label: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)/Third Binomial
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. Then $a + b$ is a third binomial : $(1): \quad a \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad b \notin \Q$ $(3): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

label: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $z, w \in \C$. Then $\dbinom z w$ is defined as: $\dbinom z w := \ds \lim_{\zeta \mathop \to z} \lim_{\omega \mathop \to w} \dfrac {\map \Gamma {\zeta + 1} } {\map \Gamma {\omega + 1} \map \Gamma {\zeta - \omega + 1} }$ where $\Gamma$ denotes the Gamma function. When $z$ is a negative integer and $w$ is not an integer, $\dbinom z w$ is infinite.

label: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $r \in \R, k \in \Z$. Then $\dbinom r k$ is defined as: $\dbinom r k = \begin {cases} \dfrac {r^{\underline k} } {k!} & : k \ge 0 \\ & \\ 0 & : k < 0 \end {cases}$ where $r^{\underline k}$ denotes the falling factorial. That is, when $k \ge 0$: $\ds \dbinom r k = \dfrac {r \paren {r - 1} \cdots \paren {r - k + 1} } {k \paren {k - 1} \cdots 1} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^k \dfrac {r + 1 - j} j$ It can be seen that this agrees with the definition for integers when $r$ is an integer. For most applications the integer form is sufficient.

label: Definition:Binomial Distribution
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_i}$ be a finite binomial experiment of length $n$ such that each of the $X_i$ in the sequence is a Bernoulli trial with parameter $p$ such that $0 \le p \le 1$. Let $X$ be the discrete probability distribution that models the number of successes in $\sequence {X_i}$ . Then $X$ is a binomial distribution with parameters $n$ and $p$.

label: Definition:Binomial Experiment
snippet: A binomial experiment is a sequence (either finite or infinite) of Bernoulli trials, each of which has the same parameter $p$. That is, a binomial experiment (with parameter $p$) is a sequence $\sequence {X_i}$ (either finite or infinite) such that: $(1): \quad$ the value of each $X_i$ is one of two values (for example: $a$ or $b$). $(2): \quad$ the probability that $X_i = a$ is the same for all $i$ (for example: $p$). $(3): \quad$ the outcomes of all the Bernoulli trials are independent. That is, it is a sequence of experiments, all of which can be modelled by the same Bernoulli distribution.

label: Definition:Bipartite Graph
snippet: A bipartite graph is a graph $G = \struct {V, E}$ where: $V$ is partitioned into two sets $A$ and $B$ such that: each edge is incident to a vertex in $A$ and a vertex in $B$. That is: no two vertices in $A$ are adjacent and no two vertices in $B$ are adjacent. It is a common practice when illustrating such a graph to draw the vertices of $A$ in one colour, and those of $B$ in another. $G$ can be denoted $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ to emphasise that $A$ and $B$ partition $V$.

label: Definition:Bipartite Graph/Partite Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ be a bipartite graph. Then $A$ and $B$ are called the partite sets of $G$.

label: Definition:Bisection
snippet: To bisect a finite geometrical object is to cut it in half, that is, into two equal parts. The act of cutting in half is known as bisection.

label: Definition:Bit
snippet: A bit is a binary digit.

label: Definition:Bivariate Distribution
snippet: A bivariate distribution is the joint distribution of two random variables $X$ and $Y$.

label: Definition:Block Basic Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$. Let $\sequence {p_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a strictly increasing sequence and let $p_0 = 0$. Let $\sequence {\alpha_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $\GF$. Define: $\ds u_n = \sum_{j \mathop = p_{n - 1} + 1}^{p_n} \alpha_j e_j$ for each $n \in \N$. We say that $\sequence {u_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a block basic sequence of $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$.

label: Definition:Block Design
snippet: Let $S$ be a set with $n$ elements. A block design is a collection of subsets $B_r$ of a set $S$ such that: each $B_r$ contains the same number $k$ of elements for every subset $T$ of $S$ with exactly $t$ elements, $T$ is a subset of exactly $\lambda$ of the $B_r$. The numbers $k$, $t$, $\lambda$ and $n$ are characteristic of the particular block design.

label: Definition:Block Matrix
snippet: A block matrix is a representation of a matrix as an array of submatrices. This may be defined as follows: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be positive integers. Let $A = \sqbrk {A_{i j} }$ be an $m \times n$ matrix of matrices over $S$. Let for every $i \in \set {1, \ldots, m}$, the elements of the $i$th row of $A$ have equal height $m_i$. Let for every $j \in \set {1,\ldots, n}$ the elements of the $j$th column of $A$ have equal width $n_i$. Define $M = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^m m_i$ and $N = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n n_i$ as indexed summations.

label: Definition:Block Multiplication
snippet: Block multiplication is (conventional) matrix multiplication in which the matrices involved are block matrices. That is, the entries are submatrices rather than single elements. The submatrices still multiply together as though they were single elements.

label: Definition:Bochner Integrable Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a Bochner measurable function. We say that $f$ is Bochner integrable there exists simple functions $s_n : I \to X$ such that: $\map {s_n} t \to \map f t$ for each $t \in I$ and: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int_I \norm {\map f t - \map {s_n} t}_X \rd \map \lambda t = 0$

label: Definition:Bochner Integral of Simple Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a simple function. Take: Lebesgue measurable subsets $\Omega_1, \ldots, \Omega_n$ of $I$ with finite Lebesgue measure $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in X$ such that: $\ds f = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x_j \chi_{\Omega_j}$ We define the Bochner integral of $f$ over $I$ by: $\ds \int_I f \rd \lambda = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x_j \map \lambda {\Omega_j}$

label: Definition:Bochner Measurable Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a function. We say that $f$ is Bochner measurable there exists a sequence of simple functions $\sequence {s_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $\ds \map f t = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map {s_n} t$ for almost all $t \in I$.

label: Definition:Body
snippet: In the context of physics and applied mathematics, a body is an object (possibly idealized) which is imagined to have a material existence in the physical universe. A body can be considered as an aggregate of particles to which it is possible to apply a force.

label: Definition:Body/Deformable
snippet: A deformable body is a body $B$ which is not rigid. That is, when under the influence of a force, the distance between any two points of $B$ may not remain constant.

label: Definition:Body/Rigid
snippet: A rigid body is a body $B$ with the property that the distance between any two points of $B$ remains constant regardless of any external forces.

label: Definition:Boolean Algebra/Also defined as
snippet: == Boolean Algebra: Also defined as == Some sources define a Boolean algebra to be what on is called a Boolean lattice. It is a common approach to define (the) Boolean algebra to be an algebraic structure consisting of: a boolean domain (that is, a set with two elements, typically $\set {0, 1}$) together with: the two operations addition $+$ and multiplication $\times$ defined as follows: $\begin{array}{c|cc} + & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{c|cc} \times & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{array}$ Hence expositions discussing such a…

label: Definition:Boolean Domain
snippet: A Boolean domain is a $2$-element set of (Aristotelian) truth values, usually defined and denoted as: $\Bbb B = \set {\T, \F}$

label: Definition:Boolean Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Then $R$ is called a Boolean ring $R$ is an idempotent ring with unity.

label: Definition:Boolean Satisfiability Problem
snippet: Let $X$ be a set of propositional variables. Let $L$ be a set of one or more propositional formulas constructed using only: elements of $X$ the $4$ unary logical connectives $\operatorname{True}$, $\operatorname{False}$, identity, and $\neg$ the $16$ binary logical connectives. The problem is to find truth values for all $x \in X$ such that all the formulas in $L$ are true. Such a problem is known as a boolean satisfiability problem.

label: Definition:Borel Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB {X, \tau}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\map \BB {X, \tau}$ such that: $\map \mu K < \infty$ for all compact $K \subseteq X$. We say that $\mu$ is a Borel measure.

label: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Borel Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\struct {S, \tau}$. The elements of $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ are called the Borel (measurable) sets of $\struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Topological Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space The Borel sigma-algebra $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ of $\struct {S, \tau}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\tau$. That is, it is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the set of open sets in $S$.

label: Definition:Bottom (Logic)
snippet: Bottom is a constant of propositional logic interpreted to mean the canonical, undoubted contradiction whose falsehood nobody could possibly ever question. The symbol used is $\bot$.

label: Definition:Boubaker Polynomials
snippet: The Boubaker polynomials are the components of the following sequence of polynomials: {{eqn | l = \map {B_0} x | r = 1 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_1} x | r = x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_2} x | r = x^2 + 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_3} x | r = x^3 + x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_4} x | r = x^4 - 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_5} x | r = x^5 - x^3 - 3 x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_6} x | r = x^6 - 2 x^4 - 3 x^2 + 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_7} x | r = x^7 - 3 x^5 - 2 x^3 + 5 x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_8} x | r = x^8 - 4 x^6 + 8 x^2 - 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_9} x | r = x^9 - 5 x^7 + 3 x^5 + 10 x^3 - 7 x }}

label: Definition:Bound Variable
snippet: A bound variable is a variable which, when it occurs in an expression, can be replaced with another variable without changing the meaning of the statement.

label: Definition:Bound of Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded. Then $B$ is a bound for $f$ : $\forall x \in S: B \ge \size {\map f x}$

label: Definition:Bound of Subset of Real Numbers
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $S$ be bounded. Then $K$ is a bound for $S$ : $\forall x \in S: \size x \le K$

label: Definition:Boundary
snippet: Geometry: Boundary: The line that goes around a geometric figure. Topology: Boundary: The elements in the closure of a set which are not in the interior of that set. Graph Theory: Boundary: The set of all the vertices of a simple graph that are adjacent to a given vertex.

label: Definition:Boundary (Geometry)
snippet: For example, the endpoints of a line segment are its boundaries.

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: == Boundary in the context of Topology: Also known as == The boundary of a subset $H$ of a topological space $T$ is also seen referred to as the frontier of $H$.

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ consists of all the points in the closure of $H$ which are not in the interior of $H$. Thus, the boundary of $H$ is defined as: $\partial H := H^- \setminus H^\circ$ where $H^-$ denotes the closure and $H^\circ$ the interior of $H$.

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ is the set of all the boundary points of $H$.

label: Definition:Boundary Condition
snippet: Let $\Phi$ be a differential equation to which a particular solution is to be found. A boundary condition is an equation relating particular values of the dependent and independent variables which the particular solution to $\Phi$ must satisfy. It is usual for such boundary condition to correspond to the physical extremities of bodies, aspects of whose internal nature is being modelled by means of $\Phi$.

label: Definition:Boundary Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Boundary Point (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z_0 \in \C$. $z_0$ is a boundary point of $S$ every $\epsilon$-neighborhood $\map {N_\epsilon} {z_0}$ of $z_0$ contains points of $\C$ in $S$ and also points of $\C$ which are not in $S$.

label: Definition:Boundary Value Problem
snippet: A boundary value problem is a differential equation for which a particular solution is to be found, such that the particular solution must satisfy certain boundary conditions.

label: Definition:Bounded Above Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Then $f$ is bounded above on $S$ by the upper bound $H$ : $\forall x \in S: \map f x \preceq H$ That is, $f \sqbrk S = \set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded above by $H$.

label: Definition:Bounded Above Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. $f$ is bounded above on $S$ by the upper bound $H$ : $\forall x \in S: \map f x \le H$ That is, the set $\set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded above in $\R$ by $H$.

label: Definition:Bounded Above Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded above : $\exists M \in T: \forall i \in \N: x_i \preceq M$

label: Definition:Bounded Above Sequence/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded above there exists no $M$ in $T$ such that: $\forall i \in \N: x_i \preceq M$ Category:Definitions/Unbounded Above Sequences Category:Definitions/Sequences

label: Definition:Bounded Above Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is bounded above (in $S$) $T$ admits an upper bound (in $S$).

label: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. A subset $T \subseteq \R$ is bounded above (in $\R$) $T$ admits an upper bound (in $\R$).

label: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Real Numbers/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ . $T \subseteq \R$ is unbounded above (in $\R$) it is not bounded above.

label: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is unbounded above (in $S$) it is not bounded above.

label: Definition:Bounded Below
snippet: Bounded Below Set Bounded Below Subset of Real Numbers Bounded Below Mapping Bounded Below Real-Valued Function Bounded Below Sequence Bounded Below Real Sequence

label: Definition:Bounded Below Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Then $f$ is said to be bounded below (in $T$) by the lower bound $L$ : $\forall x \in S: L \preceq \map f x$ That is, iff $f \sqbrk S = \set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded below by $L$.

label: Definition:Bounded Below Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Then $f$ is bounded below on $S$ by the lower bound $L$ : $\forall x \in S: L \le \map f x$ That is, the set $\set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded below in $\R$ by $L$.

label: Definition:Bounded Below Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded below : $\exists m \in T: \forall i \in \N: m \preceq x_i$

label: Definition:Bounded Below Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is bounded below (in $S$) $T$ admits a lower bound (in $S$).

label: Definition:Bounded Below Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. A subset $T \subseteq \R$ is bounded below (in $\R$) $T$ admits a lower bound (in $\R$).

label: Definition:Bounded Class/Bounded Subset of Class
snippet: Let $B$ be a class. Let $B$ be a subclass of a class $A$. Then $B$ is a bounded subset of $A$ : there exists a set $x \in A$ such that $B$ is bounded by $x$ That is, every element of $B$ is a subset of $x$.

label: Definition:Bounded Class/Bounded by Set
snippet: Let $B$ be a class. Let $x$ be a set. $B$ is bounded by $x$ : every element of $B$ is a subset of $x$.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let the image of $f$ be bounded. Then $f$ is bounded. That is, $f$ is bounded it is both bounded above and bounded below.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $f: X \to M$ be a mapping from any set $X$ into $M$. Then $f$ is a bounded mapping $f \sqbrk X$ is bounded in $M$.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space over $R$. Let $S$ be a set. Let $f : S 	o X$ be a mapping. We say that $f$ is bounded there exists a real number $M > 0$ such that: $
orm {\map f x} \le M$ for each $x \in S$.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Attaining its Bounds
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a bounded real-valued function. Let $T$ be a subset of $S$. Suppose that: $\exists a, b \in T: \forall x \in S: \map f a \le \map f x \le \map f b$ Then $f$ attains its bounds on $T$.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Unbounded
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Complex
snippet: Let $D$ be a subset of the complex plane $\C$. Then $D$ is bounded (in $\C$) there exists $M \in \R$ such that: $\forall z \in D: \cmod z \le M$

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Complex/Unbounded
snippet: Let $D$ be a subset of the complex plane $\C$. Then $D$ is unbounded (in $\C$) : $\nexists M \in \R: \forall z \in D: \cmod z \le M$ That is, if $D$ is not bounded in $\C$.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 4
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists K \in \R: \forall x \in B: \map d {x, a} \le K$ for some $a \in A$.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Euclidean
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of a Euclidean space under the usual metric. $A$ is bounded (in $\R^n$) : $\exists N \in \R: \forall x \in A: \size x \le N$ That is, every element of $A$ is within a finite distance of any point we may choose for the origin.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, d}$ be a metric space. Let $M' = \struct {Y, d_Y}$ be a subspace of $M$. Then $M'$ is unbounded (in $M$) $M'$ is not bounded in $M$.

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence
snippet: A special case of a bounded mapping is a bounded sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded $\exists m, M \in T$ such that $\forall i \in \N$: $(1): \quad m \preceq x_i$ $(2): \quad x_i \preceq M$ That is, it is bounded above and bounded below.

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $M$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a bounded sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded in $M$. That is: $\exists K \in \R: \forall n, m \in \N: \map d {x_n, x_m} \le K$

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded : $\exists K \in \R$ such that $\forall n \in \N: \norm {x_n} \le K$

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $X$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded : $\exists K \in \R$ such that $\forall n \in \N: \norm {x_n} \le K$

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Unbounded
snippet: A sequence which is not bounded is unbounded. Category:Definitions/Boundedness

label: Definition:Bounded Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$ be both bounded below and bounded above in $S$. Then $T$ is bounded in $S$.

label: Definition:Bounded Set/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is unbounded (in $S$) it is not bounded.

label: Definition:Bounded Subset of Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}}$ be a normed vector space. Let $M' \subseteq X$.

label: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Bounded Interval
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function.

label: Definition:Box-Jenkins Model/ARIMA
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let: $w_t = \nabla^d z_t$ where $\nabla^d$ denotes the $d$th iteration of the backward difference operator.

label: Definition:Box-Jenkins Model/ARMA
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $\tilde z_t, \tilde z_{t - 1}, \tilde z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be deviations from a constant mean level $\mu$: $\tilde z_t = z_t - \mu$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let $M$ be a model where the current value of $\tilde z_t$ is expressed as a combination of a finite linear aggregate of the past values along with a finite linear aggregate of the…

label: Definition:Box Topology
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $X$ be the cartesian product of $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$, that is: $\ds X := \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i$ Define: $\ds \BB := \set {\prod_{i \mathop \in I} U_i: \forall i \in I: U_i \in \tau_i}$ Then $\BB$ is a synthetic basis on $X$, as shown on Basis for Box Topology. The box topology on $X$ is defined as the topology $\tau$ generated by the synthetic basis $\BB$.

label: Definition:Brachistochrone
snippet: Let a point $A$ be joined by a wire to a lower point $B$. Let the wire be allowed to be bent into whatever shape is required. Let a bead be released at $A$ to slide down without friction to $B$. The shape of the wire so that the bead takes least time to descend from $A$ to $B$ is called the brachistochrone.

label: Definition:Braid Group
snippet: The braid group on $n$ strands is generated by $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_{n-1}$ and the following relations: $\sigma_i \sigma_j = \sigma_j\sigma_i, \forall i, j: |i-j| \ge 2$ $\sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1}, \forall i \in \{ 1, 2, \ldots, n-2 \}$

label: Definition:Brocard Angle
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the first and second Brocard points of $\triangle ABC$ respectively. Let: From Brocard Angle is Unique: $\omega = \omega'$ This angle $\omega = \omega'$ is the Brocard angle of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Brocard Points/First
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let the point $P$ be constructed such that: $\angle PAB = \angle PBC = \angle PCA$ Then $P$ is the first Brocard point of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Brocard Points/Second
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let the point $Q$ be constructed such that: $\angle QAC = \angle QCB = \angle QBA$ Then $Q$ is the second Brocard point of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Broken Line
snippet: A broken line is a line which is formed from a number of discrete straight line segments joined together. Hence a curve may be approximated by a broken line, like how a circle can be approximated by a regular polygon.

label: Definition:Brun's Constant
snippet: Brun's constant is the sum of the series consisting of the reciprocals of the twin primes: $B_2 := \paren {\dfrac 1 3 + \dfrac 1 5} + \paren {\dfrac 1 5 + \dfrac 1 7} + \paren {\dfrac 1 {11} + \dfrac 1 {13} } + \paren {\dfrac 1 {17} + \dfrac 1 {19} } + \paren {\dfrac 1 {29} + \dfrac 1 {31} } + \cdots$ Its approxmiate decimal expansion is: $B_2 \approx 1 \cdotp 90216 \, 05831 \, 04 \ldots$ Estimates of its value are occasionally refined as further work is done to establish its nature.

label: Definition:By Hypothesis
snippet: When demonstrating a proof, it is frequently necessary to refer to the specification of the result which is to be proved. This result often contains wording along the lines Suppose that ... or Let ... It is convenient to refer back to these specifications during the course of the proof. To do that, the term by hypothesis is often used.

label: Definition:C*-Subalgebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $B \subseteq A$ be a subalgebra of $A$ that is also a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. We say that $B$ is a $\text C^\ast$-subalgebra of $A$.

label: Definition:CPA Network/Edges as Activities
snippet: A CPA network with edges as activities is a CPA network such that: the nodes model the start and end times of the activities the edges model the activities themselves. The activities and their times for completion are used to label the edges. The earliest possible end time for an activity is used to label the node representing the end time of that activity. It is sometimes necessary to include dummy activities to link paths where common activities appear, but in general the paths are independent.

label: Definition:Calculation
snippet: Calculation is the process of working out the value of a mathematical or arithmetic procedure, or the output of an algorithm.

label: Definition:Calculus
snippet: Calculus is the branch of mathematics which studies change.

label: Definition:Calculus/Differential
snippet: Differential calculus is the subfield of calculus which is concerned with the study of the rates at which quantities change.

label: Definition:Calculus/Integral
snippet: Integral calculus is a subfield of calculus which is concerned with the study of the rates at which quantities accumulate. Equivalently, given the rate of change of a quantity integral calculus provides techniques of providing the quantity itself. The equivalence of the two uses are demonstrated in the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. The technique is also frequently used for the purpose of calculating areas and volumes of curved geometric figures.

label: Definition:Calculus of Variations
snippet: The calculus of variations is the subfield of analysis concerned maximizing or minimizing real functionals, which are mappings from a set of functions to the real numbers.

label: Definition:Canonical Basis of Free Module on Set
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\ds R^{\paren I} = \bigoplus_{i \mathop \in I} R$ be the free $R$-module on $I$. The canonical basis of $R^{\paren I}$ is the indexed family $\family {e_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$, defined as: $e_j = \family {\delta_{i j} }_{i \mathop \in I} \in R^{\paren I}$ where: $\delta$ denotes the Kronecker delta. $e_j$ is known as the $j$th canonical basis element of $R^{\paren I}$.

label: Definition:Canonical Order
snippet: Let $\On$ be the class of all ordinals. Let $<$ be the ordinal ordering. Let $\otimes^l$ be the lexicographic ordering on $\On \times \On$. The canonical order on $\On \times \On$, denoted $R_0$, is defined as follows, for ordinals $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$: $\tuple {\alpha, \beta} \mathrel {R_0} \tuple {\gamma, \delta}$ $\map \max {\alpha, \beta} < \map \max {\gamma, \delta}$ or $\paren {\map \max {\alpha, \beta} = \map \max {\gamma, \delta} \land \tuple {\alpha, \beta} \otimes^l \tuple {\gamma, \delta} }$

label: Definition:Canonical P-adic Expansion
snippet: Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers for prime number $p$. Let $a$ be a $p$-adic number, that is left coset, in $\Q_p$. Let $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = m}^\infty d_n p^n$ be the unique $p$-adic expansion that is a representative of $a$ where: $m \in \Z_{\le 0}$ $\forall n \in \Z_{\ge m}: d_n$ is a $p$-adic digit $m < 0 \implies d_m \ne 0$ For $m < 0$, the canonical $p$-adic expansion of $a$ is the expression: $\ldots d_n \ldots d_3 d_2 d_1 d_0 .

label: Definition:Canonical Preordering of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $A^+$ be the set of positive elements of $A$. From Set of Positive Elements of C*-Algebra is Convex Cone, $A^+$ is a convex cone. We can therefore define $\le$ to be the preordering on $A$ induced by $A^+$, defining: $a \le b$ $b - a \in A^+$. We call $\le$ the canonical preordering of $A$.

label: Definition:Cantor's Leaky Tent
snippet: Let $\CC$ denote the Cantor set on the closed unit interval $\closedint 0 1$. Let $p$ be the point $\tuple {\dfrac 1 2, \dfrac 1 2}$ in the Cartesian plane. For $c \in \CC$, let $\map L c$ denote the line segment joining $p$ to $c$. Let $X$ be the cone over $\CC$ with the vertex at $p$: That is: $X := \bigcup \set {\map L c: c \in \CC}$ Let $\EE$ denote the subset of $\CC$ which consists of the endpoints of the intervals deleted from $\closedint 0 1$ to construct $\CC$.

label: Definition:Cantor Normal Form
snippet: Let $x$ be an ordinal. The Cantor normal form of $x$ is an ordinal summation: $x = \omega^{a_1} n_1 + \dots + \omega^{a_k} n_k$ where: $k \in \N$ is a natural number $\omega$ is the minimally inductive set $\sequence {a_i}$ is a strictly decreasing finite sequence of ordinals. $\sequence {n_i}$ is a finite sequence of finite ordinals In summation notation: $x = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^k \omega^{a_i} n_i$

label: Definition:Cantor Set/Limit of Decreasing Sequence
snippet: Let $\map {I_c} \R$ denote the set of all closed real intervals. Define the mapping $t_1: \map {I_c} \R \to \map {I_c} \R$ by: $\map {t_1} {\closedint a b} := \closedint a {\dfrac 1 3 \paren {a + b} }$ and similarly $t_3: \map {I_c} \R \to \map {I_c} \R$ by: $\map {t_3} {\closedint a b} := \closedint {\dfrac 2 3 \paren {a + b} } b$ Note in particular how: $\map {t_1} {\closedint a b} \subseteq \closedint a b$ $\map {t_3} {\closedint a b} \subseteq \closedint a b$ Subsequently, define inductively: $S_0 := \set {\closedint 0 1}$ $S_{n + 1} := \map {t_1} {C_n} \cup \map {t_3} {C_n}$ and put, for…

label: Definition:Cantor Space
snippet: Let $\CC$ be the Cantor set. Let $\tau_d$ be the Euclidean topology on $\R$. Then since $\CC \subseteq \R$, we can endow $\CC$ with the subspace topology $\tau_\CC$. The topological space $\struct {\CC, \tau_\CC}$ is referred to as the Cantor space.

label: Definition:Cardinal
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Associated with $S$ there exists a set $\map \Card S$ called the cardinal of $S$. It has the properties: $(1): \quad \map \Card S \sim S$ that is, $\map \Card S$ is (set) equivalent to $S$ $(2): \quad S \sim T \iff \map \Card S = \map \Card T$

label: Definition:Cardinal Directions
snippet: The $4$ cardinal directions: North South East West are the basis of navigation and geographical coordinates.

label: Definition:Cardinal Number
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The cardinal number of $S$ is defined as follows: $\ds \card S = \bigcap \set {x \in \On : x \sim S}$ where $\On$ is the class of all ordinals.

label: Definition:Cardinality
snippet: Two sets (either finite or infinite) which are equivalent are said to have the same cardinality. The cardinality of a set $S$ is written $\card S$.

label: Definition:Cardinality/Finite
snippet: Let $S$ be a finite set. The cardinality $\card S$ of $S$ is the number of elements in $S$. That is, if: $S \sim \N_{< n}$ where: $\sim$ denotes set equivalence $\N_{<n}$ is the set of all natural numbers less than $n$ then we define: $\card S = n$ Also note that from the definition of finite: $\exists n \in \N: \card S = n \iff S$ is finite.

label: Definition:Cardinality of Continuum
snippet: The cardinality of the continuum is the cardinality of the set of real numbers, denoted $\size \R$ or $\mathfrak c$.

label: Definition:Carmichael Number
snippet: An integer $n > 0$ is a Carmichael number : $(1): \quad n$ is composite $(2): \quad \forall a \in \Z: a \perp n: a^n \equiv a \pmod n$, or, equivalently, that $a^{n - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$. That is, a Carmichael number is a composite number $n$ which satisfies $a^n \equiv a \pmod n$ for all integers $a$ which are coprime to it.

label: Definition:Cartesian 3-Space
snippet: The Cartesian $3$-space is a Cartesian coordinate system of $3$ dimensions.

label: Definition:Cartesian Closed Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Then $\mathbf C$ is called Cartesian closed $\mathbf C$ is a metacategory with finite products and with exponentials.

label: Definition:Cartesian Coordinate System
snippet: A Cartesian coordinate system is a coordinate system in which the position of a point is determined by its relation to a set of perpendicular straight lines. These straight lines are referred to as coordinate axes.

label: Definition:Cartesian Coordinate System/X Coordinate
snippet: Consider a Cartesian coordinate system $C$ with an $x$-axis. Let a point $Q$ be positioned in $C$. Let $x$ be the length of the line segment from the origin $O$ to the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to the $x$-axis. Then $x$ is known as the $x$ coordinate. If $Q$ is in the positive direction along the real number line that is the $x$-axis, then $x$ is positive. If $Q$ is in the negative direction along the real number line that is the $x$-axis, then $x$ is negative.

label: Definition:Cartesian Coordinate System/Y Coordinate
snippet: Consider a Cartesian coordinate system $C$ with a $y$-axis. Let a point $Q$ be positioned in $C$. Let $y$ be the length of the line segment from the origin $O$ to the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to the $y$-axis. Then $y$ is known as the $y$ coordinate. If $Q$ is in the positive direction along the real number line that is the $y$-axis, then $y$ is positive. If $Q$ is in the negative direction along the real number line that is the $y$-axis, then $y$ is negative.

label: Definition:Cartesian Coordinate System/Z Coordinate
snippet: Consider a Cartesian coordinate system $C$ with a $z$-axis. Let a point $Q$ be positioned in $C$. Let $z$ be the length of the line segment from the origin $O$ to the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to the $z$-axis. Then $z$ is known as the $z$ coordinate. If $Q$ is in the positive direction along the real number line that is the $z$-axis, then $z$ is positive. If $Q$ is in the negative direction along the real number line that is the $z$-axis, then $z$ is negative.

label: Definition:Cartesian Equation
snippet: A Cartesian equation is an equation defining the locus of a set of points in a Cartesian space. Such an equation is generally presented in terms of the variables: $x$ and $y$ for a $2$-dimensional space $x$, $y$ and $z$ for a $3$-dimensional space $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ for a general $n$-dimensional space

label: Definition:Cartesian Plane
snippet: A general point $Q = \tuple {x, y}$ in the Cartesian plane The Cartesian plane is a Cartesian coordinate system of $2$ dimensions. Every point on the plane can be identified uniquely by means of an ordered pair of real coordinates $\tuple {x, y}$, as follows: Identify one distinct point on the plane as the origin $O$. Select a point $P$ on the plane different from $O$. Construct an infinite straight line through $O$ and $P$ and call it the $x$-axis.

label: Definition:Cartesian Plane/Ordered Pair
snippet: == Identification of Point in Plane with Ordered Pair == Let $Q$ be a point on the Cartesian plane. Construct two straight lines through $Q$: one perpendicular to the $x$-axis, intersecting the $x$-axis at the point $x$ one perpendicular to the $y$-axis, intersecting the $y$-axis at the point $y$. The point $Q$ is then uniquely identified by the ordered pair $\tuple {x, y}$.

label: Definition:Cartesian Plane/Quadrants/First
snippet: 400px Quadrant $\text{I}: \quad$ The area above the $x$-axis and to the right of the $y$-axis is called the first quadrant. That is, the first quadrant is where both the $x$ coordinate and the $y$ coordinate of a point are positive.

label: Definition:Cartesian Plane/Quadrants/Fourth
snippet: 400px Quadrant $\text{IV}: \quad$ The area below the $x$-axis and to the right of the $y$-axis is called the fourth quadrant. That is, the fourth quadrant is where the $x$ coordinate of a point is positive and the $y$ coordinate of a point is negative.

label: Definition:Cartesian Plane/Quadrants/Second
snippet: 400px Quadrant $\text{II}: \quad$ The area above the $x$-axis and to the left of the $y$-axis is called the second quadrant. That is, the second quadrant is where the $x$ coordinate of a point is negative and the $y$ coordinate of a point is positive.

label: Definition:Cartesian Plane/Quadrants/Third
snippet: 400px Quadrant $\text{III}: \quad$ The area below the $x$-axis and to the left of the $y$-axis is called the third quadrant. That is, the third quadrant is where both the $x$ coordinate and the $y$ coordinate of a point are negative.

label: Definition:Cartesian Product
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. The cartesian product $S \times T$ of $S$ and $T$ is the set of ordered pairs $\tuple {x, y}$ with $x \in S$ and $y \in T$: $S \times T = \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in S \land y \in T}$ Another way of defining it is by: $\tuple {x, y} \in S \times T \iff x \in S, y \in T$ More specifically: $\forall p: \paren {p \in S \times T \iff \exists x: \exists y: x \in S \land y \in T \land p = \tuple {x, y} }$ $S \times T$ can be voiced $S$ cross $T$.

label: Definition:Cartesian Product/Cartesian Space
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The cartesian $n$th power of $S$, or $S$ to the power of $n$, is defined as: $\ds S^n = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n S = \set {\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}: \forall k \in \N^*_n: x_k \in S}$ Thus $S^n = \underbrace {S \times S \times \cdots \times S}_{\text{$n$ times} }$ Alternatively it can be defined recursively: $S^n = \begin {cases} S: & n = 1 \\ S \times S^{n - 1} & n > 1 \end {cases}$ The set $S^n$ called a cartesian space. An element $x_j$ of an ordered tuple $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ of a cartesian space $S^n$ is known as a basis element of $S^n$.

label: Definition:Cartesian Product/Cartesian Space/Family of Sets
snippet: Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of sets indexed by $I$. Let $\ds \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ be the Cartesian product of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $S$ be a set such that: $\forall i \in I: S_i = S$

label: Definition:Cartesian Product/Cartesian Space/Real Cartesian Space
snippet: Let $n \in \N_{>0}$. Then $\R^n$ is the cartesian product defined as follows: $\ds \R^n = \underbrace {\R \times \R \times \cdots \times \R}_{\text {$n$ times} } = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n \R$ Similarly, $\R^n$ can be defined as the set of all real $n$-tuples: $\R^n = \set {\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in \R}$

label: Definition:Cartesian Product/Cartesian Space/Real Cartesian Space/Countable
snippet: The countable cartesian product defined as: $\ds \R^\omega := \R \times \R \times \cdots = \prod_\N \R$ is called the countable-dimensional real cartesian space. Thus, $\R^\omega$ can be defined as the set of all real sequences: $\R^\omega = \set {\sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots}: x_1, x_2, \ldots \in \R}$

label: Definition:Cartesian Product/Countable
snippet: Let $\sequence {S_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence of sets. The cartesian product of $\sequence {S_n}$ is defined as: $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty S_k = \set {\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, \ldots}: \forall k \in \N: x_k \in S_k}$ It defines the concept: $S_1 \times S_2 \times \cdots \times S_n \times \cdots$ Thus $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty S_k$ is the set of all infinite sequences $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, \ldots}$ with $x_k \in S_k$.

label: Definition:Cartesian Product/Factors
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $S \times T$ be the cartesian product of $S$ and $T$. Then the sets $S$ and $T$ are called the factors of $S \times T$.

label: Definition:Cartesian Product/Finite
snippet: Let $\sequence {S_n}$ be a sequence of sets. The (finite) cartesian product of $\sequence {S_n}$ is defined as: $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n S_k = \set {\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}: \forall k \in \N^*_n: x_k \in S_k}$ where $\N^*_n$ denotes the set $\set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$. It is also denoted $S_1 \times S_2 \times \cdots \times S_n$. Thus $S_1 \times S_2 \times \cdots \times S_n$ is the set of all ordered $n$-tuples $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ with $x_k \in S_k$. In particular: $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^2 S_k = S_1 \times S_2$

label: Definition:Cartesian Product of Family/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of sets. The cartesian product of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is the set: $\ds \prod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i := \set {f \in \paren {\bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i}^I : \forall i \in I: \paren {\map f i \in S_i} }$ where $\ds \paren {\bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i}^I$ denotes the set of all mappings from $I$ to $\ds \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$.

label: Definition:Catastrophe Theory
snippet: Catastrophe theory is a branch of bifurcation theory in the study of dynamical systems. It is also a particular special case of more general singularity theory in geometry. It is based on the modelling of a dynamical system as a set of points in $n$-dimensional space. It concentrates on topological classification of such sets, connecting sudden discontinuous changes (that is, "catastrophes") with changes in topology. The theory has been applied to many fields, such as sociology, economics, engineering and linguistics.

label: Definition:Categorical Statement
snippet: Let $S$ and $P$ be predicates. A categorical statement is a statement that can be expressed in one of the following ways in natural language: In this context, the word is has the meaning of the is of predication: is $P$ means has the property $P$, or belongs to the class of things that have the property $P$ is not $P$ means does not have the property $P$, or does not belong to the class of things that have the property $P$. The word has could equally well be used: has $P$ for is $P$ does not have $P$ for is not $P$.

label: Definition:Categorical Variable
snippet: A categorical variable is a random variable whose values are categories.

label: Definition:Category
snippet: A category is an interpretation of the metacategory axioms within set theory. It consists of objects and morphisms. Because a metacategory is a metagraph, this means that a category is a graph. Let $\mathfrak U$ be a class of sets. A metacategory $\mathbf C$ is a category : $(1): \quad$ The objects form a subset $\mathbf C_0$ or $\operatorname {ob} \ \mathbf C \subseteq \mathfrak U$ $(2): \quad$ The morphisms form a subset $\mathbf C_1$ or $\operatorname{mor} \ \mathbf C$ or $\operatorname{Hom} \ \mathbf C \subseteq \mathfrak U$

label: Definition:Category (Descriptive Statistics)
snippet: Let $Q$ be a qualitative variable. Let $D$ be a finite set of $n$ observations of $Q$. Let $D$ be partitioned into a finite set of subsets of $D$. Each of the components of $D$ is known as a category.

label: Definition:Cauchy-Crofton Formula
snippet: The Cauchy-Crofton formula calculates the length of a curve by counting the number of times the curve crosses lines in the plane.

label: Definition:Cauchy Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R$. $X$ is said to have a Cauchy distribution it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\pi \lambda \paren {1 + \paren {\frac {x - \gamma} \lambda}^2} }$ for: $\lambda \in \R_{>0}$ $\gamma \in \R$ This is written: $X \sim \Cauchy \gamma \lambda$

label: Definition:Cauchy Matrix
snippet: The Cauchy matrix, commonly denoted $C_n$, can be found defined in two forms. The Cauchy matrix is an $m \times n$ matrix whose elements are in the form: either $a_{ij} = \dfrac 1 {x_i + y_j}$ or $a_{ij} = \dfrac 1 {x_i - y_j}$. where $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m$ and $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ are elements of a field $F$. They are of course equivalent, by taking $y'_j = -y_j$. Note that $x_i + y_j$ (or $x_i - y_j$, depending on how the matrix is defined) must not be zero, or the element will be undefined.

label: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Cauchy Criterion
snippet: The Cauchy criterion is the condition: For any (strictly) positive real number $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$, for a sufficiently large natural number $N \in \N$, the difference between the $m$th and $n$th terms of a Cauchy sequence, where $m, n \ge N$, will be less than $\epsilon$. Informally: For any number you care to pick (however small), if you go out far enough into the sequence, past a certain point, the difference between any two terms in the sequence is less than the number you picked. Or to put it another way, the terms get arbitrarily close together the farther out you go.

label: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a sequence in $\C$. Then $\sequence {z_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \size {z_n - z_m} < \epsilon$ where $\size {z_n - z_m}$ denotes the complex modulus of $z_n - z_m$. Considering the complex plane as a metric space, it is clear that this is a special case of the definition for a metric space.

label: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $A$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \map d {x_n, x_m} < \epsilon$

label: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {V, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $V$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \norm {x_n - x_m} < \epsilon$

label: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \N: \forall m, n \in \N: m, n \ge N: \size {x_n - x_m} < \epsilon$

label: Definition:Cauchy Sequence/Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is Cauchy : for each open neighborhood $V$ of ${\mathbf 0}_X$ there exists $N \in \N$ such that: $x_n - x_m \in V$ for each $n, m \ge N$.

label: Definition:Cayley-Dickson Construction
snippet: Let $A = \struct {A_F, \oplus}$ be a $*$-algebra. The Cayley-Dickson Construction on $A$ is the procedure which generates a new algebra $A'$ from $A$ as follows. Let: $A' = \struct {A'_F, \oplus'} = \struct {A, \oplus}^2$ where $\struct {A, \oplus}^2$ denotes the Cartesian product of $\struct {A, \oplus}$ with itself.

label: Definition:Cayley Table
snippet: A Cayley table is a technique for describing an algebraic structure (usually a finite group) by putting all the products in a square array: $\qquad \begin {array} {c|cccc} \circ & a & b & c & d \\ \hline a & a & a & b & a \\ b & b & c & a & d \\ c & d & e & f & a \\ d & c & d & a & b \\ \end {array}$ The column down the denotes the first (leading) operand of the operation. The row across the top denotes the second (following) operand of the operation.

label: Definition:Ceiling Function
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. Informally, the ceiling function of $x$ is the smallest integer greater than or equal to $x$.

label: Definition:Celestial Altitude
snippet: Let $X$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The (celestial) altitude of $X$ is defined as the angle subtended by the the arc of the vertical circle through $X$ between the celestial horizon and $X$ itself.

label: Definition:Celestial Equator
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere with observer $O$. Let $P$ be the north celestial pole. The great circle whose plane is perpendicular to $OP$ is known as the celestial equator. 480px

label: Definition:Celestial Horizon
snippet: The celestial horizon is the great circle on the celestial sphere whose plane is perpendicular to the line from the zenith to the observer. Thus the celestial horizon is the edge of the visible part of the celestial sphere. The rest of it is hidden by Earth itself. 480px

label: Definition:Celestial Mechanics
snippet: Celestial mechanics is the branch of astronomy which studies the motion of celestial bodies such as planets, stars and comets.

label: Definition:Celestial Pole
snippet: Consider the celestial sphere $C$. The celestial poles of $C$ are the north celestial pole and the south celestial pole:

label: Definition:Celsius
snippet: Celsius is a temperature scale. Its two reference points are: $0 \cels$, which is set at the melting point of water. $100 \cels$, which is set at the boiling point of water, as defined at sea level and standard atmospheric pressure. A temperature measured in Celsius is often referred to as so many degrees Celsius.

label: Definition:Center
snippet: Analysis: Center of a power series Abstract Algebra: Center of a semigroup Center of a group Center of a ring Geometry: Center of a circle Center of a sphere Center of a conic section Center of curvature of a curve at a point Graph Theory: Center of a tree Topology and metric spaces: Center of an open ball Vector spaces: Star center of a star convex set

label: Definition:Center (Abstract Algebra)/Group
snippet: The center of a group $G$, denoted $\map Z G$, is the subset of elements in $G$ that commute with every element in $G$. Symbolically: $\map Z G = \map {C_G} G = \set {g \in G: g x = x g, \forall x \in G}$ That is, the center of $G$ is the centralizer of $G$ in $G$ itself.

label: Definition:Center (Abstract Algebra)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Center in the context of Abstract Algebra == The notation $\map Z S$, conventionally used for the center of a structure $\struct {S, \circ}$, derives from the German Zentrum, meaning center. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Center (Abstract Algebra)/Ring
snippet: The center of a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$, denoted $\map Z R$, is the subset of elements in $R$ that commute under $\circ$ with every element in $R$. Symbolically: $\map Z R = \map {C_R} R = \set {x \in R: \forall s \in R: s \circ x = x \circ s}$ That is, the center of $R$ is the centralizer of $R$ in $R$ itself. It is clear that the center of a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ can be defined as the center of the semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$.

label: Definition:Center of Curvature
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve embedded in the plane. Let $N$ be the normal to $C$ at a point $P$. Let $\rho$ be the radius of curvature of $C$ at $P$. Let $Q$ be the point on $N$ which is at a distance $\rho$ from $P$ on the concave side of $C$. $Q$ is known as the center of curvature of $C$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Center of Gravity
snippet: Let $B$ be a body. The center of gravity of $B$ is that point through which the resultant of the system of parallel forces formed by the weights of all the particles constituting $B$ passes for all positions of $B$.

label: Definition:Center of Mass/Continuous
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of mass $M$. Let $B$ be of density $\map \rho {\mathbf r}$ at the point with position vector $\mathbf r$. The center of mass of $B$ is the point whose position vector $\bar {\mathbf r}$ is given by: $\ds M \bar {\mathbf r} = \int_V \map \rho {\mathbf r} \mathbf r \rd V$ where: $V$ is the volume of space occupied by $B$ $\d V$ is an infinitesimal volume element $\mathbf r$ is the position vector of $\d V$.

label: Definition:Center of Mass/Discrete
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of mass $M$. Let $B$ be made up of $n$ discrete particles each with: mass $m_i$ position vector $\mathbf r_i$ where $i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$ The center of mass of $B$ is the point whose position vector $\bar {\mathbf r}$ is given by: $\ds M \bar {\mathbf r} = \sum_{i = \mathop 1}^n m_i \mathbf r_i$

label: Definition:Center of Symmetry
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a geometric figure. A center of symmetry $C$ of $\FF$ is a point such that: every point $P$ of $\FF$ has a corresponding point $P'$ which is also in $\FF$ such that $C$ is the midpoint of the straight line segment $PP'$.

label: Definition:Center of Tree
snippet: Take a tree, and remove all the nodes whose degree is $1$, along with all their incident edges. Repeat the process until either: One node is left or: Two nodes are left, joined by a single edge. If one node is left, it is called the center of the tree. If two nodes are left, joined by a single edge, this is called the bicenter of the tree.

label: Definition:Centered Hexagonal Number
snippet: A centered hexagonal number is a figurate number which is represented by: a point in the center all other points surrounding the center at the points of a triangular lattice.

label: Definition:Centimetre/Cubic Centimetre
snippet: == Cubic Centimetre== The cubic centimetre is the CGS unit of volume. It is defined as the volume contained by a cube whose edges are $1$ centimetre long.

label: Definition:Centimetre/Square Centimetre
snippet: The square centimetre is the CGS unit of area. It is the area of a square whose sides are $1$ centimetre in length.

label: Definition:Central Binomial Coefficient
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. The binomial coefficient: $\dbinom {2 n} n$ is known as a central binomial coefficient.

label: Definition:Central Conic
snippet: A central conic is a non-degenerate conic section which has a center of symmetry. Hence a central conic is a conic section which is a circle, an ellipse or a hyperbola.

label: Definition:Central Dilatation Mapping/Scale Factor
snippet: Let $f$ be a central dilatation mapping with fixed point $C$ such that the image of the directed line segment $CP$ is $k CP$. The real non-zero constant $k$ is known as the scale factor of $f$.

label: Definition:Central Force
snippet: Consider a particle $p$ of mass $m$ moving in the plane under the influence of a force $\mathbf F$. Let the position of $p$ at time $t$ be given in polar coordinates as $\left\langle{r, \theta}\right\rangle$. Let $\mathbf F$ be expressed as: $\mathbf F = F_r \mathbf u_r + F_\theta \mathbf u_\theta$ where: $\mathbf u_r$ is the unit vector in the direction of the radial coordinate of $p$ $\mathbf u_\theta$ is the unit vector in the direction of the angular coordinate of $p$ $F_r$ and $F_\theta$ are the magnitudes of the components of $\mathbf F$ in the directions of $\mathbf u_r$ and $\mathbf…

label: Definition:Central Moment
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on some probability space with mean $\mu$. Then the $n$th central moment of $X$, usually denoted $\mu_n$, is defined as: $\mu_n = \expect {\paren {X - \mu}^n}$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$. That is, the $n$th central moment of $X$ is its $n$th moment about $\mu$.

label: Definition:Central Projection
snippet: Central Projection of $\set {A, B}$ onto $\PP_2$ from $C$ Let $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ be planes. Let $C$ be a fixed point which lies on neither $\PP_1$ nor $\PP_2$. Let $S$ be a set of points on $\PP_1$. For each point $x \in S$, let a straight line be constructed through $C$ and $x$ to intersect $\PP_2$ at $y$. The set of all $y$ is called the central projection of $S$ onto $\PP_2$.

label: Definition:Central Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ which is a subset of the center of $G$. Then $H$ is a central subgroup of $G$.

label: Definition:Centralizer/Group Element
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $a \in \struct {G, \circ}$. The centralizer of $a$ (in $G$) is defined as: $\map {C_G} a = \set {x \in G: x \circ a = a \circ x}$ That is, the centralizer of $a$ is the set of elements of $G$ which commute with $a$.

label: Definition:Centralizer/Group Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $S \subseteq G$. The centralizer of $S$ (in $G$) is the set of elements of $G$ which commute with all $s \in S$: $\map {C_G} S = \set {x \in G: \forall s \in S: x \circ s = s \circ x}$

label: Definition:Centralizer/Ring Subset
snippet: Let $S$ be a subset of a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$. The centralizer of $S$ in $R$ is defined as: $\map {C_R} S = \set {x \in R: \forall s \in S: s \circ x = x \circ s}$ That is, the centralizer of $S$ is the set of elements of $R$ which commute with all elements of $S$.

label: Definition:Centroid/Also known as
snippet: == Centroid: Also known as == A centroid is also referred to as a center of mean position. Some sources refer to it as a mean point. Approaches to this subject from the direction of physics and mechanics can be seen referring to it as a center of mass or center of gravity. However, it needs to be noted that these latter terms are merely special cases of a centroid. Beware that some sources use the term center of mass or center of gravity even when approaching the topic from a pure mathematical perspective, which can cause confusion.

label: Definition:Centroid/Set of Points
snippet: Let $S = \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n}$ be a set of $n$ points in Euclidean space.

label: Definition:Centroid/Surface
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface. Let $S$ be divided into a large number $n$ of small elements. Consider one point of each of these elements. Let a weight function be associated with this set of points. Let $G$ be the centroid of each of these weighted points. Let $n$ increase indefinitely, such that each element of $S$ converges to a point. Then the limiting position of $G$ is the centroid of $S$.

label: Definition:Centroid/Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. The centroid of $\triangle ABC$ is the point $G$ where its three medians $AL$, $MB$ and $CN$ meet. 520px

label: Definition:Centroid/Weighted Set of Points
snippet: Let $S = \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n}$ be a set of $n$ points in Euclidean space whose position vectors are given by $\mathbf a_1, \mathbf a_2, \dotsc, \mathbf a_n$ repectively. Let $W: S \to \R$ be a weight function on $S$. Let $G$ be the point whose position vector is given by: $\vec {OG} = \dfrac {w_1 \mathbf a_1 + w_2 \mathbf a_2 + \dotsb + w_n \mathbf a_n} {w_1 + w_2 + \dotsb + w_n}$ where $w_i = \map W {A_i}$ for each $i$. Then $G$ is known as the centroid of $S$ with weights $w_i, w_2, \dotsc, w_n$.

label: Definition:Cesàro Summation Operator
snippet: Let $\ell^\infty$ be the space of bounded sequences. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \ell^\infty$ be a sequence. Let $A : \ell^\infty \to \ell^\infty$ be an operator such that: $\ds \map A {x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots} = \tuple {x_1, \frac {x_1 + x_2} 2, \frac {x_1 + x_2 + x_3} 3, \ldots}$ Then $A$ is called the Cesàro summation operator.

label: Definition:Cevian
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. 400px A cevian is a line segment from a vertex of the triangle to the opposite side. In the above diagram, $CD$ is a cevian.

label: Definition:Chain (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A chain in $S$ is a totally ordered subset of $S$. Thus a totally ordered set is itself a chain in its own right.

label: Definition:Chain (Order Theory)/Subset Relation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be its power set. Let $N \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of $\powerset S$. Then $N$ is a chain (of sets) : $\forall X, Y \in N: X \subseteq Y$ or $Y \subseteq X$

label: Definition:Chain Complex
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an abelian category. A chain complex in $\AA$ is a family of objects: $\family {C_i}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ of $\AA$ and a family of morphisms: $\family {d_i : C_i \to C_{i - 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ such that for all $i \in \Z$, the composition $d_{i - 1} \circ d_i$ is the zero morphism $0 : C_i \to C_{i - 2}$.

label: Definition:Champernowne Constant
snippet: The Champernowne constant is the real number whose decimal expansion is formed by concatenating the positive integers in ascending order: $C_{10} = 0 \cdotp 12345 \, 67891 \, 01112 \, 13141 \, 51617 \, 18192 \, 02122 \ldots$

label: Definition:Change of Basis Matrix

label: Definition:Chaos Theory
snippet: Chaos theory is the branch of nonlinear systems that studies the behavior and condition of dynamical systems that are highly sensitive to initial conditions.

label: Definition:Character (Banach Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach algebra over $\C$. Let $\phi : A \to \C$ be a non-zero algebra homomorphism on $A$. We say that $\phi$ is a character on $A$.

label: Definition:Character (Number Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a finite abelian group. Let $\struct {\C_{\ne 0}, \times}$ be the multiplicative group of complex numbers. A character of $G$ is a group homomorphism: $\chi: G \to \C_{\ne 0}$

label: Definition:Character (Representation Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field $F$. Consider a linear representation: $\rho: G \to \GL V$ of $G$ where $\GL V$ denotes the general linear group over $V$. For $g \in G$, let $\map \tr {\map \rho g}$ denote the trace of $\map \rho g$. The character associated with $\rho$ is defined as: $\chi_\rho: G \to F$ where $\map {\chi_\rho} g = \map \tr {\map \rho g}$.

label: Definition:Character (Representation Theory)/Degree
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space over a field $F$. Consider a linear representation: $\rho: G \to \GL V$ of $G$ where $\GL V$ denotes the general linear group over $V$. For $g \in G$, let $\map \tr {\map \rho g}$ denote the trace of $\map \rho g$. Let $\chi_\rho: G \to F$ denote the character associated with $\rho$. The degree of $\chi_\rho$ is defined as the dimension of $V$.

label: Definition:Character Table
snippet: A character table is a tabulation of the irreducible characters of a finite group $G$. This provides a concise summary of a lot of useful information about $G$ and its normal subgroups. Because Character is Constant on Conjugacy Class, only one representation needs to be shown per conjugacy class. The character in the first row is the trivial character. The first column contains the degrees of the characters.

snippet: A characteristic function is a member of the class of functions which in some way allows one to sum up a number of characteristics of a particular mathematical object.

snippet: The concept of a characteristic function of a subset carries over directly to relations. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. The characteristic function of $\RR$ is the mapping $\chi_\RR: S \times T \to \set {0, 1}$ defined as: $\map {\chi_\RR} {x, y} = \begin {cases} 1 & : \tuple {x, y} \in \RR \\ 0 & : \tuple {x, y} \notin \RR \end{cases}$ It can be expressed in Iverson bracket notation as: $\map {\chi_\RR} {x, y} = \sqbrk {\tuple {x, y} \in \RR}$ More generally, let $\ds \mathbb S = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i = S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$ be the cartesian product of…

label: Definition:Characteristic Function of Random Variable
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The characteristic function of $X$ is the mapping $\phi: \R \to \C$ defined by: $\map \phi t = \expect {e^{i t X} }$ where: $i$ is the imaginary unit $\expect \cdot$ denotes expectation.

label: Definition:Chart
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold of dimension $d$. A $d$-dimensional chart of $M$ is an ordered pair $\struct {U, \phi}$, where: $U$ is an open subset of $M$ $\phi: U \to D$ is a homeomorphism of $U$ onto an open subset $D$ of Euclidean space $\R^d$.

label: Definition:Chebyshev Distance
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $A_1 \times A_2$ be the cartesian product of $A_1$ and $A_2$. The Chebyshev distance on $A_1 \times A_2$ is defined as: $\map {d_\infty} {x, y} := \max \set {\map {d_1} {x_1, y_1}, \map {d_2} {x_2, y_2} }$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2} \in A_1 \times A_2$.

label: Definition:Chebyshev Polynomials/First Kind
snippet: The Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind are defined as polynomials such that: {{eqn | l = \map {T_n} x | r = \map \cos {n \arccos x} }} where $n \in \N$.

label: Definition:Chebyshev Polynomials/Second Kind
snippet: The Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind are defined as polynomials such that: {{eqn | l = \map {U_n} x | r = \dfrac {\map \sin {\paren {n + 1} \arccos x} } {\map \sin {\arccos x} } }}

label: Definition:Chemistry
snippet: Chemistry is the branch of science which studies the physical properties of substances. It is often considered a branch of applied physics.

label: Definition:Chess/Chessboard
snippet: A chessboard is an array (usually square) of alternating dark and light squares (conventionally referred to as black and white, even though they may well not be those actual colours). This may be referred to as an $m \times n$ chessboard, where: $m$ is the number of ranks $n$ is the number of files. For the conventional chessboard, as depicted above, $m = n = 8$. This is the chessboard upon which chess would be played.

label: Definition:Chess/Chessboard/File
snippet: A column of a chessboard is known as a file. It is identified by letter: $\text a$ is the file on the edge of the board to the left of white (that is, to the right of black) The files are lettered sequentially up to the file on the edge of the board to the left of black (that is, to the right of white). Category:Definitions/Chess

label: Definition:Chess/Chessboard/Rank
snippet: A row of a chessboard is known as a rank. It is identified by number: $1$ is the rank nearest white The ranks are numbered sequentially to the rank nearest black. Category:Definitions/Chess

label: Definition:Chess/Piece/Knight
snippet: The knight File:Chess nlt45.svg can be moved two squares in any orthogonal direction (up, down, left or right), and then one square at right angles to that direction. It passes over intervening pieces and does not stop until reaching the end of its move. It cannot be moved onto a square occupied by another piece of the same colour. The white circles indicate the squares to which the white knight may move. The black circles indicate the squares to which the black knight may move. Note the pieces on the intervening squares.

label: Definition:Chess/Player
snippet: The two players in a game of chess are identified by the colour of the pieces they are using. The sets of pieces are made from materials of two contrasting colours, conventionally referred to as black and white. Most everyday chess sets actually are black and white.

label: Definition:Chi-Squared Test/Goodness of Fit
snippet: The chi-squared test for goodness of fit is a test of goodness of fit of observations to some theoretical probability distribution. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$. Let a value $x_i$ for $i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$ be expected to occur $E_i$ times. Let $x_i$ actually occur $O_i$ times. Then the statistic: $\ds \chi^2 = \sum_i \dfrac {\paren {O_i - E_i}^2} {E_i}$ has a $\chi$-squared distribution with $n - p$ degrees of freedom where $p$ is the number of distribution parameters estimated from the data and used to compute the $E_i$.

label: Definition:Choice Function
snippet: Let $\mathbb S$ be a set of sets such that: $\forall S \in \mathbb S: S \ne \O$ that is, none of the sets in $\mathbb S$ may be empty. A choice function on $\mathbb S$ is a mapping $f: \mathbb S \to \ds \bigcup \mathbb S$ satisfying: $\forall S \in \mathbb S: \map f S \in S$ That is, for a given set in $\mathbb S$, a choice function selects an element from that set. The domain of $f$ is $\mathbb S$.

label: Definition:Choice Function/Power Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\mathbb S = \powerset S \setminus \set \O$ be the power set of $S$ excluding the empty set $\O$. A choice function for $S$ is a mapping $f: \mathbb S \to S$ satisfying: $\forall x \in \mathbb S: \map f x \in x$ That is, for a given set in $\mathbb S$, a choice function selects an element from that set. The domain of $f$ is $\mathbb S$.

label: Definition:Cholesky Factorization
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a positive definite matrix. A Cholesky factorization of $\mathbf A$ is an expression of the form: $\mathbf A = \mathbf R^\intercal \mathbf R$ where: $\mathbf R$ is an upper triangular matrix with diagonal entries which are (strictly) positive $\mathbf R^\intercal$ denotes the transpose of $\mathbf R$.

label: Definition:Chord of Conic Section
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conic section. Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct points on $\KK$. Then the straight line segment $AB$ is a chord of $\KK$.

label: Definition:Chord of Conic Section/Ellipse
snippet: 400px A chord of an ellipse is a straight line segment whose endpoints are on the perimeter of the ellipse. In the diagram above, the line $AB$ is a chord.

label: Definition:Chord of Conic Section/Hyperbola
snippet: 400px A chord of a hyperbola is a straight line segment whose endpoints are on the hyperbola. In the diagram above, the lines $AB$, $CD$ and $EF$ are all chords.

label: Definition:Chord of Curve
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve. A chord of $\CC$ is a straight line segment whose endpoints lie on $\CC$. Hence it is a segment of a secant line $\LL$ between the points of intersection of $\CC$ with $\LL$.

label: Definition:Cipher
snippet: Arithmetic: Cipher: An outdated term for the zero digit, especially when used as a placeholder in a number expressed in basis representation form. Cipher: An outdated term for any of the Arabic numerals. Cipher: An archaic term for act of calculation, particularly using the process of algorism. Cryptography: Cipher: An algorithm for converting plaintext into ciphertext.

label: Definition:Cipher (Cryptography)
snippet: A cipher, in the context of cryptography, is an algorithm used to transform a message into another string of symbols in order to hide its meaning from a third party. A cipher operates by replacing each symbol in the original string with a word in some alphabet. The specific nature of the replacement depends on the specifics of the cipher.

label: Definition:Cipher (Cryptography)/Ciphertext
snippet: In the context of cryptography, the ciphertext is the ciphered string after the plaintext has been processed by the cipher.

label: Definition:Cipher (Cryptography)/Key
snippet: In the context of cryptography, a key is a piece of information which: is used to convert plaintext to ciphertext allows the ciphertext to be transformed back into the original plaintext. These two processes may use different keys.

label: Definition:Cipher (Cryptography)/Plaintext
snippet: In the context of cryptography, the plaintext is the message being transformed into an encrypted string.

label: Definition:Circle/Arc
snippet: 300px An arc of a circle is a part of its circumference between two given points. Hence for two given points $A$ and $B$ on the circumference of a circle, there are two such arcs so defined.

label: Definition:Circle/Arc/Major
snippet: 300px Let $a$ and $b$ be two points on the circumference of a circle. The major arc joining $a$ and $b$ is the longer of the two arcs joining $a$ and $b$. In the above diagram: the arc $ECBDF$ is the major arc defined by $E$ and $F$ the arc $CEFDB$ is the major arc defined by $B$ and $C$ and so on.

label: Definition:Circle/Arc/Minor
snippet: 300px Let $a$ and $b$ be two points on the circumference of a circle. The minor arc joining $a$ and $b$ is the shorter of the two arcs joining $a$ and $b$. In the above diagram: the arc $EF$ is the minor arc defined by $E$ and $F$ the arc $BC$ is the minor arc defined by $B$ and $C$ and so on.

label: Definition:Circle/Circumference
snippet: The circumference of a circle is the line that forms its boundary.

label: Definition:Circle/Circumference/Concave
snippet: The concave circumference of a circle $C$ is the circumference $C$ from a point inside $C$.

label: Definition:Circle/Circumference/Convex
snippet: The convex circumference of a circle $C$ is the circumference $C$ from a point outside $C$.

label: Definition:Circle Group

label: Definition:Circuit (Graph Theory)
snippet: A circuit is a closed trail with at least one edge.

label: Definition:Circular Definition
snippet: A circular definition is a definition of a concept $A$ in terms of another concept $B$ such that the definition of $B$ itself refers (either directly or indirectly) to the definition of $A$. It is a truism that circular definitions are always to be avoided.

label: Definition:Circular Proof
snippet: A circular proof is a proof $A$ in terms of another proof $B$ such that the truth value of $B$ depends (either directly or indirectly) on the truth value of $A$. A circular proof is valid, as every statement implies itself. The problem of a circular proof is that if the truth of a conclusion is , premises that are equally dubious provide no reason to support the conclusion.

label: Definition:Circumcircle

snippet: The circumcircle of a triangle is the circle that passes through all three of the triangle's vertices. This circle is said to circumscribe the triangle. 320px

label: Definition:Class (Class Theory)/Proper Class
snippet: A proper class is a class which is not a set. That is, $A$ is a proper class : $\neg \exists x: x = A$ where $x$ is a set.

label: Definition:Class (Class Theory)/Zermelo-Fraenkel
snippet: Denote with $\textrm{ZF}$ the language of set theory endowed with the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms. A class in $\textrm{ZF}$ is a formal vehicle capturing the intuitive notion of a class, namely a collection of all sets such that a particular condition $P$ holds. In $\textrm{ZF}$, classes are written using class-builder notation: $\set {x : \map P x}$ where $\map P x$ is a well-formed formula containing $x$ as a free variable.

label: Definition:Class Union/General Definition
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. The union of $A$ is: $\bigcup A := \set {x: \exists y: x \in y \land y \in A}$ That is, the class of all elements of all elements of $A$ which are themselves sets.

label: Definition:Class of All Cardinals

snippet: Classical mechanics is the study of the physical laws describing the motion of and forces on bodies under the action of a system of forces, based on Newton's Laws of Motion.

label: Definition:Closed Ball/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a positive real number. snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $\R^n$ denote the real Euclidean space of dimension $n$. Let $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$ denote the Euclidean norm. Let $a \in \R^n$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The closed (Euclidean) ball of $\R^n$ of center $a$ and radius $\epsilon$ is the subset: $\map { { {\overline B}_\epsilon}^n} a = \set {x \in \R^n : \norm {x - a} \le \epsilon}$ If the dimension $n$ has already been established, then it is commonplace to simplify the notation and present it as $\map { {\overline B}_\epsilon} a$.

label: Definition:Closed Extension Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $p$ be a new element for $S$ such that $S^*_p := S \cup \set p$. Let $\tau^*_p$ be the set defined as: $\tau^*_p := \set {U \cup \set p: U \in \tau} \cup \set \O$ That is, $\tau^*_p$ is the set of all sets formed by adding $p$ to all the open sets of $\tau$ and including the empty set. Then: $\tau^*_p$ is the closed extension topology of $\tau$ and: $T^*_p := \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_p}$ is the closed extension space of $T = \struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Closed Form Expression
snippet: An expression is a closed form expression it can be expressed in terms of a bounded number of elementary functions. Informally is it in apposition to a recurrence relation, which defines a sequence of terms from earlier terms in that sequence.

label: Definition:Closed Geodesic Ball in Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$. Let $\exp_p$ be the restricted exponential map. Let $\exp_p$ on $V$ be a diffeomorphism onto its image. Let $V \subseteq T_p M$ be an open set. Let $\map {B_\epsilon^-} 0 \subseteq V$ be the closed ball in $T_p M$ with $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ such that $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism from $\map {B_\epsilon} 0$ to its image. Then the image set $\map {\exp_p} {\map {B_\epsilon^-} 0 }$ is called the closed geodesic ball in $M$.

label: Definition:Closed Interval/Integer Interval
snippet: Let $S$ be the set $\N$ of natural numbers or $\Z$ of integers. Let $\struct {S, \le}$ be the totally ordered set formed from $S$ and the usual ordering $\le$ on numbers. Let $m, n \in S$. The integer interval between $m$ and $n$ is denoted and defined as: $\closedint m n = \begin {cases} \set {x \in S: m \le x \le n} & : m \le n \\ \O & : n where $\O$ is the empty set.

label: Definition:Closed Linear Span
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space, and let $A \subseteq H$ be a subset. Then the closed linear span of $A$, denoted $\vee A$, is defined in the following ways: $(1): \quad \ds \vee A = \bigcap \Bbb M$, where $\Bbb M$ consists of all closed linear subspaces $M$ of $H$ with $A \subseteq M$ $(2): \quad \vee A$ is the smallest closed linear subspace $M$ of $H$ with $A \subseteq M$ $(3): \quad \vee A = \map \cl {\map \span A}$, where $\cl$ denotes closure, and $\span$ denotes linear span.
