label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer
snippet: Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers. Let $x, y \in \Z$. Then $x$ is a divisor of $y$ is defined as: $x \divides y \iff \exists t \in \Z: y = t \times x$

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer/Aliquant Part
snippet: An aliquant part of an integer $n$ is a positive integer which is less than $n$ but is not a divisor of $n$.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer/Aliquot Part
snippet: An aliquot part of an integer $n$ is a divisor of $n$ which is strictly not equal to $n$.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Real Number
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $x, y \in \R$. Then $x$ divides $y$ is defined as: $x \divides y \iff \exists t \in \Z: y = t \times x$ where $\Z$ is the set of integers. That is, that $y$ is an integer multiple of $x$.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Ring with Unity
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be an ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $x, y \in D$. We define the term $x$ divides $y$ in $R$ as follows: $x \mathrel {\divides_R} y \iff \exists t \in R: y = t \circ x$ When no ambiguity results, the subscript is usually dropped, and $x$ divides $y$ in $R$ is just written $x \divides y$.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Terminology
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be a ring. Let $x, y \in R$. Let $x \divides y$ denote that $x$ is a divisor of $y$. Then the following terminology can be used: $x$ divides $y$ $y$ is a multiple of $x$ $y$ is divisible by $x$. In the field of Euclidean geometry, in particular: $x$ measures $y$. To indicate that $x$ does not divide $y$, we write $x \nmid y$.

label: Definition:Divisor Count Function
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ge 1$. The divisor count function is defined on $n$ as being the total number of positive integer divisors of $n$. It is denoted on as $\sigma_0$ (the Greek letter sigma). That is: $\ds \map {\sigma_0} n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} 1$ where $\ds \sum_{d \mathop \divides n}$ is the sum over all divisors of $n$.

label: Definition:Divisor Sum Function
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ge 1$. The divisor sum function $\map {\sigma_1} n$ is defined on $n$ as being the sum of all the positive integer divisors of $n$. That is: $\ds \map {\sigma_1} n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} d$ where $\ds \sum_{d \mathop \divides n}$ is the sum over all divisors of $n$.

label: Definition:Divisor Topology
snippet: Let $S = \set {x \in \Z: x \ge 2}$ denote the set of integers greater than $1$. Let $\BB$ be the set of all sets $U_n$ defined for all $n \ge 2$ as: $U_n = \set {x \in \Z_{>0}: x \divides n}$ where $\divides$ denotes the divisor relation. Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Then $\tau$ is referred to as the divisor topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the divisor space.

label: Definition:Divisor of Polynomial
snippet: Let $D$ be an integral domain. Let $D \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $D$. Let $f, g \in D \sqbrk x$ be polynomials. Then: $f$ divides $g$ $f$ is a divisor of $g$ $g$ is divisible by $f$ $\exists h \in D \sqbrk x : g = f h$ This is denoted: $f \divides g$

label: Definition:Dodecahedron/Regular
snippet: A regular dodecahedron is a dodecahedron whose $12$ faces are all congruent regular pentagons. It has: $12$ faces $30$ edges $20$ vertices.

label: Definition:Domain
snippet: Set theory: The concept of domain in the contexts of mapping theory, relation theory and abstract algebra. The domain of a variable. Category theory The concept of domain. Abstract algebra: The concept of integral domain in ring theory. Analysis: Domain: another term for an open region.

label: Definition:Domain (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $f: X \to Y$ be a morphism. Then the domain of $f$ is defined to be the object $X$. This is usually denoted $X = \Dom f$ or $X = \map D f$.

label: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Binary Operation
snippet: Let $\circ: S \times S \to T$ be a binary operation. The domain of $\circ$ is the set $S$ and can be denoted $\Dom \circ$. This definition can be considered as the same as that for the domain of a mapping, where the domain would be defined as $S \times S$. Category:Definitions/Abstract Algebra

label: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The domain of $f$ is $S$, and can be denoted $\Dom f$.

label: Definition:Domain of Exponential Map
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g, \nabla}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold without boundary endowed with the Levi-Civita connection. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $v \in T_p M$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be an open real interval. Let $\gamma_v : I \to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic such that: $\map {\gamma '} 0 = v$ where $\gamma'$ is the velocity of $\gamma$. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$.

label: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.

label: Definition:Domino
snippet: A domino is a $2$-omino: 200px That is, it is a polyomino consisting of exactly $2$ unit squares.

label: Definition:Dominoes
snippet: Dominoes are a set of (usually) wooden tiles: in the shape of an oblong $2$ units by $1$ unit (of the order of an inch) with two numbers, usually in the form of dots, usually between $0$ and $6$, one at each end, divided by a line between them, on one side only such that each of the numbers appears paired with every number (including itself) exactly once such that the opposite sides of the dominoes are unmarked so as to make them indistinguishable when upside down (although of course they may have a pretty design on them).

label: Definition:Dot Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $n$ dimensions: {{eqn | l = \mathbf a | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k \mathbf e_k }} {{eqn | l = \mathbf b | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_k \mathbf e_k }} where $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

label: Definition:Dot Product/Complex
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers.

label: Definition:Dot Product/General Context
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $n$ dimensions: {{eqn | l = \mathbf a | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k \mathbf e_k }} {{eqn | l = \mathbf b | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_k \mathbf e_k }} where $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

label: Definition:Double Centralizer of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $L, R : A \to A$ be bounded linear transformations such that: $\map L {a b} = \map L a b$ $\map R {a b} = a \map R b$ $\map R a b = a \map L b$ for each $a, b \in A$. We call $\tuple {L, R}$ a double centralizer for $A$.

label: Definition:Double Factorial
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.

label: Definition:Double Pointed Topology
snippet: Let $T_S = \struct {S, \tau_S}$ be a topological space. Let $A = \set {a, b}$ be a doubleton. Let $D = \struct {A, \set {\O, A} }$ be the indiscrete space on $A$. Let $\struct {T_S \times D, \tau}$ be the product space of $T_S$ and $D$. Then: $\tau$ is known as the double pointed topology on $T_S$ $\struct {T_S \times D, \tau}$ is known as the double pointed space on $T_S$. It is seen that $T_S \times D$ is conceptually equivalent to taking the space $T_S$ and replacing each point with a pair of topologically indistinguishable points.

label: Definition:Doubleton
snippet: A doubleton is a set that contains exactly two elements. The doubleton containing the distinct elements $a$ and $b$ can be written $\set {a, b}$. The set $\set {a, b}$ is known as the doubleton of $a$ and $b$.

label: Definition:Doubleton/Class Theory
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be sets. The class $\set {a, b}$ is a doubleton (class). It is defined as the class of all $x$ such that $x = a$ or $x = b$: $\set {a, b} = \set {x: x = a \lor x = b: a \ne b}$

label: Definition:Dozen
snippet: A dozen is another name for a set whose cardinality is $12$.

label: Definition:Drag
snippet: Drag is defined as the resistance to motion of a body $B$ through a fluid $F$. The amount of drag depends on: the velocity of $B$ the size and shape of $B$ the density and viscosity of $F$. There is no adequate formula for drag which can be applied in every situation.

label: Definition:Dual
snippet: Relation Theory: Dual Relation Order Theory: Dual Ordering Dual Statement Dual Isomorphism Dual Order Embedding Dual Pairs Self-Dual Linear Algebra: Algebraic Dual Double Dual Ordered Dual Basis Dual Vector Space Normed Dual Space Second Normed Dual Dual Mapping Category Theory: Dual Category Dual Statement Geometry: Dual Polyhedron Projective Geometry: Projective Dual Graph Theory: Dual Graph The concept of duality also appears in the context of De Morgan's Laws.

label: Definition:Dual Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Its dual category, denoted $\mathbf C^{\text{op} }$, is defined as follows: {{DefineCategory |ob = $X^{\text{op} }$, for all $X \in \operatorname{ob}\mathbf C$ |mor = $f^{\text{op} }: D^{\text{op} } \to C^{\text{op} }$ for all $f: C \to D$ in $\mathbf C_1$ |comp = $\left({f^{\text{op} } \circ g^{\text{op} } }\right) := \left({g \circ f}\right)^{\text{op} }$, whenever this is defined |id = $\operatorname{id}_{X^{\text{op} } } := \operatorname{id}_X^{\text{op} }$ }} It can be seen that this comes down to the metacategory obtained by reversing the direction of…

label: Definition:Dual Elements
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual elements are types of object such that one type of object has a specific connection with the other type of object.

label: Definition:Dual Operations
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual operations are types of operation such that one type of operation has a specific connection with the other type of operation.

label: Definition:Dual Statements
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual statements are statements in which: the name of each object is replaced by its dual element each operation is replaced by its dual operation.

label: Definition:Dual System
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $E$ and $F$ be vector spaces over $K$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : E \times F \to K$ be a bilinear mapping. We say that the tuple $\tuple {E, F, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a dual system over $K$ : {{item||$\innerprod {x_0} y {\mathbf 0}_K$ for all $y \in F$ implies that $x_0 {\mathbf 0}_E$}} {{item||$\innerprod x {y_0} {\mathbf 0}_K$ for all $x \in E$ implies that $y_0 {\mathbf 0}_F$}} The dual system $\tuple {E, F, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is frequently denoted as $\innerprod E F$.

label: Definition:Duality (Geometry)/Plane Geometry
snippet: In the context of plane geometry, the straight line and the point are dual elements: a straight line can be defined by two points a point can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

label: Definition:Duality (Geometry)/Solid Geometry
snippet: In the context of solid geometry, the plane and the point are dual elements: a plane can be defined by two straight lines a point can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

label: Definition:Dudeney Number
snippet: A Dudeney number is a natural number which is equal to the sum of the digits of its cube when expressed in decimal notation.

label: Definition:Dynamic Equilibrium
snippet: A body $B$ is in dynamic equilibrium : $B$ is moving with constant (non-zero) velocity the vector sum of all the forces acting upon $B$ is zero.

label: Definition:Dynamical System
snippet: A dynamical system is a nonlinear system in which a function describes the time dependence of a point in a geometrical space $X$. It is an iterative procedure consisting of: a mapping $T$ of a $X$ onto itself and: an iteration $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$. Hence positions of points in $X$ evolve iteratively under $T$.

label: Definition:Dynamical System/Flow
snippet: In a dynamical system, a set of time-dependent equations is known as flow.

label: Definition:Dynamical System/Orbit
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system consisting of a mapping $T$ and iteration $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$. The orbit of $x_0$ is the set of points $\set {x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots}$ When $T$ is invertible, the orbit usually includes the points $x_{-1} = \inv T x, x_{-2} = \inv T {x_{-1} }, \ldots$ For a flow, the orbit of a point $x$ is the union of all the points $\map x t$ for all $t$.

label: Definition:Dynkin System
snippet: Let $X$ be a set, and let $\DD \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then $\DD$ is called a Dynkin system (on $X$) it satisfies the following conditions: {{item|(3):|For all pairwise disjoint sequences $\sequence {D_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\DD$, $\ds \bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} D_n \in \DD$}}

label: Definition:Dynkin System Generated by Collection of Subsets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then the Dynkin system generated by $\GG$, denoted $\map \delta \GG$, is the smallest Dynkin system on $X$ that contains $\GG$. That is, $\map \delta \GG$ is subject to: $(1):\quad \GG \subseteq \map \delta \GG$ $(2):\quad \GG \subseteq \DD \implies \map \delta \GG \subseteq \DD$ for any Dynkin system $\DD$ on $X$ In fact, $\map \delta \GG$ always exists, and is unique, as proved on Existence and Uniqueness of Dynkin System Generated by Collection of Subsets.

label: Definition:Earth
snippet: Earth is the planet on which we live. It is the third planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Venus and Mars.

label: Definition:East Point of Horizon
snippet: Let an observer $O$ be facing the north point of the horizon $N$, facing directly away from the south point of the horizon $S$. Let the celestial equator meet the celestial horizon at the points $E$ and $W$. Let $E$ be the point on the right of $O$. This is called the east point of the horizon. 480px In the above diagram, the east point of the horizon is indicated by $E$.

label: Definition:Eastern Hemisphere
snippet: The eastern hemisphere of Earth is the hemisphere immediately to the east of the prime meridian. Points in the eastern hemisphere have longitude between $0 \degrees \, \mathrm E$ (the prime meridian itself) and $180 \degrees \, \mathrm E$.

label: Definition:Echelon Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix.

label: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Echelon Matrix: Also known as == An echelon matrix and a matrix in echelon form are the same thing. A matrix in echelon form is also sometimes seen as being in row echelon form. The definition of column echelon form is directly analogous.

label: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Echelon Form
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix whose order is $m \times n$. $\mathbf A$ is in echelon form :

label: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Echelon Form/Non-Unity Variant
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix whose order is $m \times n$.

label: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Reduced Echelon Form
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix in echelon form whose order is $m \times n$. The matrix $\mathbf A$ is in reduced echelon form , in addition to being in echelon form, the leading $1$ in any non-zero row is the only non-zero element in the column in which that $1$ occurs. Such a matrix is called a reduced echelon matrix.

label: Definition:Ecliptic
snippet: The ecliptic is the great circle that is the intersection of the plane that holds Earth's orbit with the celestial sphere.

label: Definition:Economics
snippet: Economics is the branch of applied mathematics which studies the movement of money.

label: Definition:Edge
snippet: Graph theory: the edge of a graph Solid geometry: the edge of a polyhedron the edge of a polyhedral angle Analytic geometry, analysis, number theory, etc.: the edge of a half-plane Category Theory: Edge: another word for morphism

label: Definition:Edge Deletion
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an (undirected) graph. Let $F \subseteq E$ be a set of edges of $G$. Then the graph obtained by deleting $F$ from $G$, denoted by $G \setminus F$, is the subgraph of $G$ containing the same vertices as $G$ but with all the elements of $F$ removed. That is: $G \setminus F = \struct {V, E \setminus F}$ Informally, $G \setminus F$ is the graph obtained from $G$ by removing all edges in $F$.

label: Definition:Edge Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. The set $E$ of edges in $G$ is called the edge set. It consists of (unordered) pairs of elements of the vertex set $V$. It is often convenient to refer to the edge set for a given graph $G$ as $\map E G$, especially if there is at any one time more than one graph under consideration.

label: Definition:Edgeless Graph
snippet: An edgeless graph is a graph with no edges. That is, an edgeless graph is a graph of size zero. Equivalently, an edgeless graph is a graph whose vertices are all isolated. The edgeless graph of order $n$ is denoted $N_n$ and can be referred to as the $n$-edgeless graph.

label: Definition:Effective Domain of Convex Real Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $f: X \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. We define the effective domain of $f$ by: $\Dom f = \set {x \in X : \map f x < \infty}$

label: Definition:Effective Procedure
snippet: An effective procedure is an algorithm for determining whether or not a given object has a given property.

label: Definition:Effective Transformation Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action. Then $G$ is an effective transformation group for $\phi$ $\phi$ is faithful.

label: Definition:Effectively Computable Function
snippet: Let $f$ be a function. $f$ is an effectively computable function , given the arguments of $f$, there exists an algorithm that determines its value.

label: Definition:Eigenbasis/Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. An eigenbasis for $V$ is a basis for $V$ which consists of eigenvectors.

label: Definition:Eigenfunction
snippet: An eigenfunction is a non-trivial solution to a differential equation subject to boundary conditions involving a parameter, for certain values of that parameter.

label: Definition:Eigenspace/Linear Operator
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $A : V \to V$ be a linear operator. Let $I : V \to V$ be the identity mapping on $V$. Let $\lambda \in K$ be an eigenvalue of $A$. Let $\map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ be the kernel of $A - \lambda I$. We say that $\map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ is the eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$.

label: Definition:Eigenvalue
snippet: An eigenvalue is a characteristic value of an expression in a given context.

label: Definition:Eigenvalue/Linear Operator
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $A : V \to V$ be a linear operator. $\lambda \in K$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ : $\map \ker {A - \lambda I} \ne \set {0_V}$ where: $0_V$ is the zero vector of $V$ $I : V \to V$ is the identity mapping on $V$ $\map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ denotes the kernel of $A - \lambda I$. That is, $\lambda \in K$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ the kernel of $A - \lambda I$ is non-trivial.

label: Definition:Eigenvector/Linear Operator
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $A : V \to V$ be a linear operator. Let $\lambda \in K$ be an eigenvalue of $A$. A non-zero vector $v \in V$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda$ : $v \in \map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ where: $I : V \to V$ is the identity mapping on $V$ $\map \ker {A - \lambda I}$ denotes the kernel of $A - \lambda I$. That is, : $A v = \lambda v$

label: Definition:Eighth Power
snippet: A eighth power is an integer which can be expressed as the $8$th power of an integer. The sequence of eighth powers begins: $1, 256, 6561, 65 \, 536, 390 \, 625, 1 \, 679 \, 616, 5 \, 764 \, 801, \ldots$

label: Definition:Einstein Summation Convention
snippet: The Einstein summation convention is a notational device used in the manipulation of matrices and vectors, in particular square matrices in the context of physics and applied mathematics. If the same index occurs twice in a given expression involving matrices, then summation over that index is automatically assumed. Thus the summation sign can be omitted, and expressions can be written more compactly.

label: Definition:Eisenstein Integer
snippet: An Eisenstein integer is a complex number of the form $a + b \omega$ where $a$ and $b$ are both integers and: $\omega = e^{2 \pi i / 3} = \dfrac 1 2 \paren {i \sqrt 3 - 1}$ that is, the (complex) cube roots of unity. The set of all Eisenstein integers can be denoted $\Z \sqbrk \omega$: $\Z \sqbrk \omega = \set {a + b \omega: a, b \in \Z}$

label: Definition:Elastic Collision
snippet: An elastic collision is a collision in which the total kinetic energy of the interacting bodies is the same after the collision as it was before.

label: Definition:Electric Charge
snippet: Electric charge is a physical quantity of matter which causes it to experience a force when near other electrically charged matter. It is a scalar quantity. It has been discovered by experiment that the corresponding force depends on the magnitudes of those electric charges, their displacements from each other, and their velocities.

label: Definition:Electric Charge Density
snippet: Let $A$ be a point in space in which an electric field acts. Let $\delta V$ be a volume element containing $A$. The (electric) charge density $\map \rho {\mathbf r}$ at $A$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \map \rho {\mathbf r} | r = \lim_{\delta V \mathop \to 0} \dfrac Q {\delta V} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\d Q} {\d V} | c = }} where: $Q$ denotes the electric charge within $\delta V$ $\mathbf r$ denotes the position vector of $A$. Thus the electric charge density is the quantity of electric charge per unit volume, at any given point in that volume:

label: Definition:Electric Current Density
snippet: Electric current density is a vector quantity that measures the amount of electric charge that moves through a surface with unit area that is perpendicular to the motion of the charges. It is defined as $\mathbf J \cdot \mathbf n \rd S = \d I$ where $\mathbf J$ is the electric current density $\d S$ is the infinitesimal surface area that the charges are passing through $\mathbf n$ is the normal vector to $\d S$ $\d I$ is the infinitesimal electric current passing through $\d S$.

label: Definition:Electric Displacement Field
snippet: The electric displacement field is a vector quantity defined as the electric field strength multiplied by the permittivity of the medium through which it passes: $\mathbf D = \varepsilon \mathbf E$ where: $\varepsilon$ is the permittivity of the medium $\mathbf E$ is the electric field strength

label: Definition:Electric Field
snippet: An electric field is a vector field that associates to each point in space the (electrostatic or Coulomb) force per unit of charge exerted on an infinitesimal positive test charge at rest at that point.

label: Definition:Electric Field Strength
snippet: Electric field strength is the measure of the intensity of an electric field. It is defined as: $\mathbf E = \dfrac {\mathbf F} q$ where: $\mathbf E$ denotes the electric field strength at a given point $\mathbf F$ denotes the force exerted on a test charge $q$ by $\mathbf E$ at that point. Electric field strength is a vector quantity.

label: Definition:Electric Flux Density
snippet: Electric flux density is the measure of the intensity of an electric field inside a substance $S$. It is defined as: $\mathbf D = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mathbf E$ where: $\mathbf E$ denotes the electric field strength at a given point within $S$ $\varepsilon_0$ denotes the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_r$ denotes the relative permittivity of $S$ Electric flux density is a vector quantity.

label: Definition:Electricity
snippet: Electricity is a phenomenon of physics associated with the behavior of matter that has a property of electric charge.

label: Definition:Electromagnetic Force
snippet: The electromagnetic force is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. It is the dominant force in the interactions of atoms and molecules.

label: Definition:Electromagnetic Radiation
snippet: Electromagnetic radiation is a physical process whereby a changing electric field brings about a changing magnetic field, which in turn brings about a changing electric field. These effects propagate through space in the form of waves. The components of the vectors comprising the electric field and magnetic field oscillate in planes perpendicular both to each other and the direction of travel of the wave.

label: Definition:Electromagnetism
snippet: Electromagnetism is a phenomenon of physics associated with the interactions of electricity and magnetism.

label: Definition:Electronic Circuit
snippet: An electronic circuit is a configuration of electrical components whose collective properties can be modelled by means of a network each of whose edges corresponds to a specific component. Its purpose is to guide and direct energy within a device.

label: Definition:Electrostatics
snippet: Electrostatics is the branch of physics concerned with the study of stationary electrically charged bodies, and the forces and fields they give rise to.

label: Definition:Element
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. An element of $S$ is a member of $S$.

label: Definition:Elementary Embedding/Partial Elementary Embedding
snippet: Let $\MM$ and $\NN$ be $\LL$-structures with universes $M$ and $N$ respectively. Let $A \subseteq M$ be a subsets of $M$. $j: A \to \NN$ is a partial elementary embedding it is a partial $\LL$-embedding which preserves truth for elements of $A$; that is: $\MM \models \map \phi {a_1, \ldots, a_n} \iff \NN \models \map \phi {\map j {a_1}, \ldots, \map j {a_n} }$ holds for all $n \in \N$, all $\LL$-formulas $\phi$ with $n$ free variables, and for all $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in A$.

label: Definition:Elementary Event
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment. An elementary event of $\EE$, often denoted $\omega$ (Greek lowercase omega) is one of the elements of the sample space $\Omega$ (Greek capital omega) of $\EE$.

label: Definition:Elementary Operation/Column
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over a field $K$. The elementary column operations on $\mathbf A$ are operations which act upon the columns of $\mathbf A$ as follows. For some $i, j \in \closedint 1 n: i \ne j$: {{axiom | n = \text {ECO} 1 | t = For some $\lambda \in K_{\ne 0}$, multiply column $i$ by $\lambda$ | m = \kappa_i \to \lambda \kappa_i }} {{axiom | n = \text {ECO} 2 | t = For some $\lambda \in K$, add $\lambda$ times column $j$ to column $i$ | m = \kappa_i \to \kappa_i + \lambda \kappa_j }} {{axiom | n = \text {ECO} 3 | t = Interchange columns $i$ and $j$…

label: Definition:Elementary Operation/Row
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over a field $K$. The elementary row operations on $\mathbf A$ are operations which act upon the rows of $\mathbf A$ as follows. For some $i, j \in \closedint 1 m: i \ne j$: {{axiom | n = \text {ERO} 1 | t = For some $\lambda \in K_{\ne 0}$, multiply row $i$ by $\lambda$ | m = r_i \to \lambda r_i }} {{axiom | n = \text {ERO} 2 | t = For some $\lambda \in K$, add $\lambda$ times row $j$ to row $i$ | m = r_i \to r_i + \lambda r_j }} {{axiom | n = \text {ERO} 3 | t = Exchange rows $i$ and $j$ | m = r_i \leftrightarrow r_j }}

label: Definition:Elementary Particle
snippet: An elementary particle is one of the basic building blocks of matter. To a first degree of approximation, those building blocks can be considered to be protons, neutrons and electrons. Modern research in particle physics suggests the existence of smaller constituents of protons and neutrons, but at time of writing, electrons are believe to be truly, fundamentally indivisible.

label: Definition:Elevated/Point
snippet: Let $P$ be a plane. An elevated point (relative to $P$) is a point in space which does not lie on $P$. Category:Definitions/Solid Geometry

label: Definition:Ellipse/Axis
snippet: Let $K$ be an ellipse whose foci are at $F_1$ and $F_2$.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Covertex
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$. A covertex of $K$ is either one of the endpoints of the minor axis of $K$. In the above diagram, $C_1$ and $C_2$ are the covertices of $K$.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Directrix
snippet: Let $K$ be the ellipse specified as the locus of points $P$ to a straight line $D$ and a point $F$ such that $PD$ and $PF$ are related by the condition: $\size {PF} = e \size {PD}$ where $0 < e < 1$. The line $D$ is known as the directrix of the ellipse.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Eccentricity
snippet: Let $K$ be the ellipse specified as the locus of points $P$ to a straight line $D$ and a point $F$ such that $PD$ and $PF$ are related by the condition: $\size {PF} = e \size {PD}$ where $0 < e < 1$. The constant $e$ is known as the eccentricity of the ellipse.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Equidistance
snippet: 400px Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be two points in the plane. Let $d$ be a length greater than the distance between $F_1$ and $F_2$. Let $K$ be the locus of points $P$ which are subject to the condition: $d_1 + d_2 = d$ where: $d_1$ is the distance from $P$ to $F_1$ $d_2$ is the distance from $P$ to $F_2$. Then $K$ is an ellipse. This property is known as the equidistance property. The points $F_1$ and $F_2$ are the foci of $K$.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Focus
snippet: Let $K$ be an ellipse specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ a given constant $\epsilon$ such that $0 < \epsilon < 1$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ and the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$ are related by the condition: $q = \epsilon \, p$ The point $F$ is known as the focus of the ellipse.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Focus-Directrix
snippet: 400px Let $D$ be a straight line. Let $F$ be a point. Let $e \in \R: 0 < e < 1$. Let $K$ be the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ and the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$ are related by the condition: $e p = q$ Then $K$ is an ellipse.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Major Axis
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$ whose foci are $F_1$ and $F_2$.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Major Axis/Semimajor Axis
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$. A semimajor axis of $K$ is either half of the major axis of $K$ from its midpoint to its endpoint. In the above diagram, $O V_1$ and $O V_2$ are the semimajor axes of $K$.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Minor Axis
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$ whose foci are $F_1$ and $F_2$.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Minor Axis/Semiminor Axis
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$. A semiminor axis of $K$ is either half of the minor axis of $K$ from its midpoint to its endpoint. In the above diagram, $O C_1$ and $O C_2$ are the semiminor axes of $K$.

label: Definition:Ellipse/Vertex
snippet: 500px Let $K$ be an ellipse. A vertex of $K$ is either of the two endpoints of the major axis of $K$. In the above diagram, $V_1$ and $V_2$ are the vertices of $K$.

label: Definition:Ellipsoid
snippet: An ellipsoid is a conicoid whose plane sections are circles or ellipses.

label: Definition:Elliptic Curve
snippet: An elliptic curve is a non-singular plane curve $C$ embedded in the Cartesian plane such that: $C$ can be defined by a polynomial equation such that: the coefficients of $C$ are rational the genus of $C$ is $1$ $C$ has at least $1$ rational lattice point.

label: Definition:Elliptical Cylinder
snippet: An elliptical cylinder is a cylinder which has a base whose shape is an ellipse.

label: Definition:Embedded Submanifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $S \subseteq M$ be a subset. Suppose $S$ is a topological manifold in the subspace topology. Suppose $S$ is endowed with the smooth differentiable structure such that the inclusion map $i_S : S \to M$ is a smooth embedding. Then $S$ is called the embedded submanifold of $M$.

label: Definition:Embedding
snippet: Topology: Embedding Model Theory: Embedding Abstract Algebra: Embedding (Galois Theory) Ring Embedding Category Theory: Embedding of Categories

label: Definition:Embedding (Galois Theory)
snippet: Let $K$ and $L$ be fields. A (field) monomorphism $\phi: K \to L$ is called an embedding of $K$ in $L$.

label: Definition:Embedding (Model Theory)
snippet: Let $\MM$ and $\NN$ be $\LL$-structures with universes $M$ and $N$ respectively. $j: \MM \to \NN$ is an $\LL$-embedding it is an injective map $M \to N$ which preserves interpretations of all symbols in $\LL$; that is, such that: $\map j {\map {f^\MM} {a_1, \dots, a_{n_f} } } = \map {f^\NN} {\map j {a_1}, \ldots, \map j {a_{n_f} } }$ for all function symbols $f$ in $\LL$ and $a_1, \dots, a_{n_f}$ in $M$ $\tuple {a_1, \ldots, a_{n_R} } \in R^\MM \iff \tuple {\map j {a_1}, \dots, \map j {a_{n_R} } } \in R^\NN$ for all relation symbols $R$ in $\LL$ and $a_1, \dots, a_{n_R}$ in $M$ $\map j…

label: Definition:Embedding (Topology)
snippet: Let $A, B$ be topological spaces. Let $f: A \to B$ be a mapping. Let the image of $f$ be given the subspace topology. Let the restriction $f {\restriction_{A \times f\sqbrk A }}$ of $f$ to its image be a homeomorphism. Then $f$ is an embedding (of $A$ into $B$).

label: Definition:Embedding of Categories
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor.

label: Definition:Emirp
snippet: An emirp is a prime number whose reversal is a different prime number.

label: Definition:Empty
snippet: Set Theory and Class Theory: Empty set Empty class Empty mapping Empty relation Graph Theory: Empty graph, also known as an edgeless graph Algebra and Abstract Algebra: Empty sum Descriptive Statistics: Empty class, also known as an empty class interval Category Theory: Empty category Logic: An empty term is the same as a vacuous term: a term of a categorical syllogism $\map F x$ such that nothing in the universe of discourse has the property of the predicate $F$.

label: Definition:Empty Class (Class Theory)
snippet: A class is defined as being empty it has no elements. That is: $\forall x: x \notin A$ or: $\neg \exists x: x \in A$ The empty class is usually denoted $\O$ or $\emptyset$. On the preferred symbol is $\O$.

label: Definition:Empty Mapping
snippet: Let $T$ be a set. Then the mapping $e: \O \to T$ whose domain is the empty set and whose codomain is $T$ is called the empty mapping: $e \subseteq \O \times T = \O$

label: Definition:Empty Set
snippet: The empty set is a set which has no elements. That is, $x \in \O$ is false, whatever $x$ is. It is usually denoted by some variant of a zero with a line through it, for example $\O$ or $\emptyset$, and can always be represented as $\set {}$.

label: Definition:Empty Topological Space
snippet: Let $\O$ denote the empty set. The topological space $\struct {\O, \set \O}$ is called the empty topological space.

label: Definition:Endomorphism
snippet: An endomorphism is a homomorphism from an algebraic structure into itself.

label: Definition:Endomorphism Ring/Abelian Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $\map \End G$ be the set of endomorphisms of $G$. The endomorphism ring of $G$ is the algebraic structure: $\struct {\map \End G, \oplus, \circ}$ where: $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings $\oplus$ denotes the pointwise operation on $\map \End G$ induced by $+$.

label: Definition:Endorelation
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on $S \times S$. Then $\RR$ is referred to as an endorelation on $S$. An endorelation can be defined as the ordered triple: $\RR = \tuple {S, S, R}$ where $R \subseteq S \times S$.

label: Definition:Energy
snippet: Energy is a property of physical bodies which can be defined as the ability to do work. Like time, it is difficult to define exactly what energy actually is. Energy is a scalar quantity.

label: Definition:Engineering
snippet: Engineering is the science of designing and building things.

label: Definition:Enough Injectives
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an abelian category. $\AA$ has enough injectives : for all objects $X$ of $\AA$ there exists: an injective object $I$ a monomorphism $X \to I$.

label: Definition:Entourage
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU \subseteq \powerset {S \times S}$ be a quasiuniformity on $S$. An element $u \in \UU$ of such a quasiuniformity is known as an entourage of $\UU$.

label: Definition:Entropic Operation
snippet: Let $\circ$ be an operation on a set $S$ such that: $\forall a, b, c, d \in S: \paren {a \circ b} \circ \paren {c \circ d} = \paren {a \circ c} \circ \paren {b \circ d}$ Then $\circ$ is entropic.

label: Definition:Entropy (Physics)
snippet: Entropy is a property of a thermodynamic system. It quantifies the number $\Omega$ of microstates that are consistent with the macroscopic quantities that characterize the system. The entropy of a system is equal to the expectation of the value: $k \ln P$ where: $k$ is a constant which relates the mean kinetic energy and absolute temperature of the system $P$ is the coefficient of probability of the system.

label: Definition:Entropy of Finite Sub-Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\AA \subseteq \Sigma$ be a finite sub-$\sigma$-algebra. The entropy of $\AA$ is defined as: $\ds \map H \AA := \map H {\map \xi \AA}$ where: $\map \xi \AA$ is the finite partition generated by $\AA$ $\map H \cdot$ on the denotes the entropy of finite partition

label: Definition:Envelope/Plane Geometry
snippet: An envelope is a curve which is tangent to every element of a given set of curves.

label: Definition:Epicycloid
snippet: Let a circle $C_1$ roll around the outside of another circle $C_2$. The locus of a given point on the circumference of $C_1$ is known as an epicycloid. 600px

label: Definition:Epigraph
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. The epigraph of $f$ is the set: $\map {\operatorname {epi} } f := \set {\tuple {x, \alpha} \in S \times \R: \map f x \le \alpha}$

label: Definition:Epimorphism (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: A homomorphism which is a surjection is an epimorphism.

label: Definition:Epimorphism (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. An epimorphism is a morphism $f \in \mathbf C_1$ such that: $g \circ f = h \circ f \implies g = h$ for all morphisms $g, h \in \mathbf C_1$ for which these compositions are defined. That is, an epimorphism is a morphism which is right cancellable. One writes $f: C \twoheadrightarrow D$ to denote that $f$ is an epimorphism.

label: Definition:Epitrochoid
snippet: Let a circle $C_1$ of radius $b$ roll around the outside of another circle $C_2$ of radius $a$. Consider a point $P$ on the line of a radius of $C_1$ at a distance $d$ from the center of $C_1$. The curve traced out by $P$ is called an epitrochoid.

label: Definition:Epitrochoid/Curtate
snippet: Let a circle $C_1$ of radius $b$ roll around the outside of another circle $C_2$ of radius $a$. Consider a point $P$ on the line of a radius of $C_1$ at a distance $d$ from the center of $C_1$. Let $d < b$. The curve traced out by $P$ is called a curtate epitrochoid.

label: Definition:Epitrochoid/Prolate
snippet: Let a circle $C_1$ of radius $b$ roll around the outside of another circle $C_2$ of radius $a$. Consider a point $P$ on the line of a radius of $C_1$ at a distance $d$ from the center of $C_1$. Let $d > b$. The curve traced out by $P$ is called a prolate epitrochoid.

label: Definition:Epsilon-Net
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. An $\epsilon$-net (that is: epsilon-net) for $M$ is a subset $S \subseteq A$ such that: $\ds A \subseteq \bigcup_{x \mathop \in S} \map {B_\epsilon} x$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} x$ denotes the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $M$. That is, it is a subset of $A$ such that the set of all open $\epsilon$-balls of elements of that set forms a cover for $A$.

label: Definition:Epsilon-Net/Finite Net
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. A finite $\epsilon$-net for $M$ is an $\epsilon$-net for $M$ which is a finite set.

label: Definition:Epsilon Relation
snippet: In the language of set theory $\in$, the membership primitive, is neither a class nor a set, but a primitive predicate. To simplify formulations, it is useful to introduce a class which behaves identically to the standard membership relation $\in$ for sets. This class, denoted $\Epsilon$, will be referred to as the epsilon relation. In class-builder notation: $\Epsilon := \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in y}$ Thus, explicitly, $\Epsilon$ is a relation, taking arguments from ordered pairs of sets $x$ and $y$. It consists of precisely those ordered pairs $\paren {x, y}$ satisfying $x \in y$.

label: Definition:Epsilon Relation/Restriction
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The restriction of the epsilon relation on $S$ is defined as the endorelation $\Epsilon {\restriction_S} = \struct {S, S, \in_S}$, where: ${\in_S} := \set {\tuple {x, y} \in S \times S: x \in y}$

label: Definition:Equalizer
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f, g: C \to D$ be morphisms with common domain and codomain. An equalizer for $f$ and $g$ is the limit of the diagram $C \underset f{\overset g\rightrightarrows} D$, that is, a morphism $e: E \to C$ such that: $f \circ e = g \circ e$ and subject to the following universal mapping property:

label: Definition:Equalizer UMP
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f, g: C \to D$ be morphisms with common domain and codomain. An object $E$ and a morphism $e: E \to C$: $f \circ e = g \circ e$ is said to satisfy the (equalizer) universal mapping property or UMP :

label: Definition:Equation
snippet: An equation is a mathematical statement that asserts that two expressions are equal. For expressions $A$ and $B$, this would usually be portrayed: $A = B$ where $A$ is known as the and $B$ the .

label: Definition:Equation of Geometric Figure
snippet: Let there be a coordinate system. Let the variables $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \ldots$ be used to identify points within that coordinate system. Let the variables be related to each other by means of an equation. Then the equations define the set of points which form a geometric figure. This equation is known as the equation of the geometric figure.

label: Definition:Equatorial Coordinate System
snippet: The equatorial coordinate system is an astronomical coordinate system in which measurements are based on the celestial equator. Hence a point on the celestial sphere is located by means of $2$ angular measurements: the right ascension $\alpha$, which is the angular distance measured eastwards along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox the declination $\delta$, which is the angular distance measured north or south of the terrestrial equator.

label: Definition:Equidecomposable Sets
snippet: Two sets $S, T \subset \R^n$ are said to be equidecomposable there exists a set: $X = \set {A_1, \ldots, A_m} \subset \powerset {\R^n}$ where $\powerset {\R^n}$ is the power set of $\R^n$, such that both $S$ and $T$ are decomposable into the elements of $X$.

label: Definition:Equidistance
snippet: Equidistance is one of the undefined terms in Tarski's Geometry. Intuitively, two points $a, b$ are equidistant with respect to $c, d$ if the length of line segment $a b$ is the same as that of line segment $c d$. However, at this point in the game, we have not yet defined line segment, or even distance. As such, let the following ostensive definition suffice. File:Equidistance.png In the diagram, points $a, b$ are equidistant to points $c, d$, and we write $a b \equiv c d$.

label: Definition:Equilibrium
snippet: Time Series Analysis Statistical Equilibrium Mechanics: Equilibrium: Stable Equilibrium Unstable Equilibrium Neutral Equilibrium Dynamic Equilibrium Equilibrium Position of Spring Game Theory Equilibrium Point Competitive Equilibrium Equilibrium Strategy Nash Equilibrium

label: Definition:Equimultiples
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be numbers. Then equimultiples of $a$ and $b$ are numbers of the form $c a$ and $c b$ where $c$ is also a number. That is, they are products arising from the multiplications of two numbers by the same common number.

label: Definition:Equinox
snippet: The equinoxes are the points on the celestial sphere where the ecliptic intersects the celestial equator. These are the points at which the sun, in its apparent annual motion, crosses the celestial equator.

label: Definition:Equiprobable Outcomes
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a finite probability space. Let $\Omega = \set {\omega_1, \omega_1, \ldots, \omega_n}$. Suppose that $\map \Pr {\omega_i} = \map \Pr {\omega_j}$ for all the $\omega_i, \omega_j \in \Omega$. Then from Probability Measure on Equiprobable Outcomes: $\forall \omega \in \Omega: \map \Pr \omega = \dfrac 1 n$ $\forall A \subseteq \Omega: \map \Pr A = \dfrac {\card A} n$ Such a probability space is said to have equiprobable outcomes, and is sometimes referred to as an equiprobability space.

label: Definition:Equivalence
snippet: Logic: Logical equivalence, which occurs in symbolic logic as: Semantic equivalence Provable equivalence Set theory: Set equivalence Matrix theory: Row equivalence Column equivalence Topology: Topological equivalence Relation theory: An equivalence relation is often referred to just as an equivalence. Category theory: Equivalence of categories

label: Definition:Equivalence Class
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $x \in S$. Then the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$ is the set: $\eqclass x \RR = \set {y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR}$ If $\RR$ is an equivalence on $S$, then each $t \in S$ that satisfies $\tuple {x, t} \in \RR$ (or $\tuple {t, x} \in \RR$) is called a $\RR$-relative of $x$. That is, the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$ is the set of all $\RR$-relatives of $x$.

label: Definition:Equivalence Class/Representative
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $x \in S$. Let $\eqclass x \RR$ be the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$. Let $y \in \eqclass x \RR$. Then $y$ is a representative of $\eqclass x \RR$.

label: Definition:Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$.

label: Definition:Equivalence Relation Induced by Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $\RR_f \subseteq S \times S$ be the relation defined as: $\tuple {s_1, s_2} \in \RR_f \iff \map f {s_1} = \map f {s_2}$ Then $\RR_f$ is known as the equivalence (relation) induced by $f$.

label: Definition:Equivalence Relation Induced by Partition
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\Bbb S$ be a partition of $S$. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be the relation defined as: $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in S \times S: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR \iff \exists T \in \Bbb S: \set {x, y} \subseteq T$ Then $\RR$ is the (equivalence) relation induced by (the partition) $\Bbb S$.

label: Definition:Equivalence Relation Induced by Preordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure such that $\RR$ is a preordering. Let a relation $\sim_\RR$ be defined on $S$ by: $x \sim_\RR y$ $x \mathrel \RR y$ and $y \mathrel \RR x$ Then $\sim_\RR$ is known as the equivalence (relation) induced by $\RR$.

label: Definition:Equivalent Metrics
snippet: Let $X$ be a set upon which there are two metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$. That is, $\struct {X, d_1}$ and $\struct {X, d_2}$ are two different metric spaces on the same set $X$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $n \to \infty$. Suppose that $x_n \to x$ in $\struct {X, d_1}$ $x_n \to x$ in $\struct {X, d_2}$. Then $d_1$ and $d_2$ are equivalent metrics. label: Definition:Erdős Number
snippet: A person's Erdős number is the minimum number of coauthored publications away from a publication with . The Erdős number of himself is defined as $0$.

label: Definition:Ergodic Measure-Preserving Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation.

label: Definition:Ergodic Theory
snippet: Ergodic theory is the branch of mathematics which focuses on the long-term behaviour of dynamical systems with an invariant measure.

label: Definition:Erlang Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \hointr 0 \infty$. Let $k$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $\lambda$ be a strictly positive real number. $X$ is said to have an Erlang distribution with parameters $k$ and $\lambda$ it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac {\lambda^k x^{k - 1} e^{- \lambda x} } {\map \Gamma k}$ where $\Gamma$ denotes the gamma function. This is written: $X \sim \map {\operatorname {Erlang} } {k, \lambda}$

label: Definition:Erlangen Program
snippet: The Erlangen program is a method of characterizing systems of geometry based on group theory and projective geometry.

label: Definition:Error
snippet: Let $x_0$ be an approximation to a (true) value $x$. The error $\Delta x$ is an indicator of how much difference there is between $x$ and $x_0$.

label: Definition:Error/Percentage
snippet: Let $x_0$ be an approximation to a (true) value $x$. The percentage error of $x_0$ in $x$ is defined as the relative error expressed as a percentage: $\delta x \, \% := \delta x \times 100$ where $\delta x$ denotes the relative error of $x_0$ in $x$. This, like the relative error, can be defined only when $x \ne 0$.

label: Definition:Essential Singularity
snippet: A (complex) singular point which is neither a removable singularity nor a pole is called an essential singularity.

label: Definition:Essentially Bounded Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a $\Sigma$-measurable function. We say that $f$ is essentially bounded there exists a real number $c$ such that: $\map \mu {\set {x \in X : \size {\map f x} > c} } = 0$

label: Definition:Estimator
snippet: An estimator is a statistic used to establish an approximate value of a population parameter. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be random variables. Let the joint distribution of $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be indexed by a population parameter $\theta$. Let $\delta: \R^n \to \R$ be a real-valued function. The random variable $\hat \theta = \map \delta {X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n}$ is called an estimator of $\theta$.

label: Definition:Euclid Number
snippet: A Euclid number is a natural number of the form: $E_n := p_n\# + 1$ where $p_n\#$ is the primorial of the $n$th prime number.

label: Definition:Euclid Prime
snippet: A Euclid prime is a natural number which is both a Euclid number and a prime number.

label: Definition:Euclidean Geometry
snippet: Euclidean geometry is the branch of geometry in which the parallel postulate applies. An assumption which is currently under question is whether or not ordinary space is itself Euclidean. Euclidean geometry adheres to Euclid's postulates.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric
snippet: Let $M_{1'} = \struct {A_{1'}, d_{1'} }$ and $M_{2'} = \struct {A_{2'}, d_{2'} }$ be metric spaces. Let $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}$ and $A_{2'}$. The Euclidean metric on $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ is defined as: $\map {d_2} {x, y} := \paren {\paren {\map {d_{1'} } {x_1, y_1} }^2 + \paren {\map {d_{2'} } {x_2, y_2} }^2}^{1/2}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2} \in A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $\C$ be the complex plane. The Euclidean metric on $\C$ is defined as: $\forall z_1, z_2 \in \C: \map d {z_1, z_2} := \size {z_1 - z_2}$ where $\size {z_1 - z_2}$ denotes the modulus of $z_1 - z_2$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note == himself did not in fact conceive of the Euclidean metric and its associated Euclidean space, Euclidean topology and Euclidean norm. They bear that name because the geometric space which it gives rise to is Euclidean in the sense that it is consistent with Euclid's fifth postulate. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Real Number Line
snippet: Consider the Euclidean space $\struct {\R^n, d}$. On the real number line, the Euclidean metric can be seen to degenerate to: $\map d {x, y} := \sqrt {\paren {x - y}^2} = \size {x - y}$ where $\size {x - y}$ denotes the absolute value of $x - y$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. The Euclidean metric on $\R^n$ is defined as: $\ds \map {d_2} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {x_i - y_i}^2}^{1 / 2}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n} \in \R^n$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $x \in \R^n$ be a point. Let $\tuple {x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ be the standard coordinates. Let $T_x \R^n$ be the tangent space of $\R^n$ at $x$. Let $T_x \R^n$ be identified with $\R^n$: $T_x \R^n \cong \R^n$ Let $v, w \in T_x \R^n$ be vectors such that: $\ds v = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n v^i \valueat {\partial_i} x$ $\ds w = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n w^i \valueat {\partial_i} x$ Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric such that: $\ds g_x = \innerprod v w_x = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n v^i w^i$ Then $g$ is called the Euclidean metric.

label: Definition:Euclidean Number Theory
snippet: Euclidean number theory concerns aspects of number theory and real analysis as presented in . Particular attention is paid to certain properties of the irrational numbers.

label: Definition:Euclidean Plane
snippet: For any real number $a$ let: $L_a = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: x = a}$ Furthermore, define: $L_A = \set {L_a: a \in \R}$ For any two real numbers $m$ and $b$ let: $L_{m, b} = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: y = m x + b}$ Furthermore, define: $L_{M, B} = \set {L_{m, b}: m, b \in \R}$ Finally let: $L_E = L_A \cup L_{M, B}$ The abstract geometry $\struct {\R^2, L_E}$ is called the Euclidean plane.

label: Definition:Euclidean Plus Metric
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $\set {r_i}$ be an enumeration of the rational numbers $\Q$. The Euclidean plus metric $d: \R \times \R \to \R$ is the metric defined as: $\map d {x, y} := \size {x - y} + \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty 2^{-i} \map \inf {1, \size {\max_{j \mathop \le i} \frac 1 {\size {x - r_j} } - \max_{j \mathop \le i} \frac 1 {\size {y - r_j} } } }$ Thus $d$ adds to the Euclidean metric between $x$ and $y$ a contribution which measures the relative distances of $x$ and $y$ from $\Q$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $S$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$. Let $S^n$ be a cartesian space for $n \in \N_{\ge 1}$. Let $d: S^n \times S^n \to \R$ be the usual (Euclidean) metric on $S^n$. Then $\tuple {S^n, d}$ is a Euclidean space.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Euclidean Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$. Let $S^n$ be a cartesian space for $n \in \N_{\ge 1}$. Let $M = \struct {S^n, d}$ be a Euclidean space. The topology $\tau_d$ induced by the Euclidean metric $d$ is called the Euclidean topology.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Euclidean Topology/Real Number Line
snippet: Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let $d: \R \times \R \to \R$ denote the Euclidean metric on $\R$. Let $\tau_d$ denote the topology on $\R$ induced by $d$. The topology $\tau_d$ induced by $d$ is called the Euclidean topology. Hence $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ is referred to as the real number line with the Euclidean topology.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Euclidean Topology/Real Number Plane
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let $M = \struct {\R^2, d}$ be a real Euclidean space of $2$ dimensions. The topology $\tau_d$ induced by the Euclidean metric $d$ is called the Euclidean topology. The space $\struct {\R^2, \tau_d}$ is known as the (real) Euclidean plane.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Real
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let the Euclidean metric $d$ be applied to $\R^n$. Then $\struct {\R^n, d}$ is a (real) Euclidean $n$-space.

label: Definition:Euler's Equation for Vanishing Variation
snippet: Let $\map y x$ be a real function. Let $\map F {x, y, z}$ be a real function belonging to $C^2$ all its variables. Let $J \sqbrk y$ be a functional of the form: $\ds \int_a^b \map F {x, y, y'} \rd x$ Then Euler's equation for vanishing variation is defined a differential equation, resulting from condition: $\ds \delta \int_a^b \map F {x, y, y'} \rd x = 0$ In other words: $F_y - \dfrac \d {\d x} F_{y'} = 0$

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Limit of Sequence
snippet: The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ defined as $x_n = \paren {1 + \dfrac 1 n}^n$ converges to a limit as $n$ increases without bound. That limit is called Euler's number and is denoted $e$.

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Limit of Series
snippet: The series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac 1 {n!}$ converges to a limit. This limit is Euler's number $e$.

label: Definition:Euler-Lagrange Equation
snippet: The Euler–Lagrange equation is an equation satisfied by a mapping $\mathbf q$ of a real variable $t$ which is a stationary point of the functional: $\forall t \in \R: \ds \map S {\mathbf q} = \int_a^b \map L {t, \map {\mathbf q} t, \map {\mathbf q'} t} \rd t$ where: $\mathbf q$ is the function to be found: $\mathbf q: \closedint a b \subset \R \to X : t \mapsto x = \map {\mathbf q} t$ such that: $\mathbf q$ is differentiable $\map {\mathbf q} a = \mathbf x_a$ $\map {\mathbf q} b = \mathbf x_b$ $\mathbf q'$ is the derivative of $\mathbf q$: $\mathbf q': \closedint a b \to T_{\map {\mathbf q}…

label: Definition:Euler-Mascheroni Constant
snippet: The Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ is the real number that is defined as: {{eqn | l = \gamma | o = := | r = \lim_{n \mathop \to +\infty} \paren {\sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \frac 1 k - \int_1^n \frac 1 x \rd x} }} {{eqn | r = \lim_{n \mathop \to +\infty} \paren {H_n - \ln n} }} where $\sequence {H_n}$ are the harmonic numbers and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm.

label: Definition:Euler Diagram
snippet: An Euler diagram is a graphical technique for illustrating the relationships between sets. It differs from a Venn diagram in that whereas the latter illustrates all possible intersections between a number of general sets, an Euler diagram depicts only those which are relevant for the situation being depicted.

label: Definition:Euler Numbers
snippet: The Euler Numbers $E_n$ are a sequence of integers defined by the exponential generating function: $\ds \sech x = \frac {2 e^x} {e^{2 x} + 1} = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {E_n x^n} {n!}$ where $\size x < \dfrac \pi 2$.

label: Definition:Euler Phi Function
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$, that is, a strictly positive integer. The Euler $\phi$ (phi) function is the arithmetic function $\phi: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ defined as: $\map \phi n = $ the number of strictly positive integers less than or equal to $n$ which are prime to $n$ That is: $\map \phi n = \card {S_n}: S_n = \set {k: 1 \le k \le n, k \perp n}$ That is, the number of totitives to $n$.

label: Definition:Euler Product
snippet: Let $a_n : \N \to \C$ be an arithmetic function. Let $\ds \map f s = \sum_{n \mathop \in \N} a_n n^{-s}$ be its Dirichlet series. Let $\sigma_a$ be its abscissa of absolute convergence. From Product Form of Sum on Completely Multiplicative Function, for $\map \Re s > \sigma_a$ we have: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n n^{-s} = \prod_p \frac 1 {1 - a_p p^{-s} }$ where $p$ ranges over the primes. This representation for $f$ is called an Euler product for the Dirichlet series. {{stub|Completely multiplicative hypothesis not mentioned.

label: Definition:Euler Substitution/Third
snippet: == Proof Technique == Euler's third substitution is a technique for evaluating primitives of the form: $\ds \map R {x, \sqrt {a x^2 + b x + c} } \rd x$ where $R$ is a rational function of $x$ and $\sqrt {a x^2 + b x + c}$. Let $a x^2 + b x + c$ have real roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Euler's third substitution is the substitution: $\ds \sqrt {a x^2 + b x + c} = \sqrt {a \paren {x - \alpha} \paren {x - \beta} } = \paren {x - \alpha} t$ Then: $x = \dfrac {a \beta - \alpha t^2} {a - t^2}$ and hence $\d x$ is expressible as a rational function of $x$.

label: Definition:Eulerian Circuit
snippet: An Eulerian circuit is a circuit that passes through every vertex of a graph and uses every edge exactly once.

label: Definition:Eulerian Graph
snippet: A loop-multigraph or loop-multidigraph is called Eulerian it contains an Eulerian circuit.

label: Definition:Evaluation Mapping (Topology)
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\family {Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces for some indexing set $I$. Let $\family {f_i : X \to Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of continuous mappings. Let $\ds Y = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} Y_i$ be the product space of $\family {Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $f : X \to Y$ be the mapping defined by: $\forall x \in X : \map f x = \family{\map {f_i} x}_{i \mathop \in I}$ Then $f$ is said to be the evaluation mapping induced by the family $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$

label: Definition:Even Integer/Even-Times Even
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer. Then $n$ is even-times even it has $4$ as a divisor. The first few non-negative even-times even numbers are: $0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, \ldots$

label: Definition:Even Integer/Even-Times Odd
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer. Then $n$ is even-times odd it has $2$ as a divisor and also an odd number. The first few non-negative even-times odd numbers are: $2, 6, 10, 12, 14, 18, \ldots$

label: Definition:Even Integer/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Even Integer == The concept of classifying numbers as odd or even appears to have originated with the Pythagoreans. It was their belief that even numbers are female, and odd numbers are male. A commentator on used the term isosceles number for an even number, in correspondence with the concept of an isosceles triangle. In a similar way an odd number was described as scalene.

label: Definition:Evenly Spaced Integer Topology
snippet: Let $\Z$ denote the set of integers. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets defined as: $\BB = \set {a + k \Z: a, k \in \Z, k \ne 0}$ where $a + k \Z := \set {a + k \lambda: \lambda \in \Z}$. Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Then $\tau$ is referred to as the evenly spaced integer topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the evenly spaced integer space.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Then the following real-world interpretations of the occurrence of events can be determined: If $\omega \in A$, then $A$ occurs. If $\omega \notin A$, that is $\omega \in \Omega \setminus A$, then $A$ does not occur.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Certainty
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A \in \Sigma$ be an event of $\EE$ whose probability of occurring is equal to $1$. Then $A$ is described as certain. That is, it is a certainty that $A$ occurs.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Difference
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\omega \in A \setminus B$, where $A \setminus B$ denotes the difference of $A$ and $B$. Then $A$ occurs but $B$ does not occur.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Impossibility
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A \in \Sigma$ be an event of $\EE$ whose probability of occurring is equal to $0$. Then $A$ is described as impossible. That is, it is an impossibility for $A$ to occur.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Intersection
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\omega \in A \cap B$, where $A \cap B$ denotes the intersection of $A$ and $B$. Then both $A$ and $B$ occur. This can be referred to as the intersection of $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Symmetric Difference
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\omega \in A \symdif B$, where $A \symdif B$ denotes the symmetric difference of $A$ and $B$. Then either $A$ occurs or $B$ occurs, but not both.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Union
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\omega \in A \cup B$, where $A \cup B$ denotes the union of $A$ and $B$. Then either $A$ or $B$ occur. This is known as the union of the events $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Event/Simple Event
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment. A simple event in $\EE$ is an event in $\EE$ which consists of exactly $1$ elementary event. That is, it is a singleton subset of the sample space $\Omega$ of $\EE$.

label: Definition:Event Space
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment whose probability space is $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The event space of $\EE$ is usually denoted $\Sigma$ (Greek capital sigma), and is the set of all outcomes of $\EE$ which are interesting. By definition, $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma}$ is a measurable space. Hence the event space $\Sigma$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$.

label: Definition:Eventually Constant Sequence
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a convergent sequence in $S$. Then $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is eventually constant : $\exists m \in \R: \forall n \in \N, n \ge m: x_{n + 1} = x_n$

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $Y \subseteq X$ be a subset of $X$. Suppose: $\forall x \in X: \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists y \in Y: \norm {x - y} < \epsilon$ Then $Y$ is (everywhere) dense in $X$.

label: Definition:Evolute
snippet: Consider a curve $\CC$ embedded in a plane.

label: Definition:Exact Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ be a functor. Then $F$ is an exact functor $F$ is both a left exact and a right exact functor.

label: Definition:Exact Sequence of Modules
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \cdot}$ be a ring. Let: $(1): \quad \cdots \longrightarrow M_i \stackrel {d_i} {\longrightarrow} M_{i + 1} \stackrel {d_{i + 1} } {\longrightarrow} M_{i + 2} \stackrel {d_{i + 2} } {\longrightarrow} \cdots$ be a sequence of $R$-modules $M_i$ and $R$-module homomorphisms $d_i$. Then the sequence $(1)$ is exact : $\forall i: \Img {d_i} = \map \ker {d_{i + 1} }$ where $\Img {d_i}$ and $\map \ker {d_{i + 1} }$ denote the image and kernel of homomorphisms respectively.

label: Definition:Excess Kurtosis
snippet: Excess kurtosis is defined as the difference between the kurtosis of a particular probability distribution and that of the normal distribution. Let $X$ be a random variable with kurtosis $\alpha_4$. By Kurtosis of Normal Distribution, the kurtosis of a normal distribution is equal to $3$. So the excess kurtosis of $X$, usually denoted $\gamma_2$, is given by: $\gamma_2 = \alpha_4 - 3$

label: Definition:Excircle of Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle whose sides are $a$, $b$ and $c$ opposite vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. Let sides $b$ and $c$ be produced beyond the vertices $C$ and $B$ respectively. Let a circle be constructed tangent to both of these extensions to $b$ and $c$ lines and also to $a$. The circle so constructed is called the excircle of $\triangle ABC$ $a$. 490px There are three excircles for every triangle.

label: Definition:Excircle of Triangle/Excenter
snippet: 490px The center of an excircle of a triangle is called an excenter of the triangle. In the above diagram, $I_a$ is the excenter of $\triangle ABC$ $a$.

label: Definition:Excircle of Triangle/Exradius
snippet: 490px A radius of an excircle of a triangle is called an exradius of the triangle. In the above diagram, $r_a$ is the exradius of $\triangle ABC$ $a$.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. We define a subset $\tau_{\bar p}$ of the power set $\powerset S$ as: $\tau_{\bar p} = \set {A \subseteq S: p \notin A} \cup \set S$ That is, all the subsets of $S$ which do not include $p$, along with the set $S$. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is a topology called the excluded point topology on $S$ by $p$, or just an excluded point topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is called the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$, or just an excluded point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology/Countable
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ be the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be a countably infinite set. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is a countable excluded point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is a countable excluded point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology/Finite
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ be the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be a finite set. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is a finite excluded point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is a finite excluded point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology/Uncountable
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ be the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be an uncountable set. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is an uncountable excluded point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is an uncountable excluded point space.

label: Definition:Exhausting Sequence of Sets
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ be a nested sequence of subsets of $S$ such that: $(1): \quad \forall k \in \N: S_k \subseteq S_{k + 1}$ $(2): \quad \ds \bigcup_{k \mathop \in \N} S_k = S$ Then $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ is an exhausting sequence of sets (in $\SS$). That is, it is an increasing sequence of subsets of $S$, whose union is $S$. It is common to write $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N} \uparrow S$ to indicate an exhausting sequence of sets.

label: Definition:Existential Quantifier
snippet: The symbol $\exists$ is called the existential quantifier. It expresses the fact that, in a particular universe of discourse, there exists (at least one) object having a particular property. That is: $\exists x:$ means: There exists at least one object $x$ such that ... In the language of set theory, this can be formally defined: $\exists x \in S: \map P x := \set {x \in S: \map P x} \ne \O$ where $S$ is some set and $\map P x$ is a propositional function on $S$.

label: Definition:Expansion of Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$ such that $\tau_1 \subseteq \tau_2$. Then $\tau_2$ is an expansion of $\tau_1$.

label: Definition:Expectation/Also known as
snippet: == Expectation: Also known as == The expectation of a random variable $X$ is also called the expected value of $X$ or the mean value of $X$. For a given random variable, the expectation is often denoted $\mu$. The terminology is appropriate, as it can be seen that an expectation is an example of a normalized weighted mean. This follows from the fact that a probability mass function is a normalized weight function. Various forms of $E$ can be seen to denote expectation: $\map E X$ $\map {\mathrm E} X$ $E \sqbrk X$ $\mathop {\mathbb E} \sqbrk X$ and so on.

label: Definition:Expectation/Continuous
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The expectation of $X$ is defined and denoted by: $\ds \expect X = \int_\R x \map f x \rd x$ where $f$ is the probability density function of $X$.

label: Definition:Expectation/Discrete
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The expectation of $X$, written $\expect X$, is defined as: $\expect X := \ds \sum_{x \mathop \in \image X} x \map \Pr {X = x}$ whenever the sum is absolutely convergent, that is, when: $\ds \sum_{x \mathop \in \image X} \size {x \map \Pr {X = x} } < \infty$ where $\map \Pr {X = x}$ is the probability mass function of $X$.

label: Definition:Expectation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be an integrable real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The expectation of $X$, written $\expect X$, is defined by: $\ds \expect X = \int X \rd \Pr$ where the integral sign denotes the $\Pr$-integral of $X$.

label: Definition:Experiment
snippet: An experiment can be defined in natural language as a test to see what happens.

label: Definition:Experimental Design
snippet: Let us want to set up a series of comparative experiments to compare the effects of administering $2$ or more treatments of some kind, for example: different medicines for patients different fertilizers for plots of land different lubricants for machines to a number of experimental units. An experimental design is a crafted system of experiments defined by a set of rules which defines how experimental units are grouped, in order to maximise the efficiency and precision of the experiments.

label: Definition:Exponent of Convergence
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of nonzero complex numbers. The exponent of convergence of $\sequence {a_n}$ is the infimum of $\tau \ge 0$ for which the series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \size {a_n}^{-\tau}$ converges. The exponent of convergence of a finite sequence is $0$.
