snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $I$ be a subset of $S$. $I$ is ideal in $\struct {S, \preceq}$ : $I$ is non-empty directed and lower.

label: Definition:Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {J, +}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {R, +}$. Then $J$ is an ideal of $R$ : $\forall j \in J: \forall r \in R: j \circ r \in J \land r \circ j \in J$ that is, : $\forall r \in R: J \circ r \subseteq J \land r \circ J \subseteq J$ The letter $J$ is frequently used to denote an ideal.

label: Definition:Ideal of Ring/Proper Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. A proper ideal $J$ of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is an ideal of $R$ such that $J$ is a proper subset of $R$. That is, such that $J \subseteq R$ and $J \ne R$.

label: Definition:Idempotence/Element
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\circ: S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation on $S$. Let $x \in S$ have the property that $x \circ x = x$. Then $x \in S$ is described as idempotent under the operation $\circ$.

label: Definition:Idempotence/Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is idempotent : $\forall x \in S: \map f {\map f x} = \map f x$ That is, applying the same mapping a second time to an argument gives the same result as applying it once. And of course, that means the same as applying it as many times as you want. The condition for idempotence can also be written: $f \circ f = f$ where $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings.

label: Definition:Idempotence/Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\circ: S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation on $S$. If all the elements of $S$ are idempotent under $\circ$, then the term can be applied to the operation itself: The binary operation $\circ$ is idempotent : $\forall x \in S: x \circ x = x$

label: Definition:Idempotent Operator
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Then $A$ is said to be (an) idempotent (operator) $A^2 = A$.

label: Definition:Idempotent Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. $R$ is an idempotent ring its ring product $\circ$ is an idempotent operation.

label: Definition:Identically Zero
snippet: Let $f$ be a mapping whose codomain is a subset of one of the standard number systems $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ or $\C$. Let $f$ be such that: $\forall x \in \Dom f: \map f x = 0$ That is, $f$ is the constant mapping $f_0$. Then $f$ is described as being identically zero on its domain. Category:Definitions/Analysis

label: Definition:Identification Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $S_2$ be a set. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. The identification topology on $S_2$ $f$ and $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ is defined as: $\tau_2 = \set {V \in \powerset {S_2}: f^{-1} \sqbrk V \in \tau_1}$ That is, it is the set of all subsets of $S_2$ whose preimages under $f$ are elements of $\tau_1$. The identification topology is seen to depend both on $f$ and $\tau_1$.

label: Definition:Identification Topology/Identification Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $S_2$ be a set. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. Let $\tau_2$ be the identification topology on $S_2$ with respect to $f$ and $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$. The mapping $f: S_1 \to S_2$ in this context is called the identification mapping.

label: Definition:Identity (Abstract Algebra)/Two-Sided Identity
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. An element $e \in S$ is called an identity (element) it is both a left identity and a right identity: $\forall x \in S: x \circ e = x = e \circ x$ In Identity is Unique it is established that an identity element, if it exists, is unique within $\struct {S, \circ}$. Thus it is justified to refer to it as the identity (of a given algebraic structure). This identity is often denoted $e_S$, or $e$ if it is clearly understood what structure is being discussed.

label: Definition:Identity Arithmetic Function
snippet: The identity arithmetic function $\iota: S \to \Z$ is defined for $n \ge 1$ by: $\forall n \in S: \map \iota n = \delta_{n 1}$ where: $S$ is (in theory) any set, but in this context is usually one of the standard number sets $\Z, \Q, \R, \C$ $\delta$ is the Kronecker delta. That is: $\forall n \in S: \map \iota n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 1\\ 0 & : n \ne 1 \end {cases}$

label: Definition:Identity Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. The identity functor on $\mathbf C$ is the functor $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf C$ defined by: {{axiom | lc= For all objects $C$ of $\mathbf C$: | ml = \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C} C | mo = := | mr = C }} {{axiom | lc= For all morphisms $f: C_1 \to C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: | ml = \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C} f | mo = := | mr = f }} That $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}$ constitutes a functor is shown on Identity Functor is Functor.

label: Definition:Identity Mapping
snippet: The identity mapping of a set $S$ is the self-map $I_S: S \to S$ defined as: $I_S = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in S \times S: x = y}$ or alternatively: $I_S = \set {\tuple {x, x}: x \in S}$ That is: $I_S: S \to S: \forall x \in S: \map {I_S} x = x$ That is, it is a mapping in which every element is a fixed element.

label: Definition:Identity Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $X$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. The identity morphism of $X$, denoted $\operatorname{id}_X$, is a morphism of $\mathbf C$ subject to: $\operatorname{dom} \operatorname{id}_X = \operatorname{cod} \operatorname{id}_X = X$ $f \circ \operatorname{id}_X = f$ $\operatorname{id}_X \circ g = g$ whenever $X$ is the domain of $f$ or the codomain of $g$, respectively. In most metacategories, the identity morphisms can be viewed as a representation of "doing nothing", in a sense suitable to the metacategory under consideration.

label: Definition:Identity Natural Transformation
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a covariant functor. The identity natural transformation $\operatorname{id}_F$ from $F$ to $F$, denoted $\operatorname{id}_F: F \to F$, is defined as: $\forall X \in \mathbf C : \paren{\operatorname{id}_F}_X = \operatorname{id}_{FX}$ where $\operatorname{id}_{FX}$ is the identity morphism of $FX$ in $\mathbf D$.

label: Definition:Image/Also denoted as
snippet: The notation $\Img f$ to denote the image of a mapping $f$ is specific to . The usual notation is $\map {\mathrm {Im} } f$ or a variant, but this is too easily confused with $\map \Im z$, the imaginary part of a complex number. Hence the non-standard usage $\Img f$. Some sources use $f \sqbrk S$, where $S$ is the domain of $f$. Others just use $\map f S$, but that notation is deprecated on so as not to confuse it with the notation for the image of an element.

label: Definition:Image (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a locally small category. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism in $\CC$. An image of $f$ consists of an object $I$ and a monomorphism $m: I \to Y$ such that: $(1): \quad$ There exists a morphism $e : X \to I$ such that $f = m \circ e$. $(2): \quad$ For any object $I'$ with a morphism $e' : X \to I'$ and a monomorphism $m' : I' \to Y$ such that $f = m' \circ e'$, there exists a unique morphism $v : I \to I'$ such that $m = m' \circ v$.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)
snippet: The definition of a relation as a subset of the Cartesian product of two sets gives a "static" sort of feel to the concept. However, we can also consider a relation as being an operation, where you feed an element $s \in S$ (or a subset $S_1 \subseteq S$) in at one end, and you get a set of elements $T_s \subseteq T$ out of the other. Thus we arrive at the following definition.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Element
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $s \in S$. The image of $s$ (under $f$) is defined as: $\Img s = \map f s = \ds \bigcup \set {t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in f}$ That is, $\map f s$ is the element of the codomain of $f$ related to $s$ by $f$. By the nature of a mapping, $\map f s$ is guaranteed to exist and to be unique for any given $s$ in the domain of $f$.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Subset
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Element
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. Let $s \in S$. The image of $s$ by (or under) $\RR$ is defined as: $\map \RR s := \set {t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$ That is, $\map \RR s$ is the set of all elements of the codomain of $\RR$ related to $s$ by $\RR$. Thus: $\map \RR s$ is another way to write: $\RR \sqbrk {\set s}$ where $\RR \sqbrk {\set s}$ denotes the image of a subset of $\RR$.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Subset
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then the image set (of $X$ by $\RR$) is defined as: $\RR \sqbrk X := \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$

label: Definition:Image Filter
snippet: Let $S_1, S_2$ be sets. Let $\powerset {S_1}$ and $\powerset {S_2}$ be the power sets of $S_1$ and $S_2$ respectively. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ a mapping. Let $\FF \subset \powerset {S_1}$ be a filter on $S_1$. Then $f \sqbrk \FF := \set {U \subseteq S_2: f^{-1} \sqbrk U \in \FF}$ is the image filter of $\FF$ (on $S_2$) with respect to $f$.

label: Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Image of Subset under Mapping == In parallel with the notation $f \sqbrk X$ for the direct image mapping of $f$, also employs the notation $\map {f^\to} X$. This latter notation is used in, for example, , and is referred to as the mapping induced by $f$: It should be noted that most mathematicians write $\map f X$ for $\map {f^\to} X$. Now it is quite clear that the mappings $f$ and $f^\to$ are not the same, so we shall retain the notation $f^\to$ to avoid confusion. ...

label: Definition:Immediate Successor Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. Then $a$ is an immediate successor (element) to $b$ $b$ is an immediate predecessor (element) to $a$. That is, : $(1): \quad b \prec a$ $(2): \quad \nexists c \in S: b \prec c \prec a$ That is, there exists no element strictly between $b$ and $a$ in the ordering $\preceq$. That is: $a \prec b$ and $\openint a b = \O$ where $\openint a b$ denotes the open interval from $a$ to $b$. We say that $a$ immediately succeeds $b$.

label: Definition:Impedance of Free Space
snippet: Impedance of free space is a physical constant relating the magnitudes of the electric and magnetic fields of electromagnetic radiation travelling through a vacuum. It is defined as: the quotient of the magnitudes of the electric field and magnetic fields of electromagnetic radiation travelling through a vacuum: $\dfrac {\size {\mathbf E} } {\size {\mathbf H} }$ the vacuum permeability multiplied by the speed of light: $\mu_0 c$ the square root of the quotient of the vacuum permeability by the vacuum permittivity: $\sqrt {\dfrac {\mu_0} {\varepsilon_0} }$

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Foot
snippet: The square foot is an imperial unit of area. One square foot is equal to a square of side $1$ foot in length.

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Inch
snippet: The square inch is an imperial unit of area. One square inch is equal to a square of side $1$ inch in length. The definition is exact.

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Rod, Pole or Perch
snippet: The square rod, pole or perch is an imperial unit of area. One square rod, pole or perch is equal to a square of side $1$ rod, pole or perch in length. {{eqn | r = 30 \tfrac 1 4 | rr= = \paren {5 \tfrac 1 2}^2 | c = square yards }} {{eqn | r = 272 \tfrac 1 4 | rr= = \paren {16 \tfrac 1 2}^2 | c = square feet }}

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Yard
snippet: The square yard is an imperial unit of area. One square yard is equal to a square of side $1$ yard in length.

label: Definition:Imperial/Volume
snippet: The imperial units of volume are based on a binary system, in which each unit is a factor of $2$ larger than the next smaller unit.

label: Definition:Implicit Function
snippet: Consider a (real) function of two independent variables $z = \map f {x, y}$. Let a relation between $x$ and $y$ be expressed in the form $\map f {x, y} = 0$ defined on some subset of $\R^2$. If there exists a function: $y = \map g x$ defined on some real interval $\mathbb I$ such that: $\forall x \in \mathbb I: \map f {x, \map g x} = 0$ then the relation $\map f {x, y} = 0$ defines $y$ as an implicit function of $x$.

label: Definition:Implicit Function/General
snippet: Let: $f: \R^{n + 1} \to \R, \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z} \mapsto \map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z}$ be a real-valued function on $\R^{n + 1}$, where: $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \in \R^n, z \in \R$ Let a relation between $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ and $z$ be expressed in the form: $\map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z} = 0$ defined on some subset $S \subseteq \R^n$.

label: Definition:Inaccessible by Directed Suprema
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an up-complete ordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is inaccessible by directed suprema : for all directed subsets $D$ of $S$: $\sup D \in X \implies X \cap D \ne \O$

label: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Planar Graph
snippet: 220px Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a planar graph: Then a face of $G$ is incident to an edge $e$ of $G$ if $e$ is one of those which surrounds the face. Similarly, a face of $G$ is incident to a vertex $v$ of $G$ if $v$ is at the end of one of those incident edges. In the above graph, for example, the face $BCEF$ is incident to: the edges $BC, CE, EF, FB$ the vertices $B, C, E, F$.

label: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Undirected Graph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an undirected graph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $G$. Let $e = \set {u, v} \in E$ be an edge of $G$: 320px Then: $u$ and $v$ are each incident with $e$ $e$ is incident with $u$ and incident with $v$.

label: Definition:Incircle
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $C$ be a circle which is inscribed within $P$. 300px Then $C$ is an incircle of $P$.

label: Definition:Incircle of Triangle
snippet: The incircle of a triangle is the circle tangent to each side of the triangle. This circle is said to be inscribed in the triangle. 410px

label: Definition:Incircle of Triangle/Incenter
snippet: 410px The center of an incircle of a triangle is called an incenter of the triangle.

label: Definition:Incircle of Triangle/Inradius
snippet: 410px A radius of an incircle of a triangle is called an inradius of the triangle. In the above diagram, $r$ is an inradius.

label: Definition:Inclination/Straight Line to Plane
snippet: 500px Let $P$ be a plane. Let $L$ be a straight line which intersects $P$ at the point $A$. Let $Q$ be the perpendicular from a point $B$ on $L$. Let $C$ be the point where $Q$ intersects $P$. The inclination of $L$ to $P$ is defined as the angle $BAC$. In the above diagram, this has been marked as $\theta$.

label: Definition:Included Set Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-null. Let $H \subseteq S$ be some subset of $S$. We define a subset $\tau_H$ of the power set $\powerset S$ as: $\tau_H = \set {A \subseteq S: H \subseteq A} \cup \set \O$ that is, all the subsets of $S$ which are supersets of $H$, along with the empty set $\O$. Then $\tau_H$ is a topology called the included set topology on $S$ by $H$, or just an included set topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_H}$ is called the included set space on $S$ by $H$, or just an included set space.

label: Definition:Inclusion-Reversing Mapping
snippet: Let $A, B$ be sets of sets and $\phi: A \to B$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is inclusion-reversing : for every pair of sets $a_1, a_2 \in A$ such that $a_1 \subseteq a_2$: $\map \phi {a_2} \subseteq \map \phi {a_1}$

label: Definition:Inclusion Mapping
snippet: Let $T$ be a set. Let $S\subseteq T$ be a subset. The inclusion mapping $i_S: S \to T$ is the mapping defined as: $i_S: S \to T: \forall x \in S: \map {i_S} x = x$

label: Definition:Inclusion Relation on Subobjects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } C$ be the category of subobjects of $C$. The inclusion relation $\subseteq$ on subobjects of $C$ is defined as follows: $m \subseteq m'$ there exists a morphism $f: m \to m'$

label: Definition:Inconsistent (Logic)
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$.

label: Definition:Increasing/Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is increasing : $\forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \implies \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$ Note that this definition also holds if $S = T$.

label: Definition:Increasing/Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $A$ be a subset of the natural numbers $\N$. Then a sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in A}$ of terms of $S$ is increasing : $\forall j, k \in A: j < k \implies a_j \preceq a_k$

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Events
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {A_n}$ be a sequence of events in $\Sigma$. Then $\sequence {A_n}$ is described as increasing : $\forall i \in \N: A_i \subseteq A_{i + 1}$

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Extended Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, f_n: S \to \overline{\R}$ be a sequence of extended real-valued functions. Then $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to be an increasing sequence (of extended real-valued functions) : $\forall s \in S: \forall m, n \in \N: m \le n \implies \map {f_m} s \le \map {f_n} s$ That is, $m \le n \implies f_m \le f_n$, where the second $\le$ denotes pointwise inequality.

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, f_n: S \to \R$ be a sequence of real-valued functions. Then $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to be an increasing sequence (of real-valued functions) : $\forall s \in S: \forall m, n \in \N: m \le n \implies \map {f_m} s \le \map {f_n} s$ That is, $m \le n \implies f_m \le f_n$, where the second $\le$ denotes pointwise inequality.

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Sets
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ be a nested sequence of subsets of $S$ such that: $\forall k \in \N: S_k \subseteq S_{k + 1}$ Then $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ is an increasing sequence of sets (in $\SS$).

label: Definition:Increasing Union
snippet: Let $S_0, S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_i, \ldots$ be a nested sequence of sets, that is: $S_0 \subseteq S_1 \subseteq S_2 \subseteq \ldots \subseteq S_i \subseteq \ldots$ Let $S$ be the set: $\ds S = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in \N} S_i$ where $\bigcup$ denotes set union. Then $S$ is called the increasing union of $S_0, S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_i, \ldots$

label: Definition:Increment/Functional
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $y, h: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R$ be a functional defined on a normed vector space. Consider the following difference: $ \Delta J \sqbrk {y; h} = J \sqbrk {y + h} - J \sqbrk y$ Then $\Delta J \sqbrk {y; h}$ is known as the increment of the functional $J$.

label: Definition:Independence System
snippet: Let $S$ be a finite set. Let $\mathscr F$ be a set of subsets of $S$ satisfying the independence system axioms: The ordered pair $I = \struct {S, \mathscr F}$ is called an independence system on $S$.

label: Definition:Independent Events
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events of $\EE$ such that $\map \Pr A > 0$ and $\map \Pr B > 0$.

label: Definition:Independent Events/General Definition
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\AA = \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of events of $\EE$. Then $\AA$ is independent , for all finite subsets $J$ of $I$: $\ds \map \Pr {\bigcap_{i \mathop \in J} A_i} = \prod_{i \mathop \in J} \map \Pr {A_i}$ That is, the occurrence of any finite collection of $\AA$ has the same probability as the product of each of those sets occurring individually.

label: Definition:Independent Random Variables/Dependent
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are defined as dependent (on each other) $X$ and $Y$ are not independent (of each other).

label: Definition:Independent Shocks
snippet: Let $M$ be a stochastic model which describes a time series in which adjacent observations are highly dependent. Then $M$ may be able to be modelled by a time series whose elements are of the form: $\map z t = \map {z_d} t + \map {z_r} t$ where: $\map {z_d} t$ has a deterministic model $\map {z_r} t$ has a stochastic model which consists of a sequence of independent random variables from a specified probability distribution (usually a white noise process). The terms of the sequence $\sequence {z_r}$ are known as independent shocks.

label: Definition:Independent Subgroups
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $\sequence {H_n}$ be a sequence of subgroups of $G$.

label: Definition:Index
snippet: Set Theory: Index: an element of an indexing set Index set, set of indices: other names for an indexing set Sequences: Index: the index of a term $x_k$ of a sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ is $k$ Group Theory: Index of Subgroup: order of coset space Index of Group Element: another term for discrete logarithm Matrix Theory: Index of Matrix Element: one of the two parameters which specifies an element of a matrix Arithmetic: Index notation: another word for scientific notation Algebra and Analysis: Index (Algebra): the $y$ term in expressions such as $x^y$, more commonly known as the exponent of $x$…

label: Definition:Index Number
snippet: An index number in the context of statistics and economics is a measure of a change in some business activity over time. It is constructed based on reliable information on relevant components, usually weighted according to importance. An index number is usually defined relative to a specific base year, at which time the value of the index number would be assigned a round number, usually $100$ but sometimes $1000$.

label: Definition:Index Raising
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\hat g : TM \to T^* M$ be the Riemannian metric mapping. Let $\tuple {E_i}$ and $\tuple {\epsilon^i}$ be a smooth local frame and its dual coframe. Let $g = g_{ij} \epsilon^i \epsilon^j$ be the local expression of $g$. Let $g^{ij}$ be the inverse matrix of $g_{ij}$. Let $\omega$ be a smooth covector field. Let $\map {\hat g^{-1}} \omega = \omega_i g^{ij} E_j$ be the vector field. Index raising of $\omega$, denoted by $\omega^\sharp$, is an isomorphism $\sharp : T^*M \to TM$ such that: $\omega^\sharp := \map {\hat g^{-1}} \omega$

label: Definition:Index of Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The index of $H$ (in $G$), denoted $\index G H$, is the cardinality of the left (or right) coset space $G / H$.

label: Definition:Indexed Iterated Binary Operation
snippet: Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a magma. Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers. Let $\closedint a b$ be the integer interval between $a$ and $b$. Let $f: \closedint a b \to G$ be a mapping. The indexed iteration of $*$ of $f$ from $a$ to $b$ is recursively defined and denoted: $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = a}^b \map f k = \begin {cases} \map f a & : b = a \\ \paren {\ds \prod_{k \mathop = a}^{b - 1} \map f k} * \map f b & : b > a \end {cases}$ For each ordered $n$-tuple $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$, the composite of $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ for $\oplus$ is the value at $\tuple {a_1, a_2,…

label: Definition:Indexing Set
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the elements $i \in I$ under $x$. When a mapping is used in this context, the domain $I$ of $x$ is called the indexing set of the terms $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Family
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be an indexing function for $S$. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the elements $i \in I$ under $x$. The image $\Img x$, consisting of the terms $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$, along with the indexing function $x$ itself, is called a family of elements of $S$ indexed by $I$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Family of Sets
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a set of sets. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of $\SS$ indexed by $I$. Then $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is referred to as an indexed family of sets.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Family of Subsets
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. For each $i \in I$, let $S_i$ be a corresponding subset of $S$. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of subsets of $S$ indexed by $I$. Then $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is referred to as an indexed family of subsets (of $S$ by $I$).

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Function
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the element $i \in I$ under $x$. When used in this context, the mapping $x$ is referred to as an indexing function for $S$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Index
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the element $i \in I$ under $x$. An element of the domain $I$ of $x$ is called an index.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Indexed Set
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the elements $i \in I$ under $x$. The image of $x$, that is, $x \sqbrk I$ or $\Img x$, is called an indexed set. That is, it is the set indexed by $I$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Note on Terminology
snippet: It is a common approach to blur the distinction between an indexing function $x: I \to S$ and the indexed family $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ itself, and refer to the mapping as the indexed family. This approach is in accordance with the definition of a mapping as a relation defined as an as ordered triple $\tuple {I, S, x}$, where the mapping is understood as being defined to include its domain and codomain.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Term
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the element $i \in I$ under $x$. The image of $x$ at an index $i$ is referred to as a term of the (indexed) family, and is denoted $x_i$.

label: Definition:Indicator Function
snippet: Another name for the characteristic function of a set. Another name for the Euler $\phi$ function.

label: Definition:Indicator of Group Element
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group. Let $a \in G$. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The indicator of $a$ in $H$ is the least strictly positive integer $n$ such that $a^n \in H$.

label: Definition:Indiscrete Extension of Reals
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $D$ be an everywhere dense subset of $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ with an everywhere dense complement in $\R$. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets: $\BB := \set {H: \exists U \in \tau_d: H = U \cap D}$ Let $\tau^*$ be the topology generated from $\tau_d$ by the addition of all sets of $\BB$. $\tau^* = \tau_d \cup \BB$ $\tau^*$ is then referred to as an indiscrete extension of $\R$.

label: Definition:Indiscrete Extension of Reals/Rational
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $\Q$ denote the set of rational numbers. Let $\tau^*$ be the indiscrete extension of $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$: $\tau^* = \tau_d \cup \set {H: \exists U \in \tau_d: H = U \cap \Q}$ $\tau^*$ is then referred to as the indiscrete rational extension of $\R$.

label: Definition:Indiscrete Topology
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \set {S, \O}$. Then $\tau$ is called the indiscrete topology on $S$. A topological space $\struct {S, \set {S, \O} }$ is known as an indiscrete space.

label: Definition:Induced Mapping on Spectra of Rings
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative rings with unity. Let $f : A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism. The induced mapping on spectra by $f$ is the mapping $f^* : \Spec B \to \Spec A$ between their spectra with: $\map {f^*} {\mathfrak p} = \map {f^{-1} } {\mathfrak p}$, the preimage of a prime ideal $\mathfrak p \in \Spec B$.

label: Definition:Induced Metric on Submanifold
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be a Riemannian manifold with or without a boundary. Let $M : M \subseteq \tilde M$ be a submanifold immersed in $\tilde M$. Let $i : M \to \tilde M$ be the inclusion mapping. Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric such that $g = i^* \tilde g$. Then $g$ is called the induced metric on $M$.

label: Definition:Induction Hypothesis
snippet: == Terminology of Mathematical Induction == Consider a proof by mathematical induction: The assumption that $Q$ is true for $w_p$ is called the induction hypothesis. Expressed in the various contexts of mathematical induction:

label: Definition:Induction Step
snippet: == Terminology of Mathematical Induction == Consider a proof by mathematical induction: The proof that the truth of $Q$ for $w_p$ implies the truth of $Q$ for $w_{p^+}$is called the induction step. Expressed in the various contexts of mathematical induction:

label: Definition:Inductive Argument
snippet: An inductive argument is a form of argument in which, if all the premises are true, the conclusion is probably true, but might not be. Such lines of reasoning are ubiquitous in everyday life and in most human endeavors. However, inductive arguments are only conjectures in the field of mathematics. Such arguments are not truth preserving and therefore they are not proofs.

label: Definition:Inductive Class/General
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $g: A \to A$ be a mapping on $A$. Then $A$ is inductive under $g$ : {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $A$ is closed under $g$: | q = \forall x | m = \paren {x \in A \implies \map g x \in A} }}

label: Definition:Inductive Ordered Set
snippet: An inductive ordered set is an ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound.

label: Definition:Inductive Semigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a semigroup. Let there exist $\alpha, \beta \in S$ such that the only subset of $S$ containing both $\alpha$ and $x \circ \beta$ whenever it contains $x$ is $S$ itself. That is: $\exists \alpha, \beta \in S: \forall A \subseteq S: \paren {\alpha \in A \land \paren {\forall x \in A: x \circ \beta \in A} } \implies A = S$ Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ is an inductive semigroup.

label: Definition:Inductive Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of sets. Then $S$ is inductive : {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $S$ is closed under the successor mapping: | q = \forall x | m = \paren {x \in S \implies x^+ \in S} | rc= where $x^+$ is the successor of $x$ }}

label: Definition:Inductive Set/Subset of Real Numbers
snippet: Let $I$ be a subset of the real numbers $\R$. Then $I$ is an inductive set : $1 \in I$ and $x \in I \implies \paren {x + 1} \in I$

label: Definition:Inductive Statistics
snippet: Inductive statistics is the phase of statistics which is concerned with the conditions under which conclusions about populations can be drawn from analysis of particular samples. The inferences drawn by inductive statistics are generally couched in the language of probability theory.

label: Definition:Inelastic Collision
snippet: An inelastic collision is a collision in which the total kinetic energy of the interacting bodies is not the same after the collision as it was before.

label: Definition:Inequality
snippet: An inequality is a mathematical statement that two expressions relate in one of several conventional ways: $a b$ $a \ge b$

label: Definition:Inequality/Strict
snippet: A strict inequality is an inequality which does not permit the possibility of equality. That is, an inequality of the form: $a b$

label: Definition:Inequality/Weak
snippet: A weak inequality is an inequality which permits the possibility of equality. That is, an inequality of the form: $a \le b$ $a \ge b$

label: Definition:Inertial Frame of Reference
snippet: An inertial frame of reference is a frame of reference in which a body moves at constant velocity in the absence of an external force. That is, it is a frame of reference in which Newton's First Law of Motion holds.

label: Definition:Infima Inheriting
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $R = \struct {T, \preceq'}$ be an ordered subset of $L$. Then $R$ inherits infima of $L$ for all subsets $X$ of $T$ if $X$ admits an infimum of $L$, then $X$ admits an infimum of $R$ and $\inf_R X = \inf_L X$

label: Definition:Infimum/Also known as
snippet: Particularly in the field of analysis, the infimum of a set $T$ is often referred to as the greatest lower bound of $T$ and denoted $\map {\mathrm {glb} } T$ or $\map {\mathrm {g.l.b.} } T$. Some sources refer to the infimum of a set as the infimum on a set. Some sources refer to the infimum of a set as the meet of the set and use the notation $\bigwedge T$ or $\ds \bigwedge_{y \mathop \in T} y$. Some sources introduce the notation $\ds \inf_{y \mathop \in T} y$, which may improve clarity in some circumstances.

label: Definition:Infimum of Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$. Let $f \sqbrk S$, the image of $f$, admit an infimum. Then the infimum of $f$ (on $S$) is defined by: $\ds \inf_{x \mathop \in S} \map f x = \inf f \sqbrk S$

label: Definition:Infimum of Mapping/Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded below on $S$.

label: Definition:Infimum of Sequence
snippet: A special case of an infimum of a mapping is an infimum of a sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Let $\set {x_n: n \in \N}$ admit an infimum. Then the infimum of $\sequence {x_n}$) is defined as: $\map \inf {\sequence {x_n} } = \map \inf {\set {x_n: n \in \N} }$

label: Definition:Infimum of Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$. An element $c \in S$ is the infimum of $T$ in $S$ : $(1): \quad c$ is a lower bound of $T$ in $S$ $(2): \quad d \preccurlyeq c$ for all lower bounds $d$ of $T$ in $S$. If there exists an infimum of $T$ (in $S$), we say that: $T$ admits an infimum (in $S$) or $T$ has an infimum (in $S$).

label: Definition:Infimum of Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $T \subseteq \R$. A real number $c \in \R$ is the infimum of $T$ in $\R$ : $(1): \quad c$ is a lower bound of $T$ in $\R$ $(2): \quad d \le c$ for all lower bounds $d$ of $T$ in $\R$. If there exists an infimum of $T$ (in $\R$), we say that $T$ admits an infimum (in $\R$). The infimum of $T$ is denoted $\inf T$ or $\map \inf T$.

label: Definition:Infinite Cardinal
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a cardinal. Then $\mathbf a$ is described as infinite : $\mathbf a = \mathbf a + \mathbf 1$ where $\mathbf 1$ is (cardinal) one.

label: Definition:Infinite Field
snippet: An infinite field $\struct {F, +, \cdot}$ is a field such that $F$ is a infinite set.

label: Definition:Infinite Group
snippet: A group which is not finite is an infinite group. That is, an infinite group is a group of infinite order. That is, a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is an infinite group its underlying set $G$ is infinite. That is, an infinite group is a group with an infinite number of elements.

label: Definition:Infinite Group/Countable
snippet: An infinite group whose underlying set $G$ is countable is a countably infinite group.

label: Definition:Infinite Set
snippet: A set which is not finite is called infinite. That is, it is a set for which there is no bijection between it and any $\N_n$, where $\N_n$ is the the set of all elements of $n$ less than $n$, no matter how big we make $n$.

label: Definition:Infinite Topological Space
snippet: An infinite topological space is a topological space whose underlying set is infinite.

label: Definition:Infinity
snippet: Informally, the term infinity is used to mean some infinite number, but this concept falls very far short of a usable definition. The symbol $\infty$ (supposedly invented by ) is often used in this context to mean an infinite number. However, outside of its formal use in the definition of limits its use is strongly discouraged until you know what you're talking about.

label: Definition:Information Theory
snippet: Information theory is that branch of mathematics concerned with the flow of information. It is mainly concerned with the handling of uncertainty in communication media. It can also be considered as also encompassing coding theory.

label: Definition:Initial Condition
snippet: Let $\Phi = \map F {x, y, y', y, \ldots, y^{\paren n} }$ be an ordinary differential equation. An initial condition is an ordered pair $\tuple {x_0, y_0}$ which any solution of $\Phi$ must satisfy. That is, an initial condition is the additional imposition that a solution $y = \map y x$ of $\Phi$ satisfy: $\map y {x_0} = y_0$

label: Definition:Initial Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. An initial object of $\mathbf C$ is an object $0 \in \mathbf C_0$ of $\mathbf C$ such that: For all $C \in \mathbf C_0$, there is a unique morphism $0 \to C$.

label: Definition:Initial Segment
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a well-ordered set. Let $a \in S$. The initial segment (of $S$) determined by $a$ is defined as: $S_a := \set {b \in S: b \preceq a \land b \ne a}$ which can also be rendered as: $S_a := \set {b \in S: b \prec a}$ That is, $S_a$ is the set of all elements of $S$ that strictly precede $a$. That is, $S_a$ is the strict lower closure of $a$ (in $S$). By extension, $S_a$ is described as an initial segment (of $S$).

label: Definition:Initial Segment/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $\preceq$ be a well-ordering on $A$. Let $a \in A$. The initial segment (of $A$) determined by $a$ is defined as: $A_a := \set {b \in S: b \preceq a \land b \ne a}$ which can also be rendered as: $A_a := \set {b \in S: b \prec a}$

label: Definition:Initial Segment of Natural Numbers/One-Based
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. The initial segment of the non-zero natural numbers determined by $n$: $\set {1, 2, 3, \ldots, n}$ is denoted $\N^*_{\le n}$.

label: Definition:Initial Segment of Natural Numbers/Zero-Based
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. The initial segment of the natural numbers determined by $n$: $\set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1}$ is denoted $\N_{<n}$.

label: Definition:Initial Topology
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct {Y_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces indexed by $I$. Let $\family {f_i: X \to Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of mappings indexed by $I$.

label: Definition:Initial Value Problem
snippet: Let $\map y x$ be a solution to the first order ordinary differential equation: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \map f {x, y}$ which is subject to an initial condition: $\tuple {a, b}$. That is, it is required that $y = b$ when $x = a$, that is $\map y a = b$. The finding of the resulting particular solution is known as an initial value problem.

label: Definition:Injection/Definition 4
snippet: Let $f$ be a mapping. $f$ is an injection : $\forall y \in \Img f: \card {\map {f^{-1} } y} = \card {\set {f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set y} } } = 1$ where: $\Img f$ denotes the image set of $f$ $\card {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the cardinality of a set $\map {f^{-1} } y$ is the preimage of $y$ $f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set y}$ is the preimage of the subset $\set y \subseteq \Img f$. That is, the preimage of $y$ is a singleton for all $y$ in the image set of $f$.

label: Definition:Injective
snippet: Definition:Injection Definition:Injective Object Definition:Injective Module Definition:Injective Morphism

label: Definition:Injective Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. A left $R$-module is injective it is an injective object in the category of left $R$-modules.

label: Definition:Injective Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $I$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. $I$ is an injective object : for every monomorphism $i: X \to Y$ in $\mathbf C$ and: for every morphism $f : X \to I$ there exists a morphism $g : Y \to I$, such that: $g \circ i = f$

label: Definition:Injective Path
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb I \subset \R$ be the closed unit interval $\closedint 0 1$. Let $a, b \in T$. An injective path from $a$ to $b$ is a path $f: \mathbb I \to T$ such that $f$ is injective. That is, an injective path from $a$ to $b$ is a continuous injection $f: \mathbb I \to T$ such that $\map f 0 = a$ and $\map f 1 = b$. The mapping $f$ can be described as an injective path (in $T$) joining $a$ and $b$.

label: Definition:Injective Path Component
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let us define the relation $\sim$ on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y \iff x$ and $y$ are injectively path-connected. We have that $\sim $ is an equivalence relation, so from the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, the points in $T$ can be partitioned into equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the injective path components of $T$. If $x \in T$, then the injective path component of $T$ containing $x$ (that is, the set of points $y \in T$ with $x \sim y$) can be denoted by $\map {\operatorname {IPC}_x} T$.

label: Definition:Injective on Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be injective on morphisms for all morphisms $f, g$ of $\mathbf C$: $F f = F g$ implies $f = g$ Note that it is not required that $f$ and $g$ have equal domains or codomains.

label: Definition:Injective on Objects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be injective on objects for all objects $C_1, C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: $F C_1 = F C_2$ implies $C_1 = C_2$

label: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected
snippet: Injective path-connectedness is a property of a topological space $T$ which relates to the existence of certain continuous injections from a closed real interval (in practice, usually just the closed unit interval) into $T$.

label: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Points
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$ be such that there exists an injective path from $a$ to $b$. That is, there exists a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that: Then $a$ and $b$ are injectively path-connected in $T$. It is also declared that any point $a$ is injectively path-connected to itself.

label: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Subset
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be a subset of $T$. Let $T' = \struct {U, \tau_U}$ be the subspace of $T$ induced by $U$. Then $T'$ is injectively path-connected in $T$ every two points in $U$ are injectively path-connected in $T'$. That is, $T'$ is injectively path-connected : for every $x, y \in U$, there exists a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

label: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Topological Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is injectively path-connected every two points in $T$ are injectively path-connected in $T$. That is, $T$ is injectively path-connected : $\forall x, y \in S: \exists$ a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

label: Definition:Inner Automorphism
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $x \in G$. Let the mapping $\kappa_x: G \to G$ be defined such that: $\forall g \in G: \map {\kappa_x} g = x g x^{-1}$ $\kappa_x$ is called the inner automorphism of $G$ (given) by $x$. The set of inner automorphisms of $G$ is denoted on as $\Inn G$.

label: Definition:Inner Automorphism Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. The inner automorphism group of $G$ is the algebraic structure: $\struct {\Inn G, \circ}$ where: $\Inn G$ is the set of inner automorphisms of $G$ $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings.

label: Definition:Inner Jordan Content
snippet: Let $M \subseteq \R^n$ be a bounded subspace of Euclidean $n$-space. Let: $\ds \RR = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \closedint {a_i} {b_i}$ be a closed $n$-rectangle that contains $M$. The inner Jordan content of $M$ is defined and denoted as: $\map {m_*} M = \map V \RR - \map {m^*} {\RR \setminus M}$ where: $\map {m^*} {\RR \setminus M}$ denotes the outer Jordan content of $R \setminus M$ That is, the inner Jordan content of $M$ is defined to be the outer Jordan content of the complement of $M$, relative to some fixed $\RR \supseteq M$.

label: Definition:Inner Limit
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological space. Let $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets in $X$. The inner limit of $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is defined as: $\ds \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} \ C_n := \set {x \in X: \exists N \text { cofinite set of } \N, \exists x_v \in C_v \paren {v \in N} \text { such that } x_v \to x}$ where $x_v \to x$ denotes convergence in the topology $\tau$.

label: Definition:Inner Product/Complex Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a complex subfield $\GF$. A (complex) inner product is a mapping $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \GF$ that satisfies the complex inner product axioms: That is, a (complex) inner product is a complex semi-inner product with the additional condition $(4)$.

label: Definition:Inner Product/Real Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a real subfield $\GF$. A (real) inner product is a mapping $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \GF$ that satisfies the real inner product axioms: That is, a (real) inner product is a real semi-inner product with the additional condition $(4)$.

label: Definition:Inner Product Norm
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be a subfield of $\C$. Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space over $\Bbb F$. Then the inner product norm on $V$ is the mapping $\norm {\, \cdot \,} : V \to \R_{\ge 0}$ given by: $\norm x = \sqrt {\innerprod x x}$ for each $x \in V$.

label: Definition:Inner Product Space
snippet: An inner product space is a vector space together with an associated inner product.

label: Definition:Inner Product Space/Complex Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a complex subfield $\GF$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : V \times V \to \GF$ be an complex inner product on $V$. We say that $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a (complex) inner product space. That is, a (complex) inner product space is a complex vector space together with an associated complex inner product.

label: Definition:Inner Product Space/Real Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a real subfield $\GF$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : V \times V \to \GF$ be an real inner product on $V$. We say that $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a (real) inner product space. That is, an (real) inner product space is a real vector space together with an associated real inner product.

label: Definition:Inscribe
snippet: Let a geometric figure $A$ be constructed in the interior of another geometric figure $B$ such that: $(1): \quad$ $A$ and $B$ have points in common $(2): \quad$ No part of $A$ is outside $B$. Then $A$ is inscribed inside $B$.

label: Definition:Inscribe/Circle in Polygon
snippet: A circle is inscribed in a polygon when it is tangent to each of the sides of that polygon: 300px '

label: Definition:Inscribe/Polygon in Circle
snippet: A polygon is inscribed in a circle when each of its vertices lies on the circumference of the circle: 300px That is, the vertices are concyclic. '

label: Definition:Inscribe/Polygon in Polygon
snippet: A polygon is inscribed in another polygon when each of its vertices lies on the corresponding side of the other polygon. '

label: Definition:Instant of Time
snippet: An instant is a specific point in time. Category:Definitions/Time

label: Definition:Instantaneous/Acceleration
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint t {t + h}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ be the velocity of $B$ at $t$ and $t + h$ respectively. Let $\overline {\mathbf a}$ denote the average acceleration of $B$ over $\Bbb I$. The instantaneous acceleration $\mathbf a$ of $B$ at time $t$ is defined as the limit of $\overline {\mathbf a}$ as $h \to 0$: $\mathbf a := \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\mathbf v_2 - \mathbf v_1} h$

label: Definition:Instantaneous/Velocity
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint t {t + h}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf s_1$ and $\mathbf s_2$ be the displacement of $B$ at $t$ and $t + h$ respectively. Let $\overline {\mathbf v}$ denote the average velocity of $B$ over $\Bbb I$. The instantaneous velocity $\mathbf v$ of $B$ at time $t$ is defined as the limit of $\overline {\mathbf v}$ as $h \to 0$: $\mathbf v := \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1} h$

label: Definition:Integer
snippet: The numbers $\set {\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ are called the integers. This set is usually denoted $\Z$. An individual element of $\Z$ is called an integer.

label: Definition:Integer-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a function. Let $S_1 \subseteq S$ such that $f \left({S_1}\right) \subseteq \Z$. Then $f$ is said to be integer-valued on $S_1$. That is, $f$ is defined as integer-valued on $S_1$ the image of $S_1$ under $f$ lies entirely within the set of integers $\Z$. An integer-valued function is a function $f: S \to \Z$ whose codomain is the set of integers $\Z$. That is, $f$ is integer-valued it is integer-valued over its entire domain. Category:Definitions/Integers

label: Definition:Integer/Formal Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\N, +}$ be the commutative semigroup of natural numbers under addition. From Inverse Completion of Natural Numbers, we can create $\struct {\N', +'}$, an inverse completion of $\struct {\N, +}$. From Construction of Inverse Completion, this is done as follows: Let $\boxtimes$ be the cross-relation defined on $\N \times \N$ by: $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \boxtimes \tuple {x_2, y_2} \iff x_1 + y_2 = x_2 + y_1$ From Cross-Relation is Congruence Relation, $\boxtimes$ is a congruence relation.

label: Definition:Integer/Formal Definition/Notation
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the integers defined as a set of ordered pairs of natural numbers. We have that $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxminus$ is an equivalence class of ordered pairs of natural numbers under the congruence relation $\boxminus$. As this notation is cumbersome, it is commonplace though technically incorrect to streamline it to $\eqclass {a, b} \boxminus$, or $\eqclass {a, b} {}$. This is generally considered acceptable, as long as it is made explicit as to the precise meaning of $\eqclass {a, b} {}$ at the start of any exposition. Category:Definitions/Integers

label: Definition:Integer Combination
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$. An integer $n$ of the form: $n = p a + q b: p, q \in \Z$ is an integer combination of $a$ and $b$.

label: Definition:Integer Division
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$. From the Division Theorem: $\exists_1 q, r \in \Z: a = q b + r, 0 \le r < \size b$ where $q$ is the quotient and $r$ is the remainder. The process of finding $q$ and $r$ is known as (integer) division of $a$ by $b$, and we write: $a \div b = q \rem r$

label: Definition:Integer Heronian Triangle
snippet: An integer Heronian triangle is a Heronian triangle whose sides are integers.

label: Definition:Integer Lattice
snippet: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real Euclidean space. Let $\CC$ be the Cartesian coordinate system of $n$ dimensions embedded in $\R^n$. The integer lattice in $\R^n$ is the set of points in $\R^n$ which can be defined using coordinates of $\CC$ which are integers. Thus it is the point lattice on $\R^n$ whose basis is the standard ordered basis over $\R^n$: $\BB = \set {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ where: $\mathbf e_k := \tuple {\delta_{1 k}, \delta_{2 k}, \ldots, \delta_{n k} }$ $\delta_{j k}$ is the Kronecker delta.

label: Definition:Integer Partition
snippet: A partition of a (strictly) positive integer $n$ is a way of writing $n$ as a sum of (strictly) positive integers.

label: Definition:Integer Reciprocal Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line $\R$ under the usual (Euclidean) topology $\tau_d$. Let $A \subseteq \R$ be the set of all points on $\R$ defined as: $A := \set {\dfrac 1 n : n \in \Z_{>0} }$ That is: $A := \set {1, \dfrac 1 2, \dfrac 1 3, \dfrac 1 4, \ldots}$ Then $\struct {A, \tau_d}$ is the integer reciprocal space.

label: Definition:Integer Sequence
snippet: An integer sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the set of integers $\Z$.

label: Definition:Integer Square
snippet: An integer square is a square whose sides are integers.

label: Definition:Integers Modulo m
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. The integers modulo $m$ are the set of least positive residues of the set of residue classes modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$

label: Definition:Integrable Function/Complex
snippet: Let $\mathbb I := \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $f: \mathbb I \to \C$ be a bounded complex-valued function. Define the real function $x: \mathbb I \to \R$ by: $\forall t \in \mathbb I: \map x t = \map \Re {\map f t}$ Define the real function $y: \mathbb I \to \R$ by: $\forall t \in \mathbb I: \map y t = \map \Im {\map f t}$ where: $\map \Re {\map f t}$ denotes the real part of the complex number $\map f t$ $\map \Im {\map f t}$ denotes the imaginary part of $\map f t$. Suppose that both $x$ and $y$ are Riemann integrable over $\mathbb I$.

label: Definition:Integrable Function/Lebesgue
snippet: Let $\lambda^n$ be a Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$ for some $n > 0$. Let $f: \R^n \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. Then $f$ is said to be Lebesgue integrable it is $\lambda^n$-integrable. Similarly, for all real numbers $p \ge 1$, $f$ is said to be Lebesgue $p$-integrable it is $p$-integrable under $\lambda^n$.

label: Definition:Integrable Function/Measure Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\MM_{\overline \R}$ denote the space of $\Sigma$-measurable, extended real-valued functions . Let $f \in \MM_{\overline \R}, f: X \to \overline \R$ be a measurable function. Then $f$ is said to be $\mu$-integrable : $\ds \int f^+ \rd \mu < +\infty$ and $\ds \int f^- \rd \mu < +\infty$ where $f^+$, $f^-$ are the positive and negative parts of $f$, respectively. The integral signs denote $\mu$-integration of positive measurable functions.

label: Definition:Integrable Function/Measure Space/Complex Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\struct {\C, \map \BB \C}$ be the complex numbers made into a measurable space with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $f : X \to \C$ be a $\Sigma/\map \BB C$-measurable function. Let $\map \Re f : X \to \R$ and $\map \Im f : X \to \R$ be the real part and imaginary part of $f$ respectively. We say that $f$ is $\mu$-integrable $\map \Re f$ and $\map \Im f$ are (real) $\mu$-integrable.

label: Definition:Integrable Function/p-Integrable
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f \in \MM_{\overline \R}, f: X \to \overline \R$ be a measurable function. Let $p \ge 1$ be a real number. Then $f$ is said to be $p$-integrable $\mu$ : $\ds \int \size f^p \rd \mu < +\infty$ is $\mu$-integrable.

label: Definition:Integrable Random Variable
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. We say that $X$ is integrable $X$ is $\Pr$-integrable.

label: Definition:Integral
snippet: Commutative algebra: Integral Closure Integrally Closed Integral Element of Ring Extension Integral Ring Extension Ring theory: Integral Domain Integral Polynomial Number theory: Integral Multiple Integral Part Analysis: Integral Calculus Integral: Definite Integral Indefinite Integral Integral: As a synonym for the term solution to a differential equation.

label: Definition:Integral Equation/Parameter
snippet: Consider the integral equation: of the first kind: $\map f x = \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ of the second kind: $\map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ of the third kind: $\map u x \map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ The number $\lambda$ is known as the parameter of the integral equation.

label: Definition:Integral Ideal
snippet: Let $J \subseteq \Z$ be a non-empty subset of the set of integers. Let $J$ fulfil the following conditions: Then $J$ is an integral ideal.

label: Definition:Integral Multiple/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Then $x$ is an integral multiple of $y$ $x$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $y$: $x \equiv 0 \pmod y$ That is: $\exists k \in \Z: x = 0 + k y$

label: Definition:Integral Multiple/Rings and Fields
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a ring or a field whose zero is $0_F$. Let $a \in F$. Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Then $n \cdot a$ is an integral multiple of $a$ where $n \cdot a$ is defined as: $n \cdot a := \begin {cases} 0_F & : n = 0 \\ \paren {\paren {n - 1} \cdot a} + a & : n > 1 \\ \size n \cdot \paren {-a} & : n where $\size n$ is the absolute value of $n$. Using sum notation: $\ds n \cdot a := \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n a$

label: Definition:Integral Operator
snippet: Let $X, Y$ be sets of mappings, real or complex numbers. Let $A : X \to Y$ be a mapping such that $A$ is expressible as an integral of elements of $X$ (possibly involving weight functions and kernels). Then $A$ is known as an integral operator. Category:Definitions/Operator Theory

label: Definition:Integral Transform
snippet: Let $p$ be a variable whose domain is a subset of the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval for some $a, b \in \R: a \le b$. Let $f: \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function defined on the domain $\closedint a b$. Let $\map K {p, x}$ be a real-valued function defined for all $p$ in its domain and all $x \in \closedint a b$. Let $\map f x \map K {p, x}$ be integrable $x$ for all $p$ in its domain and all $x \in \closedint a b$.

label: Definition:Integral Transform/Operator
snippet: Let $\map F p$ be an integral transform: $\map F p = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x$ This can be written in the form: $F = \map T f$ where $T$ is interpreted as the (unitary) operator meaning: Multiply this by $\map K {p, x}$ and integrate $x$ between the limits $a$ and $b$. Thus $T$ transforms the function $\map f x$ into its image $\map F p$, which is itself another real function.

label: Definition:Integrating Factor
snippet: Consider the first order ordinary differential equation: $(1): \quad \map M {x, y} + \map N {x, y} \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = 0$ such that $M$ and $N$ are real functions of two variables which are not homogeneous functions of the same degree. Suppose also that: $\dfrac {\partial M} {\partial y} \ne \dfrac {\partial N} {\partial x}$ Then from Solution to Exact Differential Equation, $(1)$ is not exact, and that method can not be used to solve it.

label: Definition:Integration/Integrand
snippet: In the expression for the definite integral: $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ or primitive (that is, indefinite integral: $\ds \int \map f x \rd x$ the function $f$ is called the integrand.

label: Definition:Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a line, a curve or a surface. An intercept of $\CC$ is the intersection of $\CC$ with another line, a curve or a surface. In particular:

label: Definition:Intercept/X-Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a cartesian plane. An $x$-intercept of $\CC$ is a point where $\CC$ intersects the $x$-axis. Hence it can also be used for the length of the line segment between that point and the origin.

label: Definition:Intercept/Y-Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a cartesian plane. A $y$-intercept of $\CC$ is a point where $\CC$ intersects the $y$-axis. Hence it can also be used for the length of the line segment between that point and the origin.

label: Definition:Interior
snippet: Topology and metric spaces: The interior of a subset $H$ of a topological space: The largest open set contained in $H$. The interior of a subset $H$ of the complex plane $\C$: The set of all interior points of $H$ The interior of a topological manifold with boundary. Plane Geometry: Interior of a Region Interior of an Angle Interior Angle of a Transversal Interior Angle of a Polygon Complex Analysis: Interior of Jordan Curve

label: Definition:Interior (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $H \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. The interior of $H$ is the subset of $H$ which consists of the interior points of $H$.

label: Definition:Interior (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Notation
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ can be denoted: $\map {\mathrm {Int} } H$ $H^\circ$ The first is regarded by some as cumbersome, but has the advantage of being clear. $H^\circ$ is neat and compact, but has the disadvantage of being less intuitive. On , $H^\circ$ is the notation of choice.

label: Definition:Interior Multiplication
snippet: Let $V$ and $V^*$ be a vector space and its algebraic dual. Let $\omega \in \map {\Lambda^k} {V^*}$ be an alternating $k$-tensor. Let $v \in V$ be a vector. Let $v \mathop \lrcorner \omega$ be an alternating $\paren {k - 1}$-tensor such that: $\map {\paren {v \mathop \lrcorner \omega}} {w_1, \ldots, w_{k - 1}} := \map \omega {v, w_1, \ldots, w_{k - 1}}$ Then the mapping $\omega \mapsto v \mathop \lrcorner \omega$ is known as the interior multiplication by $v$. If $\omega$ is a $0$-tensor then: $v \mathop \lrcorner \omega := 0$

label: Definition:Interior Point (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z \in S$. $z$ is an interior point of $S$ $z$ has an $\epsilon$-neighborhood $\map {N_\epsilon} z$ such that $\map {N_\epsilon} z \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Interior of Simple Closed Contour
snippet: Let $C$ be a simple closed contour in the complex plane. Let $f : \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a Jordan curve. Let $\phi : \R^2 \to \C$ be defined by: $\map \phi {x, y} = x + i y$ Let $\Img C = \map \phi {\Img f}$, where $\Img C$ denotes the image of $C$, and $\Img f$ denotes the image of $f$. Then the interior of $C$ is denoted $\Int C$ and defined as: $\Int C = \map \phi {\Int f}$ where $\Int f$ denotes the interior of $f$.

label: Definition:Intermediate Field
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $F$ be a field such that: $K \subset F \subset L$ Then $F$ is an intermediate field. Category:Definitions/Field Extensions

label: Definition:Internal Direct Sum of Rings/Direct Summand
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ be a sequence of subrings of $R$. Let $\ds S = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^n S_j$ be the ring direct sum of $S_1$ to $S_n$. In Conditions for Internal Ring Direct Sum it is proved that for this to be the case, then $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ must be ideals of $R$. Such ideals are known as direct summands of $R$.

label: Definition:International Standard Book Number/ISBN-10
snippet: An International Standard Book Number is a codeword used to uniquely identify a published . The ISBN-$10$ format consists of a string of $9$ digits followed by a check digit in the set $\set {0, 1, \ldots, 9, X}$. The check digit $d$ is calculated as follows. Let $c$ be calculated as: $c = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^9 k d_k \pmod {11}$ where $d_k$ denotes the $k$th digit in the ISBN-$10$. Then the check digit $d$ is defined as: $d = \begin {cases} c & : c \le 9 \\ X &: c = 10 \end {cases}$ Hyphens may be included in the string to separate out the sections for lexicographical convenience.

label: Definition:Interpretation
snippet: Let $S$ be the codomain of a mapping $f$ whose domain consists of the set of expressions of a formal language $\FF$. Then $S$ together with $f$ are known as an interpretation.

label: Definition:Interquartile Range
snippet: The interquartile range is a measure of dispersion in statistics. Let $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ be first quartile and third quartile respectively. The interquartile range is defined and denoted as: $\operatorname {IQR} := Q_3 - Q_1$

label: Definition:Intersection
snippet: Set theory: Set intersection: the elements common to two or more sets. Geometry: Geometrical intersection: the points common to two or more geometric figures. Definition:Intersection Product

label: Definition:Intersection (Geometry)
snippet: The intersection of two lines $AB$ and $CD$ is denoted by $AB \cap CD$. The intersection of two geometric figures is the set of points shared by both figures. Note that this use of $\cap$ is consistent with that of its more usual context of set intersection. When two lines intersect, they are said to cut each other.

label: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Closed
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The closed interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\closedint a b := a^\succcurlyeq \cap b^\preccurlyeq = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \preccurlyeq s} \land \paren {s \preccurlyeq b} }$ where: $a^\succcurlyeq$ denotes the upper closure of $a$ $b^\preccurlyeq$ denotes the lower closure of $b$.

label: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Left Half-Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The left half-open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\hointl a b := a^\succ \cap b^\preccurlyeq = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \prec s} \land \paren {s \preccurlyeq b} }$ where: $a^\succ$ denotes the strict upper closure of $a$ $b^\preccurlyeq$ denotes the lower closure of $b$.

label: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\openint a b := a^\succ \cap b^\prec = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \prec s} \land \paren {s \prec b} }$ where: $a^\succ$ denotes the strict upper closure of $a$ $b^\prec$ denotes the strict lower closure of $b$.

label: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Right Half-Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The right half-open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\hointr a b := a^\succcurlyeq \cap b^\prec = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \preccurlyeq s} \land \paren {s \prec b} }$ where: $a^\succcurlyeq$ denotes the upper closure of $a$ $b^\prec$ denotes the strict lower closure of $b$.

label: Definition:Interval of Convergence
snippet: Let $\xi \in \R$ be a real number. Let $\ds \map S x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {x - \xi}^n$ be a power series in $x$ about $\xi$. The set of values of $x$ for which $\map S x$ converges is called the interval of convergence of $S$.

label: Definition:Intuitionistic Propositional Logic
snippet: The intuitionist school of mathematics is one which adopts the following philosophical position: "Although we may know that it is not the case that a statement $p$ is (provably) false, we don't necessarily know that it is (provably) true either." Thus the intuitionist school rejects the Law of the Excluded Middle. The classical school, by affirming that if a statement is not true it must be false, and if it is not false it must be true, accepts as an axiom that "not not-true" must mean "true".

label: Definition:Invariant Mapping Under Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is invariant under $\RR$ : $x \mathrel \RR y \implies \map f x = \map f y$

label: Definition:Invariant Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\theta: X \to X$ be a $\Sigma / \Sigma$-measurable mapping. Then $\mu$ is said to be a $\theta$-invariant measure or to be invariant under $\theta$ : $\forall E \in \Sigma: \map \mu {\theta^{-1} \sqbrk E} = \map \mu E$ where $\theta^{-1} \sqbrk E$ denotes the preimage of $E$ under $\theta$. In terms of a pushforward measure, this can be concisely formulated as: $\theta_* \mu = \mu$

label: Definition:Invariant Metric on Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $d$ be a metric on $X$. We say that $d$ is invariant : $\map d {x, y} = \map d {x + z, y + z}$ for each $x, y, z \in X$.

label: Definition:Invariant Pseudometric on Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $d$ be a pseudometric on $X$. We say that $d$ is invariant : $\map d {x, y} = \map d {x + z, y + z}$ for each $x, y, z \in X$.

label: Definition:Invariant Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a self-map on $S$. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then $T$ is an invariant set of $f$ : $f \sqbrk Y = Y$

label: Definition:Invariant Subspace
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B H$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of $H$. Then $M$ is said to be an invariant subspace for $A$ $h \in M \implies A h \in M$. That is, $AM \subseteq M$.

label: Definition:Inverse
snippet: Logic: The inverse of a conditional $p \implies q$ is $\neg p \implies \neg q$ Abstract Algebra: Inverse Element Ring Product Inverse Definition:Inverse Semigroup Definition:Inverse in Inverse Semigroup Linear Algebra Definition:Inverse Linear Transformation Definition:Inverse Linear Operator Relation Theory: Inverse Relation Inverse Image (also known as Preimage) Mapping Theory: Inverse Mapping Inverse of a Mapping Matrix Algebra: Inverse Matrix

label: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)/Left Inverse
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$. An element $x_L \in S$ is called a left inverse of $x$ : $x_L \circ x = e_S$

label: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)/Right Inverse
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$. An element $x_R \in S$ is called a right inverse of $x$ : $x \circ x_R = e_S$

label: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$. The inverse cosecant of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \csc x := \set {y \in \R: \map \csc y = x}$ where $\map \csc y$ is the cosecant of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$. The inverse cosine of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \cos x := \set {y \in \R: \map \cos y = x}$ where $\map \cos y$ is the cosine of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Real/Arccosine
snippet: From Shape of Cosine Function, we have that $\cos x$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on the interval $\closedint 0 \pi$. From Cosine of Multiple of Pi, $\cos \pi = -1$ and $\cos 0 = 1$. Therefore, let $g: \closedint 0 \pi \to \closedint {-1} 1$ be the restriction of $\cos x$ to $\closedint 0 \pi$. Thus from Inverse of Strictly Monotone Function, $\map g x$ admits an inverse function, which will be continuous and strictly decreasing on $\closedint {-1} 1$. This function is called the arccosine of $x$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cotangent/Complex
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \left\{{0 + i, 0 - i}\right\}$

label: Definition:Inverse Cotangent/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$. The inverse cotangent of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \cot x := \set {y \in \R: \map \cot y = x}$ where $\map \cot y$ is the cotangent of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosecant/Real/Definition 2
Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine/Real
snippet: Let $S$ denote the subset of the real numbers: $S = \set {x \in \R: x \ge 1}$

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine/Real/Principal Branch
snippet: Let $S$ denote the subset of the real numbers: $S = \set {x \in \R: x \ge 1}$ The principal branch of the real inverse hyperbolic cosine function is defined as: $\forall x \in S: \map \arcosh x := \map \ln {x + \sqrt {x^2 - 1} }$ where: $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm of a (strictly positive) real number. $\sqrt {x^2 - 1}$ specifically denotes the positive square root of $x^2 - 1$ That is, where $\map \arcosh x \ge 0$.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent/Complex
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {-1 + 0 i, 1 + 0 i}$

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Function/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Inverse Hyperbolic Function == In general, the inverse hyperbolic functions are multifunctions. When used in their multifunction form, the notation of choice on for the inverse of a hyperbolic function $\operatorname h$ is $\operatorname h^{-1}$. When the area hyperbolic function is specifically required, the following prefixes are used: $\text {ar}$ for the real inverse hyperbolic functions $\text {Ar}$ for the complex inverse hyperbolic functions where $\text{ar}$ is an abbreviation for area.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Secant/Real/Principal Branch
snippet: Let $S$ denote the subset of the real numbers: $S := \hointl 0 1$ The principal branch of the real inverse hyperbolic secant function is defined as: $\forall x \in S: \map \arsech x := \map \ln {\dfrac {1 + \sqrt {1 - x^2} } x}$ where: $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm of a (strictly positive) real number. $\sqrt {1 - x^2}$ specifically denotes the positive square root of $x^2 - 1$ That is, where $\map \arsech x \ge 0$.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent/Complex
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {-1 + 0 i, 1 + 0 i}$

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets.

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$.

label: Definition:Inverse Linear Operator
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space. Let $A : X \to X$ be an invertible (in the sense of a mapping) linear transformation with inverse mapping $A^{-1} : X \to X$. We say that $A^{-1}$ is the inverse linear operator of $A$.

label: Definition:Inverse Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $V$ and $U$ be vector spaces. Let $A : V \to U$ be an invertible (in the sense of a mapping) linear transformation with inverse mapping $A^{-1} : U \to V$. We say that $A^{-1}$ is the inverse linear transformation of $A$.

label: Definition:Inverse Matrix
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Let there exist a square matrix $\mathbf B$ of order $n$ such that: $\mathbf A \mathbf B = \mathbf I_n = \mathbf B \mathbf A$ where $\mathbf I_n$ denotes the unit matrix of order $n$. Then $\mathbf B$ is called the inverse of $\mathbf A$ and is usually denoted $\mathbf A^{-1}$.

label: Definition:Inverse Matrix/Left
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. Let $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{n m}$ be a matrix of order $n \times m$ such that: $\mathbf B \mathbf A = \mathbf I_n$ where $\mathbf I_n$ denotes the unit matrix of order $n$. Then $\mathbf B$ is known as a left inverse (matrix) of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Inverse Matrix/Right
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. Let $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{n m}$ be a matrix of order $n \times m$ such that: $\mathbf A \mathbf B = \mathbf I_m$ where $\mathbf I_m$ denotes the unit matrix of order $m$. Then $\mathbf B$ is known as a right inverse (matrix) of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Inverse Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. A morphism $g: Y \to X$ is said to be an inverse (morphism) for $f$ : $g \circ f = \operatorname{id}_X$ $f \circ g = \operatorname{id}_Y$ where $\operatorname{id}_X$ denotes the identity morphism on $X$. It follows that $f$ is an isomorphism it has an inverse (morphism).

label: Definition:Inverse Secant/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$. The inverse secant of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \sec x := \set {y \in \R: \map \sec y = x}$ where $\map \sec y$ is the secant of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Sine/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$. The inverse sine of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \sin x := \set {y \in \R: \map \sin y = x}$ where $\map \sin y$ is the sine of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Sine/Real/Arcsine
snippet: From Shape of Sine Function, we have that $\sin x$ is continuous and strictly increasing on the interval $\closedint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$. From Sine of Half-Integer Multiple of Pi: $\map \sin {-\dfrac {\pi} 2} = -1$ and: $\sin \dfrac {\pi} 2 = 1$ Therefore, let $g: \closedint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2} \to \closedint {-1} 1$ be the restriction of $\sin x$ to $\closedint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$. Thus from Inverse of Strictly Monotone Function, $g \paren x$ admits an inverse function, which will be continuous and strictly increasing on $\closedint {-1} 1$.

label: Definition:Inverse Square Law
