snippet: Two real variables $x$ and $y$ are related by an inverse square law they fulfil the relationship: $\forall x, y \in \R: x \propto \dfrac 1 {y^2} \iff \exists k \in \R, k \ne 0: x y^2 = k$

label: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Complex
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {0 + i, 0 - i}$

label: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The inverse tangent of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \tan x := \set {y \in \R: \map \tan y = x}$ where $\map \tan y$ is the tangent of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Tangent/Real/Arctangent
snippet: From Shape of Tangent Function, we have that $\tan x$ is continuous and strictly increasing on the interval $\openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$. From the same source, we also have that: $\tan x \to + \infty$ as $x \to \dfrac \pi 2 ^-$ $\tan x \to - \infty$ as $x \to -\dfrac \pi 2 ^+$ Let $g: \openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2} \to \R$ be the restriction of $\tan x$ to $\openint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$. Thus from Inverse of Strictly Monotone Function, $\map g x$ admits an inverse function, which will be continuous and strictly increasing on $\R$.

label: Definition:Inverse of Elementary Column Operation
snippet: Let $e$ be an elementary column operation which transforms a matrix $\mathbf A$ to another matrix $\mathbf B$. Let $e'$ be an elementary column operation which transforms $\mathbf B$ back to $\mathbf A$. Then $e'$ is the inverse of the elementary column operation $e$.

label: Definition:Inverse of Elementary Row Operation
snippet: Let $e$ be an elementary row operation which transforms a matrix $\mathbf A$ to another matrix $\mathbf B$. Let $e'$ be an elementary row operation which transforms $\mathbf B$ back to $\mathbf A$. Then $e'$ is the inverse of the elementary row operation $e$.

label: Definition:Inverse of Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The inverse of $f$ is its inverse relation, defined as: $f^{-1} := \set {\tuple {t, s}: \map f s = t}$ That is: $f^{-1} := \set {\tuple {t, s}: \tuple {s, t} \in f}$ That is, $f^{-1} \subseteq T \times S$ is the relation which satisfies: $\forall s \in S: \forall t \in T: \tuple {t, s} \in f^{-1} \iff \tuple {s, t} \in f$

label: Definition:Inverse of Subset/Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $X \subseteq G$. Then the inverse of the subset $X$ is defined as: $X^{-1} = \set {x \in G: x^{-1} \in X}$ or equivalently: $X^{-1} = \set {x^{-1}: x \in X}$

label: Definition:Inversive Transformation
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle in the Euclidean plane $\EE$ whose center is $O$ and whose radius is $r$. For a point $P$ such that $P \ne O$, let be used to construct a ray $\LL$ starting from $O$ and passing through $P$. Let $f: \EE \to \EE$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall P \in \EE: \map f P = P'$ such that: $P'$ is also on $OP$ $OP \times OP' = r^2$ Then $f$ is known as the inversive transformation of $\EE$ $\CC$.

label: Definition:Inversive Transformation/Inverse Point
snippet: Let $\EE$ denote the Euclidean plane. Let $f: \EE \to \EE$ be the inversive transformation on $\EE$ with respect to the circle $\CC$ whose center is $O$ and whose radius is $r$. The image $P' := \map f P$ of a point $P$ under the inversive transformation $f$ is referred to as the inverse point of $P$ under $f$. From Inverse Transformation is Involution it also follows that also $P$ is the inverse point of $P'$ under $f$.

label: Definition:Involute

label: Definition:Irrational Line Segment
snippet: An irrational line segment is a line segment such that the square of whose length is an irrational number of units of area. '

label: Definition:Irrational Number
snippet: An irrational number is a real number which is not rational. That is, an irrational number is one that can not be expressed in the form $\dfrac p q$ such that $p$ and $q$ are both integers. The set of irrational numbers can therefore be expressed as $\R \setminus \Q$, where: $\R$ is the set of real numbers $\Q$ is the set of rational numbers $\setminus$ denotes set difference.

label: Definition:Irreducible Component
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A subset $Y \subseteq S$ is an irreducible component of $T$ : $Y$ is irreducible $Y$ is not a proper subset of an irreducible subset of $S$. label: Definition:Irreducible Polynomial
snippet: An irreducible polynomial is a polynomial which is not reducible.

label: Definition:Ishango Bone
snippet: The Ishango bone is a mathematical tool made from a leg bone of a baboon, dating from approximately $25 \ 000$ years ago. It bears a system of markings which may be tally marks, but may in fact be for a more complex purpose. It was found in $1960$ by in the (now the ). It was discovered in the area of near the . One row of marks contains the prime numbers between $10$ and $20$, that is, $11$, $13$, $17$ and $19$, which total $60$. Another row contains $9$, $11$, $19$ and $21$, which also total $60$.

label: Definition:Isogonal Polygon
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $P$ be such that it has the property that each vertex can be mapped to every other vertex by means of a symmetry mapping on $P$. Then $P$ is an isogonal polygon.

label: Definition:Isolated Point (Metric Space)
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space.

label: Definition:Isolated Point (Metric Space)/Subset
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset of $A$. $a \in S$ is an isolated point of $S$ there exists an open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $M$ containing no points of $S$ other than $a$: $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} a \cap S = \set a$ That is: $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \set {x \in S: \map d {x, a} < \epsilon} = \set a$

label: Definition:Isolated Point (Topology)

snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Isolated Singularity/Pole
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of a Riemann surface. Let $z_0 \in U$. Let $f: U \setminus \set {z_0} \to \C$ be a holomorphic function.

label: Definition:Isometry (Euclidean Geometry)
snippet: Let $\EE$ be a real Euclidean space. Let $\phi: \EE \to \EE$ be a bijection such that: $\forall P, Q \in \EE: PQ = P'Q'$ where: $P$ and $Q$ are arbitrary points in $\EE$ $P'$ and $Q'$ are the images of $P$ and $Q$ respectively $PQ$ and $P'Q'$ denote the lengths of the straight line segments $PQ$ and $P'Q'$ respectively. Then $\phi$ is an isometry. That is, an isometry is a bijection which preserves distance between points.

label: Definition:Isometry (Hilbert Spaces)
snippet: Let $H$ and $K$ be Hilbert spaces. Let their inner products be $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_H$ and $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_K$ respectively. A linear map $U: H \to K$ is called an isometry : $\forall g,h \in H: \innerprod g h_H = \innerprod {U g} {U h}_K$

label: Definition:Isometry (Riemannian Manifolds)
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ and $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be Riemannian manifolds with Riemannian metrics $g$ and $\tilde g$ respectively. Let the mapping $\phi : M \to \tilde M$ be a diffeomorphism such that: $\phi^* \tilde g = g$ Then $\phi$ is called an isometry from $\struct {M, g}$ to $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$.

label: Definition:Isomorphism
snippet: Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra): An isomorphism between two algebraic structures is a bijection which preserves operations. Group isomorphism: an isomorphism between two groups. Ring isomorphism: an isomorphism between two rings. $R$-algebraic structure isomorphism: an isomorphism between two $R$-algebraic structures. Relation Theory: Relation isomorphism: An isomorphism between two relational structures is a bijection which preserves relations. Order Theory: Order isomorphism: A bijection between two ordered sets which is order-preserving in both directions.

label: Definition:Isomorphism/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Isomorphism == The word isomorphism derives from the Greek morphe (μορφή) meaning form or structure, with the prefix iso- meaning equal. Thus isomorphism means equal structure.

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: An isomorphism is a homomorphism which is a bijection. That is, it is a mapping which is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism. An algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is isomorphic to another algebraic structure $\struct {T, *}$ there exists an isomorphism from $\struct {S, \circ}$ to $\struct {T, *}$, and we can write $S \cong T$ (although notation may vary).

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Field Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {K, \oplus, *}$ be fields. Let $\phi: F \to K$ be a (field) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a field isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a field isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism.

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Group Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be groups. Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a (group) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a group isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a group isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism. If $G$ is isomorphic to $H$, then the notation $G \cong H$ can be used (although notation varies).

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Monoid Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be monoids. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a (monoid) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a monoid isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a monoid isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism. If $S$ is isomorphic to $T$, then the notation $S \cong T$ can be used (although notation varies).

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Ordered Structure Isomorphism
snippet: An ordered structure isomorphism from an ordered structure $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ to another $\struct {T, *, \preccurlyeq}$ is a mapping $\phi: S \to T$ that is both: $(1): \quad$ An isomorphism, that is a bijective homomorphism, from the structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ to the structure $\struct {T, *}$ $(2): \quad$ An order isomorphism from the ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ to the ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$.

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphism/Vector Space Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {W, +', \circ'}$ be $K$-vector spaces. Then $\phi: V \to W$ is a vector space isomorphism : $(1): \quad \phi$ is a bijection $(2): \quad \forall \mathbf x, \mathbf y \in V: \map \phi {\mathbf x + \mathbf y} = \map \phi {\mathbf x} +' \map \phi {\mathbf y}$ $(3): \quad \forall \mathbf x \in V: \forall \lambda \in K: \map \phi {\lambda \mathbf x} = \lambda \map \phi {\mathbf x}$ Category:Definitions/Isomorphisms (Abstract Algebra) Category:Definitions/R-Algebraic Structure Isomorphisms Category:Definitions/Linear Algebra

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Ring Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, \oplus, *}$ be rings. Let $\phi: R \to S$ be a (ring) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a ring isomorphism $\phi$ is a bijection. That is, $\phi$ is a ring isomorphism $\phi$ is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism.

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category, and let $X, Y$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. A morphism $f: X \to Y$ is an isomorphism there exists a morphism $g: Y \to X$ such that: $g \circ f = \operatorname{id}_X$ $f \circ g = \operatorname{id}_Y$ where $\operatorname{id}_X$ denotes the identity morphism on $X$. It can be seen that this is equivalent to $g$ being both a retraction and a section of $f$.

label: Definition:Isomorphism (Hilbert Spaces)
snippet: Let $H, K$ be Hilbert spaces. Denote by $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_H$ and $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_K$ their respective inner products. An isomorphism between $H$ and $K$ is a map $U: H \to K$, such that: $(1): \quad U$ is a linear map $(2): \quad U$ is surjective $(3): \quad \forall g, h \in H: \innerprod g h_H = \innerprod {U g} {U h}_K$ These three requirements may be summarized by stating that $U$ be a surjective isometry. Furthermore, Surjection that Preserves Inner Product is Linear shows that requirement $(1)$ is superfluous.

label: Definition:Isotoxal Polygon
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $P$ be such that it has the property that each side can be mapped to every other side by means of a symmetry mapping on $P$. Then $P$ is an isotoxal polygon.

label: Definition:Iteration
snippet: Iteration is defined as successive repetitions of a mathematical process, using the output of one stage as the input of the next.

label: Definition:Iverson's Convention
snippet: Iverson's convention is a notation which allows a compact means of assigning a value of $1$ or $0$ to a proposition $P$, depending on whether $P$ is true or false: $\sqbrk P = \begin {cases} 1 & : \text {$P$ is true} \\ 0 & : \text {$P$ is false} \end {cases}$ It is sometimes seen specified as: $\sqbrk P = \begin {cases} 1 & : \text {$P$ is true} \\ 0 & : \text {$P$ otherwise} \end {cases}$ which can be useful in fields of mathematics where the Law of Excluded Middle does not apply. In each case, $0$ is the very strong zero.

label: Definition:Jack-Knife Resampling
snippet: Jack-knife resampling is a statistical technique mainly used for estimation of bias in a sample estimator of a population parameter. It involves computation of the sample estimator with the omission of one observation at a time over the entire set of observations.

label: Definition:Jacobson Radical
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\map {\operatorname{maxspec}} R$ be the set of maximal ideals of $R$. Then the Jacobson radical of $R$ is: $\ds \map {\operatorname {Jac} } R = \bigcap_{m \mathop \in \map {\operatorname{maxspec}} R} m$ That is, it is the intersection of all maximal ideals of $R$.

Order Theory: Join (Order Theory): the supremum of the set formed by two elements of an ordered set. Graph Theory: Join (Graph Theory): an edge joins two vertices of a graph. Set Theory: A term (rarely used nowadays) for set union.

label: Definition:Join of Finite Sub-Sigma-Algebras
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\AA, \BB \subseteq \Sigma$ be finite sub-$\sigma$-algebras. The join of $\AA$ and $\BB$ is the finite sub-$\sigma$-algebra defined as: $\AA \vee \BB := \map \sigma {\AA \cup \BB}$ where $\map \sigma \cdot$ denotes the generated $\sigma$-algebra.

label: Definition:Joint Distribution
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_d$ be random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$. Define a random vector $X : \Omega \to S^d$ by: $\map X \omega = \tuple {\map {X_1} \omega, \map {X_2} \omega, \ldots, \map {X_d} \omega}$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$. Then the joint distribution of $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_d$ is defined as the probability distribution of $X$.

label: Definition:Jonckheere-Terpstra Test
snippet: The Jonckheere-Terpstra test is a non-parametric test where: the null hypothesis $H_0$ is that three or more independent samples all come from the same population the alternative hypothesis $H_1$ is that their means $\mu_i$ taken in order show a monotonic trend. That is: $H_0$: that $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k$ against: $H_1$: that either: $\mu_1 \le \mu_2 \le \cdots \le \mu_k$ or: $\mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge \cdots \ge \mu_k$ in which at least one of the inequalities is strict.

label: Definition:Jones Polynomial
snippet: A Jones Polynomial is a polynomial associated with a knot.

label: Definition:Jordan Curve
snippet: Let $f : \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a path in the Euclidean plane such that: $\map f {t_1} \ne \map f {t_2}$ for all $t_1 ,t_2 \in \hointr 0 1$ with $t_1 \ne t_2$ $\map f 0 = \map f 1$ Then $f$ is called a Jordan curve.

label: Definition:Jordan Curve/Exterior
snippet: Let $f: \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a Jordan curve. It follows from the Jordan Curve Theorem that $\R^2 \setminus \Img f$ is a union of two disjoint connected components, one of which is unbounded. This unbounded component is called the exterior of $f$, and is denoted as $\Ext f$.

label: Definition:Jordan Curve/Interior
snippet: Let $f: \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a Jordan curve. It follows from the Jordan Curve Theorem that $\R^2 \setminus \Img f$ is a union of two disjoint connected components, one of which is bounded. This bounded component is called the interior of $f$, and is denoted as $\Int f$.

label: Definition:Josephus Problem
snippet: Consider a collection of $n$ people in a circle. Let them each be eliminated sequentially by counting out every $m$th person (closing the gap after each elimination). For a given a number of people $n$, and a given step size $m$, the problem is to determine the initial position in the circle of the person who remains after all the others have been eliminated.

snippet: K-theory is a method designed to enable a loose classification of vector bundles in algebraic geometry.

label: Definition:Kaprekar's Process
snippet: Kaprekar's process is the repeated application of the Kaprekar mapping to a given positive integer.

label: Definition:Kaprekar Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Suppose that $n^2$, when expressed in number base $b$, can be split into two parts that add up to $n$. Then $n$ is a Kaprekar number for base $b$.

label: Definition:Kaprekar Triple
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Suppose that $n^3$, when expressed in number base $b$, can be split into three parts that add up to $n$. Then $n$ is a Kaprekar triple for base $b$.

label: Definition:Keith Number
snippet: Let $K \in \Z_{>9}$ be an $n$-digit integer, where $n > 1$. Let $A = \left({a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}\right)$ be the digits of $K$ in order. Let $F_A$ be the Fibonacci-like sequence on $A$. Then $K$ is a Keith number $K$ occurs somewhere in $F_A$.

label: Definition:Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance
snippet: Kendall's coefficient of concordance is a test for consistency of more than $2$ sets of rankings. Let $m$ judges independently award ranks $1$ to $n$ to a set of $n$ competitors. Let $s_i$ be the sum of the rankings awarded to competitor $i$. The mean $M$ of the values of $s_i$ is $\dfrac 1 2 m \paren {n + 1}$. The sum of the squares of the deviations from $M$ is given by: $S = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {s_i - M}^2$ and Kendall's coefficient of concordance is given by: $W = \dfrac {12 S} {m^2 n \paren {n^2 - 1} }$

label: Definition:Kendall's Rank Correlation Coefficient
snippet: Kendall's rank correlation coefficient is a test for consistency of $2$ sets of rankings $\sequence a_n$ and $\sequence b_n$ on a set $S$ of $n$ objects. The set $R$ of ordered pairs $\tuple {a_i, b_i}$ is assembled: $R = \set {\tuple {a_i, b_i}: i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n} }$ and ordered according to $\sequence a$. The number $Q$ of elements of $S$ out of ranking order from $\sequence b$ is counted. Kendall's rank correlation coefficient is then formed: $K = 1 - \dfrac {4 Q} {n \paren {n + 1} }$ which takes values between $-1$ (complete disagreement) and $+1$ (complete agreement).

label: Definition:Kepler-Poinsot Polyhedron
snippet: A Kepler-Poinsot polyhedron is any of the four regular star polyhedra.

label: Definition:Ker Function
snippet: Let $K_n$ denote the modified Bessel function of the second kind. The Ker function is defined as: $\map {\Ker_n} x = \map \Re {\map {K_n} {x \map \exp {\dfrac {\pi i} 4} } }$ where: $\exp$ denotes the exponential function $x$ is real $\map \Re z$ denotes the real part of $z$.

label: Definition:Kernel (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $f : A \to B $ be a morphism in $\mathbf C$.

label: Definition:Kernel of Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $* : G\times X\to X$ be a group action.

label: Definition:Kernel of Group Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ and $\struct {H, *}$ be groups. Let $\phi: \struct {G, \circ} \to \struct {H, *}$ be a group homomorphism. The kernel of $\phi$ is the subset of the domain of $\phi$ defined as: $\map \ker \phi := \phi^{-1} \sqbrk {e_H} = \set {x \in G: \map \phi x = e_H}$ where $e_H$ is the identity of $H$. That is, $\map \ker \phi$ is the subset of $G$ that maps to the identity of $H$.

label: Definition:Kernel of Linear Transformation/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbf V, +, \times}$ be a vector space. Let $\struct {\mathbf V', +, \times}$ be a vector space whose zero vector is $\mathbf 0'$. Let $T: \mathbf V \to \mathbf V'$ be a linear transformation. Then the kernel of $T$ is defined as: $\map \ker T := T^{-1} \sqbrk {\set {\mathbf 0'} } = \set {\mathbf x \in \mathbf V: \map T {\mathbf x} = \mathbf 0'}$

label: Definition:Kernel of Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R_1, +_1, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {R_2, +_2, \circ_2}$ be rings. Let $\phi: \struct {R_1, +_1, \circ_1} \to \struct {R_2, +_2, \circ_2}$ be a ring homomorphism. The kernel of $\phi$ is the subset of the domain of $\phi$ defined as: $\map \ker \phi = \set {x \in R_1: \map \phi x = 0_{R_2} }$ where $0_{R_2}$ is the zero of $R_2$. That is, $\map \ker \phi$ is the subset of $R_1$ that maps to the zero of $R_2$. From Ring Homomorphism Preserves Zero it follows that $0_{R_1} \in \map \ker \phi$ where $0_{R_1}$ is the zero of $R_1$.

label: Definition:Kinematics
snippet: Kinematics is the branch of the mechanics describing the motion of bodies without considering the forces that may affect this motion. Hence it is concerned with such things as the displacements, velocities and accelerations of bodies.

label: Definition:Kinetic Energy
snippet: Let $B$ be a body. The kinetic energy of $B$ is defined as the energy appertaining to $B$ due to its motion. It is a scalar quantity.

label: Definition:Kleene Closure
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The Kleene closure of $S$, denoted $S^*$, is the set of all ordered tuples in $S$. The Kleene closure is endowed with the concatenation operation $*$: $\tuple{ S^*, *}$ to form an algebraic structure.

label: Definition:Klein Four-Group
snippet: == Group Example == The Klein $4$-group, often denoted $K_4$, is a group of $4$ elements, each of which is self-inverse.

label: Definition:Knot (Knot Theory)
snippet: Let $Y$ be a manifold and $X \subset Y$ a submanifold of $Y$. Let $i: X \to Y$ be an inclusion, that is a mapping such that $i \sqbrk X = X$. Then a knotted embedding is an embedding $\phi: X \to Y$ (or the image of such an embedding) such that $\phi \sqbrk X$ is not freely homotopic to $i \sqbrk X$.

label: Definition:Knot Theory
snippet: Knot theory is the branch of geometry which studies the embedding of knots in $3$-dimensional space.

label: Definition:Koszul Connection
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $E$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\pi : E \to M$ be a smooth vector bundle. Let $\map \Gamma E$ be the space of smooth sections of $E$. Let $\map {\mathfrak{X}} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields on $M$. Let $\map {C^\infty} M$ be the space of smooth real functions on $M$. Let $\nabla : \map {\mathfrak{X}} M \times \map \Gamma E \to \map \Gamma E$ be the map be written $\tuple {X, Y} \mapsto \nabla_X Y$ where $X \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} M$, $Y \in \map \Gamma E$, and $\times$ denotes the cartesian product.

label: Definition:Kronecker Delta
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a set. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Then $\delta_{\alpha \beta}: \Gamma \times \Gamma \to R$ is the mapping on the cartesian square of $\Gamma$ defined as: $\quad \forall \tuple {\alpha, \beta} \in \Gamma \times \Gamma: \delta_{\alpha \beta} := \begin{cases} 1_R & : \alpha = \beta \\ 0_R & : \alpha \ne \beta \end{cases}$ This use of $\delta$ is known as the Kronecker delta notation or Kronecker delta convention.

label: Definition:Kronecker Delta/Number
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a set. Then $\delta_{\alpha \beta}: \Gamma \times \Gamma \to \set {0, 1}$ is the mapping on the cartesian square of $\Gamma$ defined as: $\quad \forall \tuple {\alpha, \beta} \in \Gamma \times \Gamma: \delta_{\alpha \beta} := \begin {cases} 1 & : \alpha = \beta \\ 0 & : \alpha \ne \beta \end {cases}$ This use of $\delta$ is known as the Kronecker delta notation or Kronecker delta convention.

label: Definition:Kronecker Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ and $\mathbf B = \sqbrk b_{p q}$ be matrices. The Kronecker product of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is denoted $\mathbf A \otimes \mathbf B$ and is defined as the block matrix: $\mathbf A \otimes \mathbf B = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} \mathbf B & a_{12} \mathbf B & \cdots & a_{1n} \mathbf B \\ a_{21} \mathbf B & a_{22} \mathbf B & \cdots & a_{2n} \mathbf B \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_{m1} \mathbf B & a_{m2} \mathbf B & \cdots & a_{mn} \mathbf B \end{bmatrix}$ Writing this out in full: $\mathbf A \otimes \mathbf B = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} b_{11} &…

label: Definition:Krull Dimension of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity. The Krull dimension of $R$ is the supremum of lengths of chains of prime ideals, ordered by the subset relation: {{eqn | l = \map {\operatorname {dim_{Krull} } } R | r = \sup \set {\map {\mathrm {ht} } {\mathfrak p} : \mathfrak p \in \Spec R} }} {{eqn | r = \sup \set {n \in \N: \exists p_0, \ldots, p_n \in \Spec R: \mathfrak p_0 \subsetneqq \mathfrak p_1 \subsetneqq \cdots \subsetneqq \mathfrak p_n} }} where: $\map {\mathrm {ht} } {\mathfrak p}$ is the height of $\mathfrak p$ $\Spec R$ is the prime spectrum of $R$ In particular,…

label: Definition:Krull Dimension of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Its Krull dimension $\map {\dim_{\mathrm {Krull} } } T$ is the supremum of lengths of chains of closed irreducible sets of $T$, ordered by the subset relation. Thus, the Krull dimension is $\infty$ if there exist arbitrarily long chains.

label: Definition:Kummer Theory
snippet: Kummer Theory is a branch of abstract algebra and number theory which investigates certain types of field extensions.

label: Definition:Kurtosis
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is a measure of the concentration of $X$ about its expectation.

label: Definition:L-2 Inner Product
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\map {\LL^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the Lebesgue $2$-space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. Let $\map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the $L^2$ space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. We define the $L^2$ inner product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu} \times \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu} \to \R$ by: $\ds \innerprod {\eqclass f \sim} {\eqclass g \sim} = \int \paren {f \cdot g} \rd \mu$ where: $\eqclass f \sim, \eqclass g \sim \in \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ where $\eqclass f \sim$ and $\eqclass g \sim$ are the equivalence class of…

label: Definition:L1 Metric/Closed Real Interval
snippet: Let $S$ be the set of all real functions which are continuous on the closed interval $\closedint a b$. Let the real-valued function $d: S \times S \to \R$ be defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in S: \map {d_1} {f, g} := \int_a^b \size {\map f t - \map g t} \rd t$ Then $d_1$ is the $L^1$ metric on $\closedint a b$.

label: Definition:Labeled Graph
snippet: A labeled graph is a graph whose vertices are each assigned an element from a set of symbols (letters, usually, but this is unimportant). The important thing to note is that the vertices can be distinguished one from another. Note that it is not necessary for all the vertices to be assigned different labels.

label: Definition:Labeled Tree
snippet: A labeled tree is a finite tree (which may or may not be rooted) in which each node has attached to it a label. These labels may be any symbol or other object that one can think of, but usually consist of one letter or symbol. The parent function is usually depicted by placing the ancestor above the child and connecting them with a line. The various children of a node may also be considered to be in a particular order. This is usually depicted by placing them in a left-to-right order.

label: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic
snippet: A labeled tree for propositional logic is a system containing: A rooted tree $T$; A countable set $\mathbf H$ of WFFs of propositional logic; A WFF $\map \Phi t$ attached to each non-root node $t$ of $T$. Such a structure can be denoted $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$.

label: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic/Hypothesis Set
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$ be a labeled tree for propositional logic. The countable set $\mathbf H$ of WFFs of propositional logic is called the hypothesis set. The elements of $\mathbf H$ are known as hypothesis WFFs. The hypothesis set $\mathbf H$ is considered to be attached to the root node of $T$.

label: Definition:Lagrangian Derivative
snippet: Consider a fluid flow $\FF$. The Lagrangian derivative of $\FF$ is the partial derivative $\dfrac \partial {\partial t}$ which measures the rate of change at a fixed point of $\FF$ as different material flows through that point. The rate of change of the quantity $q$ is given by: $\dfrac {\rD q} {\rD t} = \dfrac {\partial q} {\partial t} + \mathbf u \cdot \nabla q$ where $\mathbf u$ is the velocity of $q$.

label: Definition:Lambert W Function
snippet: Let $e^z: \C \to \C$ be the complex exponential function. Then $\map W z$ is defined to be the multifunction that satisfies: $\map W z e^{\map W z} = z$

label: Definition:Lambert W Function/Principal Branch/Real Valued
snippet: The principal branch of the Lambert W function is the real function $W_0: \hointr {-\dfrac 1 e} \to \to \hointr {-1} \to$ such that: $x = \map {W_0} x e^{\map {W_0} x}$

label: Definition:Language of Arithmetic
snippet: A language of arithmetic is a signature for predicate logic consisting of: the binary operation symbols: $+$ and $\times$ the unary function symbol: $s$ the binary relation symbol: $<$ the constant symbol: $0$

label: Definition:Language of Predicate Logic
snippet: There are a lot of different formal systems expressing predicate logic. Although they vary wildly in complexity and even disagree (to some extent) on what expressions are valid, generally all of these use a compatible formal language. This page defines the formal language of choice on . We will use $\LL_1$ to represent the formal language of predicate logic in what follows. In order to define $\LL_1$, it is necessary to specify: An alphabet $\AA$ A collation system with the unique readability property for $\AA$ A formal grammar (which determines the WFFs of $\LL_1$)

label: Definition:Language of Predicate Logic/Alphabet
snippet: The alphabet $\AA$ of the language of predicate logic $\LL_1$ is defined as follows:

label: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic
snippet: There are a lot of different formal systems expressing propositional logic. Although they vary wildly in complexity and even disagree (to some extent) on what expressions are valid, generally all of these use a compatible formal language. This page defines the formal language of choice on . We will use $\LL_0$ to represent the formal language of propositional logic in what follows. In order to define $\LL_0$, it is necessary to specify: An alphabet $\AA$ A collation system with the unique readability property for $\AA$ A formal grammar (which determines the WFFs of $\LL_0$)

label: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic/Alphabet/Letter
snippet: Part of specifying the language of propositional logic $\LL_0$ is to specify its letters. The letters of $\LL_0$, called propositional symbols, is an arbitrary collection $\PP_0$ of symbols which has no limit on its extent. It is usual to specify them as a limited subset of the English alphabet with appropriate subscripts. A typical set of propositional symbols would be, for example: $\PP_0 = \set {p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_n, \ldots}$

label: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic/Formal Grammar/WFF
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be approved of by the formal grammar of propositional logic. Then $\mathbf A$ is called a well-formed formula of propositional logic. Often, one abbreviates well-formed formula, speaking of a WFF of propositional logic instead. More informally, a WFF of propositional logic is any sequence of symbols containing statement variables, such that when statements are substituted for the statement variables (the same statement for any given statement variable throughout), the result is a statement.

label: Definition:Laplace's Equation
snippet: == Equation == Laplace's equation is a second order PDE of the form: $\dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial z^2} = 0$ or: $\nabla^2 \psi = 0$ where $\nabla^2$ denotes the Laplacian operator.

label: Definition:Laplacian/Also known as
snippet: == Laplacian: Also known as == The Laplacian is also known as the Laplace operator, Laplace's operator or Laplace-Beltrami operator. The last name is usually used in the context of submanifolds in Euclidean space and on (pseudo-)Riemannian manifolds. Category:Definitions/Laplacian

label: Definition:Laplacian/Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $f \in \map {C^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth mapping on $M$. Let $\grad$ be the gradient operator. Let $\operatorname {div}$ be the divergence operator. The Laplace-Beltrami operator of $f$ is defined as: $\nabla^2 f := \map {\operatorname {div} } {\grad f}$

label: Definition:Laplacian/Scalar Field
snippet: Let $\R^n$ denote the real Cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $\map U {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a scalar field over $\R^n$. Let the partial derivatives of $U$ exist throughout $\R^n$. The Laplacian of $U$ is defined as: $\ds \nabla^2 U := \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial {x_k}^2}$

label: Definition:Latitude/Celestial
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The celestial latitude of $P$ is the angle subtended by the the arc of the vertical circle through $P$ between $P$ and the ecliptic. If $P$ is closer to the north ecliptic pole, the celestial latitude is defined as latitude $\beta \degrees$ north, where $\beta \degrees$ denotes $\beta$ degrees (of angle), written $\beta \degrees \, \mathrm N$. If $P$ is closer to the south ecliptic pole, the celestial latitude is defined as latitude $\beta \degrees$ south, written $\beta \degrees \, \mathrm S$.

label: Definition:Latitude/Galactic
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The galactic latitude of $P$ is the angular distance measured north or south of the galactic equator. It ranges from: $0 \degrees$ to $90 \degrees$ north $0 \degrees$ to $90 \degrees$ south where $0 \degrees$ is the galactic latitude of the galactic equator itself. This is denoted $l$.

label: Definition:Latitude/Terrestrial
snippet: Let $J$ be a point on Earth's surface that is not one of the two poles $N$ and $S$. Let $\bigcirc NJS$ be a meridian passing through $J$, whose endpoints are by definition $N$ and $S$. Let $\bigcirc NJS$ pass through the equator at $L$. The (terrestrial) latitude of $J$ is the (spherical) angle $\sphericalangle LOJ$ , where $O$ is the center of Earth. 500px If $J$ is in the northern hemisphere of Earth, the latitude is defined as latitude $n \degrees$ north, where $n \degrees$ denotes $n$ degrees (of angle), written $n \degrees \, \mathrm N$.

label: Definition:Lattice
snippet: Lattice (Order Theory), also known as an order lattice Point Lattice

label: Definition:Lattice (Ordered Set)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a lattice : for all $x, y \in S$, the subset $\set {x, y}$ admits both a supremum and an infimum.

label: Definition:Lattice Filter
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preccurlyeq}$ be a lattice. Let $F \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Lattice Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $I \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Lattice Point
snippet: Let $\R^m$ be the $m$-dimensional real Euclidean space. Let $\BB = \set {\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2, \ldots, \mathbf v_n}$ be a linearly independent set of vectors of $\R^m$. Let $\LL$ be the point lattice in $\R^m$ whose basis is $\BB$. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ be an ordered $n$-tuple of integers. Let: {{eqn | l = P | r = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n a_i \mathbf v_i | c = }} Then $P$ is a lattice point of $\LL$.

label: Definition:Lattice Point/Cartesian Coordinate System
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a cartesian coordinate system of $n$ dimensions. Let $P = \tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ be a point in $\CC$. Then $P$ is a lattice point of $\CC$ $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are all integers.

label: Definition:Lattice Point/Rational
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a cartesian coordinate system of $n$ dimensions. Let $P = \tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ be a point in $\CC$. $P$ is a rational lattice point of $\CC$ $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are all rational numbers.

label: Definition:Lattice Theory
snippet: Lattice theory is the branch of abstract algebra concerned with the structure and properties of lattices in the specific context of order theory.

label: Definition:Lattice of Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau_{_S} }$ be a topological space. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let $\R^S$ be the set of mappings from $S$ to $\R$. The lattice of real-valued mappings from $S$, denoted $\struct{\R^S, \vee, \wedge, \le}$, is the set of all mappings $\R^S$ with (pointwise) lattice operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$ defined by: $\forall f, g \in \R^S : f \vee g : S \to \R$ is defined by: $\forall s \in S : \map {\paren{f \vee g}} s = \max \set{\map f s, \map g s}$ $\forall f, g \in \R^S : f \wedge g : S \to \R$ is defined by: $\forall s \in S : \map {\paren{f \wedge g}} s = \min…

label: Definition:Latus Rectum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Latus Rectum == The term latus rectum is a compound of the Latin: latus, meaning side rectum, meaning straight or right, as in straight line or right angle. Hence it literally means right side or straight side. Its plural is latera recta.

label: Definition:Laurent Series
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in \C$ such that: $f$ is analytic in $U := \set {z \in \C: r_1 \le \cmod {z - z_0} \le r_2}$ where $r_1, r_2 \in \overline \R$ are points in the extended real numbers. A Laurent series is a summation: $\forall z \in \C: r_1 < \cmod {z - z_0} < r_2: \map f z = \ds \sum_{n \mathop \in \Z} a_n \paren {z - z_0}^n$ where: $a_n = \dfrac 1 {2 \pi i} \ds \int_C \map f z \paren {z - z_0}^{n + 1} \rd z$ $C$ is a circle with center $z_0$ and radius $r$ for $r_1 < r < r_2$ $\ds \int_C \map f z \paren {z - z_0}^{n + 1} \rd z$ is the contour integral over…

label: Definition:Leading Coefficient of Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix. The leading coefficient of each row of $\mathbf A$ is the leftmost non-zero element of that row. A zero row has no leading coefficient.

label: Definition:Leading Term
snippet: Let $P = a \circ b$ be an expression. The term $a$ is known as the leading term of $P$.

label: Definition:Leap Year
snippet: The number of days in a year is not an integer, but lies somewhere between $365$ and $366$. However, it is convenient to assign an integer number of days to any given year. It is also desirable to ensure that a particular day of the year occurs at approximately the same time each year. In the Julian and Gregorian calendars: some years are assigned $365$ days and: some years are assigned $366$ days. The years which have $366$ days are called leap years.

label: Definition:Least Significant Digit
snippet: Let $b \in \Z: b \ge 2$ be a number base Let $n$ be a number which is reported to $r$ significant figures, to base $b$, that is: $n = d_1 \times b^k + d_2 \times b^{k - 1} + \dotsb + d_{r - 1} \times b^{k - r + 2} + d_r \times b^{k - r + 1}$ where: $d_1, d_2, \dotsc, d_r$ are the significant figures of $n$ $b^k$ is the largest power of $b$ less than or equal to $n$. Then the digit $d_r$ is known as the least significant digit of $n$. Note that the usual situation is when $b = 10$, but in the field of computer science, binary is usual.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Integral
snippet: Let $\lambda^n$ be a Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$. Let $f: \R^n \to \overline \R$ be a Lebesgue integrable function, where $\overline \R$ denote the set of extended real numbers. Then the $\lambda^n$-integral of $f$: $\ds \int f \rd \lambda^n$ is called the Lebesgue integral of $f$. The definition proceeds in several steps.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Measure
snippet: Let $\JJ_{ho}^n$ be the set of half-open $n$-rectangles. Let $\map \BB {\R^n}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R^n$. Let $\lambda^n$ be the $n$-dimensional Lebesgue pre-measure on $\JJ_{ho}^n$. A measure $\mu$ extending $\lambda^n$ to $\map \BB {\R^n}$ is called $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. That is, $\mu$ is an $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure it satisfies: $\mu \restriction_{\JJ_{ho}^n} = \lambda^n$ where $\restriction$ denotes restriction. Usually, this measure is also denoted by $\lambda^n$, even though this may be considered abuse of notation.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Number
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\UU$ be an open cover of $M$. A fixed strictly positive real number $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ is called a Lebesgue number for $\UU$ : $\forall x \in A: \exists \map U x \in \UU: \map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq \map U x$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} x$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $M$.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space, and let $p \in \R$, $p \ge 1$. The (real) Lebesgue $p$-space of $\mu$ is defined as: $\map {\LL^p} \mu := \set {f: X \to \R: f \in \map \MM \Sigma, \ds \int \size f^p \rd \mu < \infty}$ where $\map \MM \Sigma$ denotes the space of $\Sigma$-measurable functions.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Space/L-Infinity
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. The Lebesgue $\infty$-space for $\mu$, denoted $\map {\LL^\infty} \mu$, is defined as: $\map {\LL^\infty} \mu := \set {f \in \map \MM \Sigma: f \text{ is essentially bounded} }$ and so consists of all $\Sigma$-measurable $f: X \to \R$ that are essentially bounded.

label: Definition:Lebombo Bone
snippet: The Lebombo bone is a baboon's leg bone bearing $29$ notches which were carved into it between $33 \ 000$ B.C.E. and $42 \ 000$ B.C.E. It is the earliest known instance of a system of tally marks. It was found in in in the , near the border with . Various untestable hypotheses have been raised concerning this artefact, notably that it was created by an early African woman to count the days between her menses. However, as the bone appears to be broken at one end, it is possible that the count of $29$ is not the complete set of notches that were originally carved.

label: Definition:Left-Hand Derivative
snippet: Let $B$ be a Banach space over the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $f: \R \to B$ be a mapping from $\R$ to $B$. The left-hand derivative of $f$ is defined as the left-hand limit: $\ds \map {f'_-} x = \lim_{h \mathop \to 0^-} \frac {\map f {x + h} - \map f x} h$ If the left-hand derivative exists, then $f$ is said to be left-hand differentiable at $x$.

label: Definition:Left-Total Relation/Multifunction
snippet: A multifunction is a left-total relation $\RR$ which is specifically not many-to-one or one-to-one. That is, for each element $s$ of the domain of $\RR$, there exists more than one $t$ in the codomain of $\RR$ such that $\tuple {s, t} \in \RR$. Hence a multifunction is not strictly speaking a mapping. However, if $\RR$ is regarded as a mapping from $S$ to the power set of $T$, then left-totality of $\RR$ is the same as totality of this lifted function. See the definition of a direct image mapping.

label: Definition:Left-Truncatable Prime
snippet: A left-truncatable prime is a prime number which remains prime when any number of digits are removed from the left hand end. Zeroes are excluded, in order to eliminate, for example, prime numbers of the form $10^n + 3$ for arbitrarily large $n$.

label: Definition:Left Adjoint Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ be locally small categories. Let $F : \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ and $G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be functors. $F$ is a left adjoint functor of $G$ there exists an adjunction $\struct {F, G, \alpha}$.

label: Definition:Left Cancellable Mapping
snippet: A mapping $f: Y \to Z$ is left cancellable (or left-cancellable) : $\forall X: \forall \struct {g_1, g_2: X \to Y}: f \circ g_1 = f \circ g_2 \implies g_1 = g_2$ That is, for any set $X$, if $g_1$ and $g_2$ are mappings from $X$ to $Y$: If $f \circ g_1 = f \circ g_2$ then $g_1 = g_2$.

label: Definition:Left Exact Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ be a functor. Then $F$ is left exact $F$ preserves finite limits.

label: Definition:Left Inverse
snippet: Mapping Theory: Left Inverse Mapping Abstract Algebra: Left Inverse Element Matrix Theory: Left Inverse Matrix

label: Definition:Left Inverse Mapping
snippet: Let $S, T$ be sets where $S \ne \O$, that is, $S$ is not empty. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $g: T \to S$ be a mapping such that: $g \circ f = I_S$ where: $g \circ f$ denotes the composite mapping $f$ followed by $g$; $I_S$ is the identity mapping on $S$. Then $g: T \to S$ is called a left inverse (mapping).

label: Definition:Left Module over Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A left module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast: R \times G \to G$, the (left) ring action, which satisfies the left module axioms:

label: Definition:Left Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. For any $x, y \in S$, the left operation on $S$ is the binary operation defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: x \gets y = x$

label: Definition:Left Order Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\tau$ be the topology on $S$ generated by the basis sets of the form: $S_a = \set {x: x \prec a}$ for $a \in S$. Then the topological space $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq, \tau}$ is known as the left order topology on $S$.

label: Definition:Legendre's Differential Equation
snippet: Legendre's differential equation is a second order ODE of the form: $\paren {1 - x^2} \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} - 2 x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + p \paren {p + 1} y = 0$ The parameter $p$ may be any arbitrary real or complex number. Solutions to Legendre's differential equation for $p \in \N$ are called Legendre polynomials of order $p$.

label: Definition:Legendre Polynomial
snippet: Consider the Legendre's differential equation: $(1): \quad \paren {1 - x^2} \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} - 2 x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + n \paren {n + 1} y = 0$ for $n \in \N$. The solutions to $(1)$ are called the Legendre polynomials of order $n$ and denoted $\map {P_n} x$. These solutions form a polynomial sequence of orthogonal polynomials on the interval $\closedint {-1} 1$.

label: Definition:Lemma
snippet: A lemma is a statement which is proven during the course of reaching the proof of a theorem. Logically there is no qualitative difference between a lemma and a theorem. They are both statements whose value is either true or false. However, a lemma is seen more as a stepping-stone than a theorem in itself (and frequently takes a lot more work to prove than the theorem to which it leads).

label: Definition:Length
snippet: Geometry: Length (Linear Measure): a formal comparison between the spatial extent of a geometric figure in a specified direction against a reference quantity (often tacitly understood). Length of a line: a formal measure of the spatial extent of a line segment. Analysis: Length of a (real) interval: the difference between the endpoints of a real interval. Length of a curve: the limit of the length of a polygonal line inscribed within the curve as the maximum length of the chords which form that polygonal line tends to zero.

label: Definition:Less Than
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \le}$ be one of the sets of numbers: $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ under the usual ordering. Let $a, b \in S$ such that $a < b$. Then $a$ is described as being less than $b$.

label: Definition:Lever
snippet: A lever is a simple machine consisting of: a rigid bar $M$ pivoted at a point $F$, called the fulcrum so that: an effort applied at one point $E$ of $M$ is transferred to: a load at another point $L$ of $M$ so as to generate a mechanical advantage.

label: Definition:Lever/Fulcrum
snippet: The fulcrum of a lever is the pivot about which the lever turns. It is the point about which the moments of the applied effort and load are calculated.

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/Rational Numbers

label: Definition:Lindelöf Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Lindelöf space every open cover of $S$ has a countable subcover.

label: Definition:Line
snippet: ' This can be interpreted to mean that a line is a construct that has no thickness. This mathematical abstraction can not of course be actualised in reality because however thin you make your line, it will have some finite width. It can be considered as a continuous succession of points. The word line is frequently used to mean infinite straight line. The context ought to make it clear if this is the case.

label: Definition:Line/Curve
snippet: A curve is a line which may or may not be straight.

label: Definition:Line/Curve/Plane
snippet: A plane curve is a curve which can be embedded in the plane.

label: Definition:Line/Endpoint
snippet: Each of the points at either end of a line segment is called an endpoint of that line segment. Similarly, the point at which an infinite half-line terminates is called the endpoint of that line. '

label: Definition:Line/Infinite
snippet: An infinite line is a line which has no endpoints. Category:Definitions/Lines

label: Definition:Line/Infinite Half-Line
snippet: An infinite half-line is a line which terminates at an endpoint at one end, but has no such endpoint at the other.

label: Definition:Line/Infinite Straight Line
snippet: An infinite straight line is a straight line which has no endpoints, or equally, a straight line which is infinite. Category:Definitions/Straight Lines

label: Definition:Line/Midpoint
snippet: Let $L = AB$ be a line segment whose endpoints are $A$ and $B$. Let $M$ be a point on $L$ such that the line segment $AM$ is equal to the line segment $MB$. That is, let $M$ be the bisector of $L$. Then $M$ is the midpoint of $L$.

label: Definition:Line/Segment
snippet: A line segment is any line (straight or not) which terminates at two points.

label: Definition:Line/Straight Line Segment
snippet: A straight line segment is a line segment which is straight. A straight line segment can be drawn joining any two points. Thus a definition for straight line which is frequently encountered is: A straight line is the shortest distance between two points. This is all very well but it assumes that the line in question terminates at two particular endpoints.

label: Definition:Line of Action
snippet: Let a force $\mathbf F$ act on a rigid body $B$. In order to completely specify how $\mathbf F$ acts on $B$, it is necessary to know the point $P$ on $B$ at which $\mathbf F$ is applied. 400px The (straight) line $L$ passing through $P$ in the direction of $\mathbf F$ is known as the line of action of $\mathbf F$ on $B$.

label: Definition:Linear
snippet: An equation or expression which concerns a polynomial of degree $1$ is called linear.

label: Definition:Linear Algebra
snippet: Linear Algebra as a branch of Mathematics In the context of Abstract Algebra: Linear Algebra: the same thing as an algebra over a field

label: Definition:Linear Algebra (Mathematical Branch)
snippet: Linear algebra is the branch of algebra which studies vector spaces and linear transformations between them.

label: Definition:Linear Code
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\Z_p$ be the set of residue classes modulo $p$. Let $\map V {n, p}$ denote the set of sequences of length $n$ of elements of $\Z_p$. A linear $\tuple {n, k}$-code is a $k$-dimensional subspace $C$ of $\map V {n, p}$ considered as a vector space over $\Z_p$ of $n$ dimensions.

label: Definition:Linear Code/Codeword
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\Z_p$ be the set of residue classes modulo $p$. Let $\map V {n, p}$ be a master code of length $n$ modulo $p$. The elements of $\map V {n, p}$ are referred to as codewords. A codeword is usually written without punctuation, so that, for example: $\tuple {\eqclass 1 p, \eqclass 0 p, \eqclass 1 p}$ is presented as: $101$

label: Definition:Linear Code/Master Code
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\Z_p$ be the set of residue classes modulo $p$. Let $\map V {n, p}$ denote the set of sequences of length $n$ of elements of $\Z_p$. From Master Code forms Vector Space, $\map V {n, p}$ is a vector space over $\Z_p$ of $n$ dimensions $\map V {n, p}$ is itself a linear $\tuple {n, n}$-code, and is referred to on as a master code (for a linear $\tuple {n, k}$-code over $\Z_p$).

label: Definition:Linear Combination of Subsets of Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$.

label: Definition:Linear Combination of Subsets of Vector Space/Dilation
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $E$ be a subset of $X$. Let $\lambda \in K$. The dilation of $E$ by $\lambda$ is defined and written as: $\lambda E := \set {\lambda x : x \in E}$ where $\lambda x$ is the scalar product of $x$ by $\lambda$.

label: Definition:Linear Congruence
snippet: A linear congruence is a polynomial congruence of the form: $a_0 + a_1 x \equiv 0 \pmod n$ That is, one where the degree of the integral polynomial is $1$.

label: Definition:Linear Eccentricity
snippet: Let $\KK$ be an central conic. The linear eccentricity of $\KK$ is defined as the distance between the center of $\KK$ and either of the foci of $\KK$.

label: Definition:Linear First Order Ordinary Differential Equation
snippet: A linear first order ordinary differential equation is a differential equation which is in (or can be manipulated into) the form: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map P x y = \map Q x$ where $\map P x$ and $\map Q x$ are functions of $x$. It is: Linear because both $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x}$ and $y$ appear to the first power, and do not occur multiplied together First order because the highest derivative is $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x}$ Ordinary because there are no partial derivatives occurring in it.

label: Definition:Linear Function
snippet: A linear function is a polynomial whose degree is $1$:

label: Definition:Linear Functional
snippet: Let $E$ be a vector space over a field $\GF$. Let $D$ be a linear subspace of $E$. A mapping $f : D \to \GF$ is called a linear functional : $\map f {\alpha x + \beta y} = \alpha \map f x + \beta \map f y$ holds for all $x, y$ in $L$ and for all $\alpha, \beta$ in $\GF$.

label: Definition:Linear Group Action
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group.

label: Definition:Linear Measure
snippet: Linear measure is the means of measurement of the magnitude of a physical displacement. As such, linear measure is a scalar quantity.

label: Definition:Linear Measure/Breadth
snippet: Breadth is linear measure in a dimension perpendicular to length. In the context of a two-dimensional geometric figure, the breadth is in the plane of that figure. In a three-dimensional figure, the choice of which direction is referred to as breadth is often arbitrary.

label: Definition:Linear Measure/Depth
snippet: Depth is linear measure in a dimension perpendicular to both length and breadth. The choice of depth is often arbitrary, although in two-dimensional diagrams of three-dimensional figures, depth is usually imagined as being the dimension perpendicular to the plane the figure is drawn in. It is typically used to measure the distance downwards from the surface of a body of liquid.

label: Definition:Linear Measure/Height
snippet: Height, like depth, is used as a term for linear measure in a dimension perpendicular to both length and breadth. However, whereas depth has connotations of down, height is used for distances up from the plane.

label: Definition:Linear Measure/Length
snippet: Length is linear measure taken in a particular direction. Usually, in multi-dimensional figures, the dimension in which the linear measure is greatest is referred to as length. It is the most widely used term for linear measure, as it is the standard term used when only one dimension is under consideration. Length is the fundamental notion of Euclidean geometry, never defined but regarded as an intuitive concept at the basis of every geometrical theorem.

label: Definition:Linear Momentum
snippet: The linear momentum of a particle is its mass multiplied by its velocity. $\mathbf p = m \mathbf v$ As mass is a scalar quantity and velocity is a vector quantity, it follows that linear momentum is a vector quantity.

label: Definition:Linear Operator
snippet: A linear operator is a linear transformation from a module into itself.

label: Definition:Linear Operator/Vector Space
snippet: A linear operator on a vector space is a linear transformation from a vector space into itself.

label: Definition:Linear Programming
snippet: Linear programming is the branch of mathematical programming which finds optimal solutions of mathematical models whose requirements are represented by linear relationships. Such optimal solutions may be maximizations or minimizations. The sort of functions which are being maximized often represent: profits volumes of goods to be produced and so on. The sort of functions which are being minimized often represent: production costs production times and so on.

label: Definition:Linear Real Function
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function. $f$ is called linear it has the form: $\forall x \in \R: \map f x = ax + b$ where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers.

label: Definition:Linear Regression
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let the regression of $Y$ on $X$ be expressible in the form: $\expect {Y \mid x} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ Then $\expect {Y \mid x}$ is known as linear regression.

label: Definition:Linear Representation/Group
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$ of finite dimension. Let $\GL V$ be the general linear group of $V$. Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. A linear representation of $G$ on $V$ is a group homomorphism $\rho: G \to \GL V$.

label: Definition:Linear Second Order ODE with Constant Coefficients
snippet: A linear second order ODE with constant coefficients is a second order ODE which can be manipulated into the form: $y' ' + p y' + q y = \map R x$ where: $p$ and $q$ are real constants $\map R x$ is a function of $x$. Thus it is a linear second order ODE: $y' ' + \map P x y' + \map Q x y = \map R x$ where $\map P x$ and $\map Q x$ are constant functions.

label: Definition:Linear Second Order Ordinary Differential Equation
snippet: A linear second order ordinary differential equation is a differential equation which is in (or can be manipulated into) the form: $\dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \map P x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map Q x y = \map R x$ where, as is indicated by the notation, $\map P x$, $\map Q x$ and $\map R x$ are functions of $x$ alone (or constants).

label: Definition:Linear Subspace
snippet: Vector Subspace However, when dealing with a Hilbert space, it may either refer to: Linear Manifold; this is the same as a vector subspace. Closed Linear Subspace, a vector subspace that is stipulated to be closed. A discussion of the differences is found here.

label: Definition:Linear Transformation
snippet: A linear transformation is a general $R$-algebraic structure homomorphism, where each of those $R$-algebraic structures is a module (usually left). Hence, let $R$ be a ring. Let $M = \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ and $N = \struct {H, +_H, \otimes}_R$ be $R$-modules. Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is a linear transformation : $(1): \quad \forall x, y \in G: \map \phi {x +_G y} = \map \phi x +_H \map \phi y$ $(2): \quad \forall x \in G: \forall \lambda \in R: \map \phi {\lambda \circ x} = \lambda \otimes \map \phi x$

label: Definition:Linear Transformation/Vector Space
snippet: Let $V, W$ be vector spaces over a field (or, more generally, division ring) $K$. A mapping $A: V \to W$ is a linear transformation : $\forall v_1, v_2 \in V, \lambda \in K: \map A {\lambda v_1 + v_2} = \lambda \map A {v_1} + \map A {v_2}$ That is, a homomorphism from one vector space to another.

label: Definition:Linearly Dependent
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group whose identity is $e$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module.

label: Definition:Linearly Dependent/Sequence
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group whose identity is $e$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module.

label: Definition:Linearly Dependent/Set
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group whose identity is $e$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module. Let $S \subseteq G$. Then $S$ is a linearly dependent set there exists a sequence of distinct terms in $S$ which is a linearly dependent sequence. That is, such that: $\ds \exists \set {\lambda_k: 1 \le k \le n} \subseteq R: \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_k \circ a_k = e$ where $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are distinct elements of $S$, and where at least one of $\lambda_k$ is not equal to $0_R$.

label: Definition:Linearly Dependent/Set/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\R^n, +, \cdot}_\R$ be a real vector space. Let $S \subseteq \R^n$. Then $S$ is a linearly dependent set there exists a sequence of distinct terms in $S$ which is a linearly dependent sequence. That is, such that: $\ds \exists \set {\lambda_k: 1 \le k \le n} \subseteq \R: \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_k \mathbf v_k = \mathbf 0$ where $\set {\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2, \ldots, \mathbf v_n} \subseteq S$, and such that at least one of $\lambda_k$ is not equal to $0$.

label: Definition:Linearly Dependent Sequence/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group whose identity is $e$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module. Let $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be a (finite) sequence of elements of $G$. Then: $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ is a linearly dependent sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ is not a linearly independent sequence .

label: Definition:Linearly Independent
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group whose identity is $e$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module.

label: Definition:Linearly Independent/Sequence
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group whose identity is $e$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module.

label: Definition:Linearly Independent/Sequence/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\R^n, +, \cdot}_\R$ be a real vector space. Let $\sequence {\mathbf v_n}$ be a sequence of vectors in $\R^n$. Then $\sequence {\mathbf v_n}$ is linearly independent : $\ds \forall \sequence {\lambda_n} \subseteq \R: \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_k \mathbf v_k = \mathbf 0 \implies \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \cdots = \lambda_n = 0$ where $\mathbf 0 \in \R^n$ is the zero vector and $0 \in \R$ is the zero scalar.

label: Definition:Linearly Independent/Set
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group whose identity is $e$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module. Let $S \subseteq G$. Then $S$ is a linearly independent set (over $R$) every finite sequence of distinct terms in $S$ is a linearly independent sequence. That is, such that: $\ds \forall \sequence {\lambda_n} \subseteq R: \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_k \circ a_k = e \implies \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \cdots = \lambda_n = 0_R$ where $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$ are distinct elements of $S$.

label: Definition:Linearly Independent/Set/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\R^n, +, \cdot}_\R$ be a real vector space. Let $S \subseteq \R^n$. Then $S$ is a linearly independent set of real vectors every finite sequence of distinct terms in $S$ is a linearly independent sequence. That is, such that: $\ds \forall \set {\lambda_k: 1 \le k \le n} \subseteq \R: \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_k \mathbf v_k = \mathbf 0 \implies \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \cdots = \lambda_n = 0$ where $\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2, \ldots, \mathbf v_n$ are distinct elements of $S$.

label: Definition:Linearly Ordered Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a linearly ordered set. Let $\tau$ be the order topology on $S$. Then $\struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ is a linearly ordered space.

label: Definition:Liouville Number
snippet: A real number $x$ is a Liouville number if for all $n \in \N$, there exist $p, q \in \Z$ (which may depend on $n$) with $q > 1$ such that: $0 < \size {x - \dfrac p q} < \dfrac 1 {q^n}$

label: Definition:Lipschitz Continuity
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ and $M' = \struct {A', d'}$ be metric spaces. Let Let $f: A \to A'$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a Lipschitz continuous mapping there exists a positive real number $K \in \R_{\ge 0}$ such that: $\forall x, y \in A: \map {d'} {\map f x, \map f y} \le K \map d {x, y}$ That is, the distance between the images of two points lies within a fixed multiple of the distance between the points.

label: Definition:Lipschitz Continuity/Lipschitz Constant
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ and $M' = \struct {A', d'}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: A \to A'$ be a (Lipschitz continuous) mapping such that: $\forall x, y \in A: \map {d'} {\map f x, \map f y} \le K \map d {x, y}$ where $K \in \R_{\ge 0}$ is a positive real number. Then $K$ is a Lipschitz constant for $f$.

label: Definition:Lipschitz Continuity/Real Function
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $I \subseteq A$ be a real interval on which: $\exists K \in \R_{\ge 0}: \forall x, y \in I: \size {\map f x - \map f y} \le K \size {x - y}$ Then $f$ is Lipschitz continuous on $I$. The constant $K$ is known as a Lipschitz constant for $f$.

label: Definition:Lipschitz Equivalence/Metric Spaces
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: M_1 \to M_2$ be a mapping such that $\exists h, k \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $\forall x, y \in A: h \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map f y} \le \map {d_1} {x, y} \le k \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map f y}$ Then $f$ is a Lipschitz equivalence, and $M_1$ and $M_2$ are described as Lipschitz equivalent.

label: Definition:Literal
snippet: A literal is either: an atom $p$ of propositional logic, that is, a statement, or the negation $\neg p$ of an atom $p$. In the language of propositional logic, these correspond to: a letter $p$ the WFF $\neg p$, where $p$ is a letter.

label: Definition:Little-O Notation
snippet: Little-$\oo$ notation occurs in a variety of contexts.

label: Definition:Little-O Notation/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Little-$\oo$ Notation == The expression $\map f n \in \map \oo {\map g n}$ is read as: $\map f n$ is little-$\oo$ of $\map g n$ Similarly, when expressed in the notation of sequences, $a_n \in \map \oo {b_n}$ is read as: $a_n$ is little-$\oo$ of $b_n$ While it is correct and accurate to write: $\map f n \in \map \oo {\map g n}$ or: $a_n \in \map \oo {b_n}$ it is a common abuse of notation to write: $\map f n = \map \oo {\map g n}$ or: $a_n = \map \oo {b_n}$ This notation offers some advantages. label: Definition:Local Basis

label: Definition:Local Compactness Property
snippet: A local compactness property is a property that specifies a form of (topological) compactness that may apply in a given neighborhood within a given topological space, but not necessarily the topological space as a whole.

label: Definition:Local Coordinates
snippet: Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional manifold. Let $p \in X$, and let $U \subseteq M$ be a neighbourhood of $p$. Let $\phi$ be the local coordinate map of $M$ such that: $\map \phi p = \tuple {\map {x_1} p, \map {x_2} p, \ldots \map {x_n} p}$ The component mappings $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n}$ of $\phi$ are known as the local coordinates around $p$.

label: Definition:Local Gravitational Constant
snippet: The local gravitational constant is the value of the acceleration $g$ caused by the gravitational field given rise to by whatever body or bodies are in a position to exert that gravitational force. In the everyday context, $g$ is the acceleration due to the gravitational field of Earth at whatever point on or near its surface the observer happens to be. Thus in this context it is approximately equal to $9 \cdotp 8 \ \mathrm {m \, s^{-2} }$.

label: Definition:Local Isometry
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ and $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $\phi : M \to \tilde M$ be a mapping such that for each $p$ there is a neighborhood $U$ such that $\bigvalueat \phi U$ is an isometry onto an open subset of $\tilde M$. Then $\phi$ is called the local isometry.

label: Definition:Locale of Topological Space
snippet: The locale of topological space $T = \struct{S, \tau}$, denoted $\map \Omega T$, is the ordered set $\struct{\tau, \subseteq}$ where $\subseteq$ denotes the subset relation on $\tau$.
