Then $a - b$ is a minor.

label: Definition:Minor Arc
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be points on the boundary $\BB$ of a simple closed curve $\CC$ in the plane. Let $a$ and $b$ divide $\BB$ into unequal parts. The shorter of the arcs described by $a$ and $b$ is referred to as the minor arc of $\BB$.

label: Definition:Minor of Determinant
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_n$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Consider the order $k$ square submatrix $\mathbf B$ obtained by deleting $n - k$ rows and $n - k$ columns from $\mathbf A$. Let $\map \det {\mathbf B}$ denote the determinant of $\mathbf B$. Then $\map \det {\mathbf B}$ is an order-$k$ minor of $\map \det {\mathbf A}$. Thus a minor is a determinant formed from the elements (in the same relative order) of $k$ specified rows and columns.

label: Definition:Mixed Tensor
snippet: Let $V$ and $V^*$ be a vector space and its algebraic dual. Then a (mixed) tensor $F$ of type $\tuple {k, l}$ is a multilinear map such that: $F : \underbrace {V \times \ldots \times V}_{\text {$k$ times} } \times \underbrace { {V^*} \times \ldots \times {V^*} }_{\text {$l$ times} } \to \R$

label: Definition:Modal Logic
snippet: Modal logic is a branch of logic in which truth values are more complex than being merely true or false, and which distinguishes between different "modes" of truth. There are two operators in classical modal logic, defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $(1): \quad$ Necessity, represented by $\nec$, defined by: $\nec P : \iff \forall w: \map P w$ $(2): \quad$ Possibility, represented by $\pos$, defined by: $\pos P: \iff \exists w: \map P w$ Modal logic may also have other operators, including: Temporal logic, which uses several operators including present and future…

label: Definition:Modal Operator/Necessity
snippet: The necessity operator $\nec$ is the unary modal operator defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $\nec P : \iff \forall w: \map P w$

label: Definition:Modal Operator/Possibility
snippet: The possibility operator $\pos$ is the unary modal operator defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $\pos P : \iff \exists w: \map P w$

label: Definition:Mode
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of quantitative data. The mode of $S$ is the element of $S$ which occurs most often in $S$. If there is more than one such element of $S$ which occurs equally most often, it is then understood that each of these is a mode. If there is no element of $S$ which occurs more often (in the extreme case, all elements are equal) then $S$ has no mode.

label: Definition:Model (Logic)/Set of Logical Formulas
snippet: Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for a logical language $\LL$. Let $\MM$ be a structure of $\mathscr M$. Let $\FF$ be a set of logical formulas of $\LL$. Then $\MM$ is a model of $\FF$ : $\MM \models_{\mathscr M} \phi$ for every $\phi \in \FF$ that is, it is a model of every logical formula $\phi \in \FF$.

label: Definition:Model (Predicate Logic)
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ be the language of predicate logic. Let $\AA$ be a structure for predicate logic. Then $\AA$ models a sentence $\mathbf A$ : $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A} = \T$ where $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A}$ denotes the value of $\mathbf A$ in $\AA$. This relationship is denoted: $\AA \models_{\mathrm{PL} } \mathbf A$ When pertaining to a collection of sentences $\FF$, one says $\AA$ models $\FF$ : $\forall \mathbf A \in \FF: \AA \models_{\mathrm{PL} } \mathbf A$ that is, it models all elements of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Model Theory
snippet: Model theory is a sub-branch of mathematical logic which studies mathematical structures by means of formal semantics for formal languages.

label: Definition:Model of Rational Choice
snippet: A model of rational choice for a player in a game consists of: $(1): \quad$ A set $A$ of moves from which the player may choose $(2): \quad$ A set $C$ of consequences of each of those moves $(3): \quad$ A consequence function $g: A \to C$ which maps a consequence to each action $(4): \quad$ A preference relation $\succsim$, which is a total ordering on $C$.

label: Definition:Modified Fort Space
snippet: Let $N$ be an infinite set. Let $\set a$ and $\set b$ be singleton sets such that $a \ne b$ and $a, b \notin N$. Let $S = N \cup \set a \cup \set b$. Let $\tau_{a, b}$ be the set of subsets of $S$ defined as: $\tau_{a, b} = \set {H \subseteq N} \cup \set {H \subseteq S: \paren {a \in H \lor b \in H} \land N \setminus H \text { is finite} }$ That is, a subset $H$ of $S$ is in $\tau_{a, b}$ either of the following hold: Then $\tau_{a, b}$ is a modified Fort topology on $a$ and $b$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_{a, b} }$ is a modified Fort space.

label: Definition:Module Defined by Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be a rings. Let $f: A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism.

label: Definition:Module Endomorphism
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. A module endomorphism of $M$ is a module homomorphism from $M$ to itself.

label: Definition:Module Theory
snippet: Module theory is the branch of abstract algebra which studies modules.

label: Definition:Module of All Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {M, +_M, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-module. Let $S$ be a set. Let $M^S$ be the set of all mappings from $S$ to $M$. Let: $+$ be the operation induced on $M^S$ by $+_M$ $\forall \lambda \in R: \forall f \in M^S: \forall x \in S: \map {\paren {\lambda \ast f} } x = \lambda \ast \paren {\map f x}$ Then $\struct {M^S, +, \ast}_R$ is the module of all mappings from $S$ to $M$.

label: Definition:Module over Group
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : G \times V \to V$ be a linear group action of $G$ on $V$, either: a left linear group action: $\phi : G \times V \to V$ or a right linear group action: $\phi : V \times G \to V$ Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a module over $G$, either a left module or a right module respectively.

label: Definition:Module over Group/Left
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : G \times V \to V$ be a left linear group action of $G$ on $V$. Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a left module over $G$.

label: Definition:Module over Group/Right
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : V \times G \to V$ be a right linear group action of $G$ on $V$. Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a right module over $G$.

label: Definition:Module over Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast$ which is either a left module or a right module, depending upon whether $\ast$ is defined as: $\ast: R \times G \to G$ or: $\ast: G \times R \to G$ respectively. As follows:

label: Definition:Module over Ring/Left and Right Modules
snippet: == Left Modules and Right Modules == In the case where the scalar ring is a commutative ring, the difference between a left module and a right module is little more than a notational difference. See: Left Module over Commutative Ring induces Right Module Right Module over Commutative Ring induces Left Module. But this is not the case for a scalar ring that is not commutative.

label: Definition:Modulo Arithmetic
snippet: Modulo arithmetic is the branch of abstract algebra which studies the residue class of integers under a modulus. As such it can also be considered to be a branch of number theory.

label: Definition:Modulo Division
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of division modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a \div_m b$ equals the integer $q \in \Z_m$ such that $b \times_m q \equiv a \pmod m$ and is possible only if $q$ is unique modulo $m$. This happens $a$ and $m$ are coprime.

label: Definition:Modulo Division/Divisor
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ For all $a, b \in \Z_m$, let $a \div_m b$ denote the operation of division modulo $m$: $a \div_m b$ equals the integer $q \in \Z_m$ such that $b \times_m q \equiv a \pmod m$ The integers $b$ and $q$ are divisors of $a$ modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Also denoted as
snippet: == Modulo Multiplication: Also denoted as == Although the operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is denoted by the symbol $\times_m$, if there is no danger of confusion, the conventional multiplication symbols $\times, \cdot$ etc. are often used instead. The notation for multiplication of two integers modulo $m$ is not usually $\eqclass a m \times_m \eqclass b m$. What is more normally seen is $a b \pmod m$. Category:Definitions/Modulo Multiplication

label: Definition:Modulo Operation
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Then the modulo operation is defined and denoted as: $x \bmod y := \begin{cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end{cases}$ where $\floor {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the floor function.

label: Definition:Modulo Operation/Modulo One
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Let the modulo operation $\bmod$ be defined as: $x \bmod y := \begin{cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end{cases}$ Then: $x \bmod 1 = x - \floor x$ from which it follows directly that: $x = \floor x + \paren {x \bmod 1}$

label: Definition:Modulus (Geometric Function Theory)
snippet: In geometric function theory, the term modulus is used to denote certain conformal invariants of configurations or curve families. More precisely, the modulus of a curve family $\Gamma$ is the reciprocal of its extremal length: $\mod \Gamma := \dfrac 1 {\map \lambda \Gamma}$

label: Definition:Moment (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on some probability space. Let $a$ be a real number. Then the $n$th moment of $X$ about $a$, usually denoted $\map {\mu_n} a$, is defined as: $\map {\mu_n} a = \expect {\paren {X - a}^n}$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$.

label: Definition:Moment Generating Function
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable. Then the moment generating function of $X$ is defined and denoted as: $\map {M_X} t = \expect {e^{t X} }$ for all $t$ such that this expectation exists.

label: Definition:Moment of Couple
snippet: Let $C$ be a couple composed of the forces $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$. The moment of $C$ is a vector given by: $\mathbf M = \mathbf F_1 \times \mathbf d$ where: $\mathbf F_1$ is one of the forces that compose $C$ $\mathbf d$ is the displacement from $\mathbf F_1$ to $\mathbf F_2$. Hence: the line of action of $\mathbf M$ is perpendicular to the plane containing $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ the magnitude of $\mathbf M$ is equal to $F d$, where: $F$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ $d$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf d$.

label: Definition:Monic Polynomial
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $f \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial in one variable over $R$. Then $f$ is monic $f$ is nonzero and its leading coefficient is $1_R$. Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}$ be a subring of $R$. Let $\ds f = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k \circ x^k$ be a polynomial in $x$ over $S$. Then $f$ is a monic polynomial its leading coefficient $a_n$ is $1_R$.

label: Definition:Monochromatic Graph
snippet: A monochromatic graph is a colored graph (either vertex-colored or edge-colored, depending on the context) in which each of the vertices or edges is assigned the same color. Category:Definitions/Graph Colorings Category:Definitions/Ramsey Theory

label: Definition:Monoid
snippet: A monoid is a semigroup with an identity element.

label: Definition:Monoid Category
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid with identity $e_S$. One can interpret $\struct {S, \circ}$ as being a category, with: {{DefineCategory | ob = Only one, say $*$ | mor = $a: * \to *$, for all $a \in S$ | comp = $a \circ b: * \to *$ is defined using the operation $\circ$ of the monoid $S$ | id = $\operatorname{id}_* := e_S: * \to *$ }} The category that so arises is called a monoid category.

label: Definition:Monoid Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be monoids. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping such that $\circ$ has the morphism property under $\phi$. That is, $\forall a, b \in S$: $\map \phi {a \circ b} = \map \phi a * \map \phi b$ Suppose further that $\phi$ preserves identities, that is: $\map \phi {e_S} = e_T$ Then $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ is a monoid homomorphism.

label: Definition:Monoid Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a monoid. Let $R^{\paren G}$ be the free $R$-module on $G$. Let $\set {e_g: g \in G}$ be its canonical basis. By Multilinear Mapping from Free Modules is Determined by Bases, there exists a unique bilinear map: $\circ: R^{\paren G} \times R^{\paren G} \to R^{\paren G}$ which satisfies: $e_g \circ e_h = e_{g \mathop * h}$ Then $R \sqbrk G = \struct {R^{\paren G}, +, \circ}$ is called the monoid ring of $G$ over $R$.

label: Definition:Monomial of Free Commutative Monoid
snippet: A monomial in the indexed set $\family {X_j: j \in J}$ is a possibly infinite product: $\ds \prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j}$ with integer exponents $k_j \ge 0$ such that $k_j = 0$ for all but finitely many $j$. Let $\mathbf X = \family {X_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ and for a multiindex $k = \paren {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ over $J$ define: $\ds \mathbf X^k = \prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j}$ Then a monomial is an object of the form $\mathbf X^k$, where $k$ is a multiindex.

label: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity.

label: Definition:Monomorphism (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: A homomorphism which is an injection is descibed as monic, or called a monomorphism.

label: Definition:Monomorphism (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. A monomorphism is a morphism $f \in \mathbf C_1$ such that: $f \circ g = f \circ h \implies g = h$ for all morphisms $g, h \in \mathbf C_1$ for which these compositions are defined. That is, a monomorphism is a morphism which is left cancellable. One writes $f: C \rightarrowtail D$ to denote that $f$ is a monomorphism.

label: Definition:Monotone
snippet: Mappings: Monotone (Order Theory): A mapping from one ordered set to another is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing. Monotone (Measure Theory): A mapping $f: \SS \to \R$ on an algebra of sets $\SS$ is monotone $A \subseteq B \iff \map f A \le \map f B$. Monotone class: A collection of subsets closed under countable intersections and unions. Monotone Galois connection In all cases, the sense is one of changing always in the same direction.

label: Definition:Monotone (Order Theory)/Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. A sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in A}$ of elements of $S$ is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing.

label: Definition:Monotone Class
snippet: Let $X$ be a set, and let $\powerset X$ be its power set. Let $\MM \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then $\MM$ is said to be a monotone class (on $X$) for every countable, nonempty, index set $I$, it holds that: $\ds \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I} \in \MM \implies \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} A_i \in \MM$ $\ds \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I} \in \MM \implies \bigcap_{i \mathop \in I} A_i \in \MM$ that is, $\MM$ is closed under countable unions and countable intersections.

label: Definition:Monotone Class Generated by Collection of Subsets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then the monotone class generated by $\GG$, $\map {\mathfrak m} \GG$, is the smallest monotone class on $X$ that contains $\GG$. That is, $\map {\mathfrak m} \GG$ is subject to: $(1): \quad \GG \subseteq \map {\mathfrak m} \GG$ $(2): \quad \GG \subseteq \MM \implies \map {\mathfrak m} \GG \subseteq \MM$ for any monotone class $\MM$ on $X$

label: Definition:Monte Carlo Method
snippet: A Monte Carlo method is a technique in statistics for investigating mathematical properties by repeated experiments a large number of times. This is useful when an analytic solution is difficult to obtain.

label: Definition:Moon
snippet: The moon is the single natural satellite of Earth.

label: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$.

label: Definition:Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. A morphism of $\mathbf C$ is an object $f$, together with: A domain $\operatorname {dom} f$, which is an object of $\mathbf C$ A codomain $\operatorname {cod} f$, also an object of $\mathbf C$ The collection of all morphisms of $\mathbf C$ is denoted $\mathbf C_1$. If $A$ is the domain of $f$ and $B$ is its codomain, this is mostly represented by writing: $f: A \to B$ or $A \stackrel f \longrightarrow B$

label: Definition:Morphism Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Its morphism category, denoted $\mathbf C^\to$, is defined as follows: {{DefineCategory |ob = The morphisms $\mathbf C_1$ of $\mathbf C$ |mor = $g: f \to f'$ is a pair $\tuple {g_1, g_2}$ of morphisms of $\mathbf C$ such that $g_2 \circ f = f' \circ g_1$ |comp = $\tuple {h_1, h_2} \circ \tuple {g_1, g_2} := \tuple {h_1 \circ g_1, h_2 \circ g_2}$, whenever this is defined |id = $\operatorname{id}_f := \tuple {\operatorname{id}_C, \operatorname{id}_D}$ for $f: C \to D$ }} The morphisms of $\mathbf C^\to$ can be made more intuitive by the following diagram:…

label: Definition:Morphism Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. A morphism functor $F$ assigns to each morphism $f$ of $\mathbf C$ a morphism $F f$ of $\mathbf D$.

label: Definition:Morphism Property
snippet: Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be a mapping from one algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ to another $\struct {T, *}$. Then $\circ$ has the morphism property under $\phi$ : $\forall x, y \in S: \map \phi {x \circ y} = \map \phi x * \map \phi y$

label: Definition:Morphism of Cones
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ be a $\mathbf J$-diagram in $\mathbf C$. Let $\struct {C, c_j}$ and $\struct {C', c'_j}$ be cones to $D$. Let $f: C \to C'$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. Then $f$ is a morphism of cones , for all objects $j$ of $\mathbf J$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+0.5em@L+2px{ C \ar[r]^*+{f} \ar[dr]_*+{c_j} & C' \ar[d]^*+{c'_j} \\ & D_j }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

label: Definition:Morphism of Schemes
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. A morphism of schemes from $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ is a morphism of locally ringed spaces from $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$.

label: Definition:Motion
snippet: A particle or a body is defined as being in motion it is not stationary with respect to the given frame of reference. Thus motion is the state of changing position.

label: Definition:Moving Average Model
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $\tilde z_t$ be the deviation from a constant mean level $\mu$: $\tilde z_t = z_t - \mu$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let $M$ be a model where the current value of $\tilde z_t$ is expressed as a finite linear aggregate of the shocks: $\tilde z_t = a_t - \theta_1 a_{t - 1} - \theta_2 a_{t - 2} - \dotsb - \theta_q a_{t - q}$ $M$ is known…

label: Definition:Muggle
snippet: A muggle is a person who is mathematically illiterate. Specifically, it refers to those who do not realise that they are indeed embarrassingly mathematically unsophisticated, and insist on peppering their speech with mathematical-sounding phrases, like Q.E.D (on believing they have won an argument) or I had $n$ pints of beer last night (being under the impression that $n$ means "a big unspecified number").

label: Definition:Multi-Digit Integer
snippet: Let $b \in \N_{>1}$ be a natural number greater than $1$. An $n$-digit integer base $b$ is an integer which has no more than $n$ digits when expressed in base $b$. That is, it is strictly less than $b^n$.

label: Definition:Multi-Value Logic
snippet: Multi-value logic is a branch of logic in which it is admissible for a statements to have a truth value other than just true or false.

label: Definition:Multifunction/Branch
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f: A \to B$ be a multifunction on $A$. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a partitioning of the codomain of $f$ such that: $\forall i \in I: f \restriction_{A \times S_i}$ is a mapping. Then each $f \restriction_{A \times S_i}$ is a branch of $f$.

label: Definition:Multifunction/Principal Branch
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f: A \to B$ be a multifunction on $A$. Let $\sequence {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a partitioning of the codomain of $f$ into branches. It is usual to distinguish one such branch of $f$ from the others, and label it the principal branch of $f$.

label: Definition:Multigraph
snippet: A multigraph is a graph that can have more than one edge between a pair of vertices. That is, $G = \struct {V, E}$ is a multigraph if $V$ is a set and $E$ is a multiset of doubleton subsets of $V$. 400px The graph above is a multigraph because of the double edge between $v_2$ and $v_3$ and the triple edge between $v_5$ and $v_6$.

label: Definition:Multinomial Coefficient
snippet: Let $k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_m \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be positive integers. The multinomial coefficient of $k_1, \ldots, k_m$ is defined as: $\dbinom {k_1 + k_2 + \cdots + k_m} {k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_m} := \dfrac {\paren {k_1 + k_2 + \cdots + k_m}!} {k_1! \, k_2! \, \ldots k_m!}$

label: Definition:Multiple/Integer
snippet: Let $\Z$ denote the set of integers. Let $x, y \in \Z$. Let $x$ be a divisor of $y$. Then $y$ is a multiple of $x$.

label: Definition:Multiple Correlation Coefficient
snippet: Context: multiple regression. Let the expectation of a random variable $Y$ be given by: $\expect y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 \cdots$ Let the least-squares regression estimators of $y$ corresponding to the observed $y_i$ be denoted $\hat y_i$. Then the multiple correlation coefficient is the product moment correlation coefficient between the $y_i$ and $\hat y_i$, and is denoted $R$.

label: Definition:Multiplication
snippet: Multiplication is the basic operation $\times$ everyone is familiar with. For example:

label: Definition:Multiplication/Complex Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of complex numbers $\C$ is written $\times$. Let $z = a + i b, w = c + i d$ where $a, b, c, d \in \R$. Then $z \times w$ is defined as: $\paren {a + i b} \times \paren {c + i d} = \paren {a c - b d} + i \paren {a d + b c}$ This follows by the facts that: Real Numbers form Field and thus real multiplication is distributive over real addition the entity $i$ is such that $i^2 = -1$.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Integers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of integers $\Z$ is written $\times$. Let us define $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$ as in the formal definition of integers. That is, $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$ is an equivalence class of ordered pairs of natural numbers under the congruence relation $\boxtimes$. $\boxtimes$ is the congruence relation defined on $\N \times \N$ by $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \boxtimes \tuple {x_2, y_2} \iff x_1 + y_2 = x_2 + y_1$. In order to streamline the notation, we will use $\eqclass {a, b} {}$ to mean $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$, as suggested.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Multiplicand
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects. The object $b$ is known as the multiplicand of $a$. That is, it is the object which is to be multiplied by the multiplier. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Multiplier
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects. The object $a$ is known as the multiplier of $b$. That is, it is the object which is to multiply the multiplicand. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Natural Numbers/Addition
snippet: Let $\N$ be the natural numbers. Let $+$ denote addition. The binary operation $\times$ is recursively defined on $\N$ as follows: $\forall m, n \in \N: \begin {cases} m \times 0 & = 0 \\ m \times \paren {n + 1} & = m \times n + m \end {cases}$ This operation is called multiplication. Equivalently, multiplication can be defined as: $\forall m, n \in \N: m \times n := \mathop {+^n} m$ where $\mathop {+^n} m$ denotes the $n$th power of $m$ under $+$.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Product
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects $a$ and $b$. Then the result $a \times b$ is referred to as the product of $a$ and $b$. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Rational Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of rational numbers $\Q$ is written $\times$. Let $a = \dfrac p q, b = \dfrac r s$ where $p, q \in \Z, r, s \in \Z \setminus \set 0$. Then $a \times b$ is defined as $\dfrac p q \times \dfrac r s = \dfrac {p \times r} {q \times s}$. This definition follows from the definition of and proof of existence of the field of quotients of any integral domain, of which the set of integers is one.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Real Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of real numbers $\R$ is written $\times$. From the definition, the real numbers are the set of all equivalence classes $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers. Let $x = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}, y = \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$, where $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ and $\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$ are such equivalence classes. Then $x \times y$ is defined as: $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {}$

label: Definition:Multiplication of Positive Cuts
snippet: Let $0^*$ denote the rational cut associated with the (rational) number $0$. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive cuts, that is, cuts such that $\alpha \ge 0^*$ and $\beta \ge 0^*$, where $\ge$ denotes the ordering on cuts. Let the operation of multiplication be defined on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as: $\gamma := \alpha \beta$ where $\gamma$ is the set of all rational numbers $r$ such that either: $r < 0$ or $\exists p \in \alpha, q \in \beta: r = p q$ where $p \ge 0$ and $q \ge 0$. In this context, $\gamma$ is known as the product of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field. Let $F^* := F \setminus \set 0$ be the set $F$ less its zero. The group $\struct {F^*, \times}$ is known as the multiplicative group of $F$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of complex numbers $\struct {\C_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of complex numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Complex Roots of Unity
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n > 0$. Let $U_n := \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$ denote the set of complex $n$th roots of unity. Let $\struct {U_n, \times}$ be the algebraic structure formed by $U_n$ under complex multiplication. Then $\struct {U_n, \times}$ is the multiplicative group of complex $n$th roots of unity.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Rational Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of rational numbers $\struct {\Q_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of rational numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Real Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of real numbers $\struct {\R_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of real numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Reduced Residues
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\Z'_m$ denote the reduced residue system modulo $m$. Consider the algebraic structure: $\struct {\Z'_m, \times_m}$ where $\times_m$ denotes multiplication modulo $m$. Then $\struct {\Z'_m, \times_m}$ is referred to as the multiplicative group of reduced residues modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Magic Square
snippet: A multiplicative magic square is an arrangement of $n^2$ distinct numbers into an $n \times n$ square array such that: the product of the elements of each row the product of the elements in each column the product of the elements along each diagonal are the same.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Magic Square/Magic Constant
snippet: The magic constant of a multiplicative magic square is the number that each of the rows and columns multiplies up to.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Monoid of Integers Modulo m
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ such that $m > 1$. The multiplicative monoid of integers modulo $m$ $\struct {\Z_m, \times_m}$ is the set of integers modulo $m$ under the operation of multiplication modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Notation
snippet: Multiplicative notation, also called product notation, is a convention for representing a binary operation of an algebraic structure. Let $S$ be such an algebraic structure, and let $x, y \in S$. $x y$ is used to indicate the result of the operation on $x$ and $y$. There is no symbol used to define the operation itself. $e$ or $1$ is used for the identity element. $x^{-1}$ is used for the inverse element. $x^n$ is used to indicate the $n$th power of $x$. This notation is usual in group theory when discussing the general group.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Order of Integer
snippet: Let $a$ and $n$ be integers. Let there exist a positive integer $c$ such that: $a^c \equiv 1 \pmod n$ Then the least such integer is called the (multiplicative) order of $a$ modulo $n$.

label: Definition:Multiplicatively Closed Subset of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {A, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity $1_A$ and zero $0_A$. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset. Then $S$ is multiplicatively closed : $(1): \quad 1_A \in S$ $(2): \quad x, y \in S \implies x \circ y \in S$

label: Definition:Multiplicity (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a function. Suppose there is $a \in \C$ such that $\map f a = 0$. Then $a$ is said to be a zero of multiplicity $k$ there exists non-zero $L \in \R$ such that: $\ds \lim_{z \mathop \to a} \dfrac {\cmod {\map f z} } {\cmod {z - a}^k} = L$ Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

label: Definition:Multiply Perfect Number
snippet: A multiply perfect number is a positive integer $n$ such that the sum of its divisors is equal to an integer multiple of $n$.

label: Definition:Multiset
snippet: A multiset is a pair $\struct {S, \mu}$ where: $S$ is a set $\mu: S \to \N_{>0}$ is a mapping to the strictly positive natural numbers For $s \in S$ the natural number $\map \mu s$ is called the multiplicity of $s$. Note that the multiplicities of elements is finite: we do not allow infinitely many occurrences of the same element, though the set $S$ itself may be finite, countably infinite or uncountably infinite.

label: Definition:Multitape Turing Machine
snippet: A multitape Turing machine is a generalization of the standard Turing machine. Instead manipulating a single tape of symbols, the machine may have any finite number thereof, each with its own read-write head. The machine chooses its moves for each tape based on the symbols read by every tape.

label: Definition:Möbius Function
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$, that is, a strictly positive integer. The Möbius function is the arithmetic function $\mu: \Z_{>0} \to \set {-1, 0, 1}$ defined as: $\map \mu n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 1 \\ 0 & : \exists p \in \mathbb P: p^2 \divides n \\ \paren {-1}^k & : n = p_1 p_2 \ldots p_k: p_i \in \mathbb P \end {cases}$ where $\mathbb P$ denotes the set of all prime numbers. That is: {{eqn | l = \map \mu n | r = \paren {-1}^k | c = if $n$ has $k$ distinct prime divisors. }}

label: Definition:N-Cube (Euclidean Space)
snippet: Let $R, c \in \R$ be real numbers with $R > 0$. Let $\struct {\R^n, d}$ be a Euclidean $n$-Space equipped with the usual metric $d$. An $n$-cube is a subset of $\struct {\R^n, d}$ defined as the cartesian product of closed real intervals of the form: $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \closedint {c - R} {c + R}_i$ where $\closedint {c - R} {c + R}_i$ is an interval in the $i$th factor of $\R^n$. The $n$-cube can be concisely expressed as: $\closedint {c - R} {c + R}^n$ in contexts where the indices of the product are unimportant.

label: Definition:NP-Complete
snippet: A decision problem $L$ is NP-complete any problem in the NP complexity class can be reduced in polynomial time and space to $L$.

label: Definition:NP Complexity Class
snippet: In computability theory, $NP$ is a complexity class in which there exists some nondeterministic Turing machine that will either: halt within $\map p {\size x}$ steps or: run forever where: $p$ is a polynomial $\size x$ is the length of the input to the Machine.

label: Definition:Naive Set Theory
snippet: Naïve set theory, in contrast with axiomatic set theory, is an approach to set theory which assumes the existence of a universal set, despite the fact that such an assumption leads to paradoxes. A popular alternative (and inaccurate) definition describes this as: a non-formalized definition of set theory which describes sets and the relations between them using natural language. However, the discipline is founded upon quite as rigid a set of axioms, namely, those of propositional and predicate logic.

label: Definition:Natural Deduction
snippet: Natural deduction is a technique for deducing valid sequents from other valid sequents by applying precisely defined proof rules, by a technique called logical inference. As such, natural deduction forms a proof system, which is focused on practical applicability.

label: Definition:Natural Deduction/Rules of Inference

Let $\eta : F \to G$ and $\xi : G \to F$ be natural transformations such that the compositions $\xi \circ \eta = \operatorname{id}_F$ and $\eta \circ \xi = \operatorname{id}_G$ are identity natural transformations. label: Definition:Natural Language
snippet: A natural language is one of the conventional, everyday languages in which people usually communicate. Although there are many natural languages in the world, we are not generally going to distinguish between them, merely lumping them all into the one concept. When natural language is referred to on , it will usually mean English.

label: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Positive Real/Definition 2
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x > 0$. The (natural) logarithm of $x$ is defined as: $\ln x := y \in \R: e^y = x$ where $e$ is Euler's number. That is: $\ln x = \log_e x$

label: Definition:Natural Logarithm/Positive Real/Definition 3
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x > 0$. The (natural) logarithm of $x$ is defined as: $\ds \ln x := \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} n \paren {\sqrt [n] x - 1}$

label: Definition:Natural Numbers/Inductive Set Definition
snippet: Let $x$ be a set which is an element of every inductive set. Then $x$ is a natural number.

label: Definition:Natural Numbers/Inductive Sets in Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $\II$ be the set of all inductive sets defined as subsets of $\R$. Then the natural numbers $\N$ are defined as: $\N := \ds \bigcap \II$ where $\ds \bigcap$ denotes intersection. It follows from the definition of inductive set that according to this definition, $0 \notin \N$.

label: Definition:Natural Numbers/Non-Zero
snippet: The natural numbers are often defined so as to exclude zero: The set $\N \setminus \set 0$ is denoted $\N_{>0}$: $\N_{>0} = \set {1, 2, 3, \ldots}$

label: Definition:Naturally Ordered Semigroup
snippet: The concept of a naturally ordered semigroup is intended to capture the behaviour of the natural numbers $\N$, addition $+$ and the ordering $\le$ as they pertain to $\N$.

label: Definition:Near-Repdigit Prime
snippet: A near-repdigit prime is a prime number with at least $3$ digits such that all digits are the same except one.

label: Definition:Negative/Complex Number
snippet: As the Complex Numbers cannot be Ordered Compatibly with Ring Structure, the concept of a negative complex number, relative to a specified zero, is not defined. However, the negative of a complex number is defined as follows: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number. Then the negative of $z$ is defined as: $-z = -a - i b$

label: Definition:Negative/Integer
snippet: The negative integers comprise the set: $\set {0, -1, -2, -3, \ldots}$ As the set of integers is the Inverse Completion of Natural Numbers, it follows that elements of $\Z$ are the isomorphic images of the elements of equivalence classes of $\N \times \N$ where two tuples are equivalent if the difference between the two elements of each tuple is the same. Thus negative can be formally defined on $\Z$ as a relation induced on those equivalence classes as specified in the definition of integers.

label: Definition:Negative/Number
snippet: The concept of negative can be applied to the following sets of numbers: $(1): \quad$ The integers $\Z$ $(2): \quad$ The rational numbers $\Q$ $(3): \quad$ The real numbers $\R$ The Complex Numbers cannot be Ordered Compatibly with Ring Structure, so there is no such concept as a negative complex number.

label: Definition:Negative/Rational Number
snippet: The negative rational numbers are the set defined as: $\Q_{\le 0} := \set {x \in \Q: x \le 0}$ That is, all the rational numbers that are less than or equal to zero.

label: Definition:Negative/Real Number
snippet: The negative real numbers are the set defined as: $\R_{\le 0} := \set {x \in \R: x \le 0}$ That is, all the real numbers that are less than or equal to zero.

label: Definition:Negative Matrix
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\GF$ denote one of the standard number systems. Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ be a $m \times n$ matrix space over $\GF$. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an element of $\map \MM {m, n}$. Then the negative (matrix) of $\mathbf A$ is denoted and defined as: $-\mathbf A := \sqbrk {-a}_{m n}$ {{eqn | r = \sqbrk {-a}_{m n} | c = }} where: $-1 \mathbf A$ denotes the matrix scalar product of $-1$ with $\mathbf A$ $-a$ is the negative of $a$.

label: Definition:Negative Part
snippet: Let $X$ be a set, and let $f: X \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. Then the negative part of $f$, $f^-: X \to \overline \R$, is the extended real-valued function defined by: $\forall x \in X: \map {f^-} x := -\min \set {0, \map f x}$ where the minimum is taken with respect to the extended real ordering. That is: $\forall x \in X: \map {f^-} x := \begin {cases} -\map f x & : \map f x \le 0 \\ 0 & : \map f x > 0 \end {cases}$ Hence the negative part of $f$ is actually defined as a positive function.

label: Definition:Negative of Real Number
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number The negative of $x$ is denoted $-x$ and is defined as: $-x := y \in \R: x + y = 0$ That is, $-x$ is the additive inverse of $x$ in $\R$.

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $z_0 \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive real number. The $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $z_0$ is defined as: $\map {N_\epsilon} {z_0} := \set {z \in \C: \cmod {z - z_0} < \epsilon}$

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Metric Space)
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset of $A$. Let $x \in S$. Let there exist $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ such that the open $\epsilon$-ball at $x$ lies completely in $S$, that is: $\map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq S$ Then $S$ is a neighborhood of $x$ in $M$.

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Real Analysis)
snippet: Let $\alpha \in \R$ be a real number.

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Real Analysis)/Epsilon
snippet: Let $\alpha \in \R$ be a real number. On the real number line with the usual metric, the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $\alpha$ is defined as the open interval: $\map {N_\epsilon} \alpha := \openint {\alpha - \epsilon} {\alpha + \epsilon}$ where $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ is a (strictly) positive real number.

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Real Analysis)/Open Subset
snippet: Let $\alpha \in \R$ be a real number. Let $N_\alpha$ be a subset of $\R$ which contains (as a subset) an open real set which itself contains (as an element) $\alpha$. Then $N_\alpha$ is a neighborhood of $\alpha$.

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space.

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Topology)/Neighborhood defined as Open
snippet: Some authorities define a neighborhood of a set $A$ as what defines as an open neighborhood: $N_A$ is a neighborhood of $A$ $N_A$ is an open set of $T$ which itself contains $A$. That is, in order to be a neighborhood of $A$ in $T$, $N_A$ must not only be a subset of $T$, but also be an open set of $T$. However, this treatment is less common, and considered by many to be old-fashioned. When the term neighborhood is used on this site, it is assumed to be not necessarily open unless so specified.

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Topology)/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$ be a point of $S$. Let $N_x$ be a subset of $S$ which contains (as a subset) an open set of $T$ which itself contains (as an element) $x$. Then $N_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$. That is: $N_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$ $\exists U \in \tau: x \in U \subseteq N_x \subseteq S$

label: Definition:Neighborhood (Topology)/Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $N_A$ be a subset of $S$ which contains (as a subset) an open set of $T$ which itself contains (as a subset) $A$. Then $N_A$ is a neighborhood of $A$. That is: $N_A$ is a neighborhood of $A$ $\exists U \in \tau: A \subseteq U \subseteq N_A \subseteq S$

label: Definition:Neighborhood Basis
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$. Let $\BB$ be a set of neighborhoods of $x$. Then $\BB$ is a neighborhood basis at $x$ : For each neighborhood $N$ of $x$, there is an $M \in \BB$ such that $M \subseteq N$.

label: Definition:Neighborhood Filter
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space.

label: Definition:Neighborhood Filter/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$. Let $\NN_x$ be the set of all neighborhoods of $x$ in $T$. Then $\NN_x$ is the neighborhood filter of $x$ (in $T$).

label: Definition:Neighborhood Space
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. For each $x \in S$, let there be given a set $\NN_x$ of subsets of $S$ which satisfy the neighborhood space axioms: The sets $\NN_x$ are the neighborhoods of $x$ in $S$. Let $\NN$ be the set of open sets of $S$: $\NN = \leftset {U \subseteq S: U}$ is a neighborhood of each of its elements$\rightset {}$ The set $S$ together with $\NN$ is called a neighborhood space and is denoted $\struct {S, \NN}$.

label: Definition:Neighborhood Space Induced by Topological Space
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $S$, thus forming the topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$. For all $x \in S$, let $\NN_x$ be the neighborhood filter of $x$ in $S$. Let $\NN$ be the set of subsets of $S$ such that: $\forall N \in \NN: N$ is a neighborhood of each of its points Then $\struct {S, \NN}$ is the neighborhood space induced by $\struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Neighborhood Sub-Basis
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$. Let $\BB$ be a set of neighborhoods of $x$. Then $\BB$ is a neighborhood sub-basis of $x$ relative to $\tau$ : for each neighborhood $N$ of $x$, there exists a finite subset $K$ of $\BB$ such that $\bigcap K \subseteq N$.

label: Definition:Neighborhood of Infinity (Real Analysis)/Positive Infinity
snippet: A neighborhood of $+\infty$ is a subset of the set of real numbers $\R$ which contains an interval $\openint a \to$ for some $a \in \R$. That is, a subset which contains all sufficiently large real numbers.

label: Definition:Nested Interval Topology
snippet: Let $S = \openint 0 1$ denote the open real interval: $\openint 0 1 = \set {x \in \R: 0 0}: U_n := \openint 0 {1 - \dfrac 1 n}$ together with $\O$ and $S$ itself. Then $\tau$ is referred to as the nested interval topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the nested interval space.

label: Definition:Nested Rectangle Space
snippet: Consider the Euclidean plane $\EE$. Let $L_1$ denote the straight line $x = 1$. Let $L_2$ denote the straight line $x = -1$. For $n \in \N$, let $R_n$ denote the boundary of the rectangle in $\EE$ such that: the center of $R_n$ is at the origin the height of $R_n$ is $2 n$ the width of $R_n$ is $\dfrac {2 n} {n + 1}$ Let $S$ be the set: $S = L_1 \cup L_2 \cup \paren {\ds \bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} R_n}$ Let $\tau$ be the topology inherited from $\EE$ The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is known as the nested rectangle space. The topology is known as the nested rectangle topology.

label: Definition:Nested Sequence
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of subsets of $S$ such that either: $\forall k \in \N: S_k \subseteq S_{k + 1}$ or: $\forall k \in \N: S_k \supseteq S_{k + 1}$ Then $\family {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ is a nested sequence (of sets).

label: Definition:Net (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $T$ be a set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a net in $T$.

label: Definition:Network (Graph Theory)
snippet: A network $N = \struct {G, w}$ is: a graph or digraph $G = \struct {V, E}$ together with: a mapping $w: E \to \R$ from the edge set $E$ of $G$ into the set $\R$ of real numbers.

label: Definition:Network Cut
snippet: Let $\NN$ be a network with a source and a sink. A network cut of $\NN$ is a set of edges of $\NN$ whose removal would create two separate components with the source in one and the sink in the other.

label: Definition:Network Theory
snippet: Network theory is the branch of mathematics concerned with the structure and properties of networks.

label: Definition:Neusis Construction
snippet: A neusis construction is a technique of drawing geometric figures using only a neusis ruler and a compass.

label: Definition:Neusis Ruler
snippet: A neusis ruler is a straightedge on which two points have been marked with a specific fixed length between them.

label: Definition:New Element
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A new element for $S$ is a set that is not an element of $S$. By Set does not Contain Itself, it may be defined as $S$ itself.

Then $S$ is known as a Newtonian potential.

label: Definition:Niemytzki Plane
snippet: The Niemytzki plane is the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ defined as: {{eqn | l = S | r = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: y \ge 0} }} {{eqn | l = \map \BB {x, y} | r = \set {\map {B_r} {x, y} \cap S: r > 0} | c = if $x, y \in \R, y > 0$ }} {{eqn | l = \map \BB {x, 0} | r = \set {\map {B_r} {x, r} \cup \set {\tuple {x, 0} }: r > 0} | c = if $x \in \R$ }} {{eqn | l = \tau | r = \set {\bigcup \GG: \GG \subseteq \bigcup_{\tuple {x, y} \mathop \in S} \map \BB {x, y} } }} where $\map {B_r} {x, y}$ denotes the open $r$-ball of $\tuple {x, y}$ in the $\R^2$ Euclidean space.

label: Definition:Nilradical of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity.

label: Definition:Non-Archimedean/Metric
snippet: A metric $d$ on a metric space $X$ is non-Archimedean : $\map d {x, y} \le \max \set {\map d {x, z}, \map d {y, z} }$ for all $x, y, z \in X$.

label: Definition:Non-Empty Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Then $S$ is said to be non-empty $S$ has at least one element. By the , this may also be phrased as: $S \ne \O$ where $\O$ denotes the empty set. Many mathematical theorems and definitions require sets to be non-empty in order to avoid erratic results and inconsistencies.

label: Definition:Non-Empty Set/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Then $A$ is non-empty $A$ has at least one element.

label: Definition:Non-Euclidean Geometry
snippet: Non-Euclidean geometry is branch of geometry in which 's fifth postulate does not hold.

label: Definition:Non-Inertial Frame of Reference
snippet: Let $P$ a particle be stationary in a given frame of reference $F_1$. However, let $P$ also be accelerating in an inertial frame of reference $F_2$. Then $F_1$ is known as a non-inertial frame of reference.

label: Definition:Non-Negative Definite Mapping
snippet: Let $\C$ be the field of complex numbers. Let $\F$ be a subfield of $\C$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\F$ Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \mathbb F$ be a mapping. Then $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \mathbb F$ is non-negative definite : $\forall x \in V: \innerprod x x \in \R_{\ge 0}$ That is, the image of $\innerprod x x$ is always a non-negative real number.

label: Definition:Non-Null Ring
snippet: A non-null ring is a ring with more than one element.

label: Definition:Non-Pythagorean Prime
snippet: A non-Pythagorean prime is an odd prime number of the form: $p = 4 n + 3$ where $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ is a positive integer.

label: Definition:Nonconstructive Proof
snippet: A nonconstructive proof is a proof in which there does not exist an effective procedure for the construction of every object in it. That is, such that it requires an infinite number of steps to complete.

label: Definition:Noncototient
snippet: A noncototient is a positive integer $n$ such that: $\nexists m \in \Z_{>0}: m - \map \phi m = n$ where $\map \phi m$ denotes the Euler $\phi$ function. That is, a noncototient is a positive integer which is not the cototient of any positive integer.

label: Definition:Nondegenerate Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. A bilinear form on $V$ which is not degenerate is nondegenerate.

label: Definition:Nondeterministic Turing Machine
snippet: A nondeterministic Turing machine (NTM) is a variation of the classical Turing machine that relaxes the restriction that all the steps in the machine must be definite. That is, given a single internal state and a single character being read on the tape the machine may have more than one possible response. If any sequence of choices puts the machine into a halting state, then the machine stops after $n$ steps, where $n$ is the minimum number of steps needed to put the machine into a halting state.

label: Definition:Nonhomogeneous Linear Second Order ODE
snippet: A nonhomogeneous linear second order ODE is a differential equation which is in (or can be manipulated into) the form: $\dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + \map P x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \map Q x y = \map R x$ where: $\map P x$, $\map Q x$ and $\map R x$ are functions of $x$ alone (or constants) $\map R x$ is not the zero constant function. That is, a nonhomogeneous linear second order ODE is a linear second order ODE which is not homogeneous.

label: Definition:Nonlinear System
snippet: A nonlinear system is a system of differential equations which are nonlinear.

label: Definition:Nonparametric Method
snippet: A nonparametric method is a technique for statistical investigation in which no assumptions are made about any parameters.

label: Definition:Nonsingular Matrix
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ be an element of the ring of square matrices $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$.

label: Definition:Nonsingular Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Nonsingular Matrix: Also known as == Nonsingular matrix can also be seen hyphenated: non-singular matrix. A nonsingular matrix is also called by some authors: an invertible matrix a regular matrix.

label: Definition:Nonstandard Analysis
snippet: Nonstandard analysis is an approach to analysis which allows for the existence of infinitesimals, placing them on a rigorous logical foundation.

label: Definition:Nontotient
snippet: A nontotient is a positive even integer $n$ such that: $\nexists m \in \Z_{>0}: \map \phi m = n$ where $\map \phi m$ denotes the Euler $\phi$ function. That is, a nontotient is a positive even integer which is not the totient of any positive integer.

snippet: Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed interval of the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $\Delta = \set {x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{n - 1}, x_n}$ form a finite subdivision of $\closedint a b$. Then the norm of $\Delta$ is defined as: $\max \set {x_1 - x_0, x_2 - x_1, \ldots, x_n - x_{n - 1} }$ and is denoted $\norm \Delta$.

label: Definition:Normal Distribution
snippet: thumb Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Then $X$ has a normal distribution the probability density function of $X$ is: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {\sigma \sqrt {2 \pi} } \map \exp {-\dfrac {\paren {x - \mu}^2} {2 \sigma^2} }$ for $\mu \in \R, \sigma \in \R_{> 0}$. This is written: $X \sim \Gaussian \mu {\sigma^2}$

label: Definition:Normal Family
snippet: Let $X = \struct {M_1, d_1}$ and $Y = \struct {M_2, d_2}$ be complete metric spaces. Let $\FF = \family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of continuous mappings $f_i: X \to Y$. Then $\FF$ is a normal family : every sequence of mappings in $\FF$ contains a subsequence which converges uniformly on compact subsets of $X$ to a continuous function $f: X \to Y$.

label: Definition:Normal Neighborhood
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold without boundary. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $\EE$ be the domain of the exponential map. Let $\EE_p = \EE \cap T_p M$. Let $\exp_p : \EE_p \to M$ be the restricted exponential map. Let $U_p \subseteq M$ be a neighborhood of $p \in M$. Suppose $U_p$ is the diffeomorphic image of $\exp_p$ of a star-shaped neighborhood of $0 \in T_p M$. Then $U_p$ is called a normal neighborhood of $p$.

label: Definition:Normal Number
snippet: A real number $r$ is normal with respect to a number base $b$ its basis expansion in number base $b$ is such that: no finite sequence of digits of $r$ of length $n$ occurs more frequently than any other such finite sequence of length $n$. In particular, for number base $b$, all digits of $r$ have the same natural density in the basis expansion of $r$.

label: Definition:Normal Operator
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\mathbf T: \HH \to \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Then $\mathbf T$ is said to be normal : $\mathbf T^* \mathbf T = \mathbf T \mathbf T^*$ where $\mathbf T^*$ denotes the adjoint of $\mathbf T$.

label: Definition:Normal Series
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. A normal series for $G$ is a sequence of (normal) subgroups of $G$: $\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_n = G$ where $G_{i - 1} \lhd G_i$ denotes that $G_{i - 1}$ is a proper normal subgroup of $G_i$.

label: Definition:Normal Series/Factor Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n}$ be a normal series for $G$: $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n} = \tuple {\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_{n - 1} \lhd G_n = G}$ The factor groups of $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n}$: $\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_n = G$ are the quotient groups: $G_1 / G_0, G_2 / G_1, \ldots, G_i / G_{i - 1}, \ldots, G_n / G_{n-1}$

label: Definition:Normal Series/Length
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n}$ be a normal series for $G$: $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n} = \tuple {\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_{n-1} \lhd G_n = G}$ The length of $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n}$ is the number of (normal) subgroups which make it. In this context, the length of $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n}$ is $n$. If such a normal series is infinite, then its length is not defined. Category:Definitions/Normal Series

snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $N$ be a subgroup of $G$. $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ : $\forall g \in G: g \circ N = N \circ g$ where $g \circ N$ denotes the subset product of $g$ with $N$.

snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $N$ be a subgroup of $G$. $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ : {{eqn | q = \forall g \in G | l = g \circ N \circ g^{-1} | o = \subseteq | r = N }} or, equivalently: {{eqn | q = \forall g \in G | l = g^{-1} \circ N \circ g | o = \subseteq | r = N }} where $g \circ N$ etc. denotes the subset product of $g$ with $N$.

Let $N$ be a subgroup of $G$. $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ : {{eqn | q = \forall g \in G | l = \leftparen {n \in N} | o = \iff | r = \rightparen {g \circ n \circ g^{-1} \in N} }} or, equivalently: {{eqn | q = \forall g \in G | l = \leftparen {n \in N} | o = \iff | r = \rightparen {g^{-1} \circ n \circ g \in N} }}

A normal subgroup is often represented by the letter $N$, as opposed to $H$ (which is used for a general subgroup which may or may not be normal). To use the notation introduced in the definition of the conjugate: $N \lhd G \iff \forall g \in G: N^g = N$ Category:Definitions/Normal Subgroups

label: Definition:Normal Vector
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface in ordinary $3$-space. Let $P$ be a point of $S$. Let $\mathbf n$ be a vector whose initial point is at $P$ such that $\mathbf n$ is perpendicular to $S$ at $P$. Then $\mathbf n$ is a normal vector to $S$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Normal to Curve
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve embedded in the plane. The normal to $C$ at a point $P$ is defined as the straight line which lies perpendicular to the tangent to $C$ at $P$ and in the same plane as $P$.

label: Definition:Normal to Surface
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface embedded in $3$-dimensional space. The normal to $S$ at a point $P$ is defined as the straight line which lies perpendicular to the tangent plane to $S$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Normalized Weight Function
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $\map W x$ be a weight function to be applied to the elements of $S$. Then $W$ is defined as being normalized : $\ds \sum_x \map W x = 1$ Category:Definitions/Algebra Category:Definitions/Statistics

label: Definition:Normalizer
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $S$ be a subset of $G$. Then the normalizer of $S$ in $G$ is the set $\map {N_G} S$ defined as: $\map {N_G} S := \set {a \in G: S^a = S}$ where $S^a$ is the $G$-conjugate of $S$ by $a$. If $S$ is a singleton such that $S = \set s$, we may also write $\map {N_G} s$ for $\map {N_G} S = \map {N_G} {\set s}$, as long as there is no possibility of confusion.

label: Definition:North Celestial Pole
snippet: Let $O$ be a celestial observer situated at the surface of Earth in the Northern hemisphere. Let $OP$ be a straight line parallel to Earth's axis. Let $P$ be the point in the visible hemisphere at which $OP$ meets the celestial sphere. Then $P$ is the north celestial pole. That is, the north celestial pole is the pole of the celestial equator which is the zenith of the North Pole. 480px In the above diagram, the north celestial pole is indicated by $P$.

label: Definition:North Point of Horizon
snippet: The point on the celestial horizon through which the principal vertical circle passes is called the north point of the horizon. 480px In the above diagram, the north point of the horizon is indicated by $N$.

label: Definition:Northern Hemisphere
snippet: The northern hemisphere of Earth is the hemisphere between the equator and the North Pole. Points in the northern hemisphere have latitude between $0 \degrees \, \mathrm N$ (the equator itself) and $90 \degrees \, \mathrm N$ (the North Pole).

label: Definition:Nowhere Dense

label: Definition:Nowhere Dense/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. $H$ is nowhere dense in $T$ : $H^-$ contains no open set of $T$ which is non-empty where $H^-$ denotes the closure of $H$.

label: Definition:Nth Root of Positive Element of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $x \in A$ be positive. We define the $n$th root $x^{1/n}$ of $x$ to be the unique positive element $y \in A$ such that $y^n = x$.

label: Definition:Null Hypothesis
snippet: In the context of a hypothesis test, the null hypothesis, usually denoted $H_0$ or $\mathrm H_0$, is the hypothesis which has been proposed for investigation.

label: Definition:Null Relation
snippet: The null relation is a relation $\RR$ in $S$ to $T$ such that $\RR$ is the empty set: $\RR \subseteq S \times T: \RR = \O$ That is, no element of $S$ relates to any element in $T$: $\RR: S \times T: \forall \tuple {s, t} \in S \times T: \neg s \mathrel \RR t$

label: Definition:Null Sequence
snippet: A null sequence is a sequence which converges to zero.

label: Definition:Null Sequence/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a sequence in $\C$ which converges to a limit of $0$: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} z_n = 0$ Then $\sequence {z_n}$ is called a (complex) null sequence. Category:Definitions/Null Sequences Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

label: Definition:Null Sequence/Normed Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed division ring with zero $0_R$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$ which converges to the limit $0_R$: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = 0_R$ Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is called a null sequence.

label: Definition:Null Sequence/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$ which converges to a limit of $0$: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n = 0$ Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is called a (real) null sequence.

label: Definition:Null Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. A set $N \in \Sigma$ is called a ($\mu$-)null set $\map \mu N = 0$.
