label: Definition:Null String
snippet: A null string is a string with no symbols in it. In particular, the null string is a word. The null string can be denoted $\epsilon$.

label: Definition:Number
snippet: There are five main classes of number: $(1): \quad$ The natural numbers: $\N = \set {0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ $(1 \text a): \quad$ The non-zero natural numbers: $\N_{>0} = \set {1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ $(2): \quad$ The integers: $\Z = \set {\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ $(3): \quad$ The rational numbers: $\Q = \set {p / q: p, q \in \Z, q \ne 0}$ $(4): \quad$ The real numbers: $\R = \set {x: x = \sequence {s_n} }$ where $\sequence {s_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\Q$ $(5): \quad$ The complex numbers: $\C = \set {a + i b: a, b \in \R, i^2 = -1}$ It is possible to categorize numbers further, for…

label: Definition:Number-Naming System
snippet: There are various number-naming systems for naming large numbers (that is: greater than $1 \, 000 \, 000$).

label: Definition:Number Base/Integer Part
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \ge 0$. Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. In the basis expansion: $x = \left[{r_m r_{m-1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0 . d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}\right]_b$ the part $r_m r_{m-1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0$ is known as the integer part.

label: Definition:Number Base/Integers
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $b \in \Z$ be an integer such that $b > 1$. By the Basis Representation Theorem, $n$ can be expressed uniquely in the form: $\ds n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m r_j b^j$ where: $m$ is such that $b^m \le n < b^{m + 1}$ all the $r_j$ are such that $0 \le r_j < b$. The number $b$ is known as the number base to which $n$ is represented. $n$ is thus described as being (written) in base $b$. Thus we can write $\ds n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m {r_j b^j}$ as: $\sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}_b$ or, if the context is clear: ${r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}_b$

label: Definition:Number Base/Radix Point
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \ge 0$. Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. In the basis expansion: $x = \sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0 \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ the dot that separates the integer part from the fractional part is called the radix point.

label: Definition:Number Field
snippet: A number field is a subfield of the field of complex numbers.

label: Definition:Number System
snippet: A number system is a technique for representing numbers.

label: Definition:Number Theory
snippet: Number theory is the branch of mathematics which studies the properties of the integers, and by extension the rational numbers and related number systems.

label: Definition:Numeral
snippet: A numeral is a symbol which is used to identify a particular number (usually a natural number). A numeral is one of a small subset of the numbers. Other numbers can be created by combining numeral using specific well-defined rules.

label: Definition:Numerators and Denominators of Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $n \in \N \cup \set \infty$ be an extended natural number. Let $C = \sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ be a continued fraction in $F$ of length $n$.

label: Definition:Numerical Analysis
snippet: Numerical analysis is the branch of applied mathematics concerned with the processes by which certain kinds of numerical solutions to problems in (mainly) physics.

label: Definition:Numerical Integration Rule
snippet: A numerical integration rule is a formula for implementing a technique of using numerical integration.

label: Definition:Object
snippet: An object is a thing. Everything that can be talked about in mathematics and logic can be referred to as an object.

label: Definition:Object (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. An object of $\mathbf C$ is an object which is considered to be atomic from a category theoretic perspective.

label: Definition:Object Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. An object functor $F$ assigns to each object $X$ of $\mathbf C$ an object $F X$ of $\mathbf D$.

label: Definition:Oblique Coordinate System
snippet: An oblique coordinate system is a coordinate system in which the position of a point is determined by its relation to a set of straight coordinate axes which are oblique. 400px

label: Definition:Observation
snippet: An observation is an item of raw data that has been obtained as the result of measurement or counting. Hence it is a particular value taken by a variable in statistics.

label: Definition:Obstinate Number
snippet: An obstinate number is a positive odd integer which cannot be expressed as the sum of a power of $2$ and a prime.

label: Definition:Obtuse Angle
snippet: An obtuse angle is an angle which has a measurement between those of a right angle and a straight angle. Note that did not consider the concept of reflex angles.

label: Definition:Octagon/Regular
snippet: A regular octagon is an octagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with $8$ sides. That is, an octagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: 300px

label: Definition:Octagonal Number
snippet: Octagonal numbers are those denumerating a collection of objects which can be arranged in the form of a regular octagon. They can be denoted: $O_1, O_2, O_3, \ldots$

label: Definition:Octahedron/Regular
snippet: 300px A regular octahedron is an octahedron whose $8$ faces are all congruent equilateral triangles. It has: $6$ vertices $12$ edges $8$ faces The regular octahedron is an example of a deltahedron.

label: Definition:Octal Notation
snippet: Octal notation is the positional number system whose base is $8$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 8^j$ where: $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}$

label: Definition:Octonion
snippet: The set of octonions, usually denoted $\Bbb O$, can be defined by using the Cayley-Dickson construction from the quaternions $\H$ as follows: From Quaternions form Algebra, $\H$ forms a nicely normed $*$-algebra. Let $a, b \in \H$. Then $\tuple {a, b} \in \Bbb O$, where: $\tuple {a, b} \tuple {c, d} = \tuple {a c - d \overline b, \overline a d + c b}$ $\overline {\tuple {a, b} } = \tuple {\overline a, -b}$ where: $\overline a$ is the conjugate of $a$ and $\overline {\tuple {a, b} }$ is the conjugation operation on $\Bbb O$.

label: Definition:Odd-Even Topology
snippet: Let $\Z_{>0}$ denote the set of strictly positive integers: $\Z_{>0} = \set {x \in \Z: x > 0}$ Let $\PP$ be the partition on $\Z_{>0}$ defined as: $\PP = \set {\set {2 k - 1, 2 k}: k \in \Z_{>0} }$ That is: $\PP = \set {\set {1, 2}, \set {3, 4}, \set {5, 6}, \ldots}$ Then the topology whose basis is $\PP$ is called the odd-even topology, and its topological space is the odd-even space.

label: Definition:Odd Integer/Odd-Times Odd
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$, i.e. let $n$ be an integer.

label: Definition:Odd Prime
snippet: Every even integer is divisible by $2$ (because this is the definition of even). Therefore, apart from $2$ itself, all primes are odd. So, referring to an odd prime is a convenient way of specifying that a number is a prime number, but not equal to $2$.

label: Definition:Odds
snippet: Let $A$ be an event. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p$.

label: Definition:Odds/On
snippet: Let $A$ be an event. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p$. The odds on $A$ is defined as: $\dfrac p {1 - p}$ where $1 - p$ is the probability of $A$ not occurring.

label: Definition:Odds Ratio
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be events. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p_A$ and the probability of $B$ occurring be $p_B$. The odds ratio of $A$ to $B$ is given by: $\theta = \dfrac {\theta_A} {\theta_B}$ where: $\theta_A$ is the odds on $A$: $\theta_A = \dfrac {p_A} {1 - p_A}$ $\theta_B$ is the odds on $B$: $\theta_B = \dfrac {p_B} {1 - p_B}$

label: Definition:Ohm
snippet: The ohm is the SI unit of electrical resistance. It is defined as being the electrical resistance between two points of an electrical conductor when a constant electric potential of $1$ volt, applied to these points, produces in the conductor an electric current of $1$ ampere, the conductor not being the seat of any electromotive force.

label: Definition:Omega-Accumulation Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. An $\omega$-accumulation point of $A$ is a limit point $x$ of $A$ such that every open set containing $x$ also contains an infinite number of points of $A$.

label: Definition:One
snippet: The immediate successor element of zero in the set of natural numbers $\N$ is called one and has the symbol $1$.

label: Definition:One-Parameter Family of Curves on Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I, J \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\Gamma : I \times J \to M$ be a continuous map, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Then $\Gamma$ is called the one-parameter family of curves on $M$.

label: Definition:One-Sided Shift of Finite Type
snippet: Let $k \in \Z_{\ge 2}$. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{kk}$ be a logical matrix. Let $\Sigma = \set {1, 2, \ldots, k}$. Let: $X_\mathbf A ^+ = \set {x = \sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} : x_n \in \Sigma, a_{x_n, x_{n + 1} } = 1}$ Let $\sigma : X_\mathbf A ^+ \to X_\mathbf A ^+$ be the forward shift operator. Then the pair $\struct {X _\mathbf A ^+, \sigma}$ is called a one-sided shift of finite type.

label: Definition:One-to-One Relation
snippet: A relation $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ is one-to-one if it is both many-to-one and one-to-many. That is, every element of the domain of $\RR$ relates to no more than one element of its codomain, and every element of the image is related to by exactly one element of its domain.

label: Definition:One (Cardinal)
snippet: The cardinal associated with the singleton $\set \O$ is called one, and is denoted $1$. More informally, this means that one is defined as being the number of elements in a singleton set.

label: Definition:One (Category)
snippet: The category one $\mathbf 1$, is the category with: {{DefineCategory |ob = One object: $*$ |mor = One morphism: the identity morphism $\operatorname{id}_*$. }}

label: Definition:One (Ordinal)
snippet: The ordinal $1$ is defined as: $1 = 0^+$ where $0^+$ denotes the successor of the ordinal $0$.

label: Definition:Ones Matrix
snippet: A ones matrix is a matrix all of whose elements are $1$.

label: Definition:Open Ball
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$ in $M$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} a := \set {x \in A: \map d {x, a} < \epsilon}$ where $d$ is the distance function on $M$. If it is necessary to show the distance function itself, then the notation $\map {B_\epsilon} {a; d}$ can be used.

label: Definition:Open Ball/Center
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $a$ is referred to as the center of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

label: Definition:Open Ball/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $x \in X$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $\struct {X, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} x = \set {y \in X: 
orm{x - y} < \epsilon}$

label: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers
snippet:
Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$ in $\struct {\Q_p, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in \Q_p: 
orm{x - a}_p < \epsilon}$

label: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers/Center
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $a$ is referred to as the center of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

label: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers/Radius
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $\epsilon$ is referred to as the radius of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

label: Definition:Open Ball/Radius
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $\epsilon$ is referred to as the radius of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

label: Definition:Open Ball/Real Analysis
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $\R^n$ denote the real Euclidean space of dimension $n$. Let $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$ denote the Euclidean norm. Let $a \in \R^n$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open (Euclidean) ball of center $a$ and radius $\epsilon$ is the subset: $\map {B_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in \R^n : \norm {x - a} < \epsilon}$

label: Definition:Open Cover
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\CC$ be a cover for $S$. Then $\CC$ is an open cover (of $T$) : $\CC \subseteq \tau$ That is, all the elements of $\CC$ are open sets.

label: Definition:Open Cover/Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H$ be a subset of $S$. Let $\CC$ be a cover of $H$. Then $\CC$ is an open cover for $H$ : $\CC \subseteq \tau$ That is, all the elements of $\CC$ are open sets.

label: Definition:Open Extension Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $p$ be a new element which is not in $S$. Let $S^*_p = S \cup \set p$. Let $\tau^*_p$ be the set defined as: $\tau^*_{\bar p} = \set {U: U \in \tau} \cup \set {S^*_p}$ That is, $\tau^*_{\bar p}$ is the set of all sets formed by taking all the open sets of $\tau$ and adding to them the set $S^*_p$. Then: $\tau^*_{\bar p}$ is the open extension topology of $\tau$ and: $T^*_{\bar p} = \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_{\bar p} }$ is the open extension space of $T = \struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Open Geodesic Ball in Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$. Let $\exp_p$ be the restricted exponential map. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} 0 \subseteq T_p M$ be the open ball in $T_p M$ with $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ such that $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism from $\map {B_\epsilon} 0$ to its image. Then the image set $\map {\exp_p} {\map {B_\epsilon} 0 }$ is called the open geodesic ball in $M$.

label: Definition:Open Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is said to be an open mapping : $\forall U \in \tau_1: f \sqbrk U \in \tau_2$ where $f \sqbrk U$ denotes the image of $U$ under $f$.

label: Definition:Open Neighborhood
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $N_A$ be a neighborhood of $A$. Let: $N_A \in \tau$ That is, let $N_A$ itself be an open set of $T$. Then $N_A$ is called an open neighborhood of $A$ in $T$.

label: Definition:Open Neighborhood/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$ be a point of $S$. Let $N_x$ be a neighborhood of $x$ in $T$. Let: $N_x \in \tau$ That is, let $N_x$ itself be an open set of $T$. Then $N_x$ is called an open neighborhood of $x$ in $T$.

label: Definition:Open Point
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $p \in S$ such that $\left\{{p}\right\} \in \tau$. That is, let $\left\{{p}\right\}$ be an open set of $T$. Then $p$ is an open point of $T$.

label: Definition:Open Rectangle
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $a_1, \ldots, a_n, b_1, \ldots, b_n$ be real numbers. The Cartesian product: $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \openint {a_i} {b_i} = \openint {a_1} {b_1} \times \cdots \times \openint {a_n} {b_n} \subseteq \R^n$ is called an open rectangle in $\R^n$ or open $n$-rectangle. The collection of all open $n$-rectangles is denoted $\JJ_o$, or $\JJ_o^n$ if the dimension $n$ is to be emphasized.

label: Definition:Open Refinement
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ and $\VV$ be covers of $S$. Then $\VV$ is an open refinement of $\UU$ : That is:

label: Definition:Open Region/Complex
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. $D$ is an open region of $\C$ $D$ is: $(1): \quad$ An open set and $(2): \quad$ connected.

label: Definition:Open Set/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $U \subseteq A$. Then $U$ is an open set in $M$ it is a neighborhood of each of its elements. That is: $\forall y \in U: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} y \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} y$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$. That is, for every point $y$ in $U$, we can find an $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$, dependent on that $y$, such that the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$ lies entirely inside $U$. Another way of saying the same thing is that one can not get out of $U$ by moving an arbitrarily small distance from any point in $U$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $V = \struct {X, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $U \subseteq X$. Then $U$ is an open set in $V$ : $\forall x \in U: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} x$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Pseudometric Space
snippet: Let $P = \struct {A, d}$ be a pseudometric space. An open set in $P$ is defined in exactly the same way as for a metric space: $U$ is an open set in $P$ : $\forall y \in U: \exists \map \epsilon y > 0: \map {B_\epsilon} y \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} y$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Real Analysis/Real Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $U \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset. Then $U$ is open (in $\R^n$) : $\forall x \in U : \exists R \in \R_{>0}: \map B {x, R} \subset U$ where $\map B {x, R}$ denotes the open Euclidean ball of radius $R$ centered at $x$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Real Analysis/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the set of real numbers. Then $I$ is open (in $\R$) : $\forall x_0 \in I: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \openint {x_0 - \epsilon} {x_0 + \epsilon} \subseteq I$ where $\openint {x_0 - \epsilon} {x_0 + \epsilon}$ is an open interval. Note that $\epsilon$ may depend on $x_0$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then the elements of $\tau$ are called the open sets of $T$. Thus: $U \in \tau$ and: $U$ is open in $T$ are equivalent statements.

label: Definition:Operation
snippet: An operation is an object, identified by a symbol, which can be interpreted as a process which, from a number of objects, creates a new object.

label: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation
snippet: A binary operation is the special case of an operation where the operation has exactly two operands. A binary operation is a mapping $\circ$ from the Cartesian product of two sets $S \times T$ to a universal set $\mathbb U$: $\circ: S \times T \to \mathbb U: \map \circ {s, t} = y \in \mathbb U$ If $S = T$, then $\circ$ can be referred to as a binary operation on $S$.

label: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\circ$ be the operation on $\struct {S, \circ}$. Let $z = x \circ y$. Then $z$ is called the product of $x$ and $y$. This is an extension of the normal definition of product that is encountered in conventional arithmetic.

label: Definition:Operation/N-Ary Operation
snippet: Let $S_1, S_2, \dots, S_n$ be sets. Let $\circ: S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n \to \mathbb U$ be a mapping from the cartesian product $S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$ to a universal set $\mathbb U$: That is, suppose that: $\circ: S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n \to \mathbb U: \forall \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n: \map \circ {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in \mathbb U$ Then $\circ$ is an $n$-ary operation. Such an $n$-ary operation needs to be defined for all ordered tuples in $S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$.

label: Definition:Operation/Unary Operation
snippet: A unary operation is the special case of an operation where the operation has exactly one operand. Thus, a unary operation on a set $S$ is a mapping whose domain and codomain are both $S$.

label: Definition:Operation Induced by Permutation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure on a set $S$. Let $\sigma: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. Let $\circ_\sigma$ be the operation on $S$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: x \circ_\sigma y := \map \sigma {x \circ y}$ Then $\circ_\sigma$ is the operation (on $S$) induced by $\sigma$.

label: Definition:Operation Induced by Restriction
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $\struct {T, \circ} \subseteq \struct {S, \circ}$. That is, let $T$ be a subset of $S$ such that $\circ$ is closed in $T$. Then the restriction of $\circ$ to $T$, namely $\circ {\restriction_T}$, is called the (binary) operation induced on $T$ by $\circ$. Note that this definition applies only if $\struct {T, \circ}$ is closed, by which virtue it is a submagma of $\struct {S, \circ}$.

label: Definition:Operations Research
snippet: Operations research is the branch of applied mathematics which studies the management of human organizations.

label: Definition:Operator Norm
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A: \HH \to \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $\norm A$ be the norm of $A$. Then $\norm A$ is referred to as the operator norm on $A$. Category:Definitions/Hilbert Spaces

label: Definition:Operator Theory
snippet: Operator theory is the study of linear operators on function spaces, beginning with differential operators and integral operators.

label: Definition:Opposite
snippet: Geometry: Opposite (in a Polygon): The opposite side (or angle) to a given side is that side (or angle) which has the same number of sides between it and the side in question. The opposite side (or angle) to a given angle is that side (or angle) which has the same number of sides between it and the angle in question. Opposite (in a Triangle): The side of a triangle which is not one of the sides adjacent to a particular angle is referred to as its opposite. Thus, each angle has an opposite side, and each side has an opposite angle.

label: Definition:Opposite Direction
snippet: Let $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ be vectors in space. We say that $\mathbf v$ is in the opposite direction to $\mathbf w$ : the lines of action of $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ are parallel but at the same time: the lines of action of $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ are not the same. Category:Definitions/Vectors

label: Definition:Optimization Theory
snippet: Optimization theory is a branch of mathematics whose aim is to find the "best" solution to a practical problem, often using techniques of numerical analysis. In this context, best is dependent upon the aim of what the solution of the problem is to achieve. Optimization theory encompasses such topics as: the calculus of variations control theory convex optimization theory decision theory game theory linear programming Markov chains network analysis queueing theory and so on.

label: Definition:Optimum Solution
snippet: The optimum solution of a problem in linear programming or optimization theory is the feasible solution which, according to the definition of the problem, is the most desirable.

label: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$.

label: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Length
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. Let $x \in X$. Let $\Orb x$ be the orbit of $x$. The length of the orbit $\Orb x$ of $x$ is the number of elements of $X$ it contains: $\size {\Orb x}$ Category:Definitions/Group Actions

label: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Set of Orbits
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $X$ be a set Let $*: G \times S \to S$ be a group action. Let $\Orb x$ denote the orbit of $x \in X$. From Group Action Induces Equivalence Relation, the relation $\RR_G$ defined as: $x \mathrel {\RR_G} y \iff y \in \Orb x$ is an equivalence relation. The quotient set $X / \RR_G$ is called the set of orbits of $X$ under the action of $G$.

label: Definition:Orbit (Physics)
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in space. The orbit of $A$ around $B$ is the path taken by $A$ as it travels around $B$ under the influence of the force acting between $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Orbit (Physics)/Period
snippet: Let body $A$ be in orbit around body $B$. The period of the orbit is the length of time it takes for $A$ to travel once around $B$ and return to its original position.

label: Definition:Order
snippet: Set Theory: Order of Set: Another word for the cardinality of a set. Abstract Algebra: Order of an Algebraic Structure Group Theory: Order of an Element in a Group Matrix Theory and Linear Algebra: Order of a Matrix Order of a Square Matrix Order of a Determinant Tensor Theory: Order of a Tensor: another term for the rank of a tensor. Number Theory: Multiplicative Order of an Integer: the least positive integer $c$ such that $a^c \equiv 1 \pmod n$. Order of a Sociable Chain: the number of members of a sociable chain.

label: Definition:Order Completion
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ be an ordered set. An ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$ is an order completion of $S$ : $(1):\quad S \subseteq T$ $(2):\quad {\preceq_T \restriction_S} = {\preceq_S}$, where $\restriction$ denotes restriction $(3):\quad \struct {T, \preceq_T}$ is a complete ordered set $(4):\quad$ For all ordered sets $\struct {T', \preceq_{T'} }$ satisfying $(1), (2)$ and $(3)$, there is a unique increasing injection $\phi: T' \to T$

label: Definition:Order Generating Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is order generating : $\forall x \in S: x^\succeq \cap X$ admits an infimum and $x = \map \inf {x^\succeq \cap X}$

label: Definition:Order Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets.

label: Definition:Order of Convergence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence of numbers or vectors in a normed vector space. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Let $p \in \R_{\ge 1}$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $\alpha$ with order $p$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {\epsilon_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $(1): \quad \size {x_n - \alpha} \le \epsilon_n$ for every $n \in \N$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\epsilon_{n + 1} } { {\epsilon_n}^p} = c$ where $c > 0$ If $p = 1$, the constant $c$ is additionally required to be less than $1$.

label: Definition:Order of Pole
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function.

label: Definition:Order of Pole/Simple Pole
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is holomorphic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$, with a pole at $z_0$. Let the order of the pole at $z_0$ be $1$. Then $z_0$ is a simple pole.

label: Definition:Order of Structure
snippet: The order of an algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is the cardinality of its underlying set, and is denoted $\order S$. Thus, for a finite set $S$, the order of $\struct {S, \circ}$ is the number of elements in $S$.

label: Definition:Order of Structure/Finite Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let the underlying set $S$ of $\struct {S, \circ}$ be finite. Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ a finite structure. That is, $\struct {S, \circ}$ is a finite structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is not an infinite structure.

label: Definition:Ordered Basis
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a free $R$-module. An ordered basis of $G$ is a sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ of elements of $G$ such that $\set {a_1, \ldots, a_n}$ is a basis of $G$.

label: Definition:Ordered Monoid
snippet: An ordered monoid is an ordered structure $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ such that $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a monoid.

label: Definition:Ordered Pair
snippet: The definition of a set does not take any account of the order in which the elements are listed. That is, $\set {a, b} = \set {b, a}$, and the elements $a$ and $b$ have the same status - neither is distinguished above the other as being more "important".

label: Definition:Ordered Pair/Kuratowski Formalization
snippet: The definition of a set does not take any account of the order in which the elements are listed. That is, $\set {a, b} = \set {b, a}$, and the elements $a$ and $b$ have the same status - neither is distinguished above the other as being more "important". The concept of an ordered pair can be formalized by the definition: $\tuple {a, b} := \set {\set a, \set {a, b} }$ This formalization justifies the existence of ordered pairs in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.

label: Definition:Ordered Set
snippet: An ordered set is a relational structure $\struct {S, \preceq}$ such that the relation $\preceq$ is an ordering. Such a structure may be: A partially ordered set (poset) A totally ordered set (toset) A well-ordered set (woset) depending on whether the ordering $\preceq$ is: A partial ordering A total ordering A well-ordering.

label: Definition:Ordered Set of All Mappings
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $X$ be a set. The ordered set of all mappings from $X$ to $L$ is defined by: $L^X := \struct {S^X, \precsim}$ where $\forall f, g \in S^X: f \precsim g \iff f \preceq g$ $\preceq$ denotes the ordering on mappings, $S^X$ denotes the set of all mappings from $X$ into $S$.

label: Definition:Ordered Structure Monomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ and $\struct {T, *, \preccurlyeq}$ be ordered structures. An ordered structure monomorphism from $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ to $\struct {T, *, \preccurlyeq}$ is a mapping $\phi: S \to T$ that is both: $(1): \quad$ A monomorphism, i.e. an injective homomorphism, from the structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ to the structure $\struct {T, *}$ $(2): \quad$ An order embedding from the ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ to the ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$.

label: Definition:Ordered Subset

snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $\N^*_n$ be the first $n$ non-zero natural numbers: $\N^*_n := \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple as Ordered Set
snippet: The rigorous definition of an ordered tuple is as a finite sequence whose domain is $\N^*_n$. However, it is possible to treat an ordered tuple as an extension of the concept of an ordered pair.

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple as Ordered Set/Ordered Triple
snippet: The ordered triple $\tuple {a, b, c}$ of elements $a$, $b$ and $c$ can be defined either as the ordered pair: $\tuple {a, \tuple {b, c} }$ or as the ordered pair: $\tuple {\tuple {a, b}, c}$ where $\tuple {a, b}$ and $\tuple {b, c}$ are themselves ordered pairs. Whichever definition is chosen does not matter much, as long as it is understood which is used. And even then, the importance is limited.

label: Definition:Ordering/Notation
snippet: Symbols used to denote a general ordering relation are usually variants on $\preceq$, $\le$ and so on. On , to denote a general ordering relation it is recommended to use $\preceq$ and its variants: $\preccurlyeq$ $\curlyeqprec$ To denote the conventional ordering relation in the context of numbers, the symbol $\le$ is to be used, or its variants: $\leqslant$ $\leqq$ $\eqslantless$ The symbol $\subseteq$ is universally reserved for the subset relation. If, for two elements $a, b \in S$, it is not the case that $a \preceq b$, then the symbols $a \npreceq b$ and $b \nsucceq a$ can be used.

label: Definition:Ordering Induced by Injection
snippet: Let $\left({T, \le}\right)$ be an ordered set, and let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection. Define $\le_f$ as the ordering induced by $f$ on $S$ by: $\forall s_1, s_2 \in S: s_1 \le_f s_2 \iff f \left({s_1}\right) \le f \left({s_2}\right)$ That $\le_f$ is in fact an ordering is shown on Ordering Induced by Injection is Ordering.

label: Definition:Ordering of Cuts/Strict
snippet: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be cuts. $\alpha$ and $\beta$ conventionally have the following strict ordering imposed on them, as follows: $\alpha$ is less than $\beta$, denoted $\alpha \alpha$.

label: Definition:Ordering on Extended Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. Extend the natural ordering $\le_\R$ on $\R$ to $\overline \R = \R \cup \set {+\infty, -\infty}$ by imposing: $\forall x \in \overline \R: -\infty \le x$ $\forall x \in \overline \R: x \le +\infty$ That is, considering the relations $\le$ and $\le_\R$ as subsets of $\overline \R \times \overline \R$: ${\le} := {\le_\R} \cup \set {\tuple {x, +\infty}: x \in \overline \R} \cup \set {\tuple {-\infty, x}: x \in \overline \R}$ where $\tuple {x, +\infty}$ and $\tuple {-\infty, x}$ denote ordered pairs in $\overline \R \times \overline \R$.

label: Definition:Ordering on Mappings
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\left({T, \preceq}\right)$ be an ordered set. Let $f, g: S \to T$ be mappings. Then ordering on mappings $f$ and $g$ denoted $f \preceq g$ is defined by $\forall s \in S: f\left({s}\right) \preceq g\left({s}\right)$

label: Definition:Ordinal/Also known as
snippet: == Ordinal: Also known as == An ordinal is also known as an ordinal number. For a given well-ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$, the expression: $\map {\mathrm {Ord} } S$ can be used to denote the unique ordinal which is order isomorphic to $\struct {S, \preceq}$.

label: Definition:Ordinal/Definition 3
snippet: An ordinal is a strictly well-ordered set $\struct {\alpha, \prec}$ such that: $\forall \beta \in \alpha: \alpha_\beta = \beta$ where $\alpha_\beta$ is the initial segment of $\alpha$ determined by $\beta$: $\alpha_\beta = \set {x \in \alpha: x \prec \beta}$

label: Definition:Ordinal/Definition 4
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be a set. $\alpha$ is an ordinal : $\alpha$ is an element of every superinductive class.

label: Definition:Ordinal/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Ordinal == The class of all ordinals can be found denoted $\On$. In order to indicate that a set $S$ is an ordinal, this notation is often seen: $\Ord S$ whose meaning is: $S$ is an ordinal. Thus $\operatorname {Ord}$ can be used as a propositional function whose domain is the class of all sets. A tradition has grown up in set theory to use lowercase Greek letters $\alpha, \ \beta, \ \gamma, \ldots$ as symbols to represent variables over ordinals. It is also customary to denote the ordering relation between ordinals as $\le$ rather than $\subseteq$ or $\preceq$.

label: Definition:Ordinal Data
snippet: Ordinal data are data which have a natural numerical ordering associated with them.

label: Definition:Ordinal Sequence
snippet: An ordinal sequence is a mapping $\theta$ whose domain is an ordinal $\alpha$. That is, the domain of $\theta$ is the set of all ordinals $\gamma$ such that $\gamma < \alpha$. Such a sequence can be referred to as an $\alpha$-sequence. Hence an $\On$-sequence is a mapping whose domain is the class of all ordinals $\On$.

label: Definition:Ordinal Sequence/Length
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal. Let $\theta$ be an ordinal sequence whose domain is $\alpha$. Then $\alpha$ can be referred to as the length of $\theta$. The length of $\theta$ can be denoted $\size \theta$.

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Closed
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. The closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$ is the set $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ of all ordinal numbers less than or equal to $\Gamma$, together with the order topology. Particular special cases of a closed ordinal space are as follows:

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Closed/Countable
snippet: Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. The countable closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$ is a particular case of a closed ordinal space $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ where $\Gamma < \Omega$. That is, it is the set $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ of all ordinal numbers less than or equal to $\Gamma < \Omega$, together with the order topology.

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Closed/Uncountable
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. The uncountable closed ordinal space on $\Omega$ is the particular case of a closed ordinal space $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ where $\Gamma = \Omega$. That is, it is the set $\closedint 0 \Omega$ of all ordinal numbers less than or equal to $\Omega$, together with the order topology.

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Open
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. The open ordinal space on $\Gamma$ is the set $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ of all ordinal numbers (strictly) less than $\Gamma$, together with the order topology. Particular special cases of an open ordinal space are as follows:

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Open/Countable
snippet: Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal such that $\Gamma < \Omega$. The countable open ordinal space on $\Gamma$ is a particular case of an open ordinal space $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ where $\Gamma < \Omega$. That is, it is the set $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ of all ordinal numbers (strictly) less than $\Gamma < \Omega$, together with the order topology.

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Open/Uncountable
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. The uncountable open ordinal space on $\Omega$ is the particular case of an open ordinal space $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ where $\Gamma = \Omega$. That is, it is the set $\hointr 0 \Omega$ of all ordinal numbers (strictly) less than $\Omega$, together with the order topology.

label: Definition:Ordinal Variable
snippet: An ordinal variable is a categorical variable whose values has a natural ordering.

label: Definition:Ordinary Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Then $S$ is an ordinary set : $S \notin S$ That is, $S$ is not an element of itself.

label: Definition:Ordinary Space
snippet: Ordinary space (or just space) is a word used to mean the universe we live in. The intuitive belief is that space is $3$-dimensional and therefore isomorphic to the real vector space $\R^3$. Hence ordinary space is usually taken as an alternative term for Euclidean $3$-dimensional space.

label: Definition:Ordinate
snippet: Consider the graph $y = \map f x$ of a real function $f$ embedded in a Cartesian plane. 500px The $y$ coordinate of a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ on $f$ is known as the ordinate of $P$.

label: Definition:Ore Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer. $n$ is an Ore number the harmonic mean of its divisors is an integer.

label: Definition:Orientation
snippet: Graph Theory Orientation: a property of digraphs Topology Orientation of Differential Manifold Analytic Geometry Orientation of Coordinate Axes: the general disposition of the coordinate axes relative to each other

label: Definition:Orientation of Contour (Complex Plane)/Negative/Simple Closed
snippet: Let $C$ be a simple closed contour in the complex plane $\C$ with parameterization $\gamma: \closedint a b \to \C$. Set $K := \set { t \in \closedint a b : \textrm{ $\gamma$ is not differentiable at $t$ } }$. Let $\Int C$ denote the interior of $C$ Then $C$ is negatively oriented, for all $t \in \openint a b \setminus K$, there exists $r \in \R_{>0}$ such that: for all $\epsilon \in \openint 0 r$ : $\map \gamma t - \epsilon i \map {\gamma'} t \in \Int C$ Alternatively, we say that $C$ has a negative orientation.

label: Definition:Orientation of Contour (Complex Plane)/Positive/Simple Closed
snippet: Let $C$ be a simple closed contour in the complex plane $\C$ with parameterization $\gamma: \closedint a b \to \C$. Set $K := \set { t \in \closedint a b : \textrm{ $\gamma$ is not differentiable at $t$ } }$. Let $\Int C$ denote the interior of $C$ Then $C$ is positively oriented, for all $t \in \openint a b \setminus K$, there exists $r \in \R_{>0}$ such that: for all $\epsilon \in \openint 0 r$ : $\map \gamma t + \epsilon i \map {\gamma'} t \in \Int C$ Alternatively, we say that $C$ has a positive orientation.

label: Definition:Orientation of Coordinate Axes/Cartesian 3-Space/Left-Handed
snippet: A Cartesian $3$-Space is defined as being left-handed if it has the following property: Let a left hand be placed such that: the thumb and index finger are at right-angles to each other the $3$rd finger is at right-angles to the thumb and index finger, upwards from the palm the thumb points along the $x$-axis in the positive direction the index finger points along the $y$-axis in the positive direction. Then the $3$rd finger is pointed along the $z$-axis in the positive direction. 320px

label: Definition:Orientation of Coordinate Axes/Cartesian 3-Space/Right-Handed
snippet: A Cartesian $3$-Space is defined as being right-handed if it has the following property: Let a right hand be placed such that: the thumb and index finger are at right-angles to each other the $3$rd finger is at right-angles to the thumb and index finger, upwards from the palm the thumb points along the $x$-axis in the positive direction the index finger points along the $y$-axis in the positive direction. Then the $3$rd finger is pointed along the $z$-axis in the positive direction. 450px

label: Definition:Orientation of Coordinate Axes/Cartesian Plane/Left-Handed
snippet: A Cartesian plane is defined as being left-handed if it has the following property: Let a left hand be placed, with palm uppermost, such that the thumb points along the $x$-axis in the positive direction, such that the thumb and index finger are at right-angles to each other. Then the index finger is pointed along the $y$-axis in the positive direction. 320px

label: Definition:Orientation of Coordinate Axes/Cartesian Plane/Right-Handed
snippet: A Cartesian plane is defined as being right-handed if it has the following property: Let a right hand be placed, with palm uppermost, such that the thumb points along the $x$-axis in the positive direction, such that the thumb and index finger are at right-angles to each other. Then the index finger is pointed along the $y$-axis in the positive direction. 320px

label: Definition:Oriented Manifold
snippet: An oriented manifold is a smooth orientable manifold together with a choice of orientation. If $M$ is an oriented $n$-manifold, then a smooth coordinate chart $\left(U,\left(x^i\right)\right)$ is said to be an oriented chart if the coordinate frame $\left(\partial / \partial x^1, \ldots, \partial / \partial x^n\right)$ is positively oriented at each point.

label: Definition:Orthic Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let $\triangle DEF$ be the triangle formed by the feet of the altitudes $AD$, $BC$ and $ED$ of $\triangle ABC$. 420px $\triangle DEF$ is known as the orthic triangle of $\triangle ABC$. That is, the orthic triangle of $\triangle ABC$ is the pedal triangle of its orthocenter.

label: Definition:Orthocenter
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. The orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$ is where its three altitudes meet. 500px

label: Definition:Orthogonal
snippet: Analytic Geometry: Orthogonal (Analytic Geometry) Orthogonal Curves Orthogonal Coordinate System: Orthogonal Curvilinear Coordinates Rectangular Coordinate System Orthogonal Trajectories Linear Algebra: Orthogonal (Linear Algebra) Orthogonal (Bilinear Form) Orthogonal (Quadratic Form) Hilbert Spaces: Orthogonal Difference Matrix Algebra: Orthogonal Matrix Group Theory: Orthogonal Group

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Bilinear Form)
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b: V \times V \to \mathbb K$ be a reflexive bilinear form on $V$. Let $v,w\in V$. Then $v$ and $w$ are orthogonal (with respect to $b$) $\map b {v, w} = \map b {w, v} = 0$ This is denoted: $v \perp w$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Bilinear Form)/Orthogonal Complement
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b : V\times V \to \mathbb K$ be a reflexive bilinear form on $V$. Let $S\subset V$ be a subset. The orthogonal complement of $S$ (with respect to $b$) is the set of all $v \in V$ which are orthogonal to all $s \in S$. This is denoted: $S^\perp$. If $S = \set v$ is a singleton, we also write $v^\perp$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Bilinear Form)/Radical
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b : V\times V \to \mathbb K$ be a reflexive bilinear form on $V$. The radical of $V$ is the orthogonal complement of $V$: $\map {\operatorname {rad} } V = V^\perp$

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Linear Algebra)/Orthogonal Complement
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $S\subseteq V$ be a subset. We define the orthogonal complement of $S$ (with respect to $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$), written $S^\perp$ as the set of all $v \in V$ which are orthogonal to all $s \in S$. That is: $S^\perp = \set {v \in V : \innerprod v s = 0 \text { for all } s \in S}$ If $S = \set v$ is a singleton, we may write $S^\perp$ as $v^\perp$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Linear Algebra)/Set
snippet: Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $S = \set {u_1, \ldots, u_n}$ be a subset of $V$. Then $S$ is an orthogonal set its elements are pairwise orthogonal: $\forall i \ne j: \innerprod {u_i} {u_j} = 0$

label: Definition:Orthogonal Basis of Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $\BB = \tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ be a basis of $V$. Then $\BB$ is an orthogonal basis $\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n$ are pairwise perpendicular.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Curves
snippet: Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ be curves that intersect at a point $P$. $C_1$ and $C_2$ are orthogonal at $P$ the tangent line to $C_1$ at $P$ is at right angles to the tangent line to $C_2$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Functions
snippet: Let $S = \set {f_1, f_2, \ldots}$ be a set of real functions that are integrable over the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. Let $S$ be such that: $\forall m, n: m \ne n \implies \innerprod {f_m} {f_n} = 0$ where $\innerprod {f_m} {f_n}$ denotes the inner product of $f_m$ and $f_n$: $\innerprod {f_m} {f_n} := \ds \int_a^b \map {f_m} x \map {f_n} x \rd x$ Then $S$ is a set of orthogonal functions.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Group
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. The ($n$th) orthogonal group (on $k$), denoted $\map {\mathrm O} {n, k}$, is the following subset of the general linear group $\GL {n, k}$: $\map {\mathrm O} {n, k} := \set {M \in \GL {n, k}: M^\intercal = M^{-1} }$ where $M^\intercal$ denotes the transpose of $M$. Further, $\map {\mathrm O} {n, k}$ is considered to be endowed with conventional matrix multiplication. That is, the ($n$th) orthogonal group (on $k$) is the set of all orthogonal order-$n$ square matrices over $k$ under (conventional) matrix multiplication.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Latin Squares
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be Latin squares of order $n$. Let $\left[{a}\right]_{i j}$ and $\left[{b}\right]_{i j}$ be the elements of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ respectively whose indices are $i$ and $j$. Then $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are orthogonal : for all $i$ and $j$, the ordered pairs $\left({\left[{a}\right]_{i j}, \left[{b}\right]_{i j}}\right)$ are distinct. That is, $\left({\left[{a}\right]_{i j}, \left[{b}\right]_{i j}}\right)$ appears no more than once for every ordered pair $\left({i, j}\right)$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf Q$ be a nonsingular square matrix over a field $\GF$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Polynomials
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of polynomials over the real numbers $\R$: $S = \set {\map {p_0} x, \map {p_1} x, \map {p_2} x, \ldots}$ such that $p_n$ is of degree $n$. The elements of $S$ are orthogonal a closed real interval $\closedint a b$ and a continuous non-negative weight function $\map w x$ on $\closedint a b$ : $\ds \int_a^b \map w x \map {p_i} x \map {p_j} x \rd x = 0$ for all $i \ne j$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Projection
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $K$ be a closed linear subspace of $H$. Then the orthogonal projection on $K$ is the mapping $P_K: H \to H$ defined by $k = \map {P_K} h \iff k \in K$ and $\map d {h, k} = \map d {h, K}$ where the latter $d$ signifies distance to a set. That $P_K$ is indeed a mapping is proved on Orthogonal Projection is Mapping. The name orthogonal projection stems from the fact that $\paren {h - \map {P_K} h} \perp K$.

label: Definition:Orthonormal Frame
snippet: Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $U \subseteq M$ be an open set. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p M$ be a tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $\tuple {E_i}$ be the local frame for $M$ on $U$. Suppose for each $p \in U$ the vectors $\bigvalueat {E_i} p$ are an orthonormal basis for $T_p M$. Then $\tuple {E_i}$ is said to be an orthonormal frame.

label: Definition:Orthonormal Subset
snippet:
Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $S \subseteq V$ be a subset of $V$. Then $S$ is an orthonormal subset (of $V$) : $(1): \quad  orall u \in S: 
orm u = 1$ where $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ is the inner product norm. $(2): \quad S$ is an orthogonal set: $ orall u, v \in S: u 
e v \implies \innerprod u v = 0$

label: Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation at Point/Infimum
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real sets. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $x \in X$. Let $\NN_x$ be the set of neighborhoods of $x$. The oscillation of $f$ at $x$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\omega_f} x := \inf_{U \mathop \in \NN_x} \map {\omega_f} {U \cap X}$ where $\map {\omega_f} {U \cap X}$ denotes the oscillation of $f$ on $U \cap X$.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation on Set
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real sets. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $A \subseteq X$ be any non-empty subset $A$ of $X$. The oscillation of $f$ on (or over) $A$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\omega_f} A := \sup_{x, y \mathop \in A} \size {\map f x - \map f y}$ where the supremum is taken in the extended real numbers $\overline \R$. Category:Definitions/Oscillation

label: Definition:Outer Jordan Content
snippet: Let $M \subseteq \R^n$ be a bounded subspace of Euclidean $n$-space. Let $\CC$ be the set of all finite coverings of $M$ by closed $n$-rectangles. The outer Jordan content of $M$ is defined as denoted as: $\ds \map {m^*} M = \inf_{C \mathop \in \CC} \sum_{R \mathop \in C} \map V R$ where: $\ds \inf_{C \mathop \in \CC}$ denotes the greatest lower bound. $\map V R$ denotes the content of the rectangle $R$.

label: Definition:Outer Measure
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\powerset X$ be the power set of $X$. An outer measure (on $X$) is a mapping: $\mu^*: \powerset X \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}$ that satisfies the following conditions: $(1): \quad \map {\mu^*} \O = 0$ $(2): \quad \forall A, B \in \powerset X: A \subseteq B \implies \map {\mu^*} A \le \map {\mu^*} B$ (that is, $\mu^*$ is monotone) $(3): \quad \ds \map {\mu^*} {\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty A_i} \le \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \map {\mu^*} {A_i}$ for all sequences $\sequence {A_i}_{i \mathop \in \N} \in \powerset X$ (that is, $\mu^*$ is countably subadditive) where…

label: Definition:Outlier
snippet: An outlier is an observation which departs significantly from the general shape of a set of data. This may either be: a genuine observation which reflects an abnormality in some measurable property being observed a mistake either in the measurement or its recording.

label: Definition:Ovals of Cassini
snippet: Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be points in the plane such that $P_1 P_2 = 2 a$ for some constant $a$. The ovals of Cassini are the loci of points $M$ in the plane such that: $P_1 M \times P_2 M = b^2$ for a real constant $b$.

label: Definition:Overlapping Interval Topology
snippet: Let $S = \closedint {-1} 1$ denote the open real interval: $\closedint {-1} 1 = \set {x \in \R: -1 \le x \le 1}$ Let $\BB$ be the set: $\BB = \set {\hointl a 1: -1 < a < 0} \cup \set {\hointr {-1} b: 0 < b < 1}$ where: $\hointl a 1$ is the half-open interval $\set {x \in \R: a < x \le 1}$. $\hointr {-1} b$ is the half-open interval $\set {x \in \R: -1 \le x < b}$. Then $\BB$ is the sub-basis for a topology $\tau$ on $\closedint {-1} 1$. $\tau$ is referred to as the overlapping interval topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the overlapping interval space.

label: Definition:P-Group
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime integer. A $p$-group (either finite or infinite) is a group whose elements are all $p$-elements.

label: Definition:P-Norm
snippet: Let $p \ge 1$ be a real number. Let $\BB$ be a Banach space. Let $\ell^p$ denote the $p$-sequence space in $\BB$: $\ds \ell^p := \set {\sequence {s_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \BB^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \norm {s_n}^p < \infty}$ Let $\mathbf s = \sequence {s_n} \in \ell^p$ be a sequence in $\ell^p$. Then the $p$-norm of $\mathbf s$ is defined as: $\ds \norm {\mathbf s}_p = \paren {\sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \size {s_n}^p}^{1 / p}$ This is often presented in expository treatments either on the real number line or the complex plane:

label: Definition:P-Norm/Real
snippet: Let $p \ge 1$ be a real number. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let ${\ell^p}_\R$ denote the real $p$-sequence space: $\ds {\ell^p}_\R := \set {\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \R^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \size {x_n}^p < \infty}$ Let $\mathbf x = \sequence {x_n} \in {\ell^p}_\R$ be a sequence in ${\ell^p}_\R$. Then the $p$-norm of $\mathbf x$ is defined as: $\ds \norm {\mathbf x}_p = \paren {\sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \size {x_n}^p}^{1 / p}$

label: Definition:P-Product Metric
snippet: Let $M_{1'} = \struct {A_{1'}, d_{1'} }$ and $M_{2'} = \struct {A_{2'}, d_{2'} }$ be metric spaces. Let $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}$ and $A_{2'}$. Let $p \in \R_{\ge 1}$. The $p$-product metric on $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ is defined as: $\map {d_p} {x, y} := \paren {\paren {\map {d_{1'} } {x_1, y_1} }^p + \paren {\map {d_{2'} } {x_2, y_2} }^p}^{1/p}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2} \in A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$. The metric space $\MM_p := \struct {A_{1'} \times A_{2'}, d_p}$ is the $p$-product (space) of $M_{1'}$ and $M_{2'}$.

label: Definition:P-Sequence Space/Real
snippet: Let $p \in \R$ be a real number such that $p \ge 1$. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. The $p$-sequence space (in $\R$), denoted ${\ell^p}_\R$, is defined as: $\ds {\ell^p}_\R := \set {\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \R^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \size {x_n}^p < \infty}$ where: $\R^\N$ is the set of all sequences in $\R$ $\size {x_n}$ denotes the absolute value of $x_n$. That is, the $p$-sequence space is the set of all sequences in $\R$ such that $\size {x_n}^p$ converges to a limit.

label: Definition:P-Series
snippet: Let $p \in \C$ be a complex number. The series defined as: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^p} = 1 + \frac 1 {2^p} + \frac 1 {3^p} + \frac 1 {4^p} + \dotsb$ is known as a $p$-series.

label: Definition:P-Value
snippet: Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test. Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be the null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis of $\delta$ respectively. Let $T$ be the test statistic which is being used to determine whether $H_0$ or $H_1$ holds. Let $C$ be the critical region of $\delta$. Let $\alpha$ be the significance level of $\delta$. The $p$-value of $\delta$ is the probability that $T$ takes a value greater than or equal to a calculated value when $H_0$ is true.

label: Definition:P-adic Digit
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. The $p$-adic digits are the natural numbers $\set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, p - 1}$.

label: Definition:P-adic Expansion
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. A $p$-adic expansion is a series in the rational numbers $\Q$ of the form: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = m}^\infty d_n p^n$ where: $m \in \Z_{\le 0}$ $\forall n \in \Z_{\ge m}: d_n$ is a $p$-adic digit $m < 0 \implies d_m \ne 0$

label: Definition:P-adic Unit
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\Z_p$ denote the $p$-adic integers. The set of $p$-adic units, denoted $\Z_p^\times$, is the set of invertible elements of $\Z_p$.

Definition:P-adically Coherent Sequence
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\sequence {\alpha_n}$ be an integer sequence such that: $(1): \quad \forall n \in \N: 0 \le \alpha_n \le p^{n + 1} - 1$ $(2): \quad \forall n \in \N: \alpha_{n + 1} \equiv \alpha_n \pmod {p^{n + 1}}$ The sequence $\sequence {\alpha_n}$ is said to be a coherent sequence. If it is necessary to emphasize the choice of prime $p$ then the sequence $\sequence {\alpha_n}$ is said to be a $p$-adically coherent sequence.

label: Definition:Pairwise Coprime/Integers
snippet: A set of integers $S$ is pairwise coprime : $\forall x, y \in S: x \ne y \implies x \perp y$ where $x \perp y$ denotes that $x$ and $y$ are coprime.

label: Definition:Pairwise Disjoint/Set of Sets
snippet: A set of sets $\Bbb S$ is said to be pairwise disjoint : $\forall X, Y \in \Bbb S: X \ne Y \implies X \cap Y = \O$ Here, $\cap$ denotes intersection, and $\O$ denotes the empty set. Hence we can say that the elements of $\Bbb S$ are pairwise disjoint.

label: Definition:Pairwise Disjoint Events
snippet: Let $\family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of events in a probability space. Then $\family {A_i}$ is pairwise disjoint : $\forall i, j \in I, i \ne j: A_i \cap A_j = \O$ That is, a set of events is pairwise disjoint every pair of them is disjoint.

label: Definition:Pairwise Orthogonal/Rows
snippet: Let $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. The rows of $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ are described as pairwise orthogonal : $\forall i, j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m}, i \ne j: {r_i}^\intercal \cdot {r_j}^\intercal = 0$ That is, the dot product of each pair of distinct rows of $\sqbrk a_{m n}$, when transposed and considered as vectors, is zero.

label: Definition:Palindromic Number
snippet: A palindromic number (base $b$) is a number which is a palindrome when expressed in number base $b$. That is, it reads the same reversed as it does forwards. When the base is not specified, it is commonplace to understand it as being $10$.

label: Definition:Palindromic Prime
snippet: A palindromic prime is a prime number which is also a palindromic number.

label: Definition:Pandigital Set
snippet: A set of integers is pandigital it contains exactly $1$ instance of each digit.

label: Definition:Pandigital Set/Penholodigital
snippet: A set of integers is penholodigital it contains exactly $1$ instance of each digit excluding $0$.

label: Definition:Parabola/Directrix
snippet: 300px Let $K$ be an [Definition:Focus-Directrix Property of Parabola|parabola]] specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ equals the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$: $p = q$ The line $D$ is known as the directrix of the parabola.

label: Definition:Parabola/Focus
snippet: 300px Let $K$ be a parabola specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ equals the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$: $p = q$ The point $F$ is known as the focus of the parabola.

label: Definition:Parabola/Focus-Directrix
snippet: 300px Let $D$ be a straight line. Let $F$ be a point. Let $K$ be the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ equals the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$: $p = q$ Then $K$ is a parabola.

label: Definition:Parabola/Vertex
snippet: 420px Let $P$ be a parabola. The vertex of $P$ is the point where the axis intersects $P$. In the above diagram, $V$ is the vertex of $P$.

label: Definition:Paraboloid
snippet: A paraboloid is a figure whose sections parallel to at least one plane are parabolas.

label: Definition:Paracompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a paracompact space : every open cover of $T$ has an open refinement which is locally finite.

label: Definition:Paradox
snippet: A paradox is a statement or group of statements that leads to one of the following:

label: Definition:Parallel
snippet: Geometry: Parallel: Parallel Lines Parallel Planes Line Parallel to Plane Matroid Theory: Parallel Elements of Matroid

label: Definition:Parallel (Geometry)/Line to Plane
snippet: Let $L$ be a straight line. Let $P$ be a plane. Then $L$ and $P$ are parallel , when produced indefinitely, they do not intersect at any point.

label: Definition:Parallel (Geometry)/Lines
snippet: ' The contemporary interpretation of the concept of parallelism declares that a straight line is parallel to itself.

label: Definition:Parallel (Geometry)/Planes
snippet: Two planes are parallel , when produced indefinitely, do not intersect at any point. The contemporary interpretation of the concept of parallelism declares that a plane is parallel to itself.

label: Definition:Parallel of Latitude
snippet: Let $J$ be a point on Earth's surface that is not one of the two poles $N$ and $S$. Let $C$ be the small circle through $J$ parallel to the plane containing the equator. Then $C$ is known as the parallel of latitude of $J$. Thus $C$ consists of all the points on Earth's surface which have the same latitude as $J$. 500px

label: Definition:Parallelepiped/Height
snippet: 400px The height of a parallelepiped is the length of the perpendicular between the planes of the bases. In the above diagram, $h$ is the height of the parallelepiped one of whose bases is $AB$.

label: Definition:Parallelogram/Altitude
snippet: 450px An altitude of a parallelogram is a line drawn perpendicular to its base, through one of its vertices to the side opposite to the base (which is extended if necessary). In the parallelogram above, line $DE$ is an altitude of the parallelogram $ABCD$. The term is also used for the length of such a line.

label: Definition:Parameter
snippet: A parameter is a constant or a variable that distinguishes special cases of a general mathematical expression.

label: Definition:Parameter Space
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population. The parameter space of $\theta$, typically denoted $\Omega$, is the domain of $\theta$. That is, it is the set of all possible values that $\theta$ can take.

label: Definition:Parameter of Differential Equation
snippet: Let $f$ be a differential equation with general solution $F$. A parameter of $F$ is an arbitrary constant arising from the solving of a primitive during the course of obtaining the solution of $f$.

label: Definition:Parameterization
snippet: A parameterization is an expression of a curve or a surface, and so on, by means of a set of parametric equations.

label: Definition:Parametric Equation
snippet: Let $\map \RR {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a relation on the variables $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$. Let the truth set of $\RR$ be definable as: $\forall k \in \N: 1 \le k \le n: x_k = \map {\phi_k} t$ where: $t$ is a variable whose domain is to be defined each of $\phi_k$ is a mapping whose domain is the domain of $t$ and whose codomain is the domain of $x_k$. Then each of: $x_k = \map {\phi_k} t$ is a parametric equation. The set: $\set {\phi_k: 1 \le k \le n}$ is a set of parametric equations specifying $\RR$.

label: Definition:Paranormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ is a paranormal subgroup in $G$ the subgroup generated by $H$ and any conjugate of $H$ is also generated by $H$ and a conjugate of $H$ within that generated subgroup. That is, $H$ is paranormal in $G$ : $\forall g \in G: \exists k \in \left\langle{H, H^g}\right\rangle: \left\langle{H, H^k}\right\rangle = \left\langle{H, H^g}\right\rangle$ where: $\left\langle{H, H^g}\right\rangle$ is the subgroup generated by $H$ and $H^g$ $H^g$ is the conjugate of $H$ by $g$.

label: Definition:Parenthesization
snippet: Let $\circ$ be a product defined on a set $S$. Let $a_1 \circ a_2 \circ \cdots a_i \circ \cdots \circ a_n$ denote a word in $S$ for some $n > 2$. To distinguish all possible products of $a_1, a_2, \dotsc, a_n$, parentheses are inserted into the word. A set of parentheses applied on a product is called a parenthesization of that word.

label: Definition:Pareto Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X \in \hointr b \infty$. $X$ is said to have a Pareto distribution it has probability density function: $\ds \map {f_X} x = \dfrac {a b^a} {x^{a + 1} }$ for $a, b \in \R_{> 0}$.

label: Definition:Parity
snippet: Number Theory: The parity of an integer: whether it is even or odd. Group Theory: The parity of a permutation of an element of the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Both concepts have the same origin: parity encapsulates the notions of oddness and evenness.

label: Definition:Parity Group
snippet: This has several forms, all of which are isomorphic: The group $\struct {\Z_2, +_2}$ $C_2$, the cyclic group of order 2 The complex square roots of unity $\struct {\set {1, -1}, \times}$ The quotient group $\dfrac {S_n} {A_n}$ of the symmetric group of order $n$ with the alternating group of order $n$ and so on.

label: Definition:Parity Ring
snippet: The parity ring is the ring of two elements which defines the nature of the parity of integers under addition and multiplication: $\struct {\set {\text{even}, \text{odd} }, +, \times}$

label: Definition:Parity of Integer
snippet: Let $z \in \Z$ be an integer. The parity of $z$ is whether it is even or odd.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Even
snippet: An integer $z$ is of even parity : $z = 2 n$ for some $n \in \Z$.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Odd
snippet: An integer $z$ is of odd parity : $z = 2 n + 1$ for some $n \in \Z$.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Opposite
snippet: Two integers $z_1$ and $z_2$ have opposite parity either: $z_1$ is even and $z_2$ is odd or: $z_2$ is even and $z_1$ is odd.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Same
snippet: Two integers $z_1$ and $z_2$ have the same parity either: $z_1$ and $z_2$ are both even or: $z_1$ and $z_2$ are both odd.

label: Definition:Partial Derivative
snippet: A partial derivative is the rate of change of a function of several variables one of those variables while keeping all the other variables constant.

label: Definition:Partial Function
snippet: Let $S \subset \N^k$. Let $f: S \to \N$ be a function. Suppose that $\forall x \in \N^k \setminus S$, $f$ is undefined at $x$. Then $f$ is known as a partial function from $\N^k$ to $\N$. Thus we can specify a function that has values for some, but not all, elements of $\N$. It can be seen that the definition of a partial function as given here is compatible with that of a partial mapping.

label: Definition:Partial Ordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then the ordering $\preceq$ is a partial ordering on $S$ $\preceq$ is not connected. That is, $\struct {S, \preceq}$ has at least one pair which is non-comparable: $\exists x, y \in S: x \npreceq y \land y \npreceq x$

label: Definition:Particle
snippet: A particle is a representation of an object in the physical universe which is idealized as having no magnitude. That is, it is modelled as being a mass concentrated at a single point.

label: Definition:Particle Physics
snippet: Particle physics is the branch of physics which studies the structure and interactions of the elementary particles of matter.

label: Definition:Particular Affirmative
snippet: A particular affirmative is a categorical statement of the form: Some $S$ is $P$ where $S$ and $P$ are predicates. In the language of predicate logic, this can be expressed as: $\exists x: \map S x \land \map P x$ Its meaning can be amplified in natural language as: There exists at least one object with the property of being $S$ which also has the property of being $P$.

label: Definition:Particular Affirmative/Set Theory
snippet: The particular affirmative $\exists x: \map S x \land \map P x$ can be expressed in set language as: $\set {x: \map S x} \cap \set {x: \map P x} \ne \O$ or, more compactly: $S \cap P \ne \O$

label: Definition:Particular Negative
snippet: A particular negative is a categorical statement of the form: Some $S$ is not $P$ where $S$ and $P$ are predicates. In the language of predicate logic, this can be expressed as: $\exists x: \map S x \land \neg \map P x$ Its meaning can be amplified in natural language as: There exists at least one object with the property of being $S$ which does not have the property of being $P$.

label: Definition:Particular Negative/Set Theory

label: Definition:Particular Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A particular point of $T$ is an element $p \in S$ which is distinguished in some manner from the other elements of $S$.

label: Definition:Particular Point Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be an arbitrary particular point of $S$. We define a subset $\tau_p$ of the power set $\powerset S$ as: $\tau_p = \set {A \subseteq S: p \in A} \cup \set \O$ that is, all the subsets of $S$ which include $p$, along with the empty set. Then $\tau_p$ is a topology called the particular point topology on $S$ by $p$, or just a particular point topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_p}$ is called the particular point space on $S$ by $p$, or just a particular point space.

label: Definition:Particular Point Topology/Countable
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be an arbitrary particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_p}$ be the particular point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be a countably infinite set. Then $\tau_p$ is a countable particular point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_p}$ is a countable particular point space.

label: Definition:Particular Point Topology/Finite
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be an arbitrary particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_p}$ be the particular point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be a finite set. Then $\tau_p$ is a finite particular point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_p}$ is a finite particular point space.

label: Definition:Particular Point Topology/Infinite
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be an arbitrary particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_p}$ be the particular point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be an infinite set. Then $\tau_p$ is an infinite particular point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_p}$ is an infinite particular point space.

label: Definition:Particular Point Topology/Uncountable
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be an arbitrary particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_p}$ be the particular point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be an uncountable set. Then $\tau_p$ is an uncountable particular point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_p}$ is an uncountable particular point space.

label: Definition:Partition
snippet: Set theory: Set Partition: a set of non-empty pairwise disjoint subsets that cover a set Topology: Partition (Topology) Partition of Unity: a collection of continuous mappings with some specific properties Probability Theory: Partition (Probability Theory) Combinatorics: Integer Partition: an expression of an integer as a sum of (strictly) positive integers Number theory: Goldbach Partition: an expression of an integer as the sum of a pair of primes (also known as a Goldbach decomposition) Real analysis: Partition of Interval: Another name for a subdivision of a closed real interval.

label: Definition:Partition (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. A partition of $\Omega$ is a family $\family {B_i: i \in I}$ of pairwise disjoint events such that $\ds \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} B_i = \Omega$.

label: Definition:Partition Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\PP$ be a partition of $S$. Let $\tau$ be the set of subsets of $S$ defined as: $a \in \tau \iff a$ is the union of sets of $\PP$ Then $\tau$ is a partition topology on $S$, and $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a partition (topological) space. The partition $\PP$ is the basis of $\struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Partitioning
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of subsets of $S$ such that: $(1): \quad \forall i \in I: S_i \ne \O$, that is, none of $S_i$ is empty $(2): \quad \ds S = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$, that is, $S$ is the union of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ $(3): \quad \forall i, j \in I: i \ne j \implies S_i \cap S_j = \O$, that is, the elements of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ are pairwise disjoint. Then $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is a partitioning of $S$. The image of this partitioning is the set $\set {S_i: i \in I}$ and is called a partition of $S$.

label: Definition:Path
snippet: Topology: Path: a continuous mapping $f: \closedint a b \to T$. Complex Analysis: Path (Complex Plane). Graph Theory: Path: a trail in which all vertices are distinct. Path in a Digraph: as a path in an undirected graph but taking into account the direction of the arcs Analytic Geometry Path (Analytic Geometry)

label: Definition:Path-Connected
snippet: Path-connectedness is a property of a topological space $T$ which relates to the existence of certain continuous mappings from a closed real interval (in practice, usually just the closed unit interval) into $T$.

label: Definition:Path-Connected/Metric Space/Subset
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset of $M$. Then $S$ is path-connected (in $M$) : $\forall m, n \in S: \exists f: \closedint 0 1 \to S: \map f 0 = m, \map f 1 = n$ where $f$ is a continuous mapping.

label: Definition:Path-Connected/Points
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$ be such that there exists a path from $a$ to $b$. That is, there exists a continuous mapping $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that: Then $a$ and $b$ are path-connected in $T$.

label: Definition:Path-Connected/Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $T' = \struct {U, \tau_U}$ be the subspace of $T$ induced by $U$. Then $U$ is a path-connected set in $T$ every two points in $U$ are path-connected in $T\,'$. That is, $U$ is a path-connected set in $T$ : for every $x, y \in U$, there exists a continuous mapping $f: \closedint 0 1 \to U$ such that: $\map f 0 = x$ and: $\map f 1 = y$

label: Definition:Path-Connected/Topological Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then $T$ is a path-connected space $S$ is a path-connected set of $T$. That is, $T$ is a path-connected space : for every $x, y \in S$, there exists a continuous mapping $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that: $\map f 0 = x$ and: $\map f 1 = y$

label: Definition:Path (Graph Theory)/Digraph
snippet: Let $D = \struct {V, E}$ be a digraph. A path $P$ in $D$ is: a sequence of vertices $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ in $V$ and a sequence of arcs $e_1, e_2, \ldots{}, e_{n - 1}$ in $E$ such that: $P$ begins with $v_1$ and ends with $v_n$ in which each arc $e_j$ is incident from $v_j$ and incident to $v_{j + 1}$ all arcs are distinct all vertices (except perhaps the first and last ones) are distinct. A path between two vertices $u$ and $v$ is called a path from $u$ to $v$.

label: Definition:Path (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $I \subset \R$ be the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. A path in $T$ is a continuous mapping $\gamma: I \to S$. The mapping $\gamma$ can be referred as: It is common to refer to a point $z = \map \gamma t$ as a point on the path $\gamma$, even though $z$ is in fact on the image of $\gamma$.

label: Definition:Path (Topology)/Endpoint
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $I \subset \R$ be the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. Let $\gamma: I \to T$ be a path in $T$. The initial point and final point of $\gamma$ can be referred to as the endpoints of $\gamma$ Category:Definitions/Path-Connected Spaces

label: Definition:Path (Topology)/Final Point
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $I \subset \R$ be the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. Let $\gamma: I \to T$ be a path in $T$. The final point of $\gamma$ is $\map \gamma b$. That is, the path ends (or finishes) at $\map \gamma b$.

label: Definition:Path (Topology)/Initial Point
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $I \subset \R$ be the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. Let $\gamma: I \to T$ be a path in $T$. The initial point of $\gamma$ is $\map \gamma a$. That is, the path starts (or begins) at $\map \gamma a$.

label: Definition:Path Component
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space.

label: Definition:Path Graph
snippet: A path graph is a tree which has a path which passes through all its vertices. The path graph with $n$ vertices is denoted $P_n$.

label: Definition:Payoff Function
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $N$ be the set of players of $G$. Let $A$ be the set of moves available to player $i \in N$. A payoff function on $A$ is a mapping $u_i$ from $A$ to the real numbers $\R$: $u_i: A \to \R$ defined by the condition: $\forall a, b \in A: a \succsim_i b \iff \map {u_i} a \ge \map {u_i} b$ where $\succsim_i$ denotes the preference relation for player $i$.

label: Definition:Payoff Table
snippet: Let $G$ be a two-person game. A payoff table for $G$ is an array which specifies the payoff to each player for each strategy of both players. $G$ is completely defined by its payoff table. {{PayoffTable|table = $\begin {array} {r c } & \text L & \text R \\ \hline \text T & w_1, w_2 & x_1, x_2 \\ \hline \text B & y_1, y_2 & z_1, z_2 \\ \hline \end {array}$}} The two numbers in the entry formed by row $r$ and column $c$ are the payoffs when the row player's moves is $r$ and the column player's moves is $c$. The first component given is the payoff to the row player.

label: Definition:Pea Pattern
snippet: A pea pattern is a generic term use for any one of a number of similar sequences. The first term $p_0$ is an arbitrary integer. $p_n$ is formed from $p_{n - 1}$ as follows. First, the distinct digits in $p_{n - 1}$ are counted, and the number of each is noted. The count of each distinct digit is concatenated with an instance of the digit itself. Then those concatenations are themselves concatenated into $p_n$ according to a predetermined order.

label: Definition:Peano Curve
