Let the pair $\tuple{R, u}$ consist of an object $R$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $u: C \to FR$ in $C$. The pair $\tuple{R, u}$ is called a universal morphism from $C$ to $F$ : $\tuple{R, u}$ is an initial object of the comma category $\paren{C \downarrow F}$ of $F$ under $C$

label: Definition:Universal Negative
snippet: A universal negative is a categorical statement of the form: No $S$ is $P$ where $S$ and $P$ are predicates. In the language of predicate logic, this can be expressed as: $\forall x: \map S x \implies \neg \map P x$ Its meaning can be amplified in natural language as: Every object which has the property of being $S$ does not have the property of being $P$.

label: Definition:Universal Negative/Set Theory
snippet: The universal negative $\forall x: \map S x \implies \neg \map P x$ can be expressed in set language as: $\set {x: \map S x} \implies \set {x: \map P x} = \O$ or, more compactly: $S \subseteq \map \complement P$

label: Definition:Universal Quantifier
snippet: The symbol $\forall$ is called the universal quantifier. It expresses the fact that, in a particular universe of discourse, all objects have a particular property. That is: $\forall x:$ means: For all objects $x$, it is true that ... In the language of set theory, this can be formally defined: $\forall x \in S: \map P x := \set {x \in S: \map P x} = S$ where $S$ is some set and $\map P x$ is a propositional function on $S$.

label: Definition:Universal Set
snippet: Sets are considered to be subsets of some large universal set. Exactly what this universal set is will vary depending on the subject and context. When discussing particular sets, it should be made clear just what that universal set is. However, note that from There Exists No Universal Set, this universal set cannot be everything that there is.

label: Definition:Universe
snippet: Predicate Logic: Universe of Discourse Set Theory: Universal Set Grothendieck Universe Class Theory: Universal Class Statistics: Universe: another word for population. Physics, etc.: Physical Universe: the actual place where we live.

label: Definition:Unknown
snippet: An unknown is an indeterminate variable in a system of equations or inequalities whose value the solver is invited to determine.

label: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine
snippet: An unlimited register machine, abbreviated URM, is an abstract machine with the following characteristics:

label: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Register
snippet: A URM has a sequence of registers which can store natural numbers: $\set {0, 1, 2, \ldots}$. Any given URM program may make use of only a finite number of these registers. Registers are usually referred to by the subscripted uppercase letters $R_1, R_2, R_3, \ldots$. The number held at any one time by a register is usually referred to by the corresponding lowercase letter $r_1, r_2, r_3, \ldots$.

label: Definition:Unordered Tuple
snippet: An unordered tuple is a small class in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory that contains a finite number of elements. It is written using roster notation and is denoted: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ that is: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} = \set {x: x = a_1 \lor x = a_2 \lor \dots \lor x = a_n}$

label: Definition:Untouchable Number
snippet: An untouchable number is a (strictly) positive integer that is not the aliquot sum of any integer.

label: Definition:Up-Complete
snippet: Let $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$ be a preordered set. Then $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$ is up-complete : every directed subset of $S$ admits a supremum in $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Let $f$ be bounded above in $T$ by $H \in T$. Then $H$ is an upper bound of $f$.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Sequence
snippet: A special case of an upper bound of a mapping is an upper bound of a sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be bounded above in $T$ by $H \in T$. Then $H$ is an upper bound of $\sequence {x_n}$.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T$ be a subset of $S$. An upper bound for $T$ (in $S$) is an element $M \in S$ such that: $\forall t \in T: t \preceq M$ That is, $M$ succeeds every element of $T$.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T$ be a subset of $\R$. An upper bound for $T$ (in $\R$) is an element $M \in \R$ such that: $\forall t \in T: t \le M$ That is, $M$ is greater than or equal to every element of $T$.

label: Definition:Upper Closure/Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a \in S$. The upper closure of $a$ (in $S$) is defined as: $a^\succcurlyeq := \set {b \in S: a \preccurlyeq b}$ That is, $a^\succcurlyeq$ is the set of all elements of $S$ that succeed $a$.

label: Definition:Upper Darboux Sum
Definition:Upper Limit (Topological Space)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f : S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real valued function. Let $x_0 \in X$. Let $\map \mho {x_0}$ be the set of open neighborhoods of $x_0$ in $\struct {S, \tau}$. We define the upper limit of $f$ at $x_0$ by: $\ds \limsup_{x \mathop \to x_0} \map f x = \inf_{V \in \map \mho {x_0} } \paren {\sup_{x \mathop \in V} \map f x}$

label: Definition:Upper Semicontinuous
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f : S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real valued function. Let $x_0 \in S$. We say that $f$ is upper semicontinuous at $x_0$ : $\ds \limsup_{x \mathop \to x_0} \map f x = \map f {x_0}$ where $\limsup$ denotes the upper limit.

label: Definition:Urysohn Function
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A, B \subseteq S$ such that $A \cap B = \O$. Let $f: S \to \closedint 0 1$ be a continuous mapping where $\closedint 0 1$ is the closed unit interval. Then $f$ is an Urysohn function for $A$ and $B$ : $f {\restriction_A} = 0, f {\restriction_B} = 1$ That is:

label: Definition:Urysohn Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is an Urysohn space : For two arbitrary distinct elements $x, y \in S$ (that is, $x \ne y$), there exists an Urysohn function for $\set x$ and $\set y$.

label: Definition:Usual Ordering
snippet: Let $X$ be one of the sets of numbers: $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$. The usual ordering on $X$ is the conventional counting and measuring order on $X$ that is learned when one is initially introduced to numbers.

label: Definition:Usual Ordering of Ordinals
snippet: Let $\On$ denote the class of all ordinals. The usual ordering $\le$ on $\On$ is the subset relation: $a \le b \iff a \subseteq b$ and its corresponding strict version: $a < b \iff a \subsetneqq b$

label: Definition:Utility Function
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. Let $C$ be the set $C$ of consequences of the moves available to $P$. A utility function on $C$ is a mapping from $C$ to the real numbers $\R$ so as to define a preference relation on $C$: $U: C \to \R$ by the condition: $\forall x, y \in C: x \succsim y \iff \map U x \ge \map U y$

label: Definition:Vacuous
snippet: Logic: A vacuous truth is a statement about a collection of objects none of which exist. By definition, such a statement is understood to be true. A vacuous term is a term of a categorical syllogism $\map F x$ such that nothing in the universe of discourse has the property of the predicate $F$. Set Theory: The vacuous set is the same thing as the empty set, that is, the set with no elements. This Empty Set is Unique. Algebra: A vacuous summation is a summation over an empty set of summands. Such a sum has a value of zero.

label: Definition:Vacuous/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vacuous == The word vacuous literally means empty. It derives from the Latin word vacuum, meaning empty space. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Vacuous Truth
snippet: Let $P \implies Q$ be a conditional statement. Suppose that $P$ is false. Then the statement $P \implies Q$ is a vacuous truth, or is vacuously true. It is frequently encountered in the form: $\forall x: \map P x \implies \map Q x$ when the propositional function $\map P x$ is false for all $x$. Such a statement is also a vacuous truth. For example, the statement: All cats who are expert chess-players are also fluent in ancient Sanskrit is (vacuously) true, because (as far as the author knows) there are no cats who are expert chess-players.

label: Definition:Vacuum Permeability
snippet: == Physical Constant == The vacuum permeability is the physical constant denoted $\mu_0$ defined as: $\mu_0:= \dfrac {2 \alpha h} {e^2 c}$ where: $e$ is the elementary charge $\alpha$ is the fine-structure constant $h$ is Planck's constant $c$ is the speed of light defined in $\mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ Of the above, only the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ is a measured value; the others are defined. It can be defined as the capability of a magnetic field to permeate a vacuum.

label: Definition:Vacuum Permittivity
snippet: == Physical Constant == The vacuum permittivity is the physical constant denoted $\varepsilon_0$ defined as: $\varepsilon_0 := \dfrac {e^2} {2 \alpha h c}$ where: $e$ is the elementary charge $\alpha$ is the fine-structure constant $h$ is Planck's constant $c$ is the speed of light defined in $\mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ Of the above, only the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ is a measured value; the others are defined. It can be defined as the capability of an electric field to permeate a vacuum.

label: Definition:Valid Argument
snippet: A valid argument is a logical argument in which the premises provide conclusive reasons for the conclusion. When an argument is valid, we may say one of the following:

label: Definition:Valuation Ideal Induced by Non-Archimedean Norm
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm{\,\cdot\,} }$ be a non-Archimedean normed division ring with zero $0_R$. The valuation ideal induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm{\,\cdot\,}$ is the set: $\PP = \set{x \in R: 
orm x \lt 1}$ That is, the valuation ideal induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm{\,\cdot\,}$ is the open ball $B_1 \paren {0_R}$.

label: Definition:Valuation Ring Induced by Non-Archimedean Norm
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a non-Archimedean normed division ring with zero $0_R$. The valuation ring induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm{\,\cdot\,}$ is the set: $\OO = \set {x \in R: 
orm x \le 1}$ That is, the valuation ring induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm{\,\cdot\,}$ is the closed ball $\map {B_1^-} {0_R}$.

label: Definition:Value
snippet: Analysis and Number Theory: Value of Variable Absolute Value Value of Continued Fraction Mapping Theory: Value: a synonym for the image of an element in the domain of a mapping Game Theory: Value of Game Value of Matrix Game Physics: Value: the number of units of a particular physical quantity that go to make up a particular physical constant.

label: Definition:Valued Field of P-adic Numbers
snippet: Let $p$ be any prime number. Let $\Q_p$ be the field of $p$-adic numbers. Let $\norm {\,\cdot\,}_p$ be the $p$-adic norm on $\Q_p$. The valued field of p-adic numbers is the valued field $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$.

label: Definition:Vanish
snippet: A variable in an equation is said to vanish when (under appropriate conditions) its value becomes zero.

label: Definition:Vanishing Ideal of Subset of Affine Space
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 0$ be a natural number. Let $k \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be the polynomial ring in $n$ variables over $k$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb A^n_k$ be a subset of the standard affine space over $k$. Its vanishing ideal is the ideal: $\map I S = \set {f \in k \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n} : \forall x \in S : \map f x = 0}$

label: Definition:Vanishing Set of Subset of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset. The vanishing set of $S$ is the set of prime ideals of $A$ containing $S$: $\map V S = \set {\mathfrak p \in \Spec A: \mathfrak p \supseteq S}$

label: Definition:Variable
snippet: A variable is a label which is used to refer to an unspecified object. A variable can be identified by means of a symbol, for example: $x, y, z, A, B, C, \phi, \psi, \aleph$ It is often convenient to append a subscript letter or number to distinguish between different objects of a similar type: $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n; S_\phi, S_{\phi_x}, \ldots$ The type of symbol used to define a variable is purely conventional. Particular types of object, as they are introduced, frequently have a particular range of symbols specified to define them, but there are no strict rules on the subject.

label: Definition:Variable/Complex
snippet: A complex variable is a symbol which can stand for any one of a set of complex numbers. The symbols most often used to denote a complex variable are $w$ and $z$.

label: Definition:Variable/Descriptive Statistics/Quantitative Variable
snippet: A quantitative variable is a variable such that: The variable can be described by numbers The performing of arithmetical operations on the data is meaningful.

label: Definition:Variable/Domain
snippet: The collection of all possible objects that a variable may refer to has to be specified. This collection is the domain of the variable.

label: Definition:Variable/Predicate Logic
snippet: In the context of predicate logic, a variable is often called an object variable or arbitrary name. As such, it is a symbol which is assigned to an arbitrarily selected object from a given universe of discourse. The understanding is that (during the scope of the argument to which it is relevant) the arbitrary name could apply equally well to any of the objects in that universe.

label: Definition:Variable/Propositional Logic
snippet: A statement variable is a variable which is used to stand for an arbitrary and unspecified statement. For a statement variable, a lowercase letter is usually used, for example: $p, q, r, \ldots{}$, and so on or lowercase Greek letters, for example: $\phi, \psi, \chi$ and so on. The citing of a statement variable can be interpreted as an assertion that the statement represented by that symbol is true. That is: $p$ means $p \text { is true}$

label: Definition:Variable/Real
snippet: A real variable is a symbol which can stand for any one of a set of real numbers. The symbols most often used to denote a real variable are $x$ and $y$.

label: Definition:Variable/Value
snippet: A variable $x$ may be (temporarily, conceptually) identified with a particular object. If so, then that object is called the value of $x$.

label: Definition:Variance
snippet: Variance is a measure of dispersion of a set of observations. Let $X$ be a random variable. The variance of $X$ is defined as the second central moment of $X$.

label: Definition:Variation/Complex Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\map P A$ be the set of finite partitions of $A$ into $\Sigma$-measurable sets. We define the variation $\cmod \mu : \Sigma \to \R$ of $\mu$ by: $\ds \map {\cmod \mu} A = \sup \set {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \cmod {\map \mu {A_j} } : \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n} \in \map P A}$ for each $A \in \Sigma$, where the supremum is taken in the set of extended real numbers $\overline \R$.

label: Definition:Variation Field of Family of Curves
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\gamma$ be an admissible curve on $M$. Let $I = \closedint a b$ is a closed real interval. Let $J$ is an open real interval. Let $\Gamma : J \times I \to M$ be the variation of $\gamma$, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product and: $\ds \forall s \in J : \forall t \in I : \tuple {s, t} \stackrel \Gamma \mapsto \map \Gamma {s, t}$ Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$.

label: Definition:Vector-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n$ be real functions of $t$. Let $\mathbb T \subseteq \R, \mathbb Y \subseteq \R^n$ (where usually $n \ge 2$). Let $\mathbf r$ be a mapping from $\mathbb T \to \mathbb Y$ that maps each $t \in \mathbb T$ to a vector $\tuple {\map {f_1} t, \map {f_2} t, \ldots, \map {f_n} t} \in \mathbb Y$. Then $\mathbf r$ is said to be a vector-valued function (of the parameter $t$). If $\mathbb T$ is not explicitly defined, it is taken to be the intersection of all the domains of $f_1 ,f_2, \cdots, f_n$.

label: Definition:Vector/Linear Algebra
snippet: Let $V = \struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a vector space over $K$, where: $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is the scalar ring of $V$. The elements of the abelian group $\struct {G, +_G}$ are called vectors.

label: Definition:Vector/Real Euclidean Space
snippet: A vector is defined as an element of a vector space. We have that $\R^n$, with the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication, forms a real Euclidean space. Hence a vector in $\R^n$ is defined as an element of the real Euclidean space $\R^n$.

label: Definition:Vector/Real Euclidean Space/Plane Vector
snippet: Consider the real Euclidean space $\R^2$. A vector in $\R^2$ can be referred to as a plane vector.

label: Definition:Vector Addition/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $V := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding vector space over $F$. The group operation $+_G$ on $V$ is known as vector addition on $V$.

label: Definition:Vector Algebra
snippet: Vector Algebra is the branch of mathematics which studies the algebra of vector spaces.

label: Definition:Vector Analysis
snippet: Vector analysis is the branch of linear algebra concerned with differentiation and integration of vector spaces, primarily in Euclidean space of $3$-dimensional space.

label: Definition:Vector Area
snippet: Let $S$ be a plane surface embedded in Cartesian $3$-space. The vector area of $S$ is a technique of representing $S$ using a vector quantity $\mathbf S$. 380px The magnitude of the vector is determined by the area of $S$, while its direction is defined as the unit normal $\mathbf {\hat n}$ to the plane of $S$. The sign of $\mathbf S = S \, \mathbf {\hat n}$ is determined by the right-hand rule according to the direction of rotation around $S$ when describing it. The shape of $S$ is arbitrary.

label: Definition:Vector Bundle
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. Then $B$ is a vector bundle over $M$ the model fiber $F$ is a topological vector space.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$. The vector cross product, denoted $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$, is defined as: $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ a_i & a_j & a_k \\ b_i & b_j & b_k \\ \end{vmatrix}$ where $\begin {vmatrix} \ldots \end {vmatrix}$ is interpreted as a determinant.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Definition 2
snippet:
Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions. The vector cross product, denoted $\mathbf a 	imes \mathbf b$, is defined as: $\mathbf a 	imes \mathbf b = 
orm {\mathbf a} 
orm {\mathbf b} \sin 	heta \, \mathbf {\hat n}$ where: $
orm {\mathbf a}$ denotes the length of $\mathbf a$ $	heta$ denotes the angle from $\mathbf a$ to $\mathbf b$, measured in the positive direction $\hat {\mathbf n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to both $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ in the direction according to the right-hand rule.

label: Definition:Vector Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field which acts on a region of space $S$. Let the point-function giving rise to $F$ be a vector quantity. Then $F$ is a vector field.

label: Definition:Vector Length
snippet: The length of a vector $\mathbf v$ in a normed vector space $\struct {V, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ is defined as $\norm {\mathbf v}$, the norm of $\mathbf v$.

label: Definition:Vector Potential
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of ordinary space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field over $R$. Let $\mathbf V$ be both rotational and solenoidal. Let $\mathbf A$ be a vector field such that $\mathbf V = \curl \mathbf A$. Then $\mathbf A$ is known as the vector potential of $\mathbf V$.

label: Definition:Vector Quantity
snippet: A vector quantity is a real-world concept that needs for its model a mathematical object with more than one component to specify it. Formally, a vector quantity is an element of a normed vector space, often the real vector space $\R^3$. The usual intellectual frame of reference is to interpret a vector quantity as having: A magnitude A direction.

label: Definition:Vector Quantity/Arrow Representation
snippet: A vector quantity $\mathbf v$ is often represented diagramatically in the form of an arrow such that: its length is proportional to the magnitude of $\mathbf v$ its direction corresponds to the direction of $\mathbf v$. The head of the arrow then indicates the positive sense of the direction of $\mathbf v$. It can be rendered on the page like so: 300px It is important to note that a vector quantity, when represented in this form, is not in general fixed in space. All that is being indicated using such a notation is its magnitude and direction, and not, in general, a point at which it acts.

label: Definition:Vector Space/Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a unitary $K$-module. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ is a vector space over $K$ or a $K$-vector space. That is, a vector space is a unitary module whose scalar ring is a division ring.

label: Definition:Vector Space/Left and Right Vector Space
snippet: == Left Vector Spaces and Right Vector Spaces == In the case where the scalar division ring is a field, the difference between a left vector space and a right vector space is little more than a notational difference. This is demonstrated in: Left Module over Commutative Ring induces Right Module Right Module over Commutative Ring induces Left Module where the commutative ring in question is the scalar field of the vector space, which is of course a type of module, under discussion. But this is not the case for a scalar division ring that is not commutative.

label: Definition:Vector Space Automorphism
snippet: Let $V$ be a $K$-vector space. Let $\phi: V \to V$ be a vector space isomorphism to itself. Then $\phi$ is a vector space automorphism.

label: Definition:Vector Space of All Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ be a $K$-vector space. Let $S$ be a set. Let $G^S$ be the set of all mappings from $S$ to $G$. Then $\struct {G^S, +_G', \circ}_K$ is a $K$-vector space, where: $+_G'$ is the (pointwise) addition induced on $G^S$ by $+_G$ $\forall \lambda \in K: \forall f \in G^S: \forall x \in S: \map {\paren {\lambda \circ f} } x = \lambda \circ \paren {\map f x}$ This is the $K$-vector space $G^S$ of all mappings from $S$ to $G$.

label: Definition:Vector Space of Matrices
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ be the $m \times n$ matrix space over a field $\GF$. Let $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +}$ denote the abelian group formed from $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ under matrix entrywise addition. Let $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +, \times}_\GF$ denote the vector space over $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ where $\times$ denotes the matrix scalar product. Then $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +, \times}_\GF$ can be referred to as the vector space of $m \times n$ matrices.

label: Definition:Vector Space over Division Ring/Left Vector Space
Definition:Vector Space over Division Ring/Right Vector Space
Definition:Vector Subspace
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$ be a $K$-algebraic structure with one operation. Let $T$ be a closed subset of $S$. Let $\struct {T, +_T, \circ_T}_K$ be a $K$-vector space where: $+_T$ is the restriction of $+$ to $T \times T$ and $\circ_T$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $K \times T$. Then $\struct {T, +_T, \circ_T}_K$ is a (vector) subspace of $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$.

label: Definition:Vector Subspace/Hilbert Spaces
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\left({S, +, \circ}\right)_K$ be a $K$-algebraic structure with one operation. Let $T$ be a closed subset of $S$. Let $\left({T, +_T, \circ_T}\right)_K$ be a $K$-vector space where: $+_T$ is the restriction of $+$ to $T \times T$ and $\circ_T$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $K \times T$. Then $\left({T, +_T, \circ_T}\right)_K$ is a (vector) subspace of $\left({S, +, \circ}\right)_K$. When considering Hilbert spaces, one wants to deal with projections onto subspaces.

label: Definition:Vector Subtraction
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $V := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding vector space over $F$. Let $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$ be vectors of $V$. Then the operation of (vector) subtraction on $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$ is defined as: $\mathbf x - \mathbf y := \mathbf x + \paren {-\mathbf y}$ where $-\mathbf y$ is the negative of $\mathbf y$. The $+$ on the is vector addition.

label: Definition:Vector Sum
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities of the same physical property.

label: Definition:Velocity
snippet: The velocity $\mathbf v$ of a body $M$ is defined as the first derivative of the displacement $\mathbf s$ of $M$ from a given point of reference time $t$: $\mathbf v = \dfrac {\d \mathbf s} {\d t}$ Informally, it is described as the rate of change of position. It is important to note that as displacement is a vector quantity, then it follows by definition of derivative of a vector that so is velocity.

label: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Centimetre per Second
snippet: == CGS unit of Velocity == The CGS unit of velocity is the centimetre per second.

label: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Foot per Second
snippet: == FPS unit of velocity == The FPS unit of velocity is the foot per second.

label: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Metre per Second
snippet: == SI unit of Velocity == The SI unit of velocity is the metre per second.

label: Definition:Venn Diagram
snippet: A Venn diagram is a technique for the graphic depiction of the interrelationship between a small number (usually $3$ or fewer) of sets. The following diagram illustrates the various operations between three sets. 500px The circles represent the sets $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$. The white surrounding box represents the universal set $\mathbb U$. Each of the areas inside the various circle represents an intersection between the various sets and their complements, as follows: The gray area represents $S_1 \cap S_2 \cap S_3$. The purple area represents $S_1 \cap S_2 \cap \overline {S_3}$.

label: Definition:Veridical Paradox
snippet: A veridical paradox is a counter-intuitive result which can be demonstrated to be true.

label: Definition:Vertex
snippet: Graph Theory: Vertex of Graph: The vertices of a graph are the points, which may or may not be joined by edges. Geometry and Solid Geometry: Vertex: A point at which $2$ or more line segments meet on the boundary of a geometric figure: Vertex of Polygon: The corners of a polygon are known as its vertices. Vertex of Polyhedron: The corners of a polyhedron are known as its vertices. Vertex of Angle: The point at which the lines containing an angle meet is known as its vertex.

label: Definition:Vertex (Geometry)
snippet: A vertex is a point on the boundary of a geometric figure at which $2$ or more line segments meet.

label: Definition:Vertex Cut
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. A vertex cut of $G$ is a set of vertices $W \subseteq \map V G$ such that the vertex deletion $G \setminus W$ is disconnected.

label: Definition:Vertex Deletion
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an (undirected) graph. Let $W \subseteq V$ be a set of vertices of $G$. Then the graph obtained by deleting $W$ from $G$, denoted by $G - W$, is the subgraph induced by $V \setminus W$. Alternatively: $G - W = \struct {V \setminus W, \set {e \in E : e \cap W = \O} }$ Informally, $G - W$ is the graph obtained from $G$ by removing all vertices in $W$ and all edges incident to those vertices. If $W$ is a singleton such that $W = \set v$, then $G - W$ may be expressed $G - v$.

label: Definition:Vertex Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. The set $V$ of vertices in $G$ is called the vertex set. It is often convenient to refer to the vertex set for a given graph $G$ as $\map V G$, especially if there is at any one time more than one graph under consideration.

label: Definition:Vertex of Simplex
snippet: Let $S$ be a $k$-simplex for some $k \in \Z_{>0}$: $S = \set {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^k \theta_i \alpha_i}$ A vertex of $S$ is one of the $k + 1$ points $\alpha_0, \alpha_1 \ldots, \alpha_k$.

label: Definition:Vertical Composition of Natural Transformations
snippet: Let $C$ and $D$ be categories. Let $F, G, H: C \to D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ and $\xi: G \to H$ be natural transformations. The vertical composition of $\eta$ and $\xi$ is the natural transformation $\xi \circ \eta : F \Rightarrow H$ with $\paren {\xi \circ \eta}_A = \xi_A \circ \eta_A$ for $A \in C$.

label: Definition:Vertical Plane
snippet: A plane is vertical it contains a vertical line.

label: Definition:Vertical Section of Function
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets. Let $f : X \times Y \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. Let $x \in X$. We define the vertical section $f_x$ of $f$ by: $\map {f_x} y = \map f {x, y}$ for each $y \in Y$.

label: Definition:Vertical Section of Set
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets. Let $E \subseteq X \times Y$. Let $x \in X$. We define the $x$-vertical section $E_x$ of $E$ by: $E_x = \set {y \in Y : \tuple {x, y} \in E}$

label: Definition:Volt
snippet: The volt is the SI unit of electromotive force and electric potential. It is defined as being the difference in electric potential between two points of an electrical conductor: when an electric current of $1$ ampere dissipates $1$ watt of power between those points that will impart $1$ joule of energy per coulomb of electric charge that passes through it.

label: Definition:Volume
snippet: Volume is the measure of the extent of a body. It has three dimensions and is specified in units of length cubed. Hence the term cube as a general vague term for a quantity in three dimensions. It is a scalar quantity.

label: Definition:Volume Element
snippet: A volume element $\delta V$ is a (usually) infinitesimal volume of space (usually) containing a particular point $P$. In the cartesian $3$-space such a volume element is modelled as a cuboid whose edges are parallel to the coordinate axes and assigned lengths $\delta x$, $\delta y$ and $\delta z$ respectively: 300px

label: Definition:Von Mangoldt Function
snippet: The von Mangoldt function $\Lambda: \N \to \R$ is defined as: $\map \Lambda n = \begin {cases} \map \ln p & : \exists m \in \N, p \in \mathbb P: n = p^m \\ 0 & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$ where $\mathbb P$ is the set of all prime numbers.

label: Definition:Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory
snippet: Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel set theory is a system of axiomatic set theory. Its main feature is that it classifies collections of objects into: sets, whose construction is strictly controlled and: classes, which have fewer restrictions on how they may be generated. All sets are classes, but not all classes are sets.

label: Definition:Von Neumann-Bounded Subset of Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $E \subseteq X$. We say that $E$ is von Neumann-bounded : for each open neighbourhood $V$ of ${\mathbf 0}_X$, there exists $s > 0$ such that $E \subseteq t V$ for each $t > s$ where $t V$ is the dilation of $V$ by $t$.

label: Definition:Von Neumann Hierarchy
snippet: Let $U$ denote the universal class. The von Neumann hierarchy is a mapping $V: \On \to U$ on the ordinals, defined via the Second Principle of Transfinite Recursion: $\map V x = \begin {cases} \O & : x = 0 \\ & \\ \powerset {\map V n} & : x = n^+ \\ & \\ \ds \bigcup_{y \mathop \in x} \map V y & : x \in \operatorname {Lim} \\ \end {cases}$ where: $\powerset x$ denotes the power set of $x$ $\operatorname {Lim}$ denotes the set of limit ordinals.

label: Definition:Walk (Graph Theory)
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. A walk $W$ on $G$ is: an alternating sequence of vertices $v_1, v_2, \ldots$ and edges $e_1, e_2, \ldots$ of $G$ beginning and ending with a vertex in which edge $e_j$ of $W$ is incident with the vertex $v_j$ and the vertex $v_{j + 1}$. A walk between two vertices $u$ and $v$ is called a $u$-$v$ walk. To describe a walk on a simple graph it is sufficient to list just the vertices in order, as the edges (being unique between vertices) are unambiguous.

label: Definition:Wave
snippet: A wave is a disturbance in a medium which propagates through that medium with the following properties: $(1): \quad$ energy is propagated between two points in space through that medium $(2): \quad$ the disturbance travels through the medium without causing the medium itself to undergo any permanent displacement.

label: Definition:Wave/Disturbance
snippet: The disturbance of a wave at a given point and time is defined as the quantity that the medium is different from its equilibrium.

label: Definition:Wave Equation
snippet: == Equation == The wave equation is a second order PDE of the form: {{eqn | l = \dfrac 1 {c^2} \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial t^2} | r = \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial z^2} | c = }}

label: Definition:Wave Profile
snippet: Let $\phi$ be a wave which is propagated along the $x$-axis with velocity $c$. At $t = 0$, let $\phi = \map f x$. Then $\map f x$ is the wave profile of $\phi$. This can be expressed as: $\paren {\map \phi x}_{t \mathop = 0} = \map f x$

label: Definition:Way Below Open
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ a preordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is way below open : $\forall x \in X: \exists y \in X: y \ll x$ where $\ll$ denotes the way below relation.

label: Definition:Weak-* Convergence (Normed Vector Space)
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of bounded linear functionals on $X$. Let $f : X \to \Bbb F$ be a bounded linear functional. Then we say that $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly-$\ast$ (read as "weakly-star") : $\map {f_n} x \to \map f x$ for each $x \in X$. We say that $f$ is a weak-$\ast$ limit of $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We denote this: $f_n \weakstarconv f$

label: Definition:Weak Cauchy Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual of $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a weak Cauchy sequence : $\sequence {\map f {x_n} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is Cauchy in $\GF$ for each $f \in X^\ast$.

label: Definition:Weak Convergence
snippet: Functional Analysis: Weak Convergence (Normed Vector Space) Probability Theory: Weak Convergence (Random Variable) Measure Theory: Weak Convergence (Measure)

label: Definition:Weak Convergence (Normed Vector Space)
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly to $x$ : $\map f {x_n} 	o \map f x$ for each $f \in X^\ast$. We say that $x$ is a weak limit of $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We denote this: $x_n \weakconv x$

label: Definition:Weakly Abnormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.

label: Definition:Weakly Compact Set
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $X$ be a topological vector space with weak topology $w$. Let $C \subseteq X$. We say that $C$ is weakly compact (or $w$-compact) in $X$ $C$ is a compact in $\struct {X, w}$. That is, for every collection of weakly open sets $\SS$ such that: $\ds C \subseteq \bigcup_{S \in \SS} S$ there exists a finite subset $\set {S_1, \ldots, S_n} \subseteq \SS$ such that: $\ds C \subseteq \bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n S_k$ Category:Definitions/Weak Topologies on Topological Vector Spaces

label: Definition:Weakly Countably Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly countably compact : every infinite subset of $S$ has a limit point in $S$.

label: Definition:Weakly Hereditary Property
snippet: Let $\xi$ be a property whose domain is the set of all topological spaces. Then $\xi$ is a weakly hereditary property : $\map \xi X \implies \map \xi Y$ where $Y$ is any closed set of $X$ when considered as a subspace. That is, whenever a topological space has $\xi$, then so does any closed subspace.

label: Definition:Weakly Locally Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly locally compact every point of $S$ has a compact neighborhood.

label: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$.

label: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation.

label: Definition:Weakly Pronormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.

label: Definition:Weakly Sigma-Locally Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly $\sigma$-locally compact : That is, $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly $\sigma$-locally compact :

label: Definition:Weakly Unconditionally Cauchy Series
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Then $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty x_n$ is weakly unconditionally Cauchy : $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \cmod {\map f {x_n} } < \infty$ for each $f \in X^\ast$.

label: Definition:Wedge Product
snippet: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be two differential forms. Let $\alpha$ be an $x$-form. Let $\beta$ be a $y$-form. The wedge product $\alpha \wedge \beta$ is defined as the linear antisymmetric map from $F^x \times F^y \to F^{x + y}$, where $F^a$ is the set of $a$-forms in some manifold. Let $x_0$ be a specific point in a manifold $X$. Let $\alpha$ be an $x$-form. Let $\phi$ be a $1$-form. Let there be a set of vectors $\mathbf u_1, \mathbf u_2, \dotsc, \mathbf u_x, \mathbf v \in \map {T_{x_0} } X$.

label: Definition:Weibull Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R_{\ge 0}$. $X$ is said to have a Weibull distribution it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \alpha \beta^{-\alpha} x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\paren {\frac x \beta}^\alpha}$ for $\alpha, \beta \in \R_{> 0}$.

label: Definition:Weight
snippet: Physics: The weight of a body is the force exerted on it by a gravitational field. Network theory: The weight of an edge or arc of a network is the functional value assigned to that edge or arc by the weight function of that network. Statistics, etc.: A weight function on a set $S$ is a mapping from $S$ to the (usually positive) real numbers. Information theory: The weight of a codeword is the number of its non-zero terms.

label: Definition:Weight Function
snippet: A weight function on a set $S$ is a mapping from $S$ to the real numbers: $w: S \to \R$ It is common for the requirements of a specific application under discussion for the codomain of $w$ to be restricted to the positive reals: $w: S \to \R_{\ge 0}$ The thing that determines whether a given mapping is a weight function depends more on how it is used.

label: Definition:Weight of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb B$ be the set of all bases of $T$.

label: Definition:Weighted Mean
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $W$ be a weight function to be applied to the terms of $S$. The weighted mean of $S$ $W$ is defined as: $\bar x := \dfrac {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} x_i} {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} }$ This means that elements of $S$ with a larger weight contribute more to the weighted mean than those with a smaller weight.

label: Definition:Well-Defined/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set determined by $\RR$. Let $\phi: S / \RR \to T$ be a mapping such that: $\map \phi {\eqclass x \RR} = \map f x$ Then $\phi: S / \RR \to T$ is well-defined : $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in \RR: \map f x = \map f y$

label: Definition:Well-Defined/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. For $x \in S$, let $\eqclass x \RR$ denote the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set of $S$ determined by $\RR$. Let $\QQ$ be a relation on $S / \RR$. Then $\QQ$ is well-defined : for arbitrary $x, y, x', y' \in S$ such that: $x \mathrel \RR x'$ $y \mathrel \RR y'$ we have that: $\tuple {\eqclass x \RR, \eqclass y \RR} \in \QQ \iff \tuple {\eqclass {x'} \RR, \eqclass {y'} \RR} \in \QQ$

label: Definition:Well-Founded Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is well-founded it satisfies the minimal condition: Every non-empty subset of $S$ has a minimal element. That is, if the ordering $\preceq$ is a well-founded relation.

label: Definition:Well-Orderable Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. If it is possible to construct an ordering $\preccurlyeq$ on $S$ such that $\preccurlyeq$ is a well-ordering, then $S$ is defined as being well-orderable.

label: Definition:Well-Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a well-ordered set the ordering $\preceq$ is a well-ordering. That is, every non-empty subset of $S$ has a smallest element: $\forall T \in \powerset S: \exists a \in T: \forall x \in T: a \preceq x$ where $\powerset S$ denotes the power set of $S$. That is, such that $\preceq$ is a well-founded total ordering.

label: Definition:Well-Ordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set.

label: Definition:Well-Ordering/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a total ordering. Then $\RR$ is a well-ordering : every non-empty subclass of $\Field \RR$ has a smallest element under $\RR$ where $\Field \RR$ denotes the field of $\RR$.

label: Definition:West Point of Horizon
snippet: Let an observer $O$ be facing the north point of the horizon $N$, facing directly away from the south point of the horizon $S$. Let the celestial equator meet the celestial horizon at the points $E$ and $W$. Let $W$ be the point on the left of $O$. This is called the west point of the horizon. 480px In the above diagram, the west point of the horizon is indicated by $W$.

label: Definition:Western Hemisphere
snippet: The western hemisphere of Earth is the hemisphere immediately to the west of the prime meridian. Points in the western hemisphere have longitude between $0 \degrees \, \mathrm W$ (the prime meridian itself) and $180 \degrees \, \mathrm W$.

label: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Double-sided Whiskered
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ be a natural transformation. Let $H : \mathbf B \to \mathbf C$ and $K : \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be covariant functors. Then: the double-sided whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $K$ and $H$, denoted by $K \eta H: K \circ F \circ H \to K \circ G \circ H$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $B \in \mathbf B: \paren{K \eta H}_B = K \eta_{_{HB} }$ described diagramatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf B \ar[rr]^H && \mathbf C…

label: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Left Whiskered
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ be a natural transformation. Let $H : \mathbf B \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Then: the left whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $H$, denoted by $\eta H: F \circ H \to G \circ H$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $B \in \mathbf B: \paren{\eta H}_B = \eta_{_{HB} }$ described diagrammatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf B \ar[rr]^H && \mathbf C \ar@/^4ex/[rr]^F_{}="f" \ar@/_4ex/[rr]_G^{}="g" && \mathbf D \ar@2^\eta "f"; "g" }$

label: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Right Whiskered
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ be a natural transformation. Let $K : \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be a covariant functor. Then: the right whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $K$, denoted by $K \eta: K \circ F \to K \circ G$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $C \in \mathbf C: \paren{K \eta}_C = K \eta_{_C}$ described diagramatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf C \ar@/^4ex/[rr]^F_{}="f" \ar@/_4ex/[rr]_G^{}="g" && \mathbf D \ar@2^\eta "f"; "g" \ar[rr]^K && \mathbf E }$

label: Definition:White Noise Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process consisting of a time series $\map {z_r} t$ such that: the terms of the sequence $\sequence {z_r}$ are independent random variables the terms of $\sequence {z_r}$ are governed by a normal distribution with zero expectation and a given variance $\sigma^2$. Then $S$ is known as a white noise process.

label: Definition:Wieferich Prime
snippet: A Wieferich prime is a prime number $p$ such that: $p^2 \divides 2^{p − 1} − 1$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.

label: Definition:Wilson Prime
snippet: A Wilson prime is a prime number $p$ such that: $p^2 \divides \paren {p - 1}! + 1$ where: $\divides$ signifies divisibility $!$ is the factorial operator.

label: Definition:Witch of Agnesi
snippet: 620px Let $OAM$ be a circle of radius $a$ whose center is at $\tuple {0, a}$. Let $M$ be the point such that $OM$ is a diameter of $OAM$. Let $OA$ be extended to cut the tangent to the circle through $M$ at $N$. Generate $NP$ perpendicular to $MN$ and $AP$ parallel to $MN$. As $A$ moves around the circle $OAM$, the point $P$ traces the curve known as the witch of Agnesi.

label: Definition:Witness Property
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a language of predicate logic. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a set of $\LL$-WFFs. Suppose that, for every $\LL$-WFF of $1$ free variable $\map \phi x$, if: $\FF \models_{\mathscr M} \exists x : \map \phi x$ then there exists some term $t$ containing no variables such that: $\FF \models_{\mathscr M} \map \phi {x := t}$ Then, $\FF$ satisfies the witness property.

label: Definition:Wolstenholme Prime
snippet: A Wolstenholme prime is a prime number $p$ such that $p > 7$ which satisfies the congruence: $\dbinom {2 p - 1} {p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod {p^4}$ where $\dbinom {2 p - 1} {p - 1}$ denotes a binomial coefficient.

label: Definition:Wonderful Demlo Number
snippet: The Wonderful Demlo numbers are the positive integers defined as the coefficients of the powers of $x$ in the expansion of: $\dfrac {1 + 10 x} {\left({1 - x}\right) \left({1 - 10 x}\right) \left({1 - 100 x}\right)}$

label: Definition:Woodall Number
snippet: A Woodall number is a positive integer of the form: $n \times 2^n - 1$

label: Definition:Woodall Prime
snippet: A Woodall prime is a Woodall number: $n \times 2^n - 1$ which is also prime.

label: Definition:Word (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $S \subseteq M$ be a subset. A word in $S$ is the product of a finite number of elements of $S$. The set of words in $S$ is denoted $\map W S$: $\map W S := \set {s_1 \circ s_2 \circ \cdots \circ s_n: n \in \N_{>0}: s_i \in S, 1 \le i \le n}$ Note that there is nothing in this definition preventing any of the elements of $S$ being repeated, neither is anything said about the order of these elements.

label: Definition:Wrench
snippet: A wrench is a force combined with a couple whose plane is perpendicular to the line of action of the force.

label: Definition:Wythoff Pair
snippet: A Wythoff pair is an ordered pair of integers of the form: $\tuple {\floor {k \phi}, \floor {k \phi^2} }$ where: $\phi$ denotes the golden section: $\phi = 1 \cdotp 618 \ldots$ $\floor x$ denotes the floor of $x$ $k$ signifies a positive integer: $k \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. Thus the coordinates of a Wythoff pair are corresponding terms of the lower and upper Wythoff sequences.

label: Definition:X-Y Plane
snippet: $x$-$y$ plane, $y$-$z$ plane and $x$-$z$ plane in Cartesian $3$-space ]] The $x$-$y$ plane is the Cartesian plane embedded in Cartesian $3$-space which contains the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis. It consists of all the points in $S$ such that $z = 0$.

label: Definition:X-Z Plane
snippet: $x$-$y$ plane, $y$-$z$ plane and $x$-$z$ plane in Cartesian $3$-space ]] The $x$-$z$ plane is the Cartesian plane embedded in Cartesian $3$-space which contains the $x$-axis and the $z$-axis. It consists of all the points in $S$ such that $x = 0$.

label: Definition:Y-Z Plane
snippet: $x$-$y$ plane, $y$-$z$ plane and $x$-$z$ plane in Cartesian $3$-space ]] The $y$-$z$ plane is the Cartesian plane embedded in Cartesian $3$-space which contains the $y$-axis and the $z$-axis. It consists of all the points in $S$ such that $x = 0$.

label: Definition:Yang-Mills Theory
snippet: Yang-Mills theory is a gauge theory based on a special unitary group $\map {SU} N$, or more generally any compact, reductive Lie algebra. Yang–Mills theory seeks to describe the behavior of elementary particles using these non-abelian Lie groups, and is at the core of the unification of the electromagnetic force and weak forces, that is $\map U 1 \times \map {SU} 2$, as well as quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force (based on $\map {SU} 3$). Thus it forms the basis of our understanding of the Standard Model of particle physics. Category:Definitions/Physics

label: Definition:Year/Calendar
snippet: A calendar year is the number of days between dates with the same designation in adjacent years. As a year is not an integral number of days, it is necessarily an approximation to the actual year. {{eqn | r = 365 \text{ or } 366 | c = days, usually, but it depends on the calendar used }}

label: Definition:Yoneda Functor/Yoneda Embedding
snippet: Let $C$ be a locally small category. Let $C^{\operatorname{op} }$ be its opposite category. Let $\mathbf {Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\sqbrk {C^{\operatorname{op} }, \mathbf {Set} }$ be the functor category between them. The Yoneda embedding of $C$ is the covariant functor $h_- : C \to \sqbrk {C^{\operatorname{op}}, \mathbf{Set} }$ which sends: {{DefineFunctor |ob = an object $X \in C$ to the contravariant hom-functor $h_X = \map {\operatorname {Hom} } {-, X}$ |mor = a morphism $f : X \to Y$ to the postcomposition natural transformation $h_f : \map {\operatorname {Hom} } {-, X} \to…

label: Definition:Z-Module Associated with Abelian Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be an abelian group with identity $e$. Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers.

label: Definition:Zeckendorf Representation
snippet: Zeckendorf representation is a system for representing a positive integer $n$ by a sequence of digits which are the indices of a sequence of $r$ Fibonacci numbers.

label: Definition:Zenith
snippet: Let an observer $O$ on the surface of Earth be assumed to be the center of the celestial sphere $C$. The zenith $Z$ is the point on $C$ which is vertically overhead. This can be determined by use of a plumb line. 480px In the above diagram, the zenith is indicated by $Z$.

label: Definition:Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem Set Theory
snippet: Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem set theory is a system of axiomatic set theory. It consists of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the inclusion of a system of first order formulas to specify the existence of properties of sets.
